basicPropertyValues.val: MOLSIM is a domain (application) ontology designed to semantically represent platform-agnostic biomolecular simulations (all-atom and coarse-grained) as FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) datasets. As an application ontology, it reuses terms from established OBO ontologies where they fit and defines its own where they do not, aiming to standardize the representation of biomolecular simulation data, processes, and methodologies across platforms and tools.

AI assistance disclosure: initial drafts of the term definitions in this ontology were produced with the assistance of large language models, primarily Google Gemini, with further drafting and curation support from Anthropic Claude; all drafts were then curated and reviewed by humans. Verification status is recorded per term and is machine-readable: a term carrying an IAO:0000117 (term editor) annotation has been checked by the named domain expert, whose ORCID is given; a definition whose text still ends with the marker (UNVERIFIED) has not yet been reviewed by a domain expert and should be treated as a draft. Terms marked owl:deprecated are retired and are exempt from verification.

Release-format note: the OWL and JSON products (molsim.owl, molsim.json and their -base/-full variants) are the complete and canonical releases. The OBO-format product (molsim.obo) is a CLASS-ONLY VIEW: OBO 1.2 cannot represent datatype properties, and named individuals are not carried through the conversion, so the data properties (per-species composition counts, boolean flags, serialised arrays) and the named individuals of this ontology are absent from it. The class hierarchy, definitions, synonyms and object properties in molsim.obo are complete and correct. Use the OWL or JSON release if you need the full content.

Scope note: MOLSIM's boundary is drawn by USE CASE, not by subject matter. The membership test for a new term is: would a complete record of a simulation dataset need to state it? That spans what was configured (timestep, thermostat, force field), what was computed (RMSD, potential of mean force, free energies), where the inputs came from (a PDB entry, a UniProt accession, a publication), and what it ran on (engine, version, hardware). Terms from neighbouring fields (quantum chemistry, computational materials science, structural biology) are admitted at most two levels below their attachment point: we record which QM engine ran and which basis set parameterised a force field, but not the internal machinery of quantum-chemical methods. This rule governs terms added from 2026-07-29 onward; earlier terms are retained. MOLSIM is the OBO-aligned ontology for biomolecular simulation metadata and is complementary to EMMO-based materials-modelling ontologies (EMMO, OSMO, VISO), with which it interoperates by SSSOM mapping rather than by adopting a shared upper ontology. Full statement: see the README.

definition.val: A denotator type indicates how a term should be interpreted from an ontological perspective.

A sequence of related actions or operations performed to achieve a specific outcome in a biomolecular simulation study. This encompasses all stages from initial system setup and simulation execution to final data analysis and interpretation.

A set of instructions and data that a computer follows to carry out a task. In molecular simulation it covers everything from a program that runs a simulation to a small script that converts one file format into another. (UNVERIFIED)

A stage of a simulation study in which the molecular system and its environment are assembled and made ready to run. It covers obtaining a structure, adding the atoms and molecules the experimental structure left out, choosing a force field, adding solvent and ions, and bringing the system to equilibrium before data is collected. (UNVERIFIED)

The stage of a biomolecular simulation process where the main simulation runs are performed according to the prepared system and defined parameters to generate trajectory data. This phase involves propagating the system forward in time using algorithms like molecular dynamics or Monte Carlo, under specific ensemble conditions. The goal is typically to sample conformational space, observe dynamic events, or calculate specific properties like free energies.

A stage of a simulation study that follows the run, in which the trajectory and energy output are processed into results. It covers everything from measuring a distance to fitting a kinetic model. It turns the raw output of a simulation into scientific findings. (UNVERIFIED)

A simulation preparation stage in which the ionization states of ionizable groups in residues and ligands, that is which protons each carries, are assigned from their estimated pKa values at the target pH of the simulation. Correct assignment matters because it sets the charges, and so the electrostatic interactions, of the model, and any pH-dependent behavior. Specialized tools are often used for this task. (UNVERIFIED)

A simplified representation used to study a real-world system, such as a molecule or collection of molecules. In biomolecular simulation, it defines the components (atoms, residues) and their properties needed for computational analysis. This framework allows scientists to simulate and predict the system's behavior. (UNVERIFIED)

comments: Distinct from 'MoDEL' (MOLSIM:001001), a named simulation data repository whose name differs from this term only by capitalisation. This term is the general class of representations used in simulation.

definition.val: A set of mathematical functions and fitted numbers used to compute the potential energy of a system of atoms from their positions alone. Instead of treating electrons explicitly, most such models use simple terms for bonds, angles, rotations about bonds and non-bonded contacts. This choice is a main factor in how accurate a classical simulation is. (UNVERIFIED)

A force field specifically designed and parameterized for simulating lipid molecules and lipid bilayers, crucial components of cell membranes. It aims to accurately capture the unique properties of lipids, including their phase behavior and interactions with other molecules. Examples include the AMBER Lipid14, Lipid17 and Lipid21 parameter sets and the lipid parameters of CHARMM36. (UNVERIFIED)

A force field specifically designed and parameterized for simulating proteins and peptides, focusing on accurately representing amino acid properties and polypeptide chain behavior. These are crucial for studying protein folding, dynamics, and interactions. Many different protein force fields exist, often differing in their parameterization philosophy and target data. (UNVERIFIED)

A force field specifically developed and parameterized for simulating Deoxyribonucleic Acid (DNA) molecules. It focuses on accurately representing the structure, dynamics, and interactions of DNA bases, sugars, and phosphate backbone, including features like sugar pucker and helical parameters. Accurate DNA force fields are essential for studying DNA replication, transcription, and drug binding.

A force field specifically developed and parameterized for simulating Ribonucleic Acid (RNA) molecules. It aims to accurately capture the complex conformational landscape and catalytic potential of RNA. Development often focuses on improving descriptions of sugar pucker, backbone torsions (especially the epsilon and zeta angles), and non-canonical base interactions.

A force field specifically designed and parameterized for simulating carbohydrate molecules (sugars or glycans). It addresses the unique challenges of modeling the flexibility of glycosidic linkages between sugar units and the numerous hydrogen bonding possibilities involving hydroxyl groups. These are important for studying glycoproteins, glycolipids, and polysaccharides like cellulose.

A force field parameterised for small organic molecules, covering the wide range of chemistry found in drug-like compounds. It must handle groups no protein or nucleic acid force field was built for. It is used together with a biomolecular force field when a ligand is simulated in a protein. (UNVERIFIED)

A force field parameterised for water alone, usually representing a molecule by 3 to 5 interaction points with fixed geometry. Water is most of the atoms in a biomolecular simulation, so the choice affects cost as much as accuracy. No model reproduces every measured property of water, so the choice depends on which properties matter for the study. (UNVERIFIED)

A set of parameters specifically developed to describe the interactions of ions (charged atoms or small molecules) within a simulation, typically in conjunction with a specific water model and other biomolecular force fields. These parameters define the ion's charge and non-bonded terms (usually Lennard-Jones parameters for size and interaction strength). Accurate ion parameters are crucial for modeling salt effects, ion channels, and metalloproteins, and often require careful tuning for compatibility with the chosen water model. (UNVERIFIED)

A chemical entity-based force field designed to give parameters for almost any organic molecule, such as a drug or a ligand, rather than for 1 class of biomolecule. It achieves that breadth by assigning atom types from rules based on each atom's chemical environment, and by supplying rules to estimate parameters that are missing. The parameters it gives for a particular molecule are approximate, so they are often checked or refined. (UNVERIFIED)

A basis set that uses a single function for each core and valence atomic orbital of an atom, with no extra functions. Because each atomic orbital is described by 1 function of fixed size, it cannot expand or contract when a bond forms, so bonding is described poorly. The STO-nG sets are common examples; they are cheap and used mainly for teaching and very rough calculations. (UNVERIFIED)

A lipid force field for the AMBER family that builds on Lipid14 and Lipid17 and extends the modular phospholipid residues to anionic head groups, polyunsaturated tails and sphingomyelin. Its bonded alkane parameters were refitted to quantum energies, and all head groups were given new partial charges. It is the lipid force field AMBER currently recommends. (UNVERIFIED)

A lipid force field for the AMBER family, released in 2014, that builds on the modular head group and tail scheme of Lipid11. It allowed lipid bilayers to be simulated at constant pressure without an artificial surface tension term, a major advance over earlier AMBER lipid parameters. It was later extended with cholesterol parameters and by Lipid17 and Lipid21. (UNVERIFIED)

A specific lipid force field parameter set developed for the AMBER simulation package, released around 2017. It was built upon the modularity of LIPID14 and provided an extension of modular phospholipid residues to include anionic head groups and polyunsaturated tails.

A specific protein force field parameter set from the AMBER family (ff), released around 2014, with optimizations primarily for side-chain (S) and backbone (B) torsion angles compared to earlier versions like ff99SB. It was widely adopted for its improved accuracy in representing protein secondary structure and dynamics. It is an all-atom force field.

A rigid water model with 3 interaction sites, 1 on each atom, using the measured geometry of an isolated water molecule. It is the water model the AMBER force fields were developed with, and the CHARMM force fields use a modified form with extra Lennard-Jones terms on hydrogen. It reproduces the density of water well, but water molecules diffuse about twice as fast as in real water, which matters for any rate taken from a simulation. (UNVERIFIED)

A force field for small organic molecules, built to be used alongside the AMBER protein and nucleic acid parameters. It defines atom types broadly enough to cover almost any organic structure, and supplies rules for filling gaps where no parameter was fitted. That breadth is why its parameters for any particular molecule should be checked rather than trusted. (UNVERIFIED)

A force field for small organic molecules that is the second version of the general AMBER force field, with parameters refitted against a larger set of quantum calculations and measurements than the first. It is the general force field AMBER recommends for ligands, and is meant to be combined with RESP or ABCG2 charges rather than with AM1-BCC charges. Its parameters differ from those of the first version, so the 2 are not interchangeable. (UNVERIFIED)

A text molecular structure format that extends the Tripos mol2 format with extra records naming the atoms through which a residue links to its neighbours. LEaP in AmberTools can load it, so that a residue built from it can be joined into a larger molecule without the links being defined again by hand. (UNVERIFIED)

A method for processing the data a simulation produces and extracting something meaningful from it. It turns a trajectory, which is a list of coordinates at successive times, into a quantity that can be compared with an experiment or with another simulation. Almost nothing useful comes out of a simulation without one. (UNVERIFIED)

A specific type of analysis method focused on understanding how chemical reactions occur within the simulated molecular system. It involves characterizing the pathways, transition states, and energy changes associated with the transformation of reactants into products. This helps elucidate reaction mechanisms and kinetics at the molecular level.

A reaction analysis that uses the positions (coordinates) of atoms to describe the progress of a chemical reaction or conformational change. It defines one or more geometric variables, collectively known as reaction coordinates, to map the transition pathway between different molecular states. This analysis helps visualize and quantify the structural changes during a reaction. (UNVERIFIED)

A type of coordinate analysis where the reaction progress is described using simple, intuitive geometric parameters like bond distances, angles, or dihedrals directly involved in the transformation. This provides a straightforward way to monitor specific structural changes assumed to be representative of the reaction pathway.

OBSOLETE. Refers to specific parameterizations or types of water models commonly used in biomolecular simulations, often used somewhat interchangeably with 'water model'. Each 'water type' (e.g., SPC, TIP3P, TIP4P-Ew) defines the geometry, number of interaction sites, and associated parameters (charges, Lennard-Jones) for representing water molecules. The choice significantly influences simulation outcomes, particularly solvation effects and dynamics.

comments: Retired 2026-08-24. Its own definition described it as 'often used somewhat interchangeably with water model', and that is what it was: a second home for water models alongside MOLSIM:000014 water model force field, which holds all 18. Its two children were re-parented rather than replaced, so there is no single successor. MOLSIM:000031 optimal point charges moved to MOLSIM:000014 beside OPC3, and MOLSIM:000476 TIP3P water model was retired as a duplicate of MOLSIM:000022 TIP3P.

definition.val: A rigid four-site water model whose partial charges and geometry were optimised together to reproduce bulk properties of liquid water, including the density, the heat of vaporisation and the dielectric constant. It reproduces several of those properties more closely than the older three-site and four-site models at a similar computational cost. (UNVERIFIED)

Specifies the geometric shape of the simulation cell used under periodic boundary conditions (PBCs), which replicate the central simulation system in three dimensions to mimic a bulk environment and avoid surface effects. The choice of shape (e.g., cubic, truncated octahedron, rhombic dodecahedron) affects the computational efficiency (volume of solvent needed) and how well the unit cell packs space. It determines the distance and geometry for interactions between a particle and its periodic images.

A specific type of simulation box shape corresponding to a dodecahedron with rhombus-shaped faces. It is one of the space-filling polyhedra that is closer to a sphere than a cube, thus often requiring less solvent volume (and fewer solvent molecules) to solvate a roughly spherical solute while maintaining a minimum distance to the periodic images. It can offer computational savings compared to a cubic box of similar minimum image distance.

A specific type of simulation box shape created by cutting off the corners of an octahedron. Like the rhombic dodecahedron, it is a space-filling polyhedron that approximates a sphere more closely than a cube, reducing the required solvent volume for solvating non-cubic solutes under periodic boundary conditions. It offers similar computational efficiency benefits as the rhombic dodecahedron for many systems.

A simulation box shape consisting of a hexagonal base extruded along a perpendicular axis. This shape is sometimes used for systems with inherent one-dimensional periodicity or symmetry, such as fibers (like DNA) or layered systems, where periodic boundary conditions are naturally applied across the hexagonal faces and along the prism axis. Its use is less common than cubic or truncated octahedral boxes for general globular protein simulations.

The simplest simulation box shape, defined by three mutually perpendicular axes (orthogonal box). If all edge lengths are equal, it is cubic; otherwise, it is rectangular (also called orthorhombic or cuboid). While straightforward to implement and visualize, cubic boxes can be inefficient for solvating non-cubic solutes, often requiring significantly more solvent molecules than more spherically approximating shapes like the truncated octahedron to achieve the same minimum distance between periodic images.

A well-defined sequence of steps or rules designed to perform a specific task or solve a particular problem. In computational science, algorithms provide the precise instructions a computer follows to reach a desired result, such as simulating molecular motion or analyzing data. (UNVERIFIED)

An algorithm used in molecular dynamics simulations to control the temperature of the simulated system, ensuring it samples configurations corresponding to a specific target temperature (e.g., for the NVT or NPT ensembles). Thermostats work by adjusting particle velocities or adding/removing kinetic energy in various ways to mimic coupling with an external heat bath. Different thermostat algorithms vary in their theoretical basis, efficiency, and how accurately they reproduce correct statistical mechanics. (UNVERIFIED)

An algorithm used in molecular dynamics simulations, typically alongside a thermostat, to control the pressure of the simulated system by adjusting the simulation box volume. This allows simulations to be performed under conditions of constant pressure and temperature (NPT ensemble), mimicking typical laboratory conditions. Different barostats vary in how they couple the volume changes to the pressure difference and whether they allow anisotropic box changes. (UNVERIFIED)

A barostat algorithm that weakly couples the system to an external pressure bath by rescaling the simulation box volume and particle coordinates based on the difference between the current instantaneous pressure and the target pressure. Similar to the Berendsen thermostat, it is computationally simple and effective for equilibration but does not rigorously sample the correct NPT ensemble. It allows isotropic or anisotropic pressure coupling. (UNVERIFIED)

A barostat algorithm in which trial changes to the simulation box volume are made at intervals during a molecular dynamics simulation and accepted or rejected with a Monte Carlo criterion. Each trial move rescales the box and the coordinates inside it. It samples the isothermal-isobaric (NPT) ensemble correctly and does not need the virial, the pressure contribution of the forces, to be computed. (UNVERIFIED)

A barostat algorithm in which the simulation box volume is treated as a dynamic variable coupled to a fictitious piston with its own mass, driven by the difference between the internal pressure of the system and the target pressure. This extended Lagrangian approach lets the volume fluctuate around the value that matches the target pressure; on its own it samples the constant-enthalpy, constant-pressure (NPH) ensemble, and combined with a thermostat it samples the NPT ensemble. It changes the volume isotropically, that is equally in all directions. (UNVERIFIED)

A barostat algorithm that extends the Andersen approach by letting all 3 box vectors change, so that both the volume and the shape of the simulation box can fluctuate. The box vectors follow their own equation of motion, driven by the difference between the pressure tensor and the target pressure. This makes it suitable for crystals and other materials under direction-dependent stress, and for phase transitions that change the shape of the box. (UNVERIFIED)

A barostat algorithm that treats the box volume as a dynamic variable coupled to a piston, as in the Andersen barostat, and adds a friction term and a random force to the piston's equation of motion, as in Langevin dynamics. The friction and random force damp the oscillations of the box volume that a purely deterministic piston shows. Combined with a thermostat on the particles, it samples the constant-temperature, constant-pressure (NPT) ensemble. (UNVERIFIED)

A Langevin thermostat is a widely used algorithm in molecular dynamics simulations that maintains a constant temperature by mimicking a solvent environment. It modifies Newton's equations of motion by adding two forces to each particle: a frictional drag force that removes kinetic energy, and a random, stochastic force that adds kinetic energy.

A thermostat algorithm that weakly couples the system to an external heat bath by rescaling particle velocities at each step based on the difference between the current instantaneous temperature and the target temperature. While computationally simple and effective at bringing the system to the target temperature, it does not rigorously generate configurations from the correct canonical (NVT) ensemble. It is often used for equilibration phases rather than production simulations. (UNVERIFIED)

A thermostat algorithm that maintains temperature by introducing stochastic collisions between randomly selected particles and fictitious heat bath particles. When a particle "collides," its velocity is reassigned from a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution corresponding to the target temperature. This method correctly generates configurations from the canonical (NVT) ensemble. (UNVERIFIED)

A deterministic thermostat algorithm that controls temperature by introducing an extended degree of freedom (a thermostat variable) that dynamically couples to the physical system's kinetic energy. This extended variable evolves according to its own equation of motion, causing the physical system's temperature to fluctuate around the target value in a way consistent with the canonical (NVT) ensemble. It avoids the stochastic elements of Langevin or Andersen thermostats. (UNVERIFIED)

An algorithm used in molecular dynamics simulations to fix certain geometric parameters, most commonly bond lengths involving light atoms like hydrogen. By constraining these fast vibrations, longer simulation time steps can be used, significantly speeding up the simulation while having minimal impact on slower, large-scale motions. These algorithms iteratively adjust particle positions or use analytical solutions to satisfy the constraint conditions. (UNVERIFIED)

An iterative constraint algorithm widely used in molecular dynamics to fix bond lengths. It adjusts the positions of atoms involved in a constraint at the end of a time step until the constraint condition (e.g., fixed bond distance) is satisfied within a defined tolerance. It handles coupled constraints involving multiple atoms connected together. (UNVERIFIED)

A constraint algorithm similar to SHAKE but designed for velocity-Verlet type integrators, ensuring that both positions and velocities satisfy the constraint conditions at the end of each time step. It involves solving constraint equations for positions first, then using those positions to solve for constrained velocities. This maintains consistency between positions and velocities under constraint. (UNVERIFIED)

A constraint algorithm that holds bond lengths fixed by correcting the positions after each integration step, solving the constraint equations directly rather than by repeated adjustment. Being non-iterative makes it fast and makes its cost predictable. It is the constraint algorithm GROMACS uses by default. (UNVERIFIED)

A force calculation algorithm that computes the electrostatic interactions between charged particles in a molecular simulation, including those at long range. Summing every pair directly costs time that grows with the square of the number of particles, so most methods reduce the cost with cutoffs, grids or multipole expansions while keeping acceptable accuracy. Examples are Ewald summation, particle mesh Ewald and reaction field. (UNVERIFIED)

A highly efficient grid-based algorithm for calculating long-range electrostatic interactions in periodic systems, based on the Ewald summation technique. It splits the calculation into a short-range part computed directly in real space and a long-range part computed efficiently in reciprocal space using Fast Fourier Transforms (FFTs) on a grid. PME is a standard method for accurate electrostatics in biomolecular simulations. (UNVERIFIED)

An approximate method for handling long-range electrostatic interactions where direct interactions are calculated only up to a certain cutoff distance. The effect of charges beyond the cutoff is approximated by embedding the cutoff sphere within a continuous dielectric medium representing the solvent. While computationally cheaper than PME, its accuracy depends on the system and parameters chosen. (UNVERIFIED)

An efficient algorithm for calculating long-range forces (like electrostatic or gravitational) in particle simulations, conceptually similar to Particle Mesh Ewald (PME). It splits the force calculation into a short-range part computed directly between nearby particles (particle-particle) and a long-range part computed using a grid and Fast Fourier Transforms (particle-mesh). PPPM is widely used in both astrophysics and molecular simulation for its performance and accuracy. (UNVERIFIED)

Refers to the classification of forces or potential energy contributions that describe how particles (atoms, ions, coarse-grained beads) affect each other within a simulation's model or force field. These types determine the structure, dynamics, and thermodynamics of the simulated system according to the chosen model.

An interaction between particles where the force or potential energy diminishes slowly with increasing distance, typically decaying as r^−n where n≤3 (e.g., electrostatic interactions decaying as 1/r). Because their influence extends significantly far, these interactions necessitate special computational techniques (like Particle Mesh Ewald (PME) or Ewald sums) in simulations using periodic boundary conditions to accurately account for contributions beyond a simple distance cutoff. They are crucial for the behavior of charged or polar molecules in condensed phases. (UNVERIFIED)

An interaction between particles where the force or potential energy decreases rapidly with increasing distance, becoming negligible beyond a certain range (typically a few molecular diameters). Van der Waals interactions (often modeled with Lennard-Jones potentials decaying as 1/(r^6) for attraction) are the primary example. These interactions can often be computationally truncated using a cutoff radius in simulations without significant loss of accuracy, improving efficiency. (UNVERIFIED)

An interaction whose strength and occurrence depend critically on the specific chemical identities, geometries, and relative orientations of the interacting partners. These often involve directional components and chemical complementarity, such as hydrogen bonds, salt bridges (ionic interactions), or π-stacking, playing key roles in molecular recognition, binding specificity, and defined structural motifs. They contrast with more general, less directional interactions like isotropic Van der Waals forces. (UNVERIFIED)

An interaction energy arising from forces that depend little on the chemical identity or the orientation of the groups involved, chiefly dispersion attraction and excluded-volume repulsion. These forces act between almost any pair of atoms, so they set overall cohesion and packing rather than specific recognition. They contrast with specific, directional interactions such as hydrogen bonds. (UNVERIFIED)

An interaction between atoms, ions, or molecules that does not involve the sharing of valence electrons to form a covalent bond. These interactions, including Van der Waals forces, electrostatic interactions (encompassing hydrogen bonds, salt bridges, dipole interactions), π-effects, and hydrophobic effects, govern molecular recognition, self-assembly, folding, and the stability of biomolecular complexes. Though individually weaker than covalent bonds (typically 0.1-10 kcal/mol vs >50 kcal/mol), their cumulative effect is critical for biological structure and function. (UNVERIFIED)

An interaction in which atoms share valence electrons, forming the bonds that hold a molecule together. Typical covalent bonds are much stronger than the thermal energy available at ordinary temperatures, so they rarely break except in chemical reactions. A classical force field represents it as a fixed connection rather than describing the sharing. (UNVERIFIED)

A short-range non-covalent interaction between atoms or molecules that combines attraction, mainly from London dispersion and from interactions of permanent or induced dipoles, with a strong repulsion when electron clouds overlap. The dispersion part arises from temporary fluctuations in electron distribution that create short-lived dipoles, and the repulsion arises from the Pauli exclusion principle. It is usually modeled with the Lennard-Jones 12-6 potential, and it determines molecular size, shape and packing and contributes to binding affinity. (UNVERIFIED)

A model that represents the effect of the surrounding solvent on a solute in a simulation. It may include individual solvent molecules explicitly, or replace them with a continuous medium carrying averaged properties. The choice sets both the cost of the simulation and which solvent effects can appear in the result. (UNVERIFIED)

A solvation model where individual solvent molecules (e.g., water molecules represented by a specific water model like TIP3P or SPC/E) are explicitly included in the simulation system alongside the solute molecule(s). This approach provides the most detailed, atomistic representation of solute-solvent interactions, capturing specific hydrogen bonding patterns, local solvent structure, and dynamic effects. However, it significantly increases the system size and computational expense due to the large number of solvent particles that must be simulated. (UNVERIFIED)

OBSOLETE. Within the context of solvation models, this typically refers to the use of an explicit solvent model where the solvent is specifically water, represented using a particular force field parameter set (e.g., TIP3P, SPC/E, TIP4P-Ew). This distinguishes it from implicit solvation approaches or explicit simulations using non-aqueous solvents. The term emphasizes that water molecules are being directly simulated using a chosen set of parameters defining their interactions.

comments: Retired 2026-08-24. It named a water model but held none: all 18 sit under MOLSIM:000014 water model force field, which its own definition pointed at by naming TIP3P, SPC/E and TIP4P-Ew as the parameter sets involved. The distinction it was reaching for, explicit solvation with water specifically, is already carried by MOLSIM:000066 explicit solvent model, whose definition names the same models. It was also asserted disjoint from MOLSIM:000066, which was wrong, since explicit water is a kind of explicit solvent rather than something separate from it.

definition.val: A solvation model that approximates the average effect of the solvent environment without explicitly representing individual solvent molecules. Instead, the solvent is treated as a continuous medium characterized by macroscopic properties, primarily its dielectric constant (ϵ) to account for electrostatic screening, and sometimes surface tension to account for nonpolar effects like cavity formation. Common examples include Generalized Born (GB) models and methods based on solving the Poisson-Boltzmann (PB) equation, often combined with a surface area term (SASA); these significantly reduce computational cost compared to explicit solvent. (UNVERIFIED)

A solvation modeling approach that combines elements of both explicit and implicit solvent representations within the same simulation. Typically, a limited number of explicit solvent molecules are retained in a specific region of interest deemed critical (e.g., the active site of an enzyme, the first solvation shell around a solute), while the bulk solvent further away is represented using an implicit continuum model. This strategy aims to capture detailed local solvent effects accurately while maintaining computational efficiency by treating the less critical bulk solvent implicitly. (UNVERIFIED)

A solvent model designed for compatibility with coarse-grained (CG) solute force fields, where the solvent representation is also simplified to match the reduced resolution of the solute. This can involve explicit CG solvent particles where each particle represents multiple (e.g., 3-4) real water molecules (like MARTINI water), or implicit CG solvent models that adapt continuum concepts to the coarse-grained scale. These models drastically reduce the number of degrees of freedom associated with the solvent, enabling simulations of very large systems or very long timescales. (UNVERIFIED)

An emerging class of solvation models where the complex relationship between a solute's structure/properties and its solvation free energy (or related solvent effects) is learned using machine learning (ML) algorithms. These algorithms are trained on large datasets generated from high-fidelity sources like explicit solvent simulations, quantum mechanical calculations, or experimental data. ML solvent models aim to achieve high accuracy approaching that of the training data but at a significantly reduced computational cost, potentially bridging the gap between fast implicit models and expensive explicit models. (UNVERIFIED)

A solvation model where the electronic structure of the solvent, or its interaction with the solute, is treated using quantum mechanics (QM). This can range from embedding a QM description of the solute within a classical solvent model (either implicit or explicit) using QM/MM techniques, to treating a number of explicit solvent molecules quantum mechanically along with the solute, or using implicit solvent models derived from QM principles (like the SMD model). These models capture electronic polarization, charge transfer, and other quantum effects involving the solvent, providing high accuracy but at a very high computational cost, reserved for specific problems like chemical reactions in solution. (UNVERIFIED)

A specific type of implicit solvent model that provides an analytical approximation to the electrostatic component of the solvation free energy, based on the Born model for solvation of a spherical ion. It calculates effective Born radii for each atom in the solute, representing the degree of solvent exposure, and uses these radii in a formula that approximates the electrostatic polarization energy typically calculated by solving the more complex Poisson-Boltzmann equation. GB models are computationally much faster than PB methods, making them popular for applications like MD simulations or energy minimization, often paired with a surface area term (GBSA). (UNVERIFIED)

An algorithm used to quantify the degree of resemblance between two objects, often molecules represented by chemical fingerprints or structural features, or between simulation data like conformations or trajectories. These methods employ various mathematical formulas (metrics or coefficients) to compute a numerical score indicating similarity or distance. They are widely used in cheminformatics, drug discovery, and simulation analysis. (UNVERIFIED)

An algorithm that measures how similar 2 molecules are as the size of what they have in common divided by the size of what they cover together. For molecular fingerprints this is the number of features present in both divided by the number present in at least 1 of them. It is the standard measure for fingerprints, runs from 0 for nothing shared to 1 for identical sets, and is also applied to overlapping molecular volumes in shape comparison. (UNVERIFIED)

A similarity calculation algorithm that compares 2 molecules by their overlap while weighting the features unique to each molecule differently, through 2 parameters, α and β. The measure ranges from 0 (nothing shared) to 1 (identical), and the weights can be set to emphasize either the reference (query) molecule or the fit (database) molecule. This asymmetry lets it find molecules that contain the reference as a substructure, or that are contained in it. (UNVERIFIED)

basicPropertyValues.val: General form, for reference: T(A,B) = |A n B| / (alpha*|A - B| + beta*|B - A| + |A n B|), where A and B are the feature sets of the two molecules being compared. alpha weights features unique to A (the reference) and beta weights features unique to B (the query or fit molecule); alpha = beta = 1 reduces to the Tanimoto coefficient, and alpha = beta = 0.5 gives the Dice coefficient. The named variants below differ only in their fixed alpha/beta values, which each of their definitions states. Note this text is a plain-string note: no OWL consumer renders mathematical notation, so it is written to be readable as-is rather than as LaTeX. Requested in GitHub issue #1.

definition.val: A similarity calculation method used to compare 2 sets (e.g., features in molecular fingerprints), closely related to the Tanimoto coefficient and Jaccard index. It measures the overlap between the sets, normalized by the average size of the 2 sets. It is often used in information retrieval and cheminformatics as an alternative similarity metric. (UNVERIFIED)

A type of statistical property representing the straight-line distance between two points in a multi-dimensional space, which may represent molecules in a property space or conformations by atom coordinates. It is calculated as the square root of the sum of squared differences between corresponding coordinates or features. Lower Euclidean distance implies higher similarity in the context of the chosen space. (UNVERIFIED)

A type of statistical property representing the distance between two points in a multi-dimensional space, calculated as the sum of the absolute differences of their coordinates. The Manhattan distance is an alternative to the Euclidean distance for measuring similarity in clustering and data analysis. This is also known as the city block distance. (UNVERIFIED)

A structural property giving the separation between 2 specified atoms, or between the centres of mass of 2 groups of atoms. It is the basic geometric measure for following interactions such as hydrogen bonds and salt bridges, or the separation between parts of a molecular system, over the course of a simulation. (UNVERIFIED)

A similarity calculation method specifically used for comparing 2 strings or bit vectors (like binary molecular fingerprints) of equal length. It counts the number of positions at which the corresponding symbols or bits are different. A lower Hamming distance indicates higher similarity between the binary representations. (UNVERIFIED)

A similarity calculation method used for comparing 2 sets, defined as the size of the intersection divided by the size of the union of the sets. It is identical to the Tanimoto coefficient when applied to binary data (like molecular fingerprints). It provides a normalized measure of overlap between feature sets, ranging from 0 (no overlap) to 1 (identical sets). (UNVERIFIED)

A similarity calculation method that measures the overlap between 2 sets, defined as the size of the intersection divided by the size of the smaller of the 2 sets. Unlike Tanimoto/Jaccard, it reaches 1 if one set is a subset of the other. It is useful for assessing containment or sub-structure relationships. (UNVERIFIED)

A Tversky index algorithm that adds the shape Tversky score and the color (chemical feature) Tversky score of 2 aligned molecules, both weighted towards the fit (database) molecule with α 0.05 and β 0.95. A high score means that the fit molecule is largely contained in the reference (query) molecule in both shape and chemistry, which helps find database molecules that are substructures of the query. The combined score normally ranges from 0 to 2. (UNVERIFIED)

A specialized variant of the Tversky Index that uses fixed parameters with the alpha (α) value of 0.95, and beta (β) value of 0.05 to heavily weight the reference molecule in the comparison. This asymmetric weighting makes it particularly effective at finding molecules that contain the reference structure as a substructure. RefTversky is commonly used in virtual screening to identify compounds that preserve key structural features of a reference molecule. (UNVERIFIED)

A similarity calculation algorithm that combines the scores of 2 or more different similarity measures into a single score. The aim is to capture several aspects of similarity at once, for example the shape of 2 molecules and the chemical features they share. The particular measures chosen and the formula that combines them define each combo score. (UNVERIFIED)

An algorithm designed to find the best path or connection between states or nodes according to some defined criteria, such as minimum cost, shortest distance, or maximum flow. These algorithms are used in various contexts, including finding minimum energy pathways for reactions, constructing minimum spanning trees for clustering, optimizing network routes, or solving complex search problems. They employ different strategies ranging from exact graph traversals to heuristic searches. (UNVERIFIED)

A greedy algorithm used to find a Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) for a connected, undirected graph with weighted edges. An MST connects all vertices together with the minimum possible total edge weight. Kruskal's algorithm iteratively adds the lowest-weight edge that does not form a cycle until all vertices are connected.

An algorithm that finds the cheapest set of connections joining every node of a network, called a minimum spanning tree, by starting from a single node and repeatedly adding the cheapest link to a node not yet reached. The result is a tree that includes every node with no redundant links. In simulation analysis, such a tree can link similar conformations for clustering. (UNVERIFIED)

An algorithm for finding the shortest path between a starting node and all other nodes in a graph with non-negative edge weights. It works by iteratively exploring the graph, maintaining the shortest distance found so far to each node, and always extending the path from the node with the current shortest distance. It is fundamental in graph theory and network routing. (UNVERIFIED)

An informed search algorithm used for finding the shortest path between a starting node and a target node in a graph, commonly used in pathfinding and planning problems. It extends Dijkstra's algorithm by using a heuristic function to estimate the cost from the current node to the target, guiding the search towards the goal more efficiently. Its performance depends on the quality of the heuristic used. (UNVERIFIED)

An algorithm that answers a question about a point by looking at whichever recorded points lie closest to it. It is used to classify, to cluster, and to build lists of which atoms are near enough to interact. It makes no assumption about the shape of the data, only that closeness is meaningful. (UNVERIFIED)

A class of heuristic optimization algorithms inspired by the process of natural selection and evolution. They maintain a population of candidate solutions (chromosomes) that evolve over generations through processes like selection, crossover (recombination), and mutation, guided by a fitness function that evaluates solution quality. Genetic algorithms are often used for complex optimization problems where exact methods are infeasible. (UNVERIFIED)

A probabilistic heuristic algorithm used for finding the global optimum of a function in a large search space, inspired by the annealing process in metallurgy. It starts with an initial solution and iteratively explores neighboring solutions, accepting worse solutions with a probability that decreases over time (controlled by a "temperature" parameter), allowing it to escape local optima. It is a metaheuristic for global optimization. (UNVERIFIED)

A probabilistic heuristic algorithm for finding good paths through graphs, inspired by the foraging behavior of ants who deposit pheromones. Artificial ants construct candidate solutions (paths) by moving through the graph, probabilistically choosing edges based on distance and accumulated artificial pheromone trails, which are updated based on the quality of solutions found. It is often applied to combinatorial optimization problems like the Traveling Salesperson Problem. (UNVERIFIED)

A class of algorithms designed to solve problems related to flows in networks (graphs where edges have capacities), such as finding the maximum flow possible between a source and a sink node. Examples include the Ford-Fulkerson algorithm and its variations (e.g., Edmonds-Karp). These algorithms are used in logistics, scheduling, network design, and resource allocation problems. (UNVERIFIED)

A binary trajectory format based on the NetCDF standard, used by the Amber simulation package. It efficiently stores atomic coordinates, velocities, forces, and periodic box dimensions from a simulation. This is the modern, recommended trajectory format for Amber.

comments: In the vast majority of scientific applications, including molecular dynamics, climate science, and oceanography, a .nc file is a NetCDF file. There is no difference in the format itself. The .nc extension is simply the most common file name suffix for a file written using the NetCDF data model. (UNVERFIED)

definition.val: Refers to the specific characteristics of a ligand molecule, particularly in the context of its interaction with a receptor molecule (like a protein). This encompasses various aspects, including whether it is bound or unbound, its specific binding pose or conformation, its protonation or tautomeric form, and its electronic state.

The state in which a ligand molecule is physically associated with its receptor molecule, typically residing within a specific binding site or pocket, stabilized by non-covalent interactions. Simulations often aim to characterize the structure, dynamics, and interaction energy of the ligand within the bound state, or calculate the free energy difference between the bound and unbound states (binding free energy).

The state in which a ligand molecule is not associated with the receptor molecule, typically solvated freely in the surrounding solvent or located far from the receptor's binding site. Defining the unbound state is necessary for calculating binding free energies, as it serves as the reference state relative to the bound state. It represents the ligand and receptor separated and independently solvated.

In chemical kinetics and simulation, the transition state refers to a specific, high-energy, transient molecular configuration along the reaction coordinate connecting two stable states (e.g., reactant and product, or bound and unbound states). It is connected to the energy barrier that must be overcome for the transition to occur. While challenging to simulate directly due to its short lifetime, characterizing the transition state is crucial for understanding reaction mechanisms and rates, often studied using specialized simulation techniques or QM methods.

A state of a system that is locally stable (residing in a minimum on the potential energy surface) but has a higher free energy than the globally stable state. The system can persist in a metastable state for a significant time if the energy barrier to reach a more stable state is high. Examples in biomolecular systems include misfolded protein conformations, transiently bound ligand poses, or specific intermediate states along a functional cycle.

A transient state occurring early in the binding process where the ligand and receptor molecules first come into close proximity and make non-specific contacts, largely driven by diffusion, before potentially rearranging into a specific, stable bound state. The encounter complex represents a collection of loosely associated configurations, often characterized by significant residual motion and non-optimal interactions, preceding the formation of the final bound pose.

A general state referring to a molecule (either ligand or receptor, or the complex) being surrounded by solvent molecules (typically a water buffer in biological contexts). This term emphasizes the presence and influence of the solvent on the molecule's structure, dynamics, and energetics. Both the bound and unbound states are typically solvated states, and solvation effects are crucial components of binding free energies and conformational preferences.

A specific three-dimensional arrangement or shape adopted by a flexible molecule, such as a protein or ligand. Molecules can typically exist in multiple conformational states, corresponding to different local minima on their potential energy surface, separated by energy barriers. Simulations are often used to explore the accessible conformational states, their relative populations, and the transitions between them, which are essential for molecular function and binding.

The condition of a molecule defined by which of its acidic and basic groups currently carry a proton. It fixes the charge on the molecule and therefore how it interacts with everything around it. It depends on the acidity of the surroundings, so a group buried in a protein may differ from the same group in water. (UNVERIFIED)

One of several forms of a molecule that differ by the position of a hydrogen atom and an accompanying shift of a double bond, and which interconvert readily. The forms are genuinely different molecules for a simulation, because their bonds and charges differ. Choosing the wrong one for a ligand is a common and silent source of error. (UNVERIFIED)

An electronic state of a molecule where one or more electrons have been promoted to higher energy levels than in the ground electronic state, typically following the absorption of light (photoexcitation). Excited states have different electron distributions, geometries, and reactivity compared to the ground state and are central to photochemistry and spectroscopy (like fluorescence). Simulating excited states requires quantum mechanical methods (like TD-DFT or CASSCF) as classical force fields are typically parameterized only for the ground electronic state. (UNVERIFIED)

A general strategy that specifies how a scientific objective is to be achieved and which procedures are followed to achieve it. In biomolecular science it covers both the physical procedures of an experiment and the calculation protocols of computational work. Knowing which strategy was used tells a reader whether a result came from physical observation or from calculation, and how the work can be repeated. (UNVERIFIED)

An integration algorithm that computes the next position and velocity from the current ones and the current force alone. It is the simplest possible scheme and the easiest to reason about. It is not used for ordinary molecular dynamics, because the energy of a system integrated this way drifts steadily upward, although Euler-type schemes are used for Brownian dynamics. (UNVERIFIED)

OBSOLETE. A type of statistical property that measures the strength and direction of the linear association between two variables. It is a value between -1 and 1, where 1 indicates a perfect positive correlation and -1 indicates a perfect negative correlation. The correlation coefficient is widely used to identify relationships between different properties in a simulation. This is often reported as r or rho.

comments: Obsoleted 2026-07-29: duplicated STATO:0000142. STATO is the canonical OBO home for statistics; reused in place of this term. Its four children were re-parented under STATO:0000142 in the same edit - retiring a parent necessarily re-points every child that named it.

definition.val: OBSOLETE. Pearson's correlation coefficient (often denoted as 'r') measures the strength and direction of the linear relationship between two continuous variables. It assumes the data are approximately normally distributed and calculates the covariance of the two variables divided by the product of their standard deviations. It is perhaps the most widely used measure of linear correlation.

comments: Obsoleted 2026-07-29: duplicated STATO:0000280. STATO is the canonical OBO home for statistics; reused in place of this term.

definition.val: A specific type of `orientation` descriptor that represents the cosine of the rotation of a vector orthogonal to a given axis.

HOLE is a computer program used to analyze the dimensions and shape of internal pathways or tunnels within a biomolecular structure. It operates by computationally squeezing a flexible sphere along a channel axis to determine the maximum pore radius at every point without overlapping the surrounding atoms.

MOLE is a software algorithm designed to automatically locate and characterize channels, tunnels, and pores within protein structures. It utilizes a Voronoi diagram approach to efficiently map the void space inside a molecule and identify paths connecting internal cavities to the surface.

A resampling method that estimates the uncertainty of a computed quantity by drawing many new samples of the same size from the existing data, with repetition allowed, and recomputing the quantity from each. The spread of the recomputed values estimates the standard error or confidence interval of the original value. It makes no assumption about how the data are distributed, but it treats data points as independent, so correlated data such as consecutive simulation frames are usually resampled in blocks. (UNVERIFIED)

It is a kinetic network model used to analyze complex conformational dynamics, such as protein folding, ligand binding, and structural rearrangements, by stitching together many short molecular dynamics (MD) simulations into a global long-timescale picture. It divides the conformations visited in simulations into discrete states and counts the transitions between them, assuming the next state depends only on the current one and not on the path taken there.

A statistical analysis that measures how different 2 probability distributions are by averaging the relative entropy (Kullback-Leibler divergence) of each from their mean distribution. The result is symmetric, giving the same value whichever distribution is taken first, and bounded, lying between 0 and 1 when base-2 logarithms are used; plain relative entropy has neither property. It is used to compare the conformations sampled by 2 simulations. (UNVERIFIED)

A statistical measure of how much information is lost when one probability distribution is used in place of another. It is not symmetric: the value depends on which distribution is treated as the reference. It is 0 only when the 2 are identical and has no upper limit, which is why the symmetric bounded version is often preferred. (UNVERIFIED)

A statistical method that re-expresses data with many variables in terms of a few, chosen to keep as much of the structure as possible. A protein trajectory has 3 coordinates per atom, which cannot be looked at directly. Reducing it to 2 or 3 numbers per frame is what makes it possible to see where the system went. (UNVERIFIED)

A statistical method that finds the directions along which data vary most, and re-expresses the data in terms of the few largest of them. Applied to a trajectory, the largest directions are the collective motions that account for most of the movement. A protein with thousands of coordinates can then be described by 2 or 3 numbers per frame. (UNVERIFIED)

A data analysis technique is a specific computational method used to extract meaningful scientific insights from the raw data generated by a simulation. These techniques can range from simple calculations, like measuring the distance between two atoms over time, to complex statistical methods that identify large-scale molecular motions. Applying these techniques is the crucial step that transforms a trajectory of atomic coordinates into an understandable story about the molecule's behavior.

Clustering analysis encompasses algorithms designed to partition a dataset into distinct groups or clusters, such that data points within the same cluster are more similar to each other than to those in other clusters based on chosen features. In molecular simulation, clustering is frequently applied to trajectory data to identify distinct conformational states visited by the system. Various algorithms exist, differing in how similarity and clusters are defined (e.g., k-means, hierarchical clustering).

A hypothesis testing analysis that decides whether to reject a null hypothesis by computing a test statistic from the sample data and comparing it with a critical value, or by computing a p-value. A p-value is the probability of observing data at least as extreme as those seen if the null hypothesis were true. Examples include t-tests, chi-squared tests and analysis of variance (ANOVA). (UNVERIFIED)

A statistical test that judges whether 2 sets of values come from the same distribution, or whether 1 set comes from a given reference distribution, by measuring the largest gap between their cumulative distributions. It makes no assumption about the shape of the distributions, but it does assume that the values are independent, which consecutive simulation frames are not. It is used, for example, to check whether 2 simulations sampled the same distribution of a property. (UNVERIFIED)

A statistical analysis that computes, from sample data such as simulation results, a range of values that would contain the true value of a quantity in a chosen share of repeated experiments, such as 95%. It states how uncertain an estimate is when the data are limited or noisy. A wider interval means greater uncertainty. (UNVERIFIED)

A statistical method that measures how far predicted values lie from observed ones. Which measure to use depends on what a large error should cost: squaring the differences makes outliers dominate, taking their size does not. Reporting more than one is usual, because each hides something the others show. (UNVERIFIED)

nodes.lbl: standard error of the mean analysis

definition.val: A statistical measure giving how far a computed average is likely to lie from the true average, based on how much the data scatter and how many independent samples there are. It shrinks as more independent data is added, unlike the spread of the data itself, which does not. For a trajectory the count of independent samples is far smaller than the number of frames, so it is usually estimated with methods that account for this, such as block averaging. (UNVERIFIED)

An error metric giving the typical size of the difference between predicted and observed values, computed by squaring the differences, averaging them and taking the square root. Squaring first makes large errors count disproportionately, so a single bad prediction moves it noticeably. It is in the same units as the quantity itself, which makes it directly interpretable. (UNVERIFIED)

An error metric giving the average size of the difference between predicted and observed values, ignoring sign. Because it does not square the differences, every error counts in proportion to its size and one large error does not dominate. It is the measure to prefer when outliers are expected and should not be allowed to control the score. (UNVERIFIED)

An error metric giving the average of the squared differences between predicted and observed values. It is the quantity most fitting procedures minimise, because squaring makes it smooth and easy to differentiate. Its units are the square of the quantity's, which is why the square root is usually reported instead. (UNVERIFIED)

A widely used all-atom force field parameter set from the CHARMM family, optimized for proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, and carbohydrates. Developed by the MacKerell Lab at the University of Maryland, it provides the mathematical parameters (atomic charges, masses, bond lengths, and angles) necessary to calculate the physical forces dictating the structure and dynamics of biomolecules. It represents a significant update over earlier CHARMM versions (like CHARMM22/27), incorporating improved parameters derived from high-level quantum calculations and experimental data. The 'm' variant (CHARMM36m) includes further refinements, particularly for proteins.

A statistical method that measures how well a model predicts data it was not fitted to, by repeatedly holding part of the data back, fitting on the rest, and testing on the held-back part. A model can always be made to fit the data it was built from, so testing on that data proves nothing. This is the standard guard against that mistake. (UNVERIFIED)

A validation method that puts an uncertainty on a result by resampling the data it came from and recomputing it many times. It is used to show that a conclusion does not rest on a few particular data points. A large spread across the resamples shows that the result is not reliable. (UNVERIFIED)

A data analysis method that judges whether a simulation has sampled enough for its results to be stable, and puts an error estimate on those results. It works from time series of the quantity of interest, or by resampling the data statistically. Without both parts, a reported value has no stated reliability. (UNVERIFIED)

A statistical method that estimates the uncertainty of an average taken from a trajectory, by dividing the data into blocks and looking at how the block averages scatter. It is needed because successive frames of a trajectory resemble each other, so the usual formula for the uncertainty of a mean underestimates it badly. Enlarging the blocks until the estimate stops changing gives the honest figure. (UNVERIFIED)

A data analysis method that compares results obtained while a parameter or collective variable is changed in one direction with those obtained while it is changed back, and reports the difference between them. A large difference means the system did not stay near equilibrium, or that sampling was insufficient. Showing that the difference is small is part of demonstrating that a free energy calculation has converged. (UNVERIFIED)

A data analysis method that computes quantitative measures of whether a simulation has sampled enough for its results to have stopped changing. Measures include the stability of a running average, the size of fluctuations in a key property, and the number of transitions observed between states. Which measure is appropriate depends on the kind of simulation and on what is being calculated. (UNVERIFIED)

A data analysis method that measures how far the configurations sampled in neighbouring simulation windows or thermodynamic states coincide. Enough overlap is needed to combine the windows with reweighting methods such as the weighted histogram analysis method (WHAM) or the multistate Bennett acceptance ratio (MBAR), and too little makes the combined free energy unreliable. Poor overlap shows that more windows or longer sampling are needed. (UNVERIFIED)

A method that studies a scientific problem by calculation on a computer, for example by simulating molecular behavior, building molecular models or analyzing the resulting data. It is distinct from an experimental method, which observes a physical sample, and from a theoretical approach, which supplies the physical principles a calculation is built on. It is defined by its algorithms and by the settings given to the program that runs it. (UNVERIFIED)

A method consisting of the physical principles and mathematical framework a calculation is built on, such as quantum mechanics or classical mechanics with an empirical potential. It sits above the algorithm and the software, and fixes what the calculation is able to represent at all. Two methods sharing an approach can still differ in every other respect. (UNVERIFIED)

A statistical metric that scores how well a model ranks a set of compounds, by checking for each pair whether the predicted order matches the measured order and weighting the pair by the difference between their measured values. A wrong order for 2 compounds with very different measured values therefore counts more than a wrong order for 2 similar ones. It is used where a model is meant to guide a choice between compounds rather than to reproduce a number. (UNVERIFIED)

A criterion applied when choosing which pairs of compounds to compare in a relative binding free energy study. The choice strongly affects whether the calculation converges, because a pair that differs by 1 atom is far easier to transform than a pair that differs by a whole ring. Such criteria cover how similar the compounds are, the range of their measured affinities, the quality of the available data and how practical the calculation is. (UNVERIFIED)

A ligand selection criterion favouring pairs of molecules that share a common core and differ only by small changes. Such pairs can be transformed into one another alchemically with few atoms changing, which helps the calculation converge and lets errors cancel. Similarity of this kind is often judged by eye or with molecular fingerprint measures. (UNVERIFIED)

A ligand selection criterion favouring molecules that resemble each other in chemical character, such as their functional groups, polarity, charge and hydrogen bonding, often measured with chemical fingerprints or descriptors. It is related to structural similarity but looks at the chemical nature of the difference rather than only at a shared core. Choosing chemically similar pairs helps keep an alchemical transformation smooth. (UNVERIFIED)

A ligand selection criterion requiring the measured binding strengths of the chosen compounds to fall within a stated range, or to differ by no more than a stated amount. Differences smaller than the typical error of the calculation cannot be told apart, and the measured values must lie within what the assay can measure reliably for the comparison to mean anything. (UNVERIFIED)

A ligand selection criterion requiring the chosen set as a whole to span a range of structures and chemistries, even though individual pairs within it should be similar. A set of near-identical compounds tests a method over a narrow region and says nothing about its general reliability. The 2 requirements apply at different levels: similarity within a pair, diversity across the set. (UNVERIFIED)

This practical criterion emphasizes selecting ligands for which reliable experimental data, particularly binding affinity measurements (like Ki, Kd, or IC50), already exist. Having high-quality experimental data is essential for validating the computational predictions and assessing the accuracy of the methods used. Availability of structural data (e.g., co-crystal structures) is also highly valuable.

A ligand selection criterion based on computed or measured properties of the compounds, such as molecular weight, lipophilicity, charge and the number of rotatable bonds. These properties predict how difficult a compound will be to simulate as well as how drug-like it is. A charged or very flexible compound needs far more sampling than a neutral rigid one. (UNVERIFIED)

A ligand selection criterion based on how large and of what kind the difference between 2 candidate compounds is. Small, local changes, such as adding a methyl group or swapping a halogen for another, usually converge quickly, while opening a ring or changing the net charge does not. Smaller changes generally give more reliable relative free energy results. (UNVERIFIED)

A ligand selection criterion asking whether the calculations a candidate would require can be completed with the time and computing available. A charged or highly flexible ligand may need many times the sampling of a neutral rigid one. It is applied before the calculation, since discovering the answer afterwards wastes the whole effort. (UNVERIFIED)

A ligand selection criterion favouring molecules and modifications that bear on an ongoing drug discovery project or a stated therapeutic aim. It is a judgement about purpose rather than about chemistry, so it cannot be computed. It is recorded because it explains why a particular set of compounds was chosen. (UNVERIFIED)

A ligand selection criterion based on how good the experimental structure of the complex is, judged by resolution, how well the model fits the data, and whether the ligand is clearly resolved. A poorly resolved ligand may be placed wrongly, and a calculation started from it inherits that error. It is assessed before the structure is used, not after a result looks wrong. (UNVERIFIED)

A ligand selection criterion based on whether the compound stays bound and in a consistent pose during a trial simulation. A ligand that drifts out of its site, or flips between poses, gives a free energy that depends on how long the run was. Testing it with a short simulation before committing to a full calculation is cheaper than discovering it afterwards. (UNVERIFIED)

A ligand selection criterion based on how tightly a compound binds relative to its size, usually measured as binding free energy divided by the number of heavy, that is non-hydrogen, atoms. It is used because binding strength tends to rise with size, so a large weak binder can look better than a small efficient one. Compounds that bind efficiently for their size are often preferred as starting points in early drug discovery. (UNVERIFIED)

The GROMACS mdp format is the specific simulation parameter format used by the GROMACS software package. The file, which typically has a ".mdp" extension, contains a series of keyword-value pairs that control every aspect of the simulation run, from the integrator and time step to the thermostat and pressure coupling methods. For GROMACS users, creating and editing the mdp file is the primary way to define the simulation protocol.

A reusable software platform that provides a common structure, tools and libraries on which simulation workflows or coupled simulation programs are built, at a higher level than a single tool or script. It may standardise how simulations are set up, how data are managed, or how separate programs exchange data during a run. Examples include workflows that automate free energy calculations and interfaces that couple a quantum chemistry program to a molecular dynamics program. (UNVERIFIED)

A software program that builds or runs a computational model of a physical system, such as a simulation engine or a modelling and setup tool. What separates it from other software is that its subject is a model of something real. (UNVERIFIED)

A text-based file format from the Amber software that stores the movement of atoms over time from a simulation. It contains a series of snapshots, or frames, where each frame lists the x, y, and z coordinates of every atom at a specific time point. It may also store the x, y, and z simulation box sizes.

Application programs specifically designed to perform molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, which calculate the motion of atoms and molecules over time based on classical mechanics and a chosen force field. These packages typically include capabilities for system preparation, simulation execution (often optimized for high-performance computing), and basic trajectory analysis. Examples include AMBER, GROMACS, NAMD, CHARMM, Desmond, and LAMMPS.

A software program that solves for the arrangement of electrons in atoms and molecules using quantum mechanics. It implements methods such as Hartree-Fock, density functional theory and the correlated methods built on them. It is what supplies an energy and a set of forces when a force field is not accurate enough. (UNVERIFIED)

A computational tool used to predict the preferred binding orientation and affinity (scoring) of one molecule (typically a small ligand) to another (usually a larger receptor like a protein or nucleic acid). Docking tools employ search algorithms to explore possible binding poses within a target site and use scoring functions to estimate the binding strength for each pose. Widely used in drug discovery and understanding molecular recognition, examples include AutoDock, Vina, Glide, GOLD, and DOCK.

A software program that turns data into images, either as interactive 3-dimensional views of molecular structures, surfaces, densities and trajectories, or as plots and graphs of numerical results. It lets a person look at a system or a result rather than only measure it. Many faults in a prepared system, such as a molecule sitting half outside its box, are obvious on sight and invisible to any numerical check. (UNVERIFIED)

Software designed to process raw data generated from biomolecular simulations (like trajectories, energy files) to calculate specific quantitative properties and extract meaningful insights. Analysis tools implement algorithms for calculating metrics like RMSD, RMSF, radius of gyration, hydrogen bonds, interaction energies, principal components (PCA), free energy estimations (MM/PBSA), clustering, etc. Examples include cpptraj (AmberTools), GROMACS analysis utilities, MDAnalysis (Python library), and specialized scripts or programs.

A tool focused on manipulating, converting, filtering, or extracting information from data files. This can involve tasks like converting file formats, extracting specific columns or frames, merging datasets, calculating simple statistics, or preparing data for input into other analysis or visualization tools.
A specific type of data processing tool dedicated to converting molecular structure, trajectory, or data files from one format to another (e.g., PDB to MOL2, XTC to netcdf).

A script specifically designed to automate a series of steps in a workflow that would otherwise need to be performed manually. In simulations, this could involve automatically setting up multiple simulation replicas, submitting jobs to a computing cluster, checking job status, and organizing output files, thereby reducing manual effort and potential errors. Workflow management systems often rely heavily on automation scripts. (UNVERIFIED)

A script written to perform specific analysis tasks on data generated from simulations, often going beyond the standard capabilities of packaged analysis tools or requiring custom calculations. Examples include scripts to calculate specific geometric parameters over time, parse log files for specific energy terms, perform advanced statistical analysis or time-series analysis on trajectory data, or generate data for custom plots.

A script that defines and executes an entire sequence of computational tasks constituting a specific workflow, often involving multiple steps like data preparation, running simulations (potentially submitting to clusters), performing analysis, and summarizing results. These scripts orchestrate the execution of various tools and other scripts, manage intermediate data, and handle dependencies between steps, ensuring the entire process runs smoothly and reproducibly. Tools like Snakemake or Nextflow help in creating robust workflow scripts. (UNVERIFIED)

A reusable part of a larger software system that provides a defined set of functions to whatever calls it. Unlike a program, it is not run on its own; it is built into something else. A library that reads a file format is the usual example. (UNVERIFIED)

A software program that helps in writing, building, installing, testing or maintaining other software, rather than in doing any science itself. Examples are compilers, build systems, package managers and version control systems. A simulation result can depend on which versions of these tools produced the software that computed it. (UNVERIFIED)

A software program that produces the topology and force field parameters a simulation needs for a molecule: which atoms are bonded, what atom type and partial charge each atom has, and the parameters for each bond, angle and dihedral. Some such programs assign existing parameters by atom type, while others derive new charges, fit new parameters or build residue templates. A wrong assignment gives a system that runs normally but represents the wrong molecule. (UNVERIFIED)

A physical theory describing how matter behaves at the scale of atoms and subatomic particles, where energy and angular momentum take discrete values. It is what chemical bonding and molecular electronic structure are explained by. In this field its equations are solved approximately to predict molecular properties. (UNVERIFIED)

A minimal basis set in which each Slater-type atomic orbital is approximated by a fixed combination of 2 Gaussian functions. Gaussian functions are used because the integrals they need are much faster to compute than those of Slater-type orbitals. With only 2 the approximation is poor, so it is used to demonstrate the method rather than to obtain results. (UNVERIFIED)

A commercial quantum chemistry engine for electronic structure calculations with ab initio, density functional and semi-empirical methods. It can also combine quantum and classical models of different parts of a system with its ONIOM method, and is often used to compute the reference data from which force field parameters, such as atomic charges, are derived. It is not designed to be a classical molecular dynamics engine for large biomolecules. (UNVERIFIED)

A quantum chemistry engine providing a broad range of wavefunction-based and density functional methods. The name is shared by 2 separately maintained programs, developed in the United States and the United Kingdom, and their inputs are not interchangeable. Which one produced a result therefore has to be recorded. (UNVERIFIED)

An open-source quantum chemistry engine specializing in high-accuracy ab initio methods, such as coupled cluster theory and symmetry-adapted perturbation theory, alongside Hartree-Fock and density functional theory. It is written in C++ with a Python interface, so calculations can be set up and combined in Python scripts. Symmetry-adapted perturbation theory splits the interaction between 2 molecules into physical parts such as electrostatics and dispersion. (UNVERIFIED)
