It combines 2 separate corrections to the standard double-zeta set. (UNVERIFIED)

A correlation-consistent triple-zeta basis set that adds both a set of diffuse functions and 1 extra optimised d type polarization function. It targets the second-row elements sodium to argon where both diffuse electron density and d orbital flexibility matter, such as anions and intermolecular complexes. It is the triple-zeta member of that combined family. (UNVERIFIED)

A correlation-consistent quadruple-zeta basis set that adds both a set of diffuse functions and 1 extra optimised d type polarization function. It is used for benchmark results on systems containing the second-row elements sodium to argon whose properties depend on both corrections. It is large enough that its use is restricted to small systems. (UNVERIFIED)

A correlation-consistent quintuple-zeta basis set that adds both a set of diffuse functions and 1 extra optimised d type polarization function. It is a specialised benchmark set for the second-row elements sodium to argon in processes that also need diffuse functions. It is close to the complete basis set limit for those elements. (UNVERIFIED)

A correlation-consistent sextuple-zeta basis set that adds both a set of diffuse functions and 1 extra optimised d type polarization function, the latter for the second-row elements sodium to argon. It is among the largest combinations available and is used only for extreme benchmark work on very small systems containing those elements. (UNVERIFIED)

A correlation-consistent double-zeta basis set that adds diffuse functions together with tight functions weighted towards core-valence correlation. The weighting concentrates the added functions where core and valence electrons actually correlate, rather than describing the core itself. It suits a small system needing both diffuse character and core-valence correlation. (UNVERIFIED)

A correlation-consistent triple-zeta basis set that adds diffuse functions together with weighted core-valence correlating functions. It is the level at which core-valence effects are usually first worth their cost. Both additions are needed for properties sensitive to diffuse electrons in systems where the core cannot be treated as inert. (UNVERIFIED)

A correlation-consistent quadruple-zeta basis set that adds diffuse functions together with weighted core-valence correlating functions. It is used for high-accuracy work where both effects must be converged rather than merely present. Its size restricts it to small molecules. (UNVERIFIED)

A correlation-consistent quintuple-zeta basis set that adds diffuse functions together with weighted core-valence correlating functions. It is a benchmark set used to approach the complete basis set limit. Its cost restricts it to atoms and very small molecules. (UNVERIFIED)

A polarization-consistent basis set at the lowest level of the pc-n family, with diffuse functions added. The family is built so results improve smoothly as the level rises, which makes extrapolation to the limit reliable. This level is the starting point of that sequence rather than a basis for production work. (UNVERIFIED)

A polarization-consistent basis set at the first level of the pc-n family, with diffuse functions added. The level corresponds roughly to polarized double-zeta quality. It is the smallest member of the family used for real calculations. (UNVERIFIED)

A polarization-consistent basis set at the second level of the pc-n family, with a set of diffuse functions added. The second level corresponds to polarized triple-zeta quality, and the family is built so that results converge smoothly as the level rises. The diffuse functions make it suitable for anions, intermolecular interactions and polarizabilities. (UNVERIFIED)

A polarization-consistent basis set at the third level of the pc-n family, with a set of diffuse functions added. The third level corresponds to polarized quadruple-zeta quality. It is used where both high accuracy and a correct description of diffuse electron density are needed. (UNVERIFIED)

A polarization-consistent basis set at the fourth level of the pc-n family, with a set of diffuse functions added. The fourth level corresponds to polarized quintuple-zeta quality and is the largest in common use in this family. It is a benchmark set for small systems whose properties depend on diffuse electrons. (UNVERIFIED)

An auxiliary basis set developed by the Ahlrichs group to fit the Coulomb part of the electron repulsion in a density fitting calculation. Fitting only the Coulomb term, rather than the whole 2-electron integral set, gives most of the speed-up at very little cost in accuracy. It is matched to the Karlsruhe orbital basis sets. (UNVERIFIED)

A set of polarization functions, of higher angular momentum than the atom occupies in its ground state, developed by the Ahlrichs group for the Karlsruhe basis sets. Polarization functions let the electron density distort away from atomic symmetry, which is what bonding requires. Without them a basis set cannot describe a bond angle correctly. (UNVERIFIED)

A basis set from the Ahlrichs group giving 2 functions per valence orbital together with polarization functions. The polarization functions let the electron cloud distort away from atomic symmetry, which is what bonding requires and which the unpolarized member of the family cannot do. It is the smallest basis set in that family suitable for real calculations. (UNVERIFIED)

A basis set from the Ahlrichs group giving 2 functions per valence orbital and no polarization functions. Without polarization functions the electron cloud cannot distort away from atomic symmetry, so bond angles are poorly described. It is used as a starting point rather than for results. (UNVERIFIED)

A basis set from the Ahlrichs group giving 3 functions per valence orbital and no polarization functions. The extra valence function improves the radial description while leaving the angular one unchanged. Like its double-zeta counterpart it is normally used with polarization functions added. (UNVERIFIED)

A type of quantum mechanics basis set consisting of periodic sine and cosine functions (waves) defined by their direction and wavelength. Plane waves are particularly well-suited for calculations on periodic systems like crystals or surfaces, often used in conjunction with Density Functional Theory and pseudopotentials. Their systematic improvability by increasing the number of waves (controlled by an energy cutoff) is a key advantage in solid-state simulations. (UNVERIFIED)

A method that represents electronic wavefunctions or densities as values on a grid of points in ordinary 3-dimensional space, rather than as coefficients of basis functions. Accuracy is then improved by making the grid finer, which is a single adjustable control. It parallelises well, because each point depends mostly on its neighbours. (UNVERIFIED)

A coordinate analysis that follows the steepest-descent path, in mass-weighted coordinates, downhill from a transition state to the reactant and product minima on the potential energy surface. The resulting path is the minimum energy path that connects reactants and products through that transition state. It shows which minima a transition state connects and describes the reaction at 0 kelvin, without thermal motion. (UNVERIFIED)

An analysis method that locates the highest point along the lowest-energy path joining reactant and product. That point is the transition state, and its height above the reactant is the reaction barrier. Finding it is what turns a computed path into a predicted rate. (UNVERIFIED)

A form of reaction analysis focused on characterizing the features of the potential energy surface (PES), which maps the system's energy as a function of its atomic coordinates. This analysis identifies critical points like energy minima (stable states), saddle points (transition states), and intersections between surfaces that govern molecular stability and reactivity. It helps visualize the energetic landscape explored during reactions or conformational changes.

A surface analysis that locates and characterises conical intersections, the molecular geometries at which 2 electronic potential energy surfaces of the same spin multiplicity have the same energy. At these points a molecule can pass very quickly from 1 electronic state to another without emitting light, which is central to photochemical reactions and to relaxation after light absorption. Their location and shape determine how efficient such transitions are. (UNVERIFIED)

A surface analysis that locates saddle points on a potential energy surface: stationary points, where all forces are zero, at which the energy is a maximum along 1 direction, the reaction path, and a minimum along all other directions. Such a point is the highest point on the lowest-energy path between reactant and product. Locating it identifies the transition state and gives the activation energy of the reaction. (UNVERIFIED)

A surface analysis that locates the minimum energy crossing point, the lowest-energy molecular geometry at which 2 potential energy surfaces of different spin states, such as a singlet and a triplet, have the same energy. Such points control the pathways of spin-forbidden reactions and of intersystem crossing, the change of a molecule from 1 spin state to another. Locating them helps to explain how a molecule changes spin state. (UNVERIFIED)

A form of reaction analysis aimed at identifying and characterizing the sequence of intermediate states and transition states that connect reactants to products, effectively mapping the reaction pathway. This can involve exploring multiple possible routes, using algorithms to find minimum energy paths, or analyzing trajectories from reaction dynamics simulations.

A pathway analysis that follows gradient extremals on a potential energy surface, which are curves along which the energy gradient points along an eigenvector of the matrix of second derivatives (the Hessian). Such curves pass through minima and saddle points, so following one uphill from a minimum can lead to a transition state. (UNVERIFIED)

A category for file formats designed to store numerical data in a specific structure that is easily parsed and read by graphing or plotting software (e.g., Grace, Gnuplot). These are structured data files typically containing columns of numbers and plotting directives.

A text-based data file format for the Grace/Xmgrace plotting program. It contains numerical data along with commands that specify the appearance of the graph, such as titles, labels, and colors. This format allows for the creation of complex, publication-quality plots. (UNVERIFIED)

A file format that represents a molecular system's topology after certain atoms, typically solvent or ions, have been removed. This format is created to simplify analysis by focusing only on the solute, while retaining the necessary parameter information for calculations. It is commonly used in post-processing steps like MM/PBSA free energy calculations. (UNVERIFIED)

A text data format in which cpptraj writes time-series results by default, as columns of numbers with the frame or time in the first column and the calculated values in the rest. It is space-delimited and carries no header structure beyond a comment line, so plotting and analysis programs read it directly. Files are commonly given the extension .dat. (UNVERIFIED)

comments: Typically with .dat extension, but could be using other file extension.

definition.val: A data file format designed to be used with the Gnuplot plotting program. It typically consists of columns of numerical data in a simple text-based layout that Gnuplot can easily parse and visualize. This format is widely used for generating scientific graphs and plots from raw data. (UNVERIFIED)

A file format associated with the XPLOR-NIH software, used for representing 3D grid data. It is a text-based format that defines a grid and the data values at each point, often used for electron density maps. This format is a common way to store volumetric data in crystallography and NMR. (UNVERIFIED)

A file format for representing data that is distributed over a three-dimensional grid. Originating from the XPLOR-NIH software, it is used to store volumetric data like electron density or potential maps. This format is used in structural biology to visualize grid-based properties around a molecule.

A file format for the OpenDX (Data Explorer) visualization program, used to represent 3D grid-based data. It stores scalar or vector data on a regular grid, making it suitable for visualizing properties like electrostatic potential or molecular density. This format is a common output for scientific programs that generate volumetric data. (UNVERIFIED)

A data format that stores the velocity of every atom of a system at each saved step of an AMBER simulation. It records velocities where a trajectory format records positions. It is needed for analyses such as velocity autocorrelation that cannot be done from coordinates alone. (UNVERIFIED)

A text data format in which AMBER records each exchange attempt of a replica exchange simulation, listing for every replica values such as its temperature, its potential energy, its condition before and after the attempt and the running success rate. The file is named rem.log by default. It is read to check how often exchanges succeed and how well the replicas mix. (UNVERIFIED)

A file format that holds the eigenvectors and eigenvalues produced by principal component analysis, normal mode analysis or quasiharmonic analysis in AMBER. The vectors come from diagonalising a covariance or mass-weighted covariance matrix, and are used in essential dynamics analysis of molecular simulations. There is no required extension: the file is usually called evecs.dat or evecs.out, and its layout is standardised so that AMBER tools such as cpptraj and ptraj can read and write it. (UNVERIFIED)

A text data format in which AMBER records the protonation state of each titratable residue at each Monte Carlo step of a constant pH simulation, with full records that also give the solvent pH, the time step and the time. The protonated fractions and pKa values of the residues are later calculated from it, for example with the cphstats program. It is an output of the simulation and is not read to start or restart one. (UNVERIFIED)

A computational procedure within structural analysis used to find the atomic coordinates corresponding to a stationary point, typically a local minimum, on the potential energy surface, representing a stable or equilibrium structure. Starting from an initial guess geometry, algorithms iteratively adjust atomic positions to minimize the energy and reduce the forces acting on the atoms until convergence criteria are met. The result is a stable structure near the starting geometry, which need not be the most stable structure overall. (UNVERIFIED)

A specific geometry optimization technique designed for large molecular systems that employs the Fragment Molecular Orbital (FMO) method. The FMO method divides the large system (like a protein or DNA segment) into smaller, manageable fragments, performs quantum mechanical calculations on fragments and fragment pairs, and combines the results to approximate the properties (energy, gradient) of the entire system. This fragmentation allows for efficient geometry optimization of very large biomolecules at a quantum mechanical level. (UNVERIFIED)

An energy analysis calculation that determines the potential energy of a molecular system for a single, fixed geometric arrangement of its atoms (a specific 'snapshot' or structure), without performing geometry optimization or simulating dynamics. This provides the energy value for that particular conformation according to the chosen theoretical method (e.g., force field or quantum mechanical level). It's often used to compare the relative energies of different pre-defined structures.

An energy analysis that computes potential energies with a high-level and computationally expensive treatment, such as coupled cluster theory or density functional theory with a large basis set. It is applied to a few chosen structures, typically optimised minima, transition states or representative conformations, rather than to a whole trajectory. The values serve as benchmarks for reaction barriers, binding energies and conformational stabilities obtained more cheaply. (UNVERIFIED)

An energy analysis technique designed to partition the total interaction energy between two or more interacting molecular fragments (e.g., in a complex) into physically meaningful components based on the underlying quantum mechanical or molecular mechanical framework. Common components include electrostatics, exchange-repulsion (Pauli repulsion), polarization (induction), and charge transfer (or dispersion in some schemes), providing insights into the nature of the forces driving the interaction. Different EDA schemes exist (e.g., Morokuma, SAPT, FMO-EDA). (UNVERIFIED)

A structural analysis technique that involves calculating the forces acting on each atom for a given molecular configuration. These forces represent the negative gradient of the potential energy and indicate the direction and magnitude of the tendency for atoms to move to lower the system's energy. Analyzing forces is crucial for geometry optimization (where forces are minimized), understanding structural strain, and driving molecular dynamics simulations. (UNVERIFIED)

A binary data format that stores 3-dimensional volumetric data on a regular grid, most often electron density from X-ray crystallography or a map from cryogenic electron microscopy. It is closely related to, and largely compatible with, the MRC format. It lets the shape of a protein or nucleic acid be seen and interpreted. (UNVERIFIED)

A binary data format in which cpptraj stores the pre-calculated pairwise distances between trajectory frames, so that a cluster analysis can reuse them instead of computing them again. It has no mandatory extension, but .cmatrix is the conventional one. (UNVERIFIED)

A type of analysis, often performed using data from simulations or specialized calculations complementary to MD, focused on determining the thermodynamic properties governing molecular systems. This includes calculating state functions like enthalpy, entropy, and particularly free energy, which dictate stability, equilibrium constants, and the spontaneity of molecular processes. Such analysis provides insights into the energetic driving forces behind biomolecular behavior. (UNVERIFIED)

A thermodynamics analysis that deals with how a system's properties change with temperature or involve heat exchange. This includes calculating quantities like heat capacity (how much energy is needed to raise the temperature), coefficients of thermal expansion, or enthalpy changes associated with specific processes. These properties are important for understanding temperature dependence and energy balance in molecular systems. (UNVERIFIED)

A specific type of thermal properties analysis focused on quantifying the heat absorbed or released during chemical reactions or phase transitions, often involving the calculation of enthalpies of formation, reaction enthalpies, or activation enthalpies. Typically employing quantum mechanical methods or specialized simulation setups, this analysis provides fundamental data on the energetics of chemical transformations. It helps predict reaction feasibility and energy output/input. (UNVERIFIED)

A text data format used by AMBER to define molecular building blocks, giving for each its atoms, their types and charges, the bonds between them and its geometry, as either internal or Cartesian coordinates. It is a common way to introduce a residue that no standard library contains, and 1 file can hold many building blocks. Such files are usually written by tools such as antechamber rather than by hand. (UNVERIFIED)

A text data format used by AMBER to store a library of molecular building blocks, giving for each its atoms, their types and charges, its bonds, its coordinates and the atoms through which it joins its neighbours. A single file can hold many building blocks, and also parameter sets. The standard residue libraries of AMBER are distributed in it, usually with the extension .lib or .off. (UNVERIFIED)

comments: AMBER lib format

definition.val: A thermodynamics analysis method that computes the free energy of a system, or more often the free energy difference between 2 states such as bound and unbound or folded and unfolded. Free energy combines energy and disorder, so it, rather than energy alone, decides which state a process settles into. Obtaining it usually needs enhanced sampling, because the states of interest are separated by barriers. (UNVERIFIED)

A specific computational task within a free energy calculation framework that uses the Fragment Molecular Orbital (FMO) method to determine the energy and properties of a molecule in its unbound ('free') state. This is often required when calculating binding free energies, where the energy of the isolated components serves as a reference point (G free). Employing FMO makes such quantum mechanical calculations feasible for the large molecules often involved in biomolecular binding events. (UNVERIFIED)

A free energy analysis method that computes the solvation free energy from a 3D reference interaction site model (3D-RISM) calculation using the Gaussian fluctuation expression. This expression is not tied to a particular closure, the approximate relation used to solve the integral equations, and is used in place of the closure's own formula. It has been shown to improve absolute solvation free energies for both polar and non-polar solutes, but not necessarily relative ones. (UNVERIFIED)

A free energy analysis method that corrects the solvation free energy computed by the 3D reference interaction site model (3D-RISM), which tends to overestimate its non-polar part, with a pressure correction based on the partial molar volume of the solute. Unlike the universal correction, it has no fitted parameters. (UNVERIFIED)

A free energy analysis method that corrects the solvation free energy computed by the 3D reference interaction site model (3D-RISM) with a term based on the partial molar volume of the solute, using parameters fitted for the particular solvent model. It counters the tendency of 3D-RISM to overestimate the non-polar part of the solvation free energy, and has been used almost only for water at ambient conditions. (UNVERIFIED)

A semi-empirical quantum method derived from density functional theory by expanding its energy about a reference density and tabulating the resulting integrals in advance. Tabulating them removes almost all the cost while keeping a quantum description. It is 2 to 3 orders of magnitude faster than the theory it comes from. (UNVERIFIED)

A density-functional based tight-binding method that solves for the atomic charges self-consistently, so each atom's charge responds to the others rather than being fixed. Adding that step corrects the description of polar and charged systems, which the non-self-consistent form handles badly. (UNVERIFIED)

A tight binding method that carries the expansion of the energy one order further than the self-consistent charge form, adding a term for how an atom's response to charge itself changes with charge. That term corrects the description of charged and hydrogen-bonded systems, which the lower order handles poorly. It is the form recommended for biomolecular work. (UNVERIFIED)

An interaction that cannot be described correctly without quantum mechanics, because it depends on the wave nature of electrons or on energy taking discrete values. Bond formation, charge transfer and dispersion are all of this kind. A classical force field represents their effects approximately with fitted terms rather than describing them. (UNVERIFIED)

A quantum mechanical interaction representing the coupling between the magnetic moment associated with the spin of an electron and the magnetic moment of a nearby atomic nucleus. This interaction leads to small shifts and splittings ('hyperfine structure') in atomic and molecular energy levels, which are observable in high-resolution spectroscopy, particularly Electron Paramagnetic Resonance (EPR) for species with unpaired electrons, and also in NMR. It provides valuable information about the electron distribution (spin density) near the nucleus and thus molecular structure. (UNVERIFIED)

A relativistic quantum mechanical interaction between a particle's intrinsic spin angular momentum and its orbital angular momentum (due to its motion, e.g., an electron orbiting a nucleus). This coupling mixes electronic states and becomes increasingly significant for electrons in atoms with high atomic number (heavy atoms). Spin-orbit coupling influences electronic energy levels, causes splitting of spectral lines (fine structure), and facilitates transitions between states of different spin multiplicity (e.g., intersystem crossing in photochemistry, important for phosphorescence). (UNVERIFIED)

A physical effect arising from the intrinsic angular momentum carried by electrons and atomic nuclei. Spin gives each particle a magnetic moment, and the interactions of these moments with magnetic fields, with each other and with orbital motion produce magnetic resonance signals and the fine and hyperfine structure of spectra. A calculation that ignores spin cannot reproduce them. (UNVERIFIED)

A quantum mechanical method that obtains the energy and other properties of a system from its electron density rather than from the many-electron wavefunction. The density depends on 3 spatial coordinates however many electrons there are, which is what makes the method affordable for large systems. Its accuracy rests on the approximate functional chosen to relate density to energy. (UNVERIFIED)

A QM/MM scheme in which the partial charges of the classical region enter the quantum calculation directly, so the quantum region's electron distribution responds to its surroundings. That response is what captures how a protein environment alters the chemistry inside an active site. It costs more than the mechanical scheme and is markedly more accurate. (UNVERIFIED)

An Ewald summation method for a periodic system in which part is described quantum mechanically and the rest by a force field. It must handle 3 kinds of interaction: within the quantum region, within the classical region, and between them. Getting the third right is what distinguishes it, because the 2 descriptions represent charge differently. (UNVERIFIED)

A QM/MM method using more than 2 levels of description, such as an expensive quantum method for a reacting group, a cheaper quantum method around it, and a force field beyond that. Each boundary must be handled separately, so the arrangement is more delicate than a 2-level one. It is used where the reacting region is small but its immediate surroundings still need quantum treatment. (UNVERIFIED)

A QM/MM method in which solvent molecules change gradually between quantum and classical treatment as they cross a transition shell around the quantum region, with their partial classical character set by their distance from its centre. The energy is a weighted average over the ways of assigning the molecules in the shell to the quantum or the classical region, with weights that change smoothly as the molecules move. This avoids the sudden jumps in force that would occur if a molecule switched abruptly between the 2 descriptions. (UNVERIFIED)

A QM/MM method in which the quantum region is redefined by distance as the simulation runs, and the forces on its atoms come from a larger quantum calculation that also includes a surrounding buffer region. The buffer keeps the forces on the quantum atoms from being distorted by the nearby boundary, while the atoms outside take their forces from a second calculation with a smaller quantum region. Because the forces do not come from a single energy function, energy is not conserved and a thermostat is used to hold the temperature. (UNVERIFIED)

A structural analysis method that computes a field, most often the electrostatic potential, and displays it on the surface of a molecule. Colouring the surface by potential shows at a glance which regions would attract a positive or a negative partner. It is how electrostatic complementarity between 2 binding partners is judged. (UNVERIFIED)

An analysis method that computes the electrostatic potential a molecule's charge distribution produces at points around it. Mapped onto the molecular surface, it shows where an approaching charge would be attracted or repelled. It is how a binding site is judged to be electrostatically complementary to a ligand. (UNVERIFIED)

An analysis method that calculates the vibrational frequencies and normal modes (patterns of atomic motion) of a molecule at a stationary point on its potential energy surface, such as an energy minimum or a transition state. The frequencies can be compared with measured vibrational spectra, such as infrared or Raman spectra, to check a structure or a force field. They also show what kind of stationary point was found: a minimum has only real frequencies, and a transition state has exactly 1 imaginary frequency. (UNVERIFIED)

A refinement within frequency analysis that goes beyond the standard harmonic approximation (which assumes vibrations occur in a perfectly parabolic potential well) to account for the true, anharmonic shape of the potential energy surface. Calculating these corrections yields more accurate vibrational frequencies that better match experimental observations, particularly for large-amplitude motions or systems with significant vibrational coupling. This improves the quantitative interpretation of vibrational spectra and thermodynamic properties derived from frequencies. (UNVERIFIED)

A simulation method in which the forces at each step come from a fast approximate quantum mechanical calculation, solved fully at each new geometry. Being quantum, it can describe bonds being made and broken, which a force field cannot. Being approximate, it is fast enough to run for a useful length of time. (UNVERIFIED)

A simulation method that treats the region where bonds form and break with the ReaxFF reactive force field and the rest of the system with a conventional AMBER force field. The reactive force field costs far more, so confining it to a small region makes a large system affordable. It works in a similar way to QM/MM, with a reactive force field in place of quantum mechanics. (UNVERIFIED)

A force field that represents how a molecule's charge distribution is distorted by the electric field around it, rather than fixing the charges in advance. It matters where the environment changes markedly, as when a ligand moves from water into a protein interior. It costs several times more, because the induced response must be solved for at every step. (UNVERIFIED)

A polarizable force field in which each atom carries a multipole expansion built from Gaussian-shaped charge distributions, and responds to the field around it. Using distributed shapes rather than points lets the model describe how charge density overlaps between close atoms. It targets the short-range region where point-charge models are least reliable. (UNVERIFIED)

A correction added to a quantum chemistry calculation to supply the weak long-range attraction that most density functionals omit. The functionals fail here because the attraction arises from correlated fluctuations they do not describe. The correction is a fitted term depending on the atoms and their separation, and it is what makes density functional theory usable for stacking and binding. (UNVERIFIED)

A Gaussian-shaped constraint simulation is a type of restrained simulation where the artificial potential used to guide the system has the mathematical form of a Gaussian function. This provides a smooth, harmonic-like restraint near the target value but becomes weaker further away.

A force field parameterization method that obtains the Lennard-Jones parameters between 2 different atom types from those of each type alone, taking the arithmetic mean of their sizes and the geometric mean of their well depths. Without such a rule every pair of atom types would need its own fitted parameters. The rule is a convenience rather than physics, which is why some pairs need an explicit override. (UNVERIFIED)

A protocol for deriving atomic charges in which the electrostatic potential is computed at the Hartree-Fock level with the 6-31G* basis set, then point charges are fitted to it with a restraint pulling buried charges towards zero. That combination is not the most accurate available; it is used because it systematically overestimates polarity by about the amount a simulation in fixed-charge water requires. It is the convention behind many AMBER force fields, including the general AMBER force fields, so charges for a new molecule used with them are usually derived the same way. (UNVERIFIED)

A coarse-grained force field for proteins and nucleic acids whose beads are chosen to preserve the chemical character and the directionality of interactions such as hydrogen bonds. It keeps more chemical detail than a purely shape-based mapping, at a higher cost. It can be combined with explicit coarse-grained water. (UNVERIFIED)

A force field parameterization method that derives parameters for a metal ion and its coordination site by fitting them to reproduce experimental data for a set of known metal complexes, such as crystal structures, vibrational frequencies or binding energies. Metal ions often need this treatment because general-purpose parameterization methods do not capture their electronic structure and bonding well. (UNVERIFIED)

A free energy analysis method that estimates binding free energy using explicit water molecules near the solute and a continuum model for the bulk. It keeps the specific water-mediated contacts that a continuum model cannot represent, while avoiding the cost of explicit solvent everywhere. The energies are then combined in the usual molecular mechanics Poisson-Boltzmann surface area way. (UNVERIFIED)

A free energy analysis method that recomputes the electrostatic (decharging) step of an alchemical binding free energy calculation with a Poisson-Boltzmann continuum model, combining the energies of the snapshots with the Bennett acceptance ratio. Raising the solute dielectric constant in the continuum model lets it include the screening by electronic polarization that a standard non-polarizable force field leaves out. The atomic radii are first calibrated so that the continuum model reproduces the explicit-solvent results. (UNVERIFIED)

Kinetic map analysis is a method used to visualize the network of transitions between different conformational states that a molecule visits during a simulation. It represents the molecular states as nodes and the transitions between them as connections, often colored or weighted by their probability or rate. This provides a clear and intuitive map of the dominant pathways for conformational change, helping to understand the mechanism and timescales of processes like ligand binding or protein folding.

Commute map analysis is a method used to identify how different parts of a molecule are dynamically connected, even if they are far apart. It transforms complex molecular coordinates into a mathematical space where the Euclidean distance between points directly corresponds to the commute time (the mean time it takes for a molecule to transition between two conformations and back). This analysis helps to uncover long-range communication networks within a protein that are essential for its function, such as in allosteric regulation.

A thermodynamics analysis method that splits the total entropy change of a process into separate contributions. The split may be by kind of motion, into translational, rotational and vibrational parts, or by component, into solute and solvent. It shows which source of disorder drives a process, for example whether binding is favoured by the release of ordered water. (UNVERIFIED)

nodes.lbl: molecular reconstruction from distribution functions analysis

definition.val: An advanced analysis method that attempts to generate a 3-dimensional model of a molecule or a molecular complex using statistical information about its structure. It takes one or more distribution functions, such as the pairwise distances between atoms obtained from a simulation or experiment, and uses an optimization algorithm to find a 3D structure that is consistent with those distributions. This technique can be used to build structural models from sparse or low-resolution data. (UNVERIFIED)

A structural analysis method that separates the change in shape of a group of atoms between 2 conformations into a pure rotation and an internal deformation. It does this by factorising the matrix that maps one set of coordinates onto the other. It answers whether a domain has turned as a rigid body or genuinely changed shape. (UNVERIFIED)

A simulation method that includes quantum behaviour of the atomic nuclei themselves, by replacing each nucleus with a ring of connected copies. The spread of the ring represents the uncertainty in the particle's position, which is large for light atoms. It matters for hydrogen, where treating the nucleus as a point misplaces bond lengths and reaction barriers. (UNVERIFIED)

Replica-exchange free energy perturbation is an enhanced sampling method that combines replica-exchange with an alchemical free energy calculation. It runs multiple simulations in parallel, each at a different intermediate state (lambda value) of the alchemical transformation, and periodically attempts to swap the lambda values between replicas.

A simulation method in which groups can gain or lose an electron during the run, coupled to a chosen electrode potential. It is the redox counterpart of constant pH simulation and uses the same machinery. It is used for proteins whose function involves moving electrons, where the oxidation state is not fixed in advance. (UNVERIFIED)

X-ray refinement is the computational process of building and optimizing an atomic model of a molecule to fit the experimental data from an X-ray crystallography experiment. It is an iterative procedure where the atomic coordinates are adjusted to best match the calculated electron density map, while simultaneously ensuring that the model has realistic chemical geometry, such as proper bond lengths and angles. This process is the final and crucial step in determining a high-resolution crystal structure.

A structural analysis method that divides the simulation box into a regular 3-dimensional grid of cells and counts how often atoms of a chosen type fall in each cell across a trajectory. The counts give the average spatial density of those atoms. It is the usual way to map where water or ions gather around a solute. (UNVERIFIED)

A fundamental trajectory post-processing step used to correct the visual representation of molecules in a periodic system. When a molecule crosses a periodic boundary, it can appear 'broken' or jump across the box in the raw output. This procedure translates the atomic coordinates back into the primary simulation box, implicitly fixing broken 'image bonds' to ensure target molecules remain whole and centered. This is a mandatory prerequisite for correct visualization and accurate calculation of some structural properties.

A trajectory processing method that separates the single combined trajectory written by a locally enhanced sampling run into 1 trajectory per copy of the duplicated region. Locally enhanced sampling simulates several copies of one part of a molecule at once, and their coordinates are interleaved in the output. Splitting them is required before each copy can be analysed or the copies averaged. (UNVERIFIED)

A modelling method that changes the atomic coordinates or the composition of a molecular structure, for example by adding or deleting atoms, rotating or translating molecules, or building new polymer chains. These operations are the basic tools for building, editing and preparing molecular models for simulation. (UNVERIFIED)

An ion randomization method is a procedure for placing ions in a simulation box by randomly swapping their positions with existing solvent molecules. This is often done after an initial, simpler placement to ensure the ions are well-distributed throughout the solvent. This method helps to create a more disordered and realistic initial distribution of ions, avoiding potential artifacts from placing them in a regular grid.

A system setup procedure that builds a larger system, called a supercell, by copying the original simulation unit cell along 1 or more directions. It is commonly used in materials science simulations to model bulk crystals or surfaces from a smaller repeating unit. It is the usual way to build a periodic system large enough to reduce artifacts caused by a small simulation box. (UNVERIFIED)

A modelling method that multiplies all the atomic coordinates of a system by a scaling factor, so that the whole system expands or contracts uniformly. It is used to adjust the density of a system, and some barostats control pressure by scaling the box and the coordinates within it in this way. (UNVERIFIED)

A system setup procedure that gives atoms their initial speeds and directions at the start of a molecular dynamics simulation. The velocities are usually drawn at random from the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution for the chosen starting temperature. This starts the thermal motion of the system before equilibration. (UNVERIFIED)

An analysis method that computes a value at every point of a 3-dimensional grid covering a region of a simulation. The values may be how often solvent is found at each point, or the electrostatic potential there. The result is a map that can be viewed as a surface or a cloud rather than read as a number. (UNVERIFIED)

A procedure that removes a subset of atoms, typically solvent and ions, from a molecular topology file. It is most often used after a simulation to make smaller topology files for the receptor, the ligand and their complex, which MM/PBSA and MM/GBSA free energy calculations need. It is an essential step in preparing files for these end-point free energy methods. (UNVERIFIED)

A force field parameterization method that modifies or adds to an existing set of force field parameters without changing the main parameter files. It is usually done by reading a small extra file of new or revised parameters, which override the default values loaded from the force field library. It is the usual way to add parameters for a non-standard ligand or to apply a specific correction. (UNVERIFIED)

An average structure calculation is a structural analysis method that computes the average coordinates of all atoms over a simulation trajectory. This provides a single, representative structure that reflects the central conformation of the system during the simulation. It is important to note that this average structure may not be a physically realistic conformation itself, especially if the molecule is highly flexible.

Coordinate centering is a structural analysis method, often performed as a pre-processing step, that translates the coordinates of a molecular system so that its center of mass is at the origin of the coordinate system. This is a standard procedure to ensure that the molecule remains in the center of the simulation box for easier analysis and visualization.

An analysis method that identifies, in each frame of a trajectory, the solvent molecules nearest to a chosen solute or region. It is used to reduce a trajectory to the solute plus a fixed number of nearest solvent molecules, and to record which solvent molecules were nearest in each frame, for example to estimate how long a water stays in contact. It answers which solvent molecules are nearest, rather than how much solvent there is. (UNVERIFIED)

Trajectory frame filtering is a data processing step where a simulation trajectory is selectively reduced in size by removing certain frames based on a specific criterion. This could involve discarding an initial equilibration period or keeping only those frames where a molecule adopts a particular shape. This filtering is a common procedure used to focus an analysis on a specific time period or a subset of conformations that are most relevant to the scientific question.

A type of analysis method focused on examining the electronic properties of a molecule derived from its quantum mechanical description, such as the wavefunction or electron density. This includes analyzing the distribution of electrons (charge, spin density), the nature of molecular orbitals, chemical bonding characteristics, and electronic response properties like polarizability. It provides fundamental insights into chemical reactivity, spectroscopy, and intermolecular forces. (UNVERIFIED)

An electronic structure analysis that assigns partial charges to the individual atoms of a molecule, either by dividing up its electron density or by fitting charges to its electrostatic potential. Many schemes exist, such as Mulliken, Löwdin, Hirshfeld, natural population analysis and electrostatic potential fitting, and they can give quite different values for the same molecule. The charges are used to parameterize classical force fields and to interpret polarity and reactivity. (UNVERIFIED)

An electronic structure analysis method that directly calculates molecular properties as expectation values using the computed quantum mechanical wavefunction or density matrix. This can include properties like dipole and multipole moments, electron density at specific points (e.g., bond critical points in QTAIM), spin densities, or electric field gradients, providing detailed information about the molecule's electronic state and interactions. It leverages the full information contained within the wavefunction. (UNVERIFIED)

A form of electronic structure analysis that investigates the molecular orbitals (MOs) of a system, which represent the energy levels and spatial distributions of electrons within the molecule based on quantum mechanics. Common analyses include visualizing frontier orbitals (HOMO, LUMO), examining orbital compositions (e.g., atomic orbital contributions), analyzing orbital energies for insights into ionization potential or electron affinity, and relating MOs to chemical bonding, reactivity, and electronic transitions. It helps rationalize chemical behavior based on electron distribution in orbitals. (UNVERIFIED)

An electronic structure analysis technique that examines how the electron distribution of a molecule is distorted (polarized) in response to an external electric field or the field generated by nearby molecules. This involves calculating the induced dipole moment and the polarizability tensor, which quantify the molecule's susceptibility to charge redistribution. Understanding polarization is crucial for accurately describing intermolecular interactions, solvation effects, and responses to electromagnetic fields. (UNVERIFIED)

A system setup procedure that puts the atoms of a system into the order that simulation and analysis programs expect, for example with the atoms of each molecule numbered consecutively, or matching the order in a topology file. Atoms in the wrong order are a common source of errors when preparing a system for simulation. Fixing the order ensures that coordinates and parameters are matched correctly for every atom. (UNVERIFIED)

OBSOLETE. Image bond fixing is a post-processing step applied to simulation trajectories to correct the visual representation of molecules in a periodic system. When a molecule crosses a periodic boundary, it can appear "broken" in the raw output, with parts of it on opposite sides of the simulation box. This procedure identifies such cases and translates the atomic coordinates to make the molecule appear whole, which is essential for correct visualization and many types of analysis.

comments: Retired as redundant with its former parent 'periodic boundary imaging' (MOLSIM:000659), of which it was the only child. Bond fixing is an implicit outcome of imaging, and that term's definition now states so. Reported and approved by the term verifier in GitHub issue #45.

definition.val: An atom selection method is the procedure or syntax used to specify a particular group of atoms within a molecular system for an analysis or modification. This is typically done using a text-based selection language that allows users to choose atoms based on properties like name, residue, or position.

A polarizable force field that represents charge as smeared-out Gaussian distributions rather than as points, with both permanent and induced multipole terms. Smearing the charge removes the artificial divergence that point charges give at very short range. It is markedly more accurate and more expensive than a point-charge treatment. (UNVERIFIED)

Amber ff19SB is a modern and widely used set of rules, or a force field, for accurately simulating the structure and movement of proteins. The AMBER ff19SB protein force field is a recent refinement of the ff14SB lineage, incorporating updated quantum mechanical calculations for backbone dihedral angle parameters to improve the description of protein secondary structure balance. It is considered a state-of-the-art choice for all-atom protein simulations, offering high fidelity for studying protein folding, dynamics, and interactions.

A structural analysis method that measures the direction of vectors defined within a molecule, such as a bond vector or the normal to a plane, and how those directions change. It covers both the orientation of a single vector over time and the angle between 2 of them. It is how the orientation and rotational behaviour of specific groups is quantified. (UNVERIFIED)

An atom remapping method is a procedure used to systematically change the properties of atoms in a topology file, such as their atom types or charges. This is often required when converting a system from one force field to another or when applying specific corrections. For experts, this is an advanced manipulation used in force field development or for setting up non-standard simulations. (UNVERIFIED)

A quantum chemistry method that solves the electronic Schrödinger equation using only fundamental physical constants and the identities of the atoms, with no parameters fitted to experiment. Hartree-Fock and the correlated methods built on it, such as Møller-Plesset perturbation theory and coupled cluster, belong here. The absence of fitted parameters is what lets accuracy be improved systematically rather than by re-tuning. (UNVERIFIED)

A PDB ID is the unique four-character alphanumeric code (e.g., '1TIM', '6M0J') where the first character is always numeric. Every PDB id is assigned to a experimentally determined biomolecular structure deposited in the Protein Data Bank (PDB). This identifier serves to reference and retrieve PDB data. However these identifiers are now deprecated in favor of the Extended PDB ID.

A UniProt ID, more formally known as a UniProt Accession Number (e.g., 'P00761', 'Q8WZ42'), is the stable and unique identifier assigned to a protein sequence record in the UniProt Knowledgebase (UniProtKB). This ID provides access to comprehensive information about a protein, including its sequence, function, annotations, and cross-references to other databases. It serves as a primary key for protein sequence and functional data.

Any origin from which data used in a biomolecular study is obtained, whether a database, a document, a laboratory record or a person. It covers where a structure, a parameter or a measurement came from. Recording it is what lets a claim in a dataset be traced back and checked. (UNVERIFIED)

comments: How this branch is built. The classes here are KINDS of data source, for example protein structural database, pathway database, or simulation data repository. Each real, named resource is then added as an individual of one of those classes, not as a class of its own. PDB, UniProt, ChEMBL, Reactome, MoDEL and AlphaFold DB are individuals in this way. This is on purpose: a named database is one single thing in the world, not a kind of thing, so it fits better as an individual. Please keep this pattern, and do not turn these individuals into classes as a tidy-up. Two things to know. First, individuals are not copied into the OBO-format file (see the release-format note in the ontology header). Second, most OBO ontologies use classes for everything, so a reviewer may ask why we did this.

definition.val: A data source that is an organized, usually electronic, collection of structured data that can be searched, retrieved and updated. In the biomolecular sciences such collections hold molecular structures, sequences, experimental results and simulation trajectories. They serve as shared resources for the research community. (UNVERIFIED)

A type of database that archives original data directly submitted by researchers or generated through primary experimental efforts. These databases are foundational resources, providing the raw material (e.g., atomic coordinates, gene sequences) upon which further analysis and knowledge discovery are built. Examples include repositories for protein structures or DNA sequences.

A primary database specializing in the storage and dissemination of three-dimensional (3D) atomic coordinate data for biological macromolecules like proteins and nucleic acids. These databases are essential for understanding molecular function, designing drugs, and providing starting points for simulations. The Protein Data Bank (PDB) is a prime example.

A structural database specifically focused on archiving and distributing 3D atomic coordinates and associated experimental data for proteins and their complexes. These resources are critical for researchers studying protein architecture, function, and interactions. The PDB is the foremost example in this category. (UNVERIFIED)

A structural database dedicated to collecting and providing 3D atomic coordinates and related information for nucleic acids such as DNA and RNA, including their various forms and complexes. These databases support research into gene regulation, RNA function, and nucleic acid-drug interactions. The Nucleic Acid Database (NDB) is a key example.

A structural database that archives 3D maps and associated metadata derived from electron microscopy experiments, particularly cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), which is used to determine the structure of large biomolecular assemblies. It complements X-ray crystallography and NMR databases by providing structural information for systems often intractable by other methods. The Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB) is the main repository. (UNVERIFIED)

A primary database that stores and organizes linear sequences of amino acids (for proteins) or nucleotides (for DNA/RNA). These databases are fundamental for comparative genomics, evolutionary studies, identifying functional motifs, and linking sequence to structure and function. Examples include GenBank for nucleic acids and UniProtKB for protein sequences.

A sequence database specifically focused on collecting, annotating, and distributing protein amino acid sequences and associated functional information. These resources are vital for understanding protein evolution, function, and for identifying proteins from experimental data. UniProtKB is a comprehensive example.

A sequence database dedicated to archiving and providing access to DNA and RNA nucleotide sequences from various organisms, including genes, genomes, and transcripts. These databases are cornerstones of genomics and molecular biology research. GenBank, ENA, and DDBJ are major international examples.

A primary database that curates information about small chemical compounds, including their structures, properties, and biological activities. These resources are crucial for drug discovery, cheminformatics, and understanding ligand-protein interactions. PubChem and ChEBI are prominent examples. (UNVERIFIED)

A small molecule database primarily focused on storing and providing access to 2D and 3D chemical structures, identifiers, and physicochemical properties of diverse chemical compounds. These are fundamental for chemical information retrieval and computational chemistry. PubChem Compound and ZINC are key examples. (UNVERIFIED)

A small molecule database specifically curating information about drugs, including their chemical properties, pharmacological actions, targets, and therapeutic uses. These resources are vital for pharmacology, drug development, and clinical research. DrugBank is a well-known example. (UNVERIFIED)

A primary database that archives experimental data obtained from various spectroscopic techniques, such as Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR), mass spectrometry, or infrared spectroscopy, applied to biological molecules. These databases allow for the reanalysis of raw or processed spectral data and aid in structural and functional characterization. The Biological Magnetic Resonance Data Bank (BMRB) is an example for NMR data.

A spectroscopic database specifically designed to store, organize, and disseminate experimental data from Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) studies of biomolecules. This includes raw spectral data, assigned chemical shifts, coupling constants, and derived structural constraints, complementing 3D coordinate depositions. The BMRB is the principal repository.

A type of database that derives its content from analyzing, curating, or integrating information from one or more primary databases, often providing value-added annotations or classifications. These databases help researchers interpret primary data by, for example, grouping proteins into families or classifying structures. Pfam (protein families) and SCOP (structural classification) are examples.

A secondary database that classifies proteins into families and identifies conserved domains based on sequence similarity, structural features, or functional annotations. These resources help predict protein function and understand evolutionary relationships. Examples include Pfam, InterPro, and SMART. (UNVERIFIED)

A secondary database that organizes known protein structures into a hierarchical classification based on their evolutionary relationships and structural similarities, such as folds and superfamilies. These classifications provide insights into protein architecture and evolution. SCOP and CATH are prominent examples. (UNVERIFIED)

Databases that curate and represent information about biological pathways, such as metabolic, signaling, or regulatory networks, detailing the interactions between molecules. These resources help understand complex biological processes and the roles of individual components. KEGG and Reactome are widely used examples.

A secondary database that collects and organizes experimental data on the biological activity of chemical compounds, particularly their interactions with protein targets, such as binding affinities and inhibition constants. These are crucial for drug discovery and chemical biology research. ChEMBL and BindingDB are key examples. (UNVERIFIED)

A specialized type of database designed to store complex, structured, and unstructured information, often integrating data from multiple sources and using ontologies or controlled vocabularies to represent knowledge explicitly. Knowledge bases aim to provide a comprehensive understanding of specific biological entities or systems, facilitating inference and discovery. UniProtKB is a prime example in the protein domain. (UNVERIFIED)

A type of database primarily focused on the storage, preservation, and dissemination of datasets, often associated with specific types of studies, computational outputs, or large-scale projects. Repositories ensure data accessibility and reusability for the scientific community. Examples include those for simulation trajectories or predicted protein structures.

A repository specifically designed to store, share, and allow re-analysis of data generated from biomolecular simulations, such as molecular dynamics trajectories and analysis results. These resources promote reproducibility and enable new discoveries from existing simulation data. MDposit and MDrepo are examples.

A repository that archives and provides access to computationally predicted three-dimensional structures of proteins, often generated by large-scale initiatives or community efforts. These resources offer structural hypotheses for proteins lacking experimental structures. The AlphaFold DB is a prominent example.

A repository dedicated to storing and disseminating datasets from metabolomics experiments, which involve the comprehensive study of small molecules (metabolites) within cells, tissues, or organisms. These resources support systems biology and biomarker discovery. MetaboLights is an example. (UNVERIFIED)

A database that indexes and provides access to bibliographic information from scientific journals, conference proceedings, and other scholarly publications. These are essential tools for researchers to find relevant scientific articles and stay updated on research findings. PubMed and Scopus are widely used examples.

A web server that runs a computation on data the user supplies, rather than returning records it already holds. The user uploads a structure, the server computes something from it, and the result comes back. That is what separates it from a database server, which retrieves rather than computes. (UNVERIFIED)

A data format that holds the direct output of a prediction program, such as a predicted structure, a predicted binding site, or a predicted functional annotation. It covers the result as the program wrote it, before any curation or deposition into a public repository. A coordinate file from a local homology modelling run is an example. (UNVERIFIED)

A visualization and analysis program for molecular structures, built to handle very large data such as cryogenic electron microscopy maps and whole virus capsids. It is the successor to Chimera, rewritten for modern graphics hardware. Its speed on large structures is what distinguishes it. (UNVERIFIED)

OBSOLETE. Refers to data obtained directly from a specific laboratory experiment. This can include data reported in a scientific publication for which no separate database entry exists, or unpublished results from ongoing research.

Only the first is a kind of source, so a private unpublished PDB entry belonged under all 3. The 2 facets are now recorded by the MOLSIM:002274 data source descriptor branch instead. Raised in review by orcid:0000-0002-2294-5393; neither this term nor its former children had a single instance.

definition.val: OBSOLETE. A published research article, review, book chapter, or conference proceeding that serves as the source of specific data, findings, or methodologies. When data is cited directly from a publication without an associated database entry, the publication itself is considered the data source. This is common for specific measurements or observations not typically archived elsewhere.

The term duplicated a concept IAO already models, and its own definition enumerated exactly IAO's document types. Part of the data source refactor asked for in review by orcid:0000-0002-2294-5393, which removed the facets experimental and private from the hierarchy and left it sorting sources by what kind of resource they are.

definition.val: OBSOLETE. Data or findings originating from a laboratory experiment that have not yet been published or formally disseminated to the public or scientific community. This category covers preliminary results, ongoing research data, or information shared through informal channels before formal publication or deposition.

definition.val: OBSOLETE. A data source that is not publicly accessible, such as an internal database maintained by a private company or research institution, or data held privately by an individual researcher. This category is important for acknowledging data origins that cannot be independently verified or accessed by the wider community.

definition.val: OBSOLETE. A database developed and maintained within a specific organization (e.g., a pharmaceutical company, a research institute) for its internal use, not generally accessible to the public. These often contain proprietary data, specialized collections, or information tailored to the organization's specific research needs.

Only the first is a kind of source, so a private unpublished PDB entry belonged under all 3. The 2 facets are now recorded by the MOLSIM:002274 data source descriptor branch instead. Raised in review by orcid:0000-0002-2294-5393; neither this term nor its former children had a single instance. This one has a successor: an in house database is a database, so MOLSIM:000689 database source replaces it.

definition.val: Information or data obtained directly from an individual researcher or expert through informal means such as email, conversation, or unpublished notes, rather than through a formal publication or public database. While sometimes necessary, such sources are typically less verifiable and are often used for supplementary or preliminary information.

A type of force field classified by the level of structural detail, or resolution, used to represent the system's components. This classification distinguishes between models that represent every atom explicitly versus those that group atoms into larger pseudo-atoms or beads. The resolution impacts the balance between computational efficiency and physical accuracy. (UNVERIFIED)

A force field in which groups of atoms are represented by single interaction sites rather than individually. Cutting the number of particles cuts the cost of every step and allows a longer timestep, so much larger systems and much longer times become reachable. What is lost is any detail below the size of a site. (UNVERIFIED)

A force field that explicitly includes parameters for every atom in the simulated system, including hydrogen atoms. This approach provides a high level of detail and aims for greater physical realism compared to coarse-grained models. All-atom simulations are generally more computationally intensive due to the larger number of particles.

A force field for carbohydrates (glycans) in the AMBER family, developed by the GLYCAM group, that provides parameters for common monosaccharides and the glycosidic linkages between them. It is used to study oligosaccharides and the carbohydrate portions of glycoproteins and glycolipids. It is designed to be compatible with AMBER protein and lipid force fields. (UNVERIFIED)

A force field for carbohydrates in the AMBER family, a variant of GLYCAM06, in which extra points representing lone pairs are placed on the oxygen atoms so that it can be used with the 5-site TIP5P water model. The distance of each extra point from its oxygen was chosen to best reproduce the quantum electrostatic potential, and the fit leaves almost no charge on the oxygen nucleus itself. The extra points make hydrogen bonding more directional, which matters for sugars, whose behaviour depends strongly on hydrogen bonds. (UNVERIFIED)

A set of ion parameters for the AMOEBA polarizable force field as distributed with the AMBER suite. Because AMOEBA represents charge with atomic multipoles and explicit induced dipoles rather than fixed point charges, ions need parameters fitted for that form. Parameters from a fixed-charge force field cannot be used with it. (UNVERIFIED)

A specific protein force field parameter set from the AMBER family, representing one of the earlier polarizable force fields. Unlike fixed-charge force fields (like ff99SB), ff02 includes electronic polarizability explicitly, aiming for a more accurate description of electrostatics but at a higher computational cost. Its adoption was less widespread than fixed-charge counterparts.

A force field from the AMBER family, introduced in 2010, that combines the ff99SB protein parameters with the bsc0 correction for DNA and the chi OL3 correction for RNA. It brought together the recommended protein and nucleic acid parameters of that time in 1 set. It was later superseded by ff12SB and ff14SB for proteins and by newer nucleic acid force fields. (UNVERIFIED)

A specific protein force field parameter set from the AMBER family, representing an update released around 2012. Compared to ff99SB, ff12SB refined quantum-chemical (QM) based side-chain dihedral parameters and updated the backbone φ rotational profile to compensate for biases seen in earlier version. It served as an intermediate improvement before the release of ff14SB.

An all-atom force field for proteins and nucleic acids from the AMBER family, described by Cornell and co-workers in 1995, whose partial charges were fitted to quantum electrostatic potentials with the RESP method. Later AMBER sets such as ff96, ff99 and ff99SB revised its parameters, mainly the backbone torsion terms. It gives a poor balance between helical and extended protein structures and is now obsolete. (UNVERIFIED)

A protein force field in the AMBER family that revises the ff94 parameters, mainly the backbone torsion terms, to reduce the preference of ff94 for helical structure. It has been replaced by later AMBER protein force fields. (UNVERIFIED)

A force field for proteins and nucleic acids in the AMBER family, described by Wang, Cieplak and Kollman in 2000, that revises many torsion and other bonded parameters of ff94 against quantum calculations on small model molecules. It is the base of most later AMBER force fields, such as ff99SB for proteins and the bsc0 and OL corrections for nucleic acids. Its backbone torsions still gave a poor balance between helical and extended protein structure, which ff99SB corrected. (UNVERIFIED)

A protein force field, introduced by Sorin and Pande in 2005, that changes the backbone phi torsion terms of AMBER ff99 to reduce its overly strong preference for helical structure. It was developed to study how helical peptides fold, and it agreed better than ff99 with measured folding rates and stabilities. (UNVERIFIED)

A force field for nucleic acids, built on the AMBER ff99 parameter set with the alpha and gamma backbone dihedral terms refit by the Barcelona group. The refit removed the build-up of non-native gamma trans backbone geometries that made DNA simulations degrade on the 50 to 100 nanosecond timescale. It became the base of later AMBER DNA and RNA force fields, such as OL15 and OL3. (UNVERIFIED)

A protein force field in the AMBER family that refits the backbone torsion terms of ff99 against high-level quantum calculations on glycine and alanine tetrapeptides. It gives a much better balance between helical and extended structures and corrects the sampling of glycine. The SB in its name refers to Stony Brook, where it was developed, and it is the base of later variants such as ff99SB-ILDN and ff14SB. (UNVERIFIED)

A force field for proteins, built on the AMBER ff99SB parameter set with the side-chain torsion terms refit to high-level quantum calculations for isoleucine, leucine, aspartate and asparagine, whose 1-letter codes give the name. These 4 residues were chosen because their simulated rotamer populations differed most from Protein Data Bank statistics. The new terms agree considerably better with NMR measurements of side-chain conformations, and the rest of the parameter set is unchanged. (UNVERIFIED)

An all-atom force field parameter set from the CHARMM family, widely used for protein simulations, often paired with the CMAP (Cross-term energy Correction Map) correction for backbone torsions. Released before CHARMM27 and CHARMM36, it represented a standard for many years. Parameterization relied heavily on fitting to experimental data available at the time. (UNVERIFIED)

An earlier force field parameter set from the CHARMM family, notable for being a 'united-atom' force field for proteins. In this representation, nonpolar hydrogen atoms (e.g., on CH, CH2, CH3 groups) are implicitly included in the heavy atoms they are attached to, reducing the number of particles and computational cost compared to all-atom models.

An all-atom force field of the CHARMM family that combines the CHARMM22 protein parameters, usually with the CMAP backbone correction, with nucleic acid parameters published in 2000. In GROMACS the name refers to CHARMM22 plus CMAP for proteins. It was later replaced by CHARMM36. (UNVERIFIED)

A protein force field that is version 1 of OPEP, a coarse-grained model representing each amino acid by its backbone atoms N, H, Cα, C and O and a single bead for the side chain. Keeping the backbone atoms retains much of the detail of backbone hydrogen bonding while reducing computational cost. (UNVERIFIED)

A protein force field that is version 2 of OPEP, a coarse-grained model representing each amino acid by its backbone atoms N, H, Cα, C and O and a single bead for the side chain. Keeping the backbone atoms retains much of the detail of backbone hydrogen bonding while reducing computational cost. (UNVERIFIED)

A protein force field that is version 3 of OPEP, a coarse-grained model representing each amino acid by its backbone atoms N, H, Cα, C and O and a single bead for the side chain. Keeping the backbone atoms retains much of the detail of backbone hydrogen bonding while reducing computational cost. (UNVERIFIED)

A protein force field that is version 4 of OPEP, a coarse-grained model representing each amino acid by its backbone atoms N, H, Cα, C and O and a single bead for the side chain. Keeping the backbone atoms retains much of the detail of backbone hydrogen bonding while reducing computational cost. (UNVERIFIED)

A family of force fields developed by Jorgensen and co-workers for condensed-phase simulations, whose non-bonded parameters were fitted mainly to reproduce measured properties of organic liquids, such as density and heat of vaporisation. It includes united-atom and all-atom versions and covers organic molecules and proteins, with OPLS-AA/M the latest version for proteins. (UNVERIFIED)

A force field of the OPLS family in which every atom, including every hydrogen, is represented as a separate interaction site. Representing hydrogens explicitly describes groups such as aromatic rings and hydrogen-bonding sites in more detail than the united-atom version, at a higher cost. Its parameters exist for proteins and many organic molecules. (UNVERIFIED)

A force field of the OPLS family in which non-polar hydrogens are merged into the heavy atom they are bonded to, so that a methyl group is 1 interaction site rather than 4. Merging them cuts the particle count substantially at the cost of any detail those hydrogens carried. It was widely used for organic liquids before all-atom parameters became affordable. (UNVERIFIED)

A specific parameter set version within the OPLS-AA force field family, released around 2001. It contained parameters primarily for proteins and organic liquids available at that time. Subsequent versions like OPLS-2005 updated and expanded upon this set. (UNVERIFIED)

A significant update and expansion of the OPLS-AA force field parameter set, released around 2005. It included refined parameters for proteins, nucleic acids, and a wider range of organic functional groups compared to OPLS-2001. It remains a widely used parameter set within the OPLS family. (UNVERIFIED)

A rigid water model with 4 sites, the fourth being a massless point near the oxygen, on the bisector of the H-O-H angle, carrying that atom's negative charge. Moving the negative charge off the oxygen towards the hydrogens gives a better electrostatic field around the molecule. It costs more than a 3-site model and reproduces properties such as the dielectric constant and the temperature of maximum density better than TIP3P. (UNVERIFIED)

A specific variant of the TIP4P water model, optimized for use with Ewald summation methods for calculating long-range electrostatic interactions, which are standard in modern simulations with periodic boundary conditions. The parameters are adjusted to provide good agreement with experimental properties of liquid water (like density, enthalpy of vaporization) under typical simulation conditions (room temperature and pressure). It is a popular choice for biomolecular simulations. (UNVERIFIED)

A variant of the TIP4P water model, parameterized to reproduce the melting temperature of ordinary ice and the properties of the different ice phases. It gives a better description of water's phase diagram, particularly the solid phases, than models optimized for the liquid state. It is useful for studying freezing, melting, or ice interfaces. (UNVERIFIED)

A variant of the TIP4P water model, published by Abascal and Vega in 2005, re-parameterized to provide improved agreement with a wider range of experimental properties of liquid water over various temperatures and pressures compared to earlier TIP4P versions. It is considered one of the most accurate rigid, non-polarizable 4-point models for general liquid water simulations. It accurately predicts properties like the temperature of maximum density. (UNVERIFIED)

A rigid water model with 5 sites, adding 2 massless points in the positions the oxygen's lone pairs would occupy. Placing negative charge there makes hydrogen bonding directional in the way real water's is. It was fitted to reproduce the temperature of maximum density of water near 4 °C, at a higher cost than 3-site and 4-site models. (UNVERIFIED)

A rigid water model with 6 sites, carrying charges on all 3 atoms, on 2 lone-pair points and on a further point near the oxygen. The extra sites refine the electrostatic field further still. Its cost restricts it to studies of water itself rather than of biomolecules in water. (UNVERIFIED)

A rigid water model with 3 interaction sites, 1 on each atom, an O-H bond length of 1 Å and an H-O-H angle of 109.47 degrees, the ideal tetrahedral value, rather than the angle of an isolated molecule. Like other fixed-charge models, its charges give a dipole moment larger than that of an isolated water molecule, to represent on average the polarization of water in the liquid. It is among the oldest water models still in use, and SPC/E was derived from it. (UNVERIFIED)

A variation of the SPC water model where the normally rigid constraints on bond lengths (O-H) and/or angle (H-O-H) are replaced with flexible harmonic potentials. This allows the water molecule geometry to fluctuate during the simulation, which can affect dynamics and spectroscopic properties. It adds computational overhead compared to rigid SPC. (UNVERIFIED)

A rigid 3-site water model that keeps the geometry of its predecessor and adds a correction for the energy cost of polarizing a molecule from its gas-phase to its liquid charge distribution. That correction improves the density and the diffusion coefficient markedly. It is a common choice where bulk water properties matter more than compatibility with a particular force field. (UNVERIFIED)

A force field specifically developed and parameterized to accurately model a particular class of chemical molecules, such as proteins, lipids, or nucleic acids. Its parameters are tuned based on experimental data and/or quantum mechanical calculations relevant to that molecular type.
