This specialization aims to improve the accuracy of simulations for specific biomolecular systems. (UNVERIFIED)

A quantum chemistry engine built around density functional theory using Slater-type orbitals rather than the Gaussian functions most programs use. Slater functions have the correct shape at the nucleus, which suits properties that depend on the region near heavy atoms. It is often chosen for transition metal and relativistic calculations. (UNVERIFIED)

Abalone (Abalone II) is a general purpose molecular dynamics and molecular graphics program for simulations of bio-molecules in a periodic boundary conditions in explicit or implicit water models. Mainly designed to simulate the protein folding and DNA-ligand complexes in AMBER force field.

An open-source quantum chemistry engine for atomistic simulation of solids, liquids, molecules and biological systems, with a focus on density functional theory. Its Quickstep module uses a mixed basis of Gaussian functions and plane waves, which makes density functional calculations on large systems efficient, including ab initio molecular dynamics and QM/MM simulations that treat a small region with quantum mechanics and the rest classically. It is written to run in parallel on large computers. (UNVERIFIED)

A quantum chemistry engine for ab initio molecular dynamics, in which the forces on the atoms come from density functional theory, usually with a plane wave basis. Its main method, Car-Parrinello molecular dynamics, which gives the program its name, lets the electronic orbitals move with their own fictitious dynamics so that the electronic structure need not be fully solved again at every step. It also performs Born-Oppenheimer molecular dynamics. (UNVERIFIED)

A high-performance software package specifically designed for classical molecular dynamics simulations of biological systems, developed by D. E. Shaw Research (DESRES). Desmond is known for its exceptional speed, particularly on GPUs, and its integration with the Schrödinger Materials Science Suite. It supports standard force fields (like CHARMM, AMBER, OPLS) and offers features for system building, simulation execution (including free energy calculations), and analysis, primarily targeting drug discovery and biomolecular research.

A quantum chemistry engine offering a broad range of wavefunction and density functional methods, heavily optimised for Intel processors. It shares its origins and much of its input syntax with GAMESS (US). It was formerly distributed under the name PC GAMESS. (UNVERIFIED)

A quantum chemistry engine of the GAMESS family, developed in the United Kingdom separately from GAMESS-US although the 2 share common origins. It offers a broad range of ab initio and density functional methods for the electronic structure of molecules, and can be combined with molecular mechanics in QM/MM calculations, where a small region is treated with quantum mechanics and the rest classically. Like other quantum chemistry programs, it is used mainly for electronic structure calculations and parameterization rather than for large-scale classical molecular dynamics. (UNVERIFIED)

A quantum chemistry engine of the GAMESS family, developed in the United States and freely available, that provides methods from semi-empirical and Hartree-Fock theory through density functional theory to perturbation, coupled cluster and multi-configuration methods. It also performs geometry optimization, vibrational analysis and QM/MM calculations, which treat a small region with quantum mechanics and the rest classically. It is widely used in computational chemistry research and teaching. (UNVERIFIED)

A software package for classical molecular dynamics simulation, developed principally at ETH Zürich, covering system setup, simulation and analysis. It is distributed together with the force field family of the same name, which is a separate thing from the program. (UNVERIFIED)

A commercial molecular modeling suite for desktop computers with a graphical interface for building, viewing and simulating molecules. It combines molecular mechanics with several force fields, semi-empirical and ab initio quantum chemistry, and molecular dynamics in 1 program. (UNVERIFIED)

A commercial quantum chemistry engine from Schrödinger, used mainly for density functional and Hartree-Fock calculations, that evaluates the costly electron repulsion terms quickly with a pseudospectral method. It also offers local second-order Møller-Plesset perturbation theory (LMP2) and QM/MM calculations, which treat a small region with quantum mechanics and the rest classically. It is often used in drug discovery for reaction modeling, property prediction and force field parameterization. (UNVERIFIED)

A classical molecular dynamics engine, open source and developed at Sandia National Laboratories, that is designed to run in parallel on many processors and supports a very wide range of interaction potentials. Its applications reach from biomolecules, using force fields such as CHARMM, AMBER and OPLS, to materials science, solid-state physics and coarse-grained models. That breadth makes it suitable for simulation setups that other engines do not support. (UNVERIFIED)

A semi-empirical quantum chemistry engine that implements methods such as AM1, PM3, PM6 and PM7, which replace most of the costly integrals of ab initio theory with parameters fitted to reference data. These methods are much faster than ab initio or density functional calculations but usually less accurate, so they allow larger systems or more calculations. It is often used for fast geometry optimization, property estimates and as the quantum part of QM/MM calculations where speed matters. (UNVERIFIED)

A highly scalable, parallel molecular dynamics simulation software package developed at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, designed specifically for simulating large biomolecular systems on high-performance computers (NAnoscale Molecular Dynamics). NAMD works particularly well with the CHARMM force field (and others like AMBER) and is often used in conjunction with the VMD visualization program for setup and analysis. It is known for its excellent performance on parallel architectures, including GPUs.

An open-source quantum chemistry engine for density functional theory calculations and ab initio molecular dynamics that uses numerical atomic orbitals, confined to a region around each atom, as its basis, together with pseudopotentials. That basis keeps calculations on large systems affordable and suits parallel computers. It is used mostly in materials science and condensed matter physics, although it can also be applied to biomolecules. (UNVERIFIED)

A commercial molecular modeling and computational chemistry suite with an integrated graphical interface for building, viewing and calculating molecules. It implements molecular mechanics, semi-empirical methods such as AM1 and PM3, Hartree-Fock, density functional theory and Møller-Plesset perturbation theory. It is widely used in teaching and in research on how molecular structure relates to properties. (UNVERIFIED)

A freely available software package for molecular mechanics and molecular dynamics, best known for its implementation of polarizable force fields such as AMOEBA. It supports several standard force fields, including AMBER, CHARMM, OPLS and MMFF, and includes programs for energy minimization, molecular dynamics, free energy calculations and structural analysis. Its design is modular. (UNVERIFIED)

A molecular dynamics engine for high-performance parallel computers, developed at Fraunhofer SCAI. It supports many interaction potentials and is used mainly in nanotechnology and materials science, and also in biochemistry and biophysics. (UNVERIFIED)

A quantum chemistry program package for molecules and clusters, built for speed and parallel performance, that offers density functional theory and correlated wavefunction methods such as second-order Møller-Plesset perturbation theory and coupled cluster theory. It is widely used where high accuracy or large basis sets are needed, for example in reaction mechanism studies, spectroscopy and force field parameterization. (UNVERIFIED)

A commercially licensed quantum chemistry engine, developed at the University of Vienna, for density functional calculations on periodic systems using plane waves and the projector augmented wave method. Plane waves naturally describe an infinite repeating solid. It is one of the most widely used programs for solids, surfaces and interfaces, including ab initio molecular dynamics. (UNVERIFIED)

A software package primarily used for macromolecular structure determination based on experimental data, particularly X-ray crystallography and NMR spectroscopy data. It incorporates molecular mechanics (energy terms from force fields), molecular dynamics (often used for refinement or simulated annealing protocols), and terms representing the experimental restraints to refine structures consistent with both physics and experimental observations. While it uses MD concepts, its primary goal is structure determination rather than simulating equilibrium dynamics.

A barostat algorithm that gives the box volume its own equation of motion, as in the Andersen barostat, and combines it with a Nosé-Hoover thermostat, following the constant-pressure equations of motion proposed by Hoover. The equations are deterministic, so no random numbers are involved. They were later shown not to sample the isothermal-isobaric ensemble exactly, a problem corrected in the later equations of Martyna, Tobias and Klein. (UNVERIFIED)

A constraint algorithm that solves all the distance constraint equations of a molecule together with Newton's method, instead of correcting one constraint at a time as SHAKE does. Each iteration costs more, but the solution converges much faster, so far fewer iterations are needed. It was designed for small molecules, where solving the equations together is cheap. (UNVERIFIED)

A constraint algorithm that, before the SHAKE iteration, transforms the constraint equations with a precomputed matrix, called a preconditioner, so that they become nearly independent of one another. The decoupled constraints then converge much faster, quadratically rather than linearly, which means the error shrinks far more quickly from one iteration to the next. It suits rigid or semi-rigid molecules with many coupled constraints. (UNVERIFIED)

An analytical (non-iterative) constraint algorithm specifically designed for rigid water models like TIP3P or SPC/E, where both bond lengths and the bond angle are fixed. Because the geometry is simple and fixed, the constraint equations for a water molecule can be solved analytically, making SETTLE significantly faster than iterative methods like SHAKE for constraining water. It is highly efficient for simulations with explicit water. (UNVERIFIED)

A constraint algorithm that extends the SHAKE approach to rigid bodies of 3 or more atoms, correcting their positions after an unconstrained step by a rotation of each rigid body as a whole. It gives the same trajectory as fully converged SHAKE, but is more efficient and more accurate for groups of 3 or more atoms. It is used to keep rigid molecules or rigid fragments at their fixed geometry during a simulation. (UNVERIFIED)

A constraint algorithm that holds bond lengths fixed while using information about the atoms' velocities as well as their positions to converge faster. Holding bonds fixed removes the fastest vibrations from a system, which is what allows a longer timestep. It is an extension of the SHAKE approach rather than a separate idea. (UNVERIFIED)

A thermostat algorithm that adds an extra degree of freedom to the system, representing the heat bath, which exchanges energy with the atoms through its own equation of motion. The equations are deterministic and generate the canonical distribution provided the dynamics are ergodic, that is explore all accessible states, which is not always the case for small or stiff systems. In Nosé's original form, time is rescaled as well, which Hoover's later reformulation removes. (UNVERIFIED)

A thermostat algorithm that applies a Poincaré time transformation to the Nosé Hamiltonian, so that the extended system keeps a Hamiltonian form, as in the original Nosé thermostat, but evolves in real time, as in the Nosé-Hoover thermostat. Keeping the Hamiltonian form allows it to be integrated with symplectic, time-reversible methods that give good long-term stability. (UNVERIFIED)

A temperature control algorithm that modifies simple weak coupling by adding a random term chosen so the resulting distribution of kinetic energies is the correct one. Weak coupling alone drives every fluctuation towards the mean, which suppresses the spread a real system has. The random term restores it at no extra cost. (UNVERIFIED)

A quantum chemistry method that simplifies the equations of an ab initio or density functional method by neglecting some terms and replacing others with parameters fitted to experimental or reference data. It is much faster than ab initio methods while still describing electrons explicitly, which molecular mechanics does not. It gives a balance between cost and accuracy for properties such as molecular geometry and energy. (UNVERIFIED)

A semi-empirical method that treats every valence electron explicitly while representing the inner electrons by a fixed core. Including all valence electrons is what lets it describe molecules of any element combination rather than only conjugated ones. It is the level nearly all modern semi-empirical methods work at. (UNVERIFIED)

A semi-empirical quantum method that treats only the pi electrons of a conjugated system, holding the rest of the molecule fixed as a framework. Restricting the calculation to pi electrons made conjugated molecules computable long before general methods existed. It predicted the absorption spectra of dyes well and cannot describe anything outside the pi system. (UNVERIFIED)

A semi-empirical method that treats only the pi electrons explicitly, holding the sigma electrons and nuclei fixed as a core framework. It applies to planar conjugated molecules, where the pi electrons control properties such as ultraviolet and visible absorption. It cannot describe anything outside the pi system, so it is used mainly for qualitative studies of conjugated molecules and for teaching. (UNVERIFIED)

A semi-empirical quantum method built on the NDDO approximation, adding extra Gaussian terms to the core repulsion so that hydrogen bonding is described better than its predecessor manages. Its parameters were adjusted by hand against measured heats of formation and geometries. It remains in wide use, particularly as the basis of fast charge assignment schemes. (UNVERIFIED)

A semi-empirical all-valence-electron method, in its second parameterisation, that neglects the differential overlap, the product of 2 different atomic orbitals, in the electron repulsion integrals even when both orbitals are on the same atom. The severity of that approximation makes it very fast and correspondingly crude. It is of historical interest rather than in current use. (UNVERIFIED)

A semi-empirical all-valence-electron method that keeps the 1-centre exchange integrals between different orbitals on the same atom, which the earlier complete neglect (CNDO) scheme discards. Keeping them is what lets it describe electron spin distributions and the properties that depend on them. It is the level the MINDO and SINDO families refine. (UNVERIFIED)

A fundamental ab initio quantum chemistry method that approximates the solution to the electronic Schrödinger equation for a multi-electron system. It treats each electron as moving in an average field created by all other electrons, neglecting instantaneous electron correlation but including exact exchange interaction. It serves as a starting point for more sophisticated ab initio methods and is the foundation simplified by semi-empirical approaches. (UNVERIFIED)

A Hartree-Fock method for systems with unpaired electrons that keeps electrons of opposite spin in the same spatial orbitals wherever they are paired. The constraint means the wavefunction remains an eigenfunction of total spin, with no spin contamination. It is less flexible than the unrestricted method and usually gives a slightly higher energy. (UNVERIFIED)

An iterative computational procedure that solves for a set of molecular orbitals by repeatedly recomputing the average field each electron feels from all the others until the orbitals stop changing. It is how the Hartree-Fock equations, and those of density functional theory, are solved in practice. A calculation that fails to reach that fixed point is said not to have converged. (UNVERIFIED)

A Hartree-Fock method that lets electrons of opposite spin occupy different spatial orbitals. The extra freedom describes unpaired electrons better than forcing paired orbitals does. The price is that the resulting wavefunction is not an eigenfunction of total spin, so it can be contaminated by states of higher multiplicity. (UNVERIFIED)

A family of semi-empirical all-valence-electron methods based on the INDO (intermediate neglect of differential overlap) approximation, with parameters fitted to reproduce the heats of formation of organic molecules. Successive versions are numbered, the best known being MINDO/3. They were later replaced by methods based on the NDDO approximation, such as MNDO and AM1. (UNVERIFIED)

A semi-empirical quantum method built on the NDDO approximation, with parameters fitted to measured heats of formation, geometries and dipole moments. It described geometries and heats of formation far better than the earlier INDO-based methods. Its known failure is that it underestimates hydrogen bonding severely, which is what later methods such as AM1 set out to fix. (UNVERIFIED)

A semi-empirical approximation scheme that sets to zero every electron repulsion integral containing the product of 2 atomic orbitals centred on different atoms, while keeping those in which each product comes from orbitals on the same atom. Dropping those integrals is what makes NDDO-based calculations fast, and the approximation is less severe than in the CNDO and INDO schemes. It underlies the MNDO, AM1 and PM families of methods. (UNVERIFIED)

A modification of the PM3 and MNDO semi-empirical methods that adds a pairwise distance directed Gaussian function to the core repulsion between each pair of atoms, together with a new set of parameters. The corrections improve heats of formation markedly, particularly for organic molecules. It changes the parameters and the core repulsion rather than the underlying approximation. (UNVERIFIED)

A semi-empirical quantum method built on the NDDO approximation, with all of its parameters fitted automatically to a large set of measured molecular properties. Treating every parameter as adjustable, including some that AM1 took from spectroscopic measurements, is what distinguishes it from AM1. (UNVERIFIED)

A variant of the PM3 semi-empirical method that adds a molecular mechanics correction for the HCON (peptide) linkage, a torsion term that raises the too-low rotation barrier PM3 gives for amide bonds. Without it, semi-empirical methods tend to make the amide nitrogen pyramidal and the amide bond too easy to twist. (UNVERIFIED)

A semi-empirical quantum method built on the NDDO approximation, parameterised for most of the periodic table rather than for organic elements alone. That coverage is what distinguishes it from its predecessors, which handle few metals. It also revised the core repulsion terms, improving hydrogen bonding and the description of metal complexes. (UNVERIFIED)

A semi-empirical quantum method built on the NDDO approximation, refitting the parameters of AM1 against a larger and more modern set of measurements. It uses the same functional form as its predecessor and differs only in the parameter values. It covers the elements most common in organic and biological molecules. (UNVERIFIED)

A semi-empirical quantum method built on the NDDO approximation that computes the 2-electron repulsion integrals it keeps from a minimal basis of Gaussian functions, instead of approximating them by a multipole expansion as earlier NDDO methods do. The computed integrals are then scaled by empirical functions to reproduce experimental results. It is much less widely used than its contemporaries. (UNVERIFIED)

A semi-empirical all-valence-electron method based on the INDO (intermediate neglect of differential overlap) approximation, in which the atomic orbitals are first orthogonalised symmetrically. The orthogonalisation makes the approximations more internally consistent than in the unmodified INDO scheme. It was developed to improve on earlier INDO-based methods. (UNVERIFIED)

A modification of the AM1 semi-empirical method specifically parameterized to handle lanthanide elements (rare earth metals). Standard AM1 parameters are not available or reliable for these heavy elements, so Sparkle/AM1 replaces the core description of the lanthanide ion with a point charge dressed by Gaussian functions, adjusted to reproduce structural data. It enables AM1-level calculations on complexes containing lanthanides. (UNVERIFIED)

An all-valence-electron semi-empirical method likely based on the INDO or NDDO approximation schemes, developed by Zhidomirov and coworkers. It represents one of the many variations within the semi-empirical framework, likely with specific parameterizations or modifications to the integral approximations aimed at particular applications or accuracy improvements. Note: This method is less common than MNDO/AM1/PMx variants, and specific details might require consulting specialized literature. (UNVERIFIED)

A post-Hartree-Fock method that recovers electron correlation by treating the difference between the true electronic Hamiltonian and the Hartree-Fock one as a perturbation, and computing energy corrections order by order. Each successive order adds more correlation and costs more. The order used is written as a number after the name. (UNVERIFIED)

A Møller-Plesset method truncated at second order, which adds the correlation energy from double excitations out of the Hartree-Fock reference. It is the cheapest wavefunction method that includes electron correlation and is widely used for that reason. It describes dispersion reasonably and overestimates it for large systems. (UNVERIFIED)

A Møller-Plesset method truncated at third order. It costs substantially more than second order and does not reliably give a better answer, because the perturbation series does not converge smoothly. It is rarely used in practice. (UNVERIFIED)

A Møller-Plesset method truncated at fourth order, including single, double, triple and quadruple excitations out of the Hartree-Fock reference. The triple excitations are what make it markedly more accurate than second order and also what make it expensive. It is sometimes written with the excitation levels listed explicitly. (UNVERIFIED)

A Møller-Plesset method truncated at fifth order. It includes still higher excitations than fourth order, at a cost that rises steeply with system size. It is used almost only to study how the perturbation series itself behaves. (UNVERIFIED)

A class of advanced quantum mechanics methods required for accurately describing molecules or chemical processes where the electronic structure cannot be well represented by a single dominant electron configuration (as assumed in basic Hartree-Fock theory). These situations often involve stretched bonds, excited states, diradicals, or transition metals, necessitating the use of multiple electronic configurations to capture the essential physics. These methods are typically more computationally demanding than single-reference approaches. (UNVERIFIED)

A multi-configurational self-consistent field method that includes every possible electron configuration within a chosen set of electrons and orbitals, the active space, and optimises the orbitals at the same time. The remaining orbitals stay doubly occupied or empty. Choosing the active space is the main difficulty, because the cost grows factorially with its size, and the method is the most widely used multi-reference starting point. (UNVERIFIED)

A quantum chemistry method that optimises the shapes of the molecular orbitals and the weights of several electron configurations at the same time. A single configuration cannot describe a bond being broken or a near-degenerate ground state; several can. It is the starting point for the multi-reference correlated methods. (UNVERIFIED)

nodes.lbl: multi-reference coupled cluster with single and double excitations

definition.val: A quantum chemistry method that applies a coupled cluster treatment with single and double excitations on top of a multi-configurational reference wavefunction. It combines the size consistency of coupled cluster with a reference able to describe bond breaking. It is among the most accurate methods available and among the most expensive. (UNVERIFIED)

nodes.lbl: multi-reference configuration interaction with single and double excitations

definition.val: A quantum chemistry method that performs a configuration interaction treatment with single and double excitations starting from a multi-configurational reference rather than a single determinant. It recovers dynamic correlation on top of the static correlation the reference already describes. It is not size-consistent, which limits its use on large or dissociating systems. (UNVERIFIED)

A multi-configurational self-consistent field method that divides the active space into subspaces and limits how many electrons may be excited out of or into each, while optimising the orbitals at the same time. The restriction keeps the number of configurations manageable where a complete treatment would be too large. It trades some completeness for the ability to use a bigger active space. (UNVERIFIED)

A post-Hartree-Fock method that adds terms quadratic in the excitation coefficients to the truncated configuration interaction equations, so that the energy becomes size-consistent. Size consistency means the energy of 2 well-separated molecules equals the sum of their separate energies, which truncated configuration interaction does not give. The method is closely related to coupled cluster theory. (UNVERIFIED)

A quadratic configuration interaction method with single and double excitations that adds a perturbative estimate of triple excitations. The triples correction is what brings the method close to chemical accuracy for many properties. It costs considerably more than the calculation without it. (UNVERIFIED)

A post-Hartree-Fock method that includes single and double excitations in a configuration interaction treatment modified so that the result is size-consistent. Size consistency means the energy of 2 well-separated molecules equals the sum of their separate energies, which plain truncated configuration interaction does not satisfy. Its cost and accuracy are close to those of coupled cluster with single and double excitations. (UNVERIFIED)

A computational method that uses a simplified energy function whose parameters were fitted to experimental measurements or to more accurate calculations, rather than derived from first principles. The fitting is what makes it fast enough for large systems. It is also its limit: the method is reliable only for systems resembling those it was fitted to. (UNVERIFIED)

A method that adjusts the positions of atoms to reach a nearby arrangement of lowest energy. It moves downhill from wherever it starts, so it finds the nearest low point rather than the lowest one anywhere. It is run before a simulation to remove the severe atom overlaps that a freshly built system almost always contains. (UNVERIFIED)

Molecular dynamics (MD) is a computer simulation technique used to study the physical movement of atoms and molecules over time. It calculates the forces between particles using an empirical potential energy function (force field) and then integrates Newton's equations of motion numerically to simulate how the positions and velocities evolve in small time steps. MD simulations provide detailed information about the dynamic behavior, conformational changes, and thermodynamics of molecular systems.

The NetCDF (Network Common Data Form) format, which typically uses the .nc extension, is a set of software libraries and a file format designed for storing and sharing array-oriented scientific data. Developed and maintained by the Unidata program at the University Corporation for Atmospheric Research (UCAR), it is an open standard widely used across many scientific disciplines, such as molecular dynamics. While Amber has adopted NetCDF as its preferred, modern format for storing trajectories and other data, the format itself is not specific to Amber and is a general-purpose standard.

Enhanced sampling encompasses a diverse set of computational techniques used in molecular simulations to accelerate the exploration of a system's possible configurations or states. These methods aim to overcome the timescale limitations of standard simulations, particularly when high energy barriers separate important states or when rare events need to be sampled efficiently. They often involve modifying the potential energy surface, using multiple simulation copies, or applying biasing forces.

An enhanced sampling method that gradually builds up a force opposing the system's own along a chosen coordinate, until the system moves along that coordinate freely. Once the opposing force matches the true one, the barriers along that coordinate have been flattened. The accumulated force is itself the answer, because it gives the free energy profile. (UNVERIFIED)

Canonical adiabatic free energy sampling refers to enhanced sampling strategies where system parameters or constraints are changed very slowly (adiabatically) during a simulation performed under constant NVT conditions. It splits a system into a "subsystem" (the reactive part) and an "environment". By introducing fictitious masses and decoupling the subsystem, it allows the subsystem to evolve slowly and adiabatically on the potential of mean force while operating at a much higher temperature than the environment, speeding up rare events without altering the physical ensemble.

Forward Flux Sampling (FFS) is an enhanced sampling technique specifically designed to calculate rate constants and characterize pathways for rare events, such as transitions between stable molecular states. It involves defining a series of non-overlapping interfaces along a reaction coordinate between the initial and final states. Trajectories are initiated from these interfaces and only propagated forward if they reach the next interface, efficiently focusing computational effort on successful transition paths.

Locally Enhanced Sampling (LES) is a computational method used in molecular dynamics to accelerate the simulation of specific, localized regions of a molecule, such as a ligand binding site or a specific protein segment. It achieves this by introducing multiple non-interacting copies of the "enhanced" atoms while proportionately reducing their interaction potentials.

A statistical model of a system that moves between discrete states, in which the next state depends only on the current one and not on how the system arrived there. That assumption is what makes long-timescale behaviour computable from short observations. It holds only if the states are chosen so that everything relevant about the past is captured by which state the system is in. (UNVERIFIED)

The max-flux approach in molecular systems typically refers to a variational method used to calculate the most probable reaction pathway during a transition (like conformational changes or chemical reactions). It finds the path that maximizes the diffusive flux of distinct reactive trajectories between two metastable states.

Metadynamics is an enhanced sampling technique that accelerates the exploration of complex energy landscapes by adding a history-dependent bias potential along a few chosen collective variables (CVs). Small repulsive energy 'hills' (often Gaussian functions) are periodically deposited at the system's current location in the CV space, discouraging revisiting explored areas and eventually filling up free energy wells. The accumulated bias potential provides an estimate of the free energy surface along the selected CVs.

Milestoning sampling (or the milestoning algorithm) is an advanced molecular simulation technique designed to calculate the kinetics and thermodynamics of slow, complex processes (such as protein folding or drug binding). It breaks down computationally expensive simulations into multiple, short, independent trajectories between predefined interfaces, or "milestones".

A free energy analysis method that combines data from simulations run at many thermodynamic states at once, and returns the free energy difference between any pair of them together with equilibrium averages. It uses every sample from every state rather than only neighbouring pairs, which is what makes it statistically optimal. It generalises the 2-state Bennett acceptance ratio. (UNVERIFIED)

A machine learning model built from layers of simple units, each combining its inputs and passing the result on, whose connection strengths are adjusted to fit training data. Given enough units it can represent almost any relationship, which is why it is used where no formula is known. In this field it is used to predict energies and forces, and to find useful coordinates automatically. (UNVERIFIED)

The Nudged Elastic Band (NEB) method is primarily used to find the Minimum Energy Path (MEP) connecting two known stable states (e.g., reactant and product) on a potential energy surface. It works by optimizing a discrete chain of intermediate structures (images) linking the start and end points. Forces acting on the images perpendicular to the path are minimized, while spring forces along the path ensure continuity, guiding the chain towards the MEP, including the transition state.

An enhanced sampling method that transforms the coordinates so that regions with known energy barriers, described by a simpler reference potential, take up less of the configuration space and low-energy basins take up more. The transformation leaves the partition function unchanged, so averages computed with the transformed coordinates need no reweighting afterwards. This makes those barriers easier to cross without changing the equilibrium properties of the system. (UNVERIFIED)

Replica-exchange molecular dynamics (REMD), also known as parallel tempering, is an enhanced sampling technique that runs multiple simulations (replicas) of the same system in parallel, typically each at a different temperature. At regular intervals, attempts are made to swap the current configurations between pairs of replicas running at adjacent temperatures, accepted based on a probability criterion. This allows configurations explored at high temperatures (overcoming energy barriers) to diffuse down to lower temperatures, enhancing conformational sampling.

Steered Molecular Dynamics (sMD) is a simulation technique where an external, time-dependent force or constraint is applied to manipulate the system, often by pulling on specific atoms or controlling the distance between groups. This forces the system along a chosen pathway, allowing exploration of processes like ligand unbinding or protein monomerization-multimerization that might not occur spontaneously on simulation timescales. sMD trajectories can also be used with fluctuation theorems (like Jarzynski's equality) to estimate equilibrium free energy differences.

A computational method that finds the most likely route between 2 stable states of a system, described in terms of a few chosen coordinates. It represents the route as a line of points and repeatedly moves them downhill on the energy or free energy surface while keeping them evenly spaced along it. The line settles onto the path the system is most likely to take, which is rarely a straight one. (UNVERIFIED)

The swarm-of-trajectories approach refers to computational strategies that utilize a large number of independent, often relatively short, MD simulations launched from specific initial conditions. This "swarm" allows for efficient statistical sampling of pathways, transition probabilities between states, or average forces needed in methods like the String Method or Milestoning. It contrasts with relying on a single, very long trajectory to observe events of interest.

Targeted Molecular Dynamics (TMD) is a simulation technique used to induce a conformational transition between a known initial structure and a known target structure. It achieves this by adding an extra potential energy term that biases the system to reduce its root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) relative to the target structure over the course of the simulation. TMD provides a plausible pathway for the transition, although not necessarily the minimum energy or most probable one.

Transition Path Sampling (TPS) is a powerful simulation technique designed to study rare transition events between stable molecular states by directly sampling the ensemble of reactive pathways connecting them. Starting with one known reactive trajectory, it uses a Monte Carlo sampling in path space (generating new trial paths from old ones) to explore the set of all possible transition mechanisms without needing predefined reaction coordinates. TPS allows for the calculation of rate constants and detailed mechanistic analysis.

The Transition State Ensemble (TSE) refers to the collection of molecular configurations that lie at the top of the highest free energy barrier separating the reactant and product states of a process, such as protein folding or a chemical reaction. Structures within the TSE are equally likely to proceed forward to the product state or revert back to the reactant state (i.e., they have a committor probability of 0.5). Characterizing the structural features of the TSE is key to understanding the mechanism of the transition.

Transition Interface Sampling (TIS) is a path sampling technique, related to Forward Flux Sampling, used for calculating rate constants of rare events. It involves defining interfaces along an order parameter and then specifically sampling ensembles of trajectories that start in the reactant state and reach a particular interface, or start at one interface and reach the next. By calculating the crossing probabilities between interfaces, TIS reconstructs the overall rate constant.

An input file format that carries the keywords and data blocks instructing the Amsterdam Density Functional software how to perform a quantum chemical calculation. It specifies details like the desired computational task (e.g., geometry optimization, frequency calculation), the molecular geometry, the choice of density functional and basis set, and other calculation parameters. The format uses specific ADF keywords and block structures (e.g., ATOMS, GEOMETRY). (UNVERIFIED)

A CHARMM input file is a script containing a sequence of commands written in the CHARMM scripting language, which directs the CHARMM program to perform various tasks. These tasks can range from reading topology and coordinate files, setting up system parameters, running energy minimizations or molecular dynamics simulations, to analyzing results.

An input file format that instructs the GAMESS (US) quantum chemistry program, structured into groups identified by keywords starting with '$', such as $CONTRL, $BASIS and $DATA. Within these groups, keywords specify the type of calculation (e.g., RUNTYP=OPTIMIZE), the theoretical method (e.g., SCFTYP=RHF), basis set, molecular geometry, and other computational details. The format follows specific Fortran namelist-like conventions. (UNVERIFIED)

A text data format that specifies a molecular system and the settings for a quantum chemistry calculation to the GAMESS-UK program, using directives such as TITLE, RUNTYPE, GEOMETRY and BASIS. Its keywords and layout differ substantially from those of the separate GAMESS (US) program, so files are not interchangeable between them. (UNVERIFIED)

An input file format that instructs the Gaussian quantum chemistry software, carrying the extension .com or .gjf. It characteristically includes a route section, starting with #, containing keywords that define the theoretical method, basis set and calculation type, followed by a title section, the charge and spin multiplicity, and the molecular geometry. (UNVERIFIED)

In GROMACS, the primary molecular dynamics input file usually has an .mdp extension and contains keyword-value pairs defining the simulation parameters. Processed by the grompp tool, it controls aspects like the integration algorithm, timestep, simulation length, temperature and pressure coupling methods, and cutoff schemes. This file dictates how the MD simulation engine (mdrun) will execute the run.

A data format, written with the extension .hin, that is the native way the HyperChem modelling package stores a molecular system. It holds atomic coordinates, connectivity, force field atom types, and settings for a calculation. It serves both as input to the program and as the way a session is saved. (UNVERIFIED)

An input file format that carries the instructions for a quantum chemistry calculation in Jaguar, part of the Schrodinger suite. It uses a specific syntax with data sections delimited by &section_name (e.g., &gen, &zmat) and terminated by &, containing keywords and values controlling the calculation type, method, basis set, and molecular geometry. The structure facilitates setting up various QM tasks. (UNVERIFIED)

A data format specifying a molecule's geometry to the MOPAC semi-empirical program as 3 coordinates per atom. Each coordinate carries a flag saying whether it may be optimised or must be held fixed. That per-coordinate control is what distinguishes it from a plain coordinate list. (UNVERIFIED)

A data format specifying a molecule's geometry to the MOPAC semi-empirical program as bond lengths, angles and rotations. As with its coordinate counterpart, each value carries a flag saying whether it may be optimised. It is the form used when a particular bond or angle must be scanned or held. (UNVERIFIED)

A NAMD configuration file, typically ending in .namd, contains parameters and commands that control a molecular dynamics simulation run using the NAMD software. It uses a keyword-value pair format, often leveraging Tcl scripting capabilities, to specify input files (structure, coordinates, parameters), simulation conditions (temperature, pressure, duration), and algorithms. This file dictates the entire simulation protocol.

An NWChem input file (.nw) uses directives and nested blocks to instruct the NWChem software package on performing computational chemistry tasks. It is composed of commands, called directives, which define data (such as basis sets, geometries, and filenames) and the actions to be performed on that data. Directives are processed in the order presented in the input file, with the exception of certain start-up directives (see Input File Structure) which provide critical job control information, and are processed before all other input. Most directives are specific to a particular module and define data that is used by that module only. A few directives (see Top-level Directives) potentially affect all modules, for instance by specifying the total electric charge on the system.

An input file format that instructs the Q-Chem quantum chemistry program, using data blocks marked by $block_name and $end. Key blocks include $molecule (defining charge, multiplicity, and geometry), $rem (specifying calculation method, basis set, job type via keywords), and potentially others like $basis or $opt. This structure organizes the input required for a wide range of QM calculations. (UNVERIFIED)

A text data format in which the Amsterdam Density Functional program records a completed calculation. It holds the input as read back, the convergence history, the final energy with its breakdown into components, the final geometry and computed properties such as charges and dipole moments. (UNVERIFIED)

A binary data format, written by the Amsterdam Density Functional program with the extension .rkf and called TAPE21 in versions up to 2019, that stores the results of a calculation as named sections that can be read by keyword. It holds information such as the geometry, basis set details, molecular orbital coefficients and computed properties. It is read for analysis and visualization, and can be reused as a fragment file in a later calculation on a larger molecule. (UNVERIFIED)

The CHARMM output file is the main text log generated during a CHARMM run, typically containing an echo of the input script commands interspersed with the results produced by those commands. This includes detailed energy breakdowns, progress information during dynamics or minimization (like step number, time, temperature, pressure, energies), and outputs from analysis routines. It serves as the primary record of the CHARMM job execution.

A text data format, written with the extension .log or .out, in which the GAMESS (US) program records a completed calculation. It holds the input as read back, the basis set and geometry, convergence progress for the SCF or geometry optimisation, final energies, molecular orbital information and calculated properties. It is the file results are extracted from. (UNVERIFIED)

A text data format in which the GAMESS-UK program records a completed calculation, including the input as read back, convergence progress, final energies and calculated properties. Its structure and keywords differ from those of the separate GAMESS (US) program, so a parser written for one will not read the other. (UNVERIFIED)

A text data format, written with the extension .log, in which the Gaussian program records a completed calculation. It holds setup information, convergence progress, final energies, molecular orbital details, properties such as dipole moments and charges, and vibrational and thermochemical results when those were requested. A compact summary called the archive entry sits near the end. (UNVERIFIED)

The GROMACS MD output typically refers to the primary text log file (.log) generated by the mdrun simulation engine. It contains summary information about the simulation setup, detailed performance data (like PME load balancing and timings), step-by-step progress updates (if configured in the .mdp file), and final run statistics including energy averages and runtime. This file is crucial for monitoring performance and verifying run completion.

A text data format, written with the extension .out, in which the Jaguar program records a completed calculation. It holds the input parameters, convergence information for the SCF and geometry optimisation cycles, final energies, properties such as charges and dipole moments, and vibrational frequencies when requested. The final geometry is usually written to a separate structure file. (UNVERIFIED)

An output file format holding the results of a calculation performed by the MOPAC semi-empirical program, written with the extension .out. It typically includes an echo of the input keywords, details of geometry optimization steps (if performed), the final optimized geometry, the calculated heat of formation (ΔHf), ionization potential, dipole moment, and atomic charges. A summary section usually highlights the key results and timings. (UNVERIFIED)

A text data format, written with the extension .out or .nwout, in which the NWChem program records the tasks its input file requested. It holds the calculation setup, convergence progress, energies from whichever quantum, molecular mechanics or combined method was used, properties and timings. Because the program accepts very varied inputs, the layout of the file varies with them. (UNVERIFIED)

A text data format, written with the extension .out or .qcout, in which the Q-Chem program records a completed calculation. It holds the method and basis set used, convergence information for the SCF and geometry optimisation, final electronic energies, molecular orbital information, and properties such as charges and dipole moments. A summary section usually collects the main computed values. (UNVERIFIED)

A binary checkpoint file format that stores the state of a completed or running Gaussian calculation, including the molecular geometry, basis set details, molecular orbital coefficients, density matrix and forces. It is essential for restarting interrupted calculations (especially geometry optimizations or frequency calculations) and for post-processing tasks like generating cube files or performing wavefunction analysis. It can be converted to a formatted version (.fchk). (UNVERIFIED)

A binary data format, written with the extension .chk, in which Gaussian stores the state of a calculation so that a later job can continue from it. It holds the geometry, the wavefunction and Hessian information that a later job can read back. (UNVERIFIED)

A binary data format, written with the extension .cpt, in which GROMACS stores the complete state of a running simulation at intervals. It holds the step number, the time, the positions, the velocities, the box and the state of the thermostat and barostat. Resuming from it continues the run exactly, as though it had never stopped. (UNVERIFIED)

Restarting an NWChem calculation involves using various files generated during a previous run, depending on the calculation type. This may include the run database (.db), molecular orbital vector files (.movecs), geometry files, or specific QM/MM restart files (.rst).

A data format that stores the force on every atom of a system at each saved step of an AMBER simulation. It records forces where a trajectory format records positions. It is used for debugging a force field and for analyses that need the forces themselves. (UNVERIFIED)

The GROMACS .gro file is a simple, formatted text file used to store molecular coordinates, atom/residue names, and optionally velocities. It includes a title line, the total number of atoms, and then one line per atom specifying residue and atom information, coordinates (in nanometers), and optionally velocities. The file concludes with the periodic box vectors. It is typically used to store single structures.

A text data format used by the TINKER software to store a molecular system, giving for each atom its index, name, x, y and z coordinates, force field atom type and the indices of the atoms bonded to it. Although it shares the .xyz extension with the plain XYZ format, it is not interchangeable with it. It therefore serves as both a coordinate file and a topology file. (UNVERIFIED)

A data format in which TURBOMOLE records the Cartesian coordinates of a molecule, as a data group headed $coord that usually sits in a separate file named coord, which the control file refers to. Each line gives the x, y and z coordinates of 1 atom in atomic units (bohr), followed by its element symbol. (UNVERIFIED)

A GROMACS include topology file (.itp) contains the topology definition for a specific type of molecule (like a protein, lipid, or solvent). It typically includes sections like [ moleculetype ], [ atoms ], [ bonds ], etc., and is designed to be reusable. These .itp files are incorporated into the main system topology (.top) file using the #include directive.

A topology file format that describes an entire molecular system to be simulated with GROMACS, written with the extension .top. It typically starts by including force field parameter files and specific molecule topology files (.itp) using #include directives. Crucially, it concludes with a [ molecules ] section listing the names and counts of each type of molecule present in the simulation box. (UNVERIFIED)

A data format in which NWChem stores the topology of a system for molecular dynamics or QM/MM calculations, as a separate file that its prepare module generates from the input coordinates and the force field files. It holds the static description of the system: the atoms, the bonded interactions, the excluded pairs and the force field parameters. The quantities that change, such as coordinates and velocities, are kept in a separate restart file. (UNVERIFIED)

A Protein Structure File (.psf) defines the atoms, connectivity (bonds, angles, dihedrals, impropers), and basic atomic properties (like type indices, charges, masses) for a molecular system. Importantly, it does not contain the actual force field parameters. PSF files are used by the simulation programs CHARMM and NAMD.

basicPropertyValues.val: The format originates with X-Plor. Recorded here rather than in the definition, which was verified on 2026-09-18 without it. Source: EDAM 1.25, class format_3882 PSF (http://edamontology.org/format_3882).

definition.val: The DCD (.dcd) trajectory format is a widely used binary file format for storing atomic coordinates from molecular dynamics simulations, optionally including periodic box information. Originally developed for CHARMM, it is now supported by many simulation packages (like NAMD, LAMMPS) and analysis tools (like VMD) due to its efficiency and portability.

A binary data format in which GROMACS records the positions of atoms through a simulation, and in some forms their velocities and forces as well. The compressed forms reduce the precision of the coordinates to save space, which is acceptable for analysis but not for restarting a run exactly. Which form was written determines what the trajectory can afterwards be used for. (UNVERIFIED)

A molecular structure is the information that specifies the three-dimensional arrangement of atoms in a molecule. It is typically represented by a list of atomic coordinates (X, Y, Z) for each atom in the system. This structural information is the fundamental input for visualization and is the starting point for any molecular simulation.

OBSOLETE. Small molecule structure formats are designed primarily for representing organic and drug-like molecules, often emphasizing chemical details like bond orders, formal charges, and stereochemistry. These formats are widely used in cheminformatics, drug discovery databases, and as input for various modeling tasks. Common examples include SDF, Mol2, and SMILES strings.

comments: Retired in the file-format flattening. Classifying structure formats by molecule size was an artificial distinction: a small molecule can be stored in a PDB file and a macromolecule in a mol2 file. Its former children are now direct children of 'molecular structure format' (MOLSIM:001088). Reported in GitHub issue #20.

definition.val: The Mol2 format (.mol2) is a text-based file format originating from Sybyl software, commonly used to represent small molecules, especially in docking and cheminformatics applications. It stores atomic coordinates, atom names, connectivity (including bond orders), partial charges, and often uses specific Sybyl atom types. A single Mol2 file can contain multiple molecular structures.

The Structure-Data File (SDF, .sdf) format is widely used in cheminformatics for storing libraries of small molecules along with associated data. It essentially consists of multiple blocks defining atomic coordinates and connectivity for each molecule concatenated together, where each block can be followed by data fields like IDs or calculated properties.

basicPropertyValues.val: The format was developed by MDL Information Systems. Recorded here rather than in the definition, which was verified on 2026-09-18 without it. Source: EDAM 1.25, class format_3814 SDF (http://edamontology.org/format_3814).

definition.val: Sequence formats are standardized ways to represent the primary structure of biological macromolecules, such as the order of amino acids in a protein or nucleotides in DNA/RNA, using strings of characters. These formats usually include a header line providing an identifier and description, followed by the sequence itself using standard codes (e.g., one-letter codes). They are fundamental in bioinformatics for storing and exchanging sequence data.

A data format that stores a property varying continuously through 3-dimensional space, such as electron density or electrostatic potential, as values on a regular grid of points. A file in one of these formats states the grid's origin, its dimensions and its spacing, then lists a value for each point. They are used to visualize and analyse spatial distributions from simulation or from experiment. (UNVERIFIED)

General data formats are versatile, often standardized ways to structure and exchange data that are not tied to a specific application domain like molecular simulation. Formats like XML or JSON use tags or key-value pairs to create hierarchical and self-describing data structures. They are sometimes employed in simulation contexts for storing metadata, configuration, or for facilitating data exchange between different tools.

A script holding the sequence of commands that an analysis program or library carries out on simulation data. It records exactly what was computed and in what order, so an analysis can be repeated. It is often the only surviving record of how a published number was obtained. (UNVERIFIED)

The Fasta format is a simple and widely used text-based format for storing biological sequence data (nucleotides or amino acids). Each sequence entry begins with a single-line description header, marked by a greater-than symbol ('>'), followed by the sequence data on one or more subsequent lines. Its simplicity makes it easily readable by humans and parsable by many bioinformatics tools.

A text data format storing a property sampled on a regular 3-dimensional grid, together with the positions of the atoms it surrounds. It states the grid's origin, its axes and its spacing, then lists one value per point. Electron density, electrostatic potential and molecular orbitals are all distributed in it. (UNVERIFIED)

XML (Extensible Markup Language) is a flexible, text-based markup language used to encode data in a format that is both human-readable and machine-readable. It uses user-defined tags to structure data hierarchically with elements and attributes. XML is widely used for data exchange on the web and in various scientific domains, including bioinformatics.

A data format, built on XML, that records chemical information as structured, labelled text. It defines tags for molecular structures, reactions, spectra and calculation results, so that a file states what each number is rather than relying on position. Its purpose is exchange between programs that would otherwise each need a reader for the others' formats. (UNVERIFIED)

A text data format holding a sequence of commands for the ptraj or cpptraj trajectory analysis programs of AmberTools. A file in this format names the input trajectories with trajin, may name a reference structure, and then lists analysis commands such as rms, distance, hbond, radgyr or cluster. It is the record of how a trajectory was post-processed. (UNVERIFIED)

A category of analysis methods focused on examining the three-dimensional arrangement of atoms (geometry and conformation) and the overall shape and topology of molecules based on simulation data or optimized structures. This includes measuring geometric parameters (distances, angles, dihedrals), identifying characteristic local and global structural features, comparing structures, and quantifying structural fluctuations. It helps understand molecular architecture, flexibility, stability, and structure-function relationships.

OBSOLETE. A structural analysis focusing on the overall architecture, shape, fold, and packing of a macromolecule or molecular complex, rather than fine details. This is often characterized by metrics like the radius of gyration, principal moments of inertia, overall dimensions, secondary structure content (for proteins), or tertiary arrangement of domains. It provides a macroscopic view of the molecule's conformation and large-scale structural changes.

comments: Retired because it grouped nothing: the analyses its definition named (radius of gyration, principal moments of inertia, secondary structure) are siblings under MOLSIM:000917 structural analysis, not subclasses of this term. Raised in the August 2026 definition review.

definition.val: A generic name for a text-based file format that stores the Cartesian (x, y, z) coordinates of atoms in a molecular system. The specific layout can vary, as multiple simulation packages like CHARMM and Amber have their own distinct versions of a ".crd" file. Due to its ambiguity, it is often necessary to specify which software's CRD format is being used.

A structural analysis focusing on the detailed geometric arrangement of small groups of atoms within a molecule. This includes analyzing specific bond lengths, bond angles, dihedral angles, ring conformations (like sugar pucker), hydrogen bonding patterns, or the conformation of amino acid side chains. It provides fine-grained insights into specific interactions, conformational preferences, and flexibility at the atomic or residue level.

A fundamental local structure analysis that calculates the angle formed by three specified atoms (A-B-C), centered on atom B. These bond angles are essential parameters defining the geometry and shape of molecules. Monitoring their values and distributions during simulations reveals information about molecular flexibility and conformational preferences around specific centers. (UNVERIFIED)

A local structure analysis technique that calculates the torsion angle defined by four sequentially bonded atoms (A-B-C-D), representing the rotation around the central bond (B-C). Dihedral angles are critical for determining the three-dimensional conformation of flexible molecules, including protein backbones, side chains, and polymer chains. Analyzing their values and distributions reveals accessible rotational states and conformational dynamics.

A basic local structure analysis technique that measures the distance between any two specified atoms (bonded or non-bonded) in a molecular system. Monitoring distances is essential for tracking bond lengths, identifying close contacts, analyzing non-covalent interactions (like hydrogen bonds, salt bridges, van der Waals contacts), and assessing overall conformational changes or molecular dimensions.

A specialized local structure analysis used to describe and quantify the non-planar conformation (puckering) of cyclic molecular fragments, particularly five-membered (e.g., furanose rings in DNA/RNA, proline) or six-membered rings (e.g., pyranose rings, cyclohexane). It employs parameters like pseudorotation angles and amplitudes to precisely define the ring's shape (e.g., envelope, twist, chair, boat conformations). This analysis is vital for understanding the structure and function of nucleic acids and carbohydrates. (UNVERIFIED)

A type of structural analysis focusing on quantifying properties associated with individual atoms within the molecular structure, often reflecting their local environment or dynamics. Examples include atomic fluctuations (Root Mean Square Fluctuation, RMSF, or B-factors) indicating mobility, solvent-accessible surface area (SASA) quantifying exposure to solvent, or coordination numbers describing the local packing density. Analyzing these properties provides atom-specific insights into dynamics, interactions, and structural roles. (UNVERIFIED)

A force field for DNA from the Olomouc group that combines OL15 and OL21 and adds a refinement of the torsion terms that control sugar puckering (delta and tau1). The sugar pucker affects the balance between the A and B forms of DNA. It is the DNA force field recommended in AMBER. (UNVERIFIED)

An analysis method that groups the structures in a trajectory by how similar they are, usually measured by the distance between them after superposition. It reduces thousands of frames to a handful of representative shapes. Those representatives are what a trajectory is usually described and pictured by. (UNVERIFIED)

A specialized structure clustering approach where conformations are grouped primarily based on the values of selected dihedral angles, rather than overall coordinate RMSD. Structures are assigned to bins based on which ranges their key dihedral angles fall into, and clusters are formed by grouping structures within the same or similar bins. This method is particularly useful for analyzing conformational changes driven by specific torsions, like backbone transitions or sidechain rotations. (UNVERIFIED)

Dynamics analysis involves processing the time-series data generated from molecular dynamics simulations, primarily the trajectory files, to extract quantitative information and insights about the system's behavior. This encompasses a wide range of techniques aimed at understanding molecular motions, conformational changes, interactions, and kinetic or thermodynamic properties. The goal is to translate raw simulation output into meaningful physical or biological understanding.

A text-based file format used by the AMBER software suite to store standard force field parameters. These files (historically using the .dat extension) contain the equilibrium values and force constants for bonds, angles, dihedrals, and non-bonded interactions for specific atom types. They serve as the central parameter database loaded by system-building tools like LEaP. (UNVERIFIED)

A coordinate rotation method is a structure modification method that applies a mathematical rotation to the coordinates of a molecule or a group of atoms. This procedure changes the orientation of the selected atoms in three-dimensional space without altering their internal structure.

A dynamics analysis method that measures how the fluctuations of 2 different properties relate to each other over time, including at a time delay. A positive value means they rise and fall together, a negative value means one rises as the other falls, and near zero means they are independent. The delay at which the relationship is strongest shows which motion leads and which follows. (UNVERIFIED)

A dynamics analysis method that measures how the displacement of each atom or residue from its average position relates to that of every other, over the course of a simulation. A strongly positive value means 2 sites move in the same direction, a negative value means they move in opposite directions. The result is usually drawn as a dynamic cross-correlation map, which shows which parts of a molecule move as one. (UNVERIFIED)

comments: is it synonymous as "atomic correlation analysis"?

definition.val: Motion analysis encompasses techniques used to characterize the types, directions, and magnitudes of movements occurring within a molecular system during a simulation. These methods aim to simplify the complex, high-dimensional atomic motions into understandable patterns or dominant modes. This helps identify functionally relevant conformational changes, flexibility, and collective dynamics.

A structural analysis method that superposes structures by matching their principal axes of inertia rather than by minimising the distance between corresponding atoms. It aligns on overall mass distribution and shape, so it is unaffected by local differences that would dominate a least-squares fit. It suits comparisons of rotational motion and of overall shape. (UNVERIFIED)

A dynamics analysis method that maps the many-dimensional motion in a trajectory onto 1 or a few chosen directions. The chosen direction may be a simple geometric measure such as a distance or an angle, or a vector taken from principal component analysis. Projecting this way reduces a trajectory to a small number of curves that can be read directly. (UNVERIFIED)

A dynamics analysis method that decomposes the motion of a molecular system into a set of independent collective modes, each with a characteristic amplitude or frequency. Principal component analysis applied to a trajectory and normal mode analysis applied to a single structure are the 2 standard ways of obtaining them. The modes show the principal directions in which a molecule moves. (UNVERIFIED)

A type of dynamics analysis focused on quantifying the random translational and rotational movement of molecules or particles within the simulation environment due to thermal energy. It primarily involves calculating diffusion coefficients, which measure the rate at which particles spread out over time. This analysis provides insights into transport properties, viscosity, and mobility in fluids, membranes, or crowded cellular environments. (UNVERIFIED)

An analysis method that extracts a diffusion coefficient from a trajectory, most often by tracking how the mean squared displacement of the molecules grows with time. Over long enough times that growth is linear, and its slope gives the coefficient. Reading a slope from too short a stretch of trajectory is the usual way this measurement goes wrong. (UNVERIFIED)

A type of structural analysis focused on calculating and interpreting the potential energy associated with specific molecular structures or conformations obtained from simulations or modeling. This includes calculating single point energies, comparing energies of different conformers, or decomposing the total energy into contributing components. It helps assess the stability and likelihood of different structures.

An energy analysis that computes the net energy change when a molecular complex forms from its separated components in a stated reference state, such as the gas phase or solution. The result is the difference in potential energy or free energy between the bound complex and the unbound molecules, and a more negative value means stronger binding. Quantum mechanical methods and end-point methods such as MM-PBSA and MM-GBSA can estimate it, some of them including entropy and solvation to give a binding free energy. (UNVERIFIED)

An effective energy analysis that estimates the binding free energy of a molecular complex by combining molecular mechanics energies from simulation snapshots with a Poisson-Boltzmann calculation of the electrostatic solvation energy and a surface area term for the nonpolar solvation energy. The energies are averaged over many snapshots of the complex and of its separated parts. Solute entropy is not captured by this averaging and, when wanted, is estimated separately, for example by normal mode analysis. (UNVERIFIED)

An effective energy analysis that estimates binding free energies by combining molecular mechanics energies with a generalized Born model for the electrostatic part of the solvation free energy and a surface area term for the nonpolar part. The generalized Born model approximates the Poisson-Boltzmann equation at lower cost, which makes the method suited to large numbers of calculations such as virtual screening. In other respects it is the same as the Poisson-Boltzmann variant, MM-PBSA. (UNVERIFIED)

An energy analysis that computes the change in potential energy when 2 or more molecules or fragments are brought from infinite separation to their positions in a complex, with the geometry of the complex held fixed. It is usually the sum of the electrostatic and van der Waals interactions between the parts, or of their quantum mechanical counterparts such as electrostatics, exchange-repulsion, induction and dispersion. It normally leaves out the energy needed to distort each fragment on binding and the effect of solvation, so it is only 1 part of the total binding energy. (UNVERIFIED)

A specific type of interaction energy analysis focused on quantifying the energetic contribution of individual or collective hydrogen bonds within or between molecules. This can be estimated using specialized energy decomposition schemes, analysis of electrostatic and van der Waals terms between donor-hydrogen-acceptor atoms from a force field, or derived from quantum mechanical calculations. Quantifying H-bond energies helps understand their role in stabilizing structures and mediating molecular recognition. (UNVERIFIED)

A specific interaction energy analysis quantifying the stabilizing energetic contribution from the non-covalent interactions (primarily van der Waals/dispersions and electrostatics) between adjacent nucleobases (DNA, RNA). These interactions occur between the aromatic base rings and are essential for the stability, geometry, and mechanical properties of nucleic acid structures. Stacking interaction energies are commonly estimated using quantum mechanical methods or specially parameterized molecular mechanics force fields.

This refers to one of the file formats used by Amber to store atomic coordinates. Its extension is commonly .inpcrd, .crd or .mdcrd. It contains a list of coordinates in ASCII, usually read alongside a topology file, and may optionally include periodic box information.

comments: Amber's standard ASCII coordinate trajectory file format. The "Coordinates Data Set" or "COORDS" in Amber is not a file format, but rather a specialized, in-memory data structure used by the cpptraj analysis program. It is designed to efficiently hold and manipulate sets of coordinate frames (i.e., structures) loaded from trajectory files during an analysis session. Since the COORDS data set is an internal, in-memory representation, it does not have a file extension. Users can interact with it using file-based commands: Loading: users populate a COORDS data set by loading data from standard Amber file formats, such as restart files (.rst7), PDB files, or trajectory files (.nc, .mdcrd), using the loadcrd command. Saving: users write the contents of a COORDS data set to a file using the crdout command. The output will be in a standard coordinate or trajectory format (e.g., Amber restart, PDB, etc.), not a special "COORDS format."

definition.val: A category of analysis methods focused specifically on characterizing the structure, dynamics, and properties of the solvent molecules (most commonly water) surrounding a solute molecule within a simulation. This includes examining solvent density and distribution around the solute, analyzing hydrogen bonding networks within the solvent and between solvent and solute, calculating residence times of solvent molecules near the solute, and assessing the overall impact of the solvent on solute behavior. It provides crucial insights into solvation phenomena. (UNVERIFIED)

A hydration analysis that divides the water around a solute into concentric layers, or shells, usually by distance from the solute atoms or surface, and characterizes the water in each shell. It reports, for example, the number of water molecules, their density, preferred orientations, hydrogen bonding patterns and residence times compared with bulk water. This gives a structured description of the local solvent environment. (UNVERIFIED)

A distribution analysis that calculates the probability of finding a particle at a distance r from a reference particle or point, relative to the probability for a uniform distribution at the same density. The resulting radial distribution function, g(r), shows peaks for ordered solvation shells and approaches 1 at large distances, where the solvent behaves as bulk. Integrating it up to its first minimum gives the average number of neighbors in the first solvation shell. (UNVERIFIED)

A specific type of validation technique focused on assessing the quality of the 3-dimensional arrangement of atoms (the conformation) in simulated biomolecules. It evaluates whether the molecular geometry, including bond lengths, angles, and steric arrangements, is plausible according to known chemical and physical rules. This ensures the structural models generated or sampled during a simulation are stereochemically sound. (UNVERIFIED)

A structural analysis that plots the backbone dihedral angles phi and psi of each amino acid residue in a protein, to show whether they fall in regions that are sterically allowed or disallowed. It is used to check the quality and realism of a protein backbone structure. In simulations it also shows which backbone conformations, such as helix or sheet, a protein samples. (UNVERIFIED)

A form of conformation validation that involves examining various geometric features of a biomolecular structure beyond just backbone torsion angles. This may include verifying appropriate bond lengths, bond angles, checking for unrealistic close contacts between atoms (clashes), or assessing other stereochemical parameters against standard values. It serves as a general quality control measure for the overall molecular model.

Refers to the regular, local folding patterns occurring within the backbone of polymers like proteins or nucleic acids, such as alpha-helices and beta-sheets in proteins. These structures are defined by specific patterns of hydrogen bonds between backbone atoms and represent key building blocks of the molecule's overall three-dimensional architecture. While not a technique itself, analyzing secondary structure content and stability is often part of simulation validation and analysis.

Refers to the dynamic transformations or fluctuations observed in the secondary structure elements of a biomolecule during a simulation or over time. Monitoring these changes, such as the formation or dissolution of helices or sheets, provides insights into molecular flexibility, folding pathways, or responses to interactions. Analyzing these dynamics helps understand how molecular function relates to structural transitions.

A specific type of solvent analysis focusing on the direct interaction of water molecules with a solute molecule. It involves characterizing the arrangement, orientation, dynamics, and energetics of water molecules in the immediate vicinity of the solute, often referred to as the hydration shell(s). Understanding hydration patterns is critical as these interfacial water molecules strongly influence the solute's structure, stability, dynamics, and interactions with other molecules. (UNVERIFIED)

A solvent analysis technique focused on determining the average spatial arrangement or probability density of solvent molecules relative to the solute molecule, averaged over a simulation trajectory. This often involves calculating various distribution functions (e.g., radial, spatial, or angular) that quantify how the likelihood of finding a solvent molecule varies with position and/or orientation around the solute. It reveals preferred solvation sites and the overall structure of the solvent environment. (UNVERIFIED)

A core mathematical technique from linear algebra used to simplify a square matrix by finding its characteristic values (eigenvalues) and directions (eigenvectors), effectively transforming it into a diagonal matrix. In biomolecular simulations, this is heavily used in methods like Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to identify dominant modes of collective atomic motion from covariance matrices, or in Normal Mode Analysis (NMA) to find vibrational frequencies from Hessian matrices. Diagonalization reveals the fundamental components or modes underlying complex data or system dynamics. (UNVERIFIED)

A coarse-grained model in which groups of atoms, or whole residues, are represented as beads joined by simple springs.
