The springs are chosen to reproduce the overall shape and flexibility of the assembly rather than any chemistry, so the model can cover structures far too large to simulate atom by atom. What it can show is how the parts move relative to each other; what it cannot show is anything that depends on a specific chemical group. (UNVERIFIED)

A coarse-grained model that treats a polymer as a bendable filament described by 2 numbers: its total length, and the distance over which it stays pointing the same way. In a simulation it is built as a chain of beads whose bond and angle terms reproduce those 2 numbers. It is how DNA is modelled when what matters is how it coils and loops rather than which base is where. (UNVERIFIED)

Experimental or computational methods used alongside Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations to provide synergistic information, validate simulation accuracy, or compute properties challenging for standard MD alone. These techniques bridge simulation results with real-world measurements or provide deeper thermodynamic or structural insights. They help build a more comprehensive understanding of the molecular system under study.

An experimental Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) phenomenon that arises from the through-space dipolar coupling between nearby nuclear spins (commonly protons), used as a complementary technique to MD. Detecting NOEs allows measurement of short inter-proton distances (typically < 6 Å), providing crucial experimental restraints for determining or validating biomolecular structures and conformational ensembles in solution. MD simulations can be used to predict NOEs for comparison with experiments or refined using experimental NOE data.

An experimental technique, either using X-rays (SAXS) or neutrons (SANS), where radiation is scattered by molecules in solution at low angles, providing information complementary to MD simulations. The resulting scattering profile is sensitive to the overall size, shape, and quaternary structure (oligomerization) of the molecules, averaged over the entire ensemble present in the sample. SAS data provides valuable low-resolution structural information that can be used to validate conformational ensembles generated by MD or to guide modeling of large-scale structures. (UNVERIFIED)

Spectroscopy is the study of how matter interacts with energy, particularly electromagnetic radiation like light. By analyzing how energy is absorbed, emitted, or scattered by a substance, we can learn about its atomic and molecular structure, composition, and dynamics. It serves as a fundamental set of tools for observing the properties of molecules.

A spectroscopic technique that probes how the bonds in a molecule stretch, bend and twist, by measuring absorption in the infrared or scattering of visible light. Each vibration has a frequency set by the masses involved and the stiffness of the bond, so the spectrum reports on chemical structure. Infrared absorption and Raman scattering are its 2 main forms. (UNVERIFIED)

A spectrum recording how strongly a sample absorbs infrared light across a range of frequencies. Absorption occurs where the frequency matches a molecular vibration that changes the molecule's dipole, so the positions of the bands identify chemical groups. Its band positions can be compared with vibrational frequencies computed by quantum chemical or force field methods. (UNVERIFIED)

A spectrum recording the small shift in frequency of light scattered by a sample, which reveals the vibrations that took or gave energy to the photons. It detects vibrations that change the molecule's polarizability, while infrared absorption detects those that change its dipole, so the 2 methods often show different bands. They are therefore complementary rather than alternatives. (UNVERIFIED)

A spectrum recorded with the illuminating light tuned close to, but not at, an electronic absorption band of the sample. Approaching an absorption greatly enhances the scattering from vibrations connected with it, so a chosen part of a large molecule dominates the spectrum. It is used to study a selected site, such as the active site of a complex biomolecule. (UNVERIFIED)

A spectroscopic technique measuring the difference in infrared absorption between left and right circularly polarized light. Only molecules that are not superimposable on their mirror images show such a difference, and the sign of each band reveals which form is present. It reports on 3-dimensional structure in solution, where ordinary infrared absorption reports only on which groups are there. (UNVERIFIED)

A spectroscopic technique that probes transitions of electrons between energy levels, usually driven by ultraviolet or visible light. The energy absorbed or emitted reports on the spacing of those levels, which depends on bonding and conjugation. It is how colour, fluorescence and photochemical behaviour are studied. (UNVERIFIED)

A spectrum recording how strongly a sample absorbs light across the ultraviolet and visible range, as a function of wavelength. Absorption occurs where the photon energy matches a gap between electronic levels, so the positions of the bands report on bonding and conjugation. It is the measurement a computed electronic transition is compared against. (UNVERIFIED)

A property giving the full profile of an absorption or emission band in an electronic spectrum, including its width and any structure within it, rather than only where its peak lies. The width reports how much the molecule's geometry changes when it absorbs light, and the structure within it reveals individual vibrations. A calculation matching only the peak position can still be wrong about both. (UNVERIFIED)

A spectroscopic technique that probes the magnetic behaviour of nuclei or unpaired electrons, by observing how they respond in an applied magnetic field. The response depends on the local environment of each spin, which is what makes it report on structure. Nuclear magnetic resonance and electron paramagnetic resonance belong here. (UNVERIFIED)

An interaction between nearby unpaired electron spins that favours their pointing in opposite directions. The paired arrangement has lower energy than the aligned one, so the system has little or no net magnetism. It occurs between metal centres in many metalloproteins and determines their magnetic signature. (UNVERIFIED)

A 3-by-3 array describing how strongly an electron spin interacts with a nearby nuclear spin, and how that strength depends on direction. Its directional part reports where the unpaired electron sits relative to the nucleus. It is what electron paramagnetic resonance spectra are interpreted through. (UNVERIFIED)

A spectroscopic technique that probes transitions between a molecule's rotational energy levels, almost always in the gas phase where molecules turn freely. The spacing of the levels depends on how the molecule's mass is distributed, so the spectrum gives bond lengths and angles very precisely. It is among the most accurate structural measurements available and works only for small molecules. (UNVERIFIED)

An interaction between a molecule's vibration and its rotation, arising because a vibrating molecule changes shape and so changes how easily it turns. It means the 2 motions cannot be treated as independent. It shows in a spectrum as a shift in rotational line spacing that depends on which vibrational state the molecule is in. (UNVERIFIED)

A spectroscopic technique that measures how a sample responds differently to left and right circularly polarized light. Only molecules that are not superimposable on their mirror images give such a difference, so these techniques report on handedness. Optical rotation, circular dichroism and Raman optical activity belong here. (UNVERIFIED)

A chiroptical spectroscopy technique that measures the small difference in the intensity of Raman scattering from chiral molecules in right versus left circularly polarized light. It combines the vibrational information of Raman spectroscopy with sensitivity to a molecule's handedness and 3-dimensional structure. It is especially useful for studying the shape of biomolecules in water, close to their natural conditions. (UNVERIFIED)

The turning of the plane of polarized light as it passes through a sample of molecules that are not superimposable on their mirror images. The direction and size of the turn depend on which mirror form is present and in what excess. It is how the handedness of a sample is measured, and computing it correctly is a demanding test of a quantum method. (UNVERIFIED)

A statistical analysis that smooths short-term fluctuations in a time series and shows longer-term trends by averaging a property over a time window that slides along the series. The average is recomputed each time the window moves forward. Watching the running average of a property such as total energy or temperature is a common way to judge whether a simulation has reached a stable equilibrium. (UNVERIFIED)

A text-based file format used by the GROMOS simulation software to store the complete configuration of a molecular system. It is organized into data blocks (e.g., POSITION, VELOCITY, BOX) and contains atomic coordinates, periodic box dimensions, and optionally velocities. This format typically uses the .cnf file extension and is the primary input for coordinates in GROMOS simulations. (UNVERIFIED)

A file format for the MPDyn simulation program that stores the atomic coordinates of a molecular system. This format contains the x, y, and z positions for each atom, structured for use with the MPDyn software package. It provides the essential structural input for running simulations with MPDyn. (UNVERIFIED)

The .trj format is an ASCII (text-based) trajectory file format used by the Amber molecular dynamics software suite and other analysis programs. Its fundamental purpose is to store a time-series of atomic coordinates, capturing the dynamic motion of a system during a simulation. The file contains sequential "frames" where each frame is a complete set of X, Y, and Z coordinates for every atom in the system at a specific point in time. It can also store periodic box dimensions, although this capability is sometimes limited.

comments: The .trj format belongs to a family of older Amber text-based trajectory formats. Its role is best understood in comparison to its relatives: vs. .mdcrd: The .trj and .mdcrd formats are functionally identical. Both are safe, relatively unambiguous choices for storing Amber ASCII trajectories. A file with one extension can often be renamed to the other without causing issues in analysis software. vs. .crd: The .crd extension is highly ambiguous and problematic. It is the native format for the CHARMM simulation package and is interpreted as such by default in many tools. Using .trj avoids this critical format conflict. vs. .nc (NetCDF): The NetCDF format is the modern, binary, and recommended format for Amber trajectories. Compared to .trj, NetCDF (.nc) files are smaller, faster to read/write, and store data with higher precision. The .trj format is considered a legacy option.

definition.val: A distance matrix in molecular simulation is a 2D data set that stores the pairwise distances between a selection of particles, such as atoms or residues, calculated from a simulation trajectory. It is a common form of analysis used to study conformational changes, structural stability, and the relative movement of different parts of a molecule.

comments: Common examples include: - General Text Formats: Often saved as plain text (.txt), comma-separated values (.csv), or a generic data (.dat) file for easy parsing and use in other programs. - Program-Specific Formats: Some simulation packages output the matrix in their own specific formats. For example, GROMACS can generate a distance matrix as an .xpm file, which is a portable pixmap image format. - Binary Formats: For efficiency, especially with large matrices, they may be saved in binary formats like NumPy's .npy format, which is common in Python-based analysis workflows.

definition.val: A text data format that stores a 2-dimensional matrix, such as a distance matrix, an RMSD matrix or a hydrogen bond pattern, by encoding each value as a character standing for a colour. It is a specialised use of the general XPixMap image format, so an ordinary image viewer can open it. GROMACS writes it and converts it to PostScript with gmx xpm2ps. (UNVERIFIED)

A text data format that holds the complete static description of a molecular system for an AMBER simulation: its atoms, the bonds between them, the force field parameters that govern their interactions, and their partial charges. It carries everything the simulation engine needs except the coordinates, which come from a separate file. It is read once at the start of a run and does not change during it. (UNVERIFIED)

OBSOLETE. A file format from the Amber simulation software that describes the structure and force field parameters of a molecule. This is the traditional, ASCII-based version of the Amber parameter/topology file, containing all information needed to calculate forces on the system. It is often used interchangeably with the prmtop format.

comments: Retired 2026-08-07 as an internal duplicate of MOLSIM:001042 prmtop format. ParmEd writes one Amber topology format under two extensions, .prmtop and .parm7, so these were never two formats. Both terms also carried skos:exactMatch to the same EDAM term, EDAM:format_3881 AMBER top, which is what surfaced the duplication. prmtop survives because it is the name that actually occurs in practice: 19 occurrences against 0 for parm7 in the AMBER keyword corpus this ontology was extracted from. Its names are kept as exact synonyms on MOLSIM:001042.

definition.val: The Crystallographic Information File (cif) format is a standard text-based file format used to store information about molecular structures, especially those determined by experiments. It uses a flexible tag-based structure with key-value pairs, making it more robust and extensible for handling the large, complex structures and extensive metadata common in modern structural biology. As the official format of the Protein Data Bank (PDB), the macromolecular CIF (mmCIF) variant has superseded the older PDB format for archiving and distributing 3D coordinates of proteins and nucleic acids.

A file format used by the TINKER simulation package to store the trajectory of a molecular system. It archives the atomic coordinates from different snapshots of a simulation in a single file for later analysis. This is the standard trajectory output for TINKER simulations. (UNVERIFIED)

comments: This can also be a coordinate format from Tinker package as well.

definition.val: The original residue number is the number assigned to an amino acid in the original experimental data file. As a type of identifier, it represents the residue number as it appeared in the source file, typically a PDB file, before any renumbering may have occurred during simulation setup. This is crucial for mapping simulation results back to the standard numbering used in publications and other databases, especially when multiple chains or insertions are present.

comments: The residue number as it appeared in the original input (e.g., PDB) file

definition.val: A chain ID is a letter used to label different polymer molecules, like different protein chains, in a structure file. The chain ID usually has a limited number of characters like in the PDB format (1) or in mmCIF and PSF formats (4). It is an essential part of the atom selection syntax in analysis tools, allowing for targeting of specific molecules in a system.

comments: An identifier used in PDB files to distinguish different polymer chains.

definition.val: An insertion code is a letter used in PDB and mmCIF structure files when extra amino acids have been inserted into a sequence without renumbering every residue after the insertion, thus allowing multiple residues to share the same residue number. This code is critical for unambiguously identifying specific residues in atom selections (e.g. residue "10A" is distinct from "10B"). This is referred to in PDB files as "icode".

comments: A character used in PDB files to handle insertions in a sequence.

definition.val: A file format from the Amber software that saves the state of a simulation in plain text, allowing the run to be continued later. It contains the atomic coordinates, velocities, and periodic box dimensions at a specific point in time, in a human-readable form. The same ASCII format is written under several extensions, including .rst, .rst7 and .restrt. (UNVERIFIED)

OBSOLETE. A text-based file format from the Amber software that saves the state of a simulation. It is the ASCII version of the Amber restart file, containing coordinates, velocities, and box information in a human-readable format. This format is often used for its portability and ease of inspection.

comments: Retired 2026-08-07 as an internal duplicate of MOLSIM:001049 rst format. ParmEd writes one Amber ASCII coordinate format under several extensions, .rst7, .restrt and .inpcrd, so .rst and .rst7 were never two formats; the real division in this family is ASCII against the binary NetCDF MOLSIM:001051 ncrst format. Both terms also carried skos:closeMatch to the same EDAM term, EDAM:format_3886 RST, which is the pattern that surfaced the duplication. The curator chose rst as the surviving label; note that ParmEd itself does not write a .rst extension, so rst7 format and restrt format are kept as exact synonyms on MOLSIM:001049.

definition.val: A binary data format from AMBER, built on the NetCDF container, that saves the state of a simulation at one moment so that the run can be continued. It stores the coordinates, the velocities, the box dimensions and the time with high precision. It is the default and recommended restart format in current AMBER versions. (UNVERIFIED)

comments: A NetCDF-based restart file for Amber simulations.

definition.val: CHARMM commonly uses coordinate files in its own CARD format (.crd), which is a formatted ASCII file including atom coordinates along with atom numbers, residue names/numbers, atom types, and possibly weighting factors. It often starts with a title section describing the system.

A file format from the CHARMM simulation software that stores the atomic coordinates of a molecule. It is a binary, unformatted version of the CHARMM coordinate file, making it more compact and faster to read than its text-based counterpart. This format is often used for saving and reading structures within CHARMM workflows. (UNVERIFIED)

A binary file format from the GROMACS software that stores the full-precision trajectory of a simulation. It saves the atomic coordinates, velocities, and forces at each time step without any loss of precision. This format is used instead of XTC format when high accuracy is needed for analysis.

A compressed, binary file format from the GROMACS software for storing the trajectory of a molecular simulation. It uses a lossy compression algorithm to store atomic coordinates with reduced precision, resulting in much smaller file sizes. This is the most common trajectory format for GROMACS users when only atomic positions are needed for analysis. (UNVERIFIED)

A modern, binary file format from the GROMACS software used to store the results of a molecular simulation. It supports various compression algorithms and can store not only coordinates but also velocities, forces, and other trajectory data. This format is designed for high efficiency and flexibility in storing large simulation datasets. (UNVERIFIED)

An input file format for sqm, the semi-empirical quantum chemistry program in AmberTools, holding a title line, a namelist of calculation settings, and then 1 line per atom giving its atomic number, atom name and Cartesian coordinates. Its main use is in deriving AM1-BCC partial charges for new molecules, a step that antechamber carries out by running sqm. (UNVERIFIED)

comments: An input file format for the semi-empirical QM program SQM.

definition.val: A binary file format used by the Desmond simulation software to store the trajectory of a molecular system. It efficiently stores atomic coordinates, velocities, and other data in a block-based structure. This is the native trajectory output format for simulations run with Desmond. (UNVERIFIED)

comments: A trajectory file format used by the Desmond simulation software.

definition.val: A data format holding the lowest-energy conformations found by a low-mode (LMOD) conformational search in AmberTools, stored in order of energy with the global minimum first. It uses the standard formatted AMBER trajectory layout and is updated at intervals as the search proceeds. How many conformations it keeps, and within what energy window of the minimum, are set by the user. (UNVERIFIED)

A binary data format built on HDF5 in which the MDTraj library stores trajectories together with the topology they belong to. Keeping both in one file removes the usual need to supply a separate topology when reading a trajectory. It is the native format of that library rather than a community standard. (UNVERIFIED)

comments: An HDF5-based trajectory file format used by the MDTraj library.

definition.val: A data format for molecular simulation data, defined as a community standard on top of the general-purpose HDF5 container. It specifies where positions, velocities, forces and metadata are placed, so any program following it can read another's output. It belongs to no single simulation program, which is what distinguishes it from the engine-specific formats. (UNVERIFIED)

The PQR format is a modification of the standard Protein Data Bank (PDB) format used in computational biology to store atomic coordinate data along with atomic partial charges (Q) and radii (R). The name itself is a mnemonic, representing PDB + Q (charge) + R (radius). Its primary advantage is that it bundles the necessary structural and electrostatic parameters into a single, PDB-like file that is easily parsed by both analysis software and molecular visualization programs. These files are most commonly generated by the PDB2PQR software, which processes a standard PDB file, adds missing hydrogen atoms, and assigns atomic charges and radii based on a chosen force field.

The Molecular Operating Environment (MOE) is a comprehensive, commercial software system for drug discovery, molecular modeling, and computational chemistry developed by the Chemical Computing Group. It integrates visualization with a vast array of tools for structure preparation, docking, pharmacophore modeling, and molecular dynamics setup within a single unified interface.

A flexible version of the 3-site TIP3P water model, in which the O-H bonds and the H-O-H angle are described by harmonic terms rather than held rigid. Flexibility is needed when vibrational spectra are computed, or when the model is used with a method that cannot handle constraints. It requires a shorter timestep, because bond vibrations are the fastest motion in the system. (UNVERIFIED)

comments: A flexible three-site water model.

definition.val: A water model with 3 sites, derived from the SPC geometry, whose bonds and angle can stretch and bend. Its bonded parameters were refitted alongside the flexibility so that the liquid's density and diffusion stay correct. Making a rigid model flexible without refitting changes both. (UNVERIFIED)

comments: A flexible three-site water model.

definition.val: A text data format in which the secstruct command of cpptraj writes secondary structure results as 1 line per frame, giving the frame number and then 1 character for each residue, in the layout the older ptraj program used. It fixes no file extension, and it is kept so that the output can still be read by tools written for ptraj. (UNVERIFIED)

Xmgrace is a computer program used to make scientific graphs and plots from data. As a type of visualization tool, Xmgrace is a 2D plotting program for X Window Systems. Some simulation analysis tools, like GROMACS and cpptraj, can directly generate output files in a compatible format for easy plotting of time-series data like RMSD or energy. This tool is associated with file formats like .agr and .xvg.

A visualization tool that draws 2-dimensional and 3-dimensional graphs from data files, driven from the command line or from a script. Because it is scriptable it can be called from an analysis pipeline to produce figures without a person present. It is one of the standard ways simulation output is plotted. (UNVERIFIED)

A visualization program for displaying and animating molecular structures and trajectories in 3 dimensions. It handles systems of millions of atoms and includes Tcl and Python scripting, so analyses can be run on what is being shown. It is widely used to inspect molecular dynamics trajectories. (UNVERIFIED)

A visualization plugin for VMD that draws and animates collective modes of motion from normal mode analysis or principal component analysis. It shows a mode as arrows on the structure, or as a trajectory moving along it. It turns an eigenvector into something that can be looked at. (UNVERIFIED)

comments: A VMD plugin for visualizing and analyzing normal modes.

definition.val: A data format that records a 3-dimensional histogram as though it were the path of a single particle, writing the 3 histogram dimensions as the x, y and z coordinates of 1 atom over successive frames. That trick lets a volumetric distribution, such as where water sits around a solute, be opened in a molecular viewer as a point cloud. It is produced by the hist command of cpptraj. (UNVERIFIED)

comments: The traj3d "pseudo-trajectory" is not a standard, independent file format but rather a specialized output option available within the hist command in Amber's cpptraj analysis program. It is created by taking the three data dimensions of a 3D histogram and writing them out as the X, Y, and Z coordinates of a single "atom" over time. This reformatting creates a trajectory-like file that can be loaded into molecular visualization software. The purpose is to allow researchers to visually inspect the 3D distribution of data from the histogram in a more intuitive, interactive 3D space, rather than as a static 2D plot. There is no mandatory file extension for the output file itself.

definition.val: OBSOLETE. An information content entity is an abstract concept representing any piece of data, information, or knowledge that can be identified and described. In the context of simulations, it refers to the abstract data itself, such as the concept of a molecular structure or a simulation parameter set, separate from the specific file format used to store it. This distinction helps in organizing and standardizing the description of simulation data and metadata.

comments: Retired 2026-08-12 when MOLSIM adopted COB as its upper level. IAO:0000030 information content entity is one of COB's five roots and says the same thing, so keeping a MOLSIM class beside it was a duplicate. Its 8 direct children were re-parented onto IAO:0000030 in the same change; the 46 terms below them moved with their parents.

definition.val: A molecular system specification defines the physical and chemical properties of a molecule required for computational chemistry and quantum mechanical simulations. This specification is the complete informational blueprint of the system before any simulation is performed.

A process specification is the abstract set of instructions and parameters that define how a computational task, like a simulation or an analysis, should be performed. It represents the complete plan for the process, including the choice of algorithms, control settings, and input files. This specification must be recorded to ensure a computational experiment is reproducible.

An output file is generated by a computational program and contains the results of the calculation or simulation, along with logs, progress information, and any error messages. These files are crucial for analyzing the outcome of computational jobs.

A molecular system specification that describes what a molecular system is made of: its atoms, their types and charges, the bonds between them, and the force field parameters that apply. In most simulations it does not change during the run, which is why it is kept separate from the coordinates. Without it, a set of coordinates cannot be read as molecules. (UNVERIFIED)

A category of data formats used by the CHARMM simulation package to describe the molecular topology of a system. These formats define the atoms, connectivity, and the chemical nature of residues. (UNVERIFIED)

A data format used by CHARMM that defines a reusable template for one chemical building block, such as an amino acid or a nucleotide. It gives the atoms in that block, their types and charges, the bonds between them, and their standard geometry. A topology for a whole molecule is assembled by joining these templates in sequence. (UNVERIFIED)

A text data format used by AMBER to supply force field parameters that are missing from the main parameter files, or to override ones that are present. It lets a user add parameters for a non-standard molecule without editing the distributed force field. It is read in addition to the main files rather than in place of them. (UNVERIFIED)

The complete collection of settings that tells a program how to run one simulation, including the temperature and pressure to hold, how long to run, how often to save, and which physical approximations to use. It is normally kept as a single input file. Together with the starting structure it is what would be needed to repeat the run exactly. (UNVERIFIED)

A simulation trajectory is the record of a molecule's motion over time, captured during a simulation. It consists of a time-ordered sequence of snapshots or "frames" where each frame contains the 3D coordinates of all atoms at a specific instant. This trajectory is the primary output of a molecular dynamics simulation and is the raw data used for all subsequent analysis of the system's dynamic behavior.

A simulation log is a text file that records everything that happened during a computer simulation. As a type of process output, the simulation log is a human-readable file that contains a time-ordered record of a simulation run, including an echo of input parameters, performance data, and periodic updates of thermodynamic properties. This file is the primary source for monitoring the progress and stability of a simulation and for diagnosing errors.

A process output that holds the complete set of information needed to resume a simulation exactly where it stopped. It includes the atomic positions and velocities, the box dimensions, and the internal variables of any thermostat or barostat. Restarting from positions alone gives a different trajectory, because the missing quantities are re-initialised. (UNVERIFIED)

Analysis data is the information content that is the result of analyzing simulation data. This includes any derived quantities calculated from a trajectory, such as RMSD values over time, a potential of mean force profile, or a list of identified hydrogen bonds. This processed data represents the scientific findings extracted from the simulation.

A category for file formats designed to store information about molecules, such as their structure, movement, or the forces governing them. These formats provide standardized ways to represent molecular systems for use in computational chemistry and biology software. This class includes formats for atomic coordinates, trajectories, and force field parameters.

A prep format in which the geometry of the new building block is given as internal coordinates, that is, a bond length, an angle and a dihedral angle for each atom relative to atoms already placed. It is otherwise the same as the variant that uses Cartesian coordinates. Geometry in this form can define a building block's ideal shape without a starting 3-dimensional structure. (UNVERIFIED)

OBSOLETE. A file format specifically designed to describe the complex, three-dimensional structures of large biological molecules like proteins and DNA. These formats accommodate hierarchical descriptions, such as chains and residues, in addition to atomic coordinates. Examples include the widely used PDB and mmCIF formats.

comments: Retired in the file-format flattening. Classifying structure formats by molecule size was an artificial distinction: a small molecule can be stored in a PDB file and a macromolecule in a mol2 file. Its former children are now direct children of 'molecular structure format' (MOLSIM:001088). Reported in GitHub issue #20.

definition.val: A type of file format that describes the three-dimensional arrangement of atoms in a molecule. These formats store atomic coordinates and often include information about chemical bonds and residue identity. They are essential for visualizing molecules and providing the starting point for simulations.

OBSOLETE. A coordinate file primarily stores the three-dimensional positions (X, Y, Z coordinates) of atoms in a molecular system. It may also contain atom names, residue information, and potentially periodic box dimensions, but typically lacks detailed bonding (topology) or force field parameter information. Common examples include PDB, GRO, and XYZ formats, used for initial structures or snapshots from simulations.

comments: Retired in the same file-format flattening. Grouping coordinate formats by the software that writes them proved unhelpful, since formats are not owned by one program. Its former children are now direct children of 'molecular structure format' (MOLSIM:001088). Related discussion in GitHub issue #20.

definition.val: A trajectory file stores the history of atomic positions (and sometimes velocities, forces, energies or the simulation box size) recorded at regular intervals during a molecular dynamics simulation. It contains a series of snapshots (or frames) representing the system's movement over time. Analyzing trajectories allows researchers to study dynamic processes, conformational changes, and calculate time-averaged properties.

A file format that defines the atoms of a molecular system, how they are bonded together, and the force field parameters that apply to them. This includes atom types, partial charges, and parameters for bonds, angles, dihedral angles, and non-bonded interactions (like Lennard-Jones parameters). It essentially provides the 'rules' for how atoms interact in a molecular mechanics simulation. (UNVERIFIED)

A prep format in which the geometry of the new building block is given as Cartesian coordinates, that is, 3 numbers per atom. It is otherwise the same as the variant that uses internal coordinates. Geometry in this form is easier to produce from an existing structure file. (UNVERIFIED)

A text data format used by CHARMM that holds the numerical force field parameters: force constants, preferred bond lengths and angles, rotation terms and van der Waals values. It is paired with a separate file defining the residues those parameters apply to. The 2 together are what a CHARMM topology is built from. (UNVERIFIED)

A data format that specifies the 3-dimensional arrangement of atoms inside a Gaussian input file, either as Cartesian x, y and z coordinates or as a Z-matrix of bond lengths, angles and dihedral angles. The Z-matrix form is chosen when internal coordinates or molecular symmetry need to be held fixed; the Cartesian form is simpler and more common. Both appear in the same place in the input file. (UNVERIFIED)

A data format specifying a molecule's geometry inside a Gaussian input file as bond lengths, angles and rotations relative to atoms already placed. It is chosen when a geometry must be scanned or constrained, because one number can be varied or frozen directly. It is harder to write than plain coordinates and is not used unless that control is wanted. (UNVERIFIED)

A data format specifying a molecule's geometry inside a Gaussian input file as an element symbol followed by x, y and z coordinates for each atom. It is a simple and common way to give Gaussian a geometry, and is easy to generate from ordinary structure files. Unlike a Z-matrix, it does not single out bond lengths or angles that can be varied or held fixed. (UNVERIFIED)

A text data format holding the settings for a run of the paramfit program in AmberTools, which fits force field parameters to quantum mechanical or experimental reference data. It is written as assignments of the form variable=value, 1 per line, and says what kind of run is wanted, which parameters are to be fitted and which reference data to fit against. (UNVERIFIED)

A text data format holding the parameters of a ReaxFF reactive force field, which are far more numerous than a conventional force field needs because bonding is computed from the distances between atoms rather than fixed in advance. A single file covers every element combination the parameter set supports. Parameters fitted for different element sets are not interchangeable, so the file determines which chemistry can be simulated. (UNVERIFIED)

A data format, held in files known as Slater-Koster files, that stores the pre-calculated electronic and repulsive properties between pairs of atom types for a density functional tight binding calculation. The values are derived once from more expensive quantum mechanical calculations and then reused. That reuse is what makes the method fast while keeping a quantum mechanical description of the system. (UNVERIFIED)

A text data format listing the covalent bonds that may be cut when the core, quantum and buffer regions of an adaptive buffered force-mixing QM/MM simulation are drawn, so that region boundaries fall at chemically sensible places. Each line names 2 atoms, by atom type or by index, joined by an arrow that says from which side the bond may be broken. (UNVERIFIED)

A text data format that defines the clusters used in reservoir replica exchange molecular dynamics with dihedral bin clustering, listing the dihedral angles that define the clusters, the weight of each cluster and which cluster each reservoir structure belongs to. The weights let structures from the reservoir enter the simulation with a non-Boltzmann weighting. It can be written by the dihedral clustering analysis of cpptraj. (UNVERIFIED)

A simulation parameter format that holds the control settings for an EMIL absolute free energy calculation in AMBER, conventionally in a file named emilParameters.in. It records the reference model parameters and the integration settings that the calculation needs. (UNVERIFIED)

basicPropertyValues.val: Berryman J.T. Absolute free energies for biomolecules in implicit or explicit solvent. Physics Procedia, 2014. States that the AMBER implementation of this method is called EMIL.

Berryman J.T. and Schilling T. Free energies by thermodynamic integration relative to an exact solution, used to find the handedness-switching salt concentration for DNA. J. Chem. Theory Comput. 9(1):679-686, 2013.

definition.val: The cein format is a specialized input file used in constant redox-potential MD simulations. It defines the properties of residues that can exist in different oxidation states, such as a cysteine that can be oxidized or reduced. This file provides the necessary parameters for a constant redox potential simulation, allowing the system to dynamically change its electronic state in response to a defined electrochemical potential.

The cpein format is a complex input file for constant pH and electrochemical potential (CpH/E) MD simulations that simultaneously model changes in both protonation and electron-transfer states. It defines the properties of residues that can be affected by both the surrounding pH and the electrochemical potential. This format is required when studying complex bioenergetic processes where proton and electron transfers are coupled.

A molecular structure format, based on the macromolecular Crystallographic Information File format, that describes 1 chemical building block, giving its atom names, elements, bonds, charges and ideal coordinates. Each file acts as a dictionary entry that deposited structures refer to rather than repeat, as in the Chemical Component Dictionary of the Protein Data Bank. It is how a ligand or a modified residue is described once and reused. (UNVERIFIED)

A data format that stores the results of analysing how solvent molecules are arranged and behave around a solute. Files in these formats typically hold values on a 3-dimensional grid, such as the chance of finding a solvent atom at a point or the average interaction energy there. Examples include solvent density maps and the correlation functions produced by 3D-RISM theory. (UNVERIFIED)

A data format that stores a 3-dimensional grid giving the chance of finding a solvent molecule at each position around a solute, relative to a random distribution. The value at each point is the pair distribution function g(r): above 1 means the solvent gathers there, below 1 means it is pushed away. Peaks in the grid mark solvation shells and hydrogen bonding sites. (UNVERIFIED)

A data format that stores a 3-dimensional grid of the direct correlation function c(r) between a solute and the surrounding solvent. It isolates the solute's direct influence on a solvent molecule at each position, leaving out effects passed along through other solvent molecules. It is a basic quantity in liquid-state theories such as 3D-RISM and is used to derive thermodynamic properties of solvation. (UNVERIFIED)

A data format that stores a 3-dimensional grid of the total correlation function h(r) between a solute and the surrounding solvent. It gives the whole departure from a random solvent distribution caused by the solute, counting both direct and indirect effects, and it relates to the pair distribution function as h(r) = g(r) − 1. It is used in liquid-state theories to calculate solvation properties. (UNVERIFIED)

This file format stores a 3D map of the potential energy experienced by the solvent molecules in the space surrounding a central solute. The value at each grid point represents the average potential energy of the solvent at that location, reflecting the combined interactions with the solute and other solvent molecules. This format provides a view of the energetic landscape of the solvent, which can be used to identify energetically favorable or unfavorable regions for solvation.

A data format that stores a 3-dimensional grid of the average electric charge density contributed by solvent molecules around a solute. Unlike a map of where solvent atoms sit, it gives the net positive or negative charge at each point, averaged over the simulation. It shows how the solvent screens and responds to the solute's own charges. (UNVERIFIED)

A data format that stores a 3-dimensional grid giving the solvent charge at each grid point around a solute, as a point charge in units of the elementary charge, combining the contributions of all solvent atom types. It differs from a charge density map, which gives charge per unit volume at each point. It is an output of 3D-RISM calculations. (UNVERIFIED)

A data format that stores a 3-dimensional grid of the interaction energy a solvent molecule would feel at each position around a solute. Negative values mark positions the solvent is drawn to and positive values mark positions it is pushed away from. The grid shows the energetic landscape that determines how solvent arranges itself. (UNVERIFIED)

A text data format in which a 1D-RISM calculation writes how a property of the bulk solvent, such as the pair distribution, the direct correlation or the site-site potential, varies with distance for every pair of solvent sites. After a few header lines starting with #, each line gives a separation followed by the value for each site pair. The susceptibility file that 3D-RISM reads is written in a different format. (UNVERIFIED)

A data format that stores, for every pair of sites in a bulk solvent, the total excess coordination number: how many more sites of one type surround a site of the other type than a uniform distribution would give. It measures how strongly the solvent structures itself. It is written by 1D-RISM calculations in a file ending in .n00. (UNVERIFIED)

A data format that stores, for every pair of sites in a bulk solvent, the total excess charge of one site type gathered around the other, compared with a uniform distribution. It is laid out as a table with 1 row and 1 column per solvent site, plus the total excess charge from all sites. It is written by 1D-RISM calculations in a file ending in .q00. (UNVERIFIED)

A data format in which Gaussian writes the electrostatic potential it computed at a set of points around a molecule, together with those points' coordinates. It is the input a charge fitting program reads. The choice of where the points lie affects the charges obtained, so it is part of the fitting protocol rather than an incidental detail. (UNVERIFIED)

The mdinfo format is a text file generated by the Amber simulation software that provides a concise, real-time summary of a running simulation. It contains the most recently calculated energy terms and thermodynamic properties, such as temperature and pressure, formatted for easy monitoring. This file is continuously updated during a run, making it useful for checking the immediate status and stability of a simulation without having to parse the much larger main output file.

A database web server is an online application that provides a graphical interface for searching, visualizing, and retrieving data from a structured repository. It acts as an accessible gateway, allowing researchers to query complex datasets and download specific entries without needing direct interaction with the underlying database management system.

A standard text-based file format designed for exchanging NMR-derived information, particularly structural restraints like distances and angles. It provides a standardized way to represent experimental data used for structure calculation and simulation refinement. (UNVERIFIED)

An input variable or algorithmic setting defined prior to execution that governs the behavior, conditions, or numerical rules of a computational process (encompassing both simulation generation and post-run analysis). (UNVERIFIED)

An input setting that determines the physical interactions, boundary conditions or integration rules used to generate a trajectory. Examples are the target temperature a thermostat holds, the size of the timestep, and the distance beyond which interactions are ignored. These settings are part of what a result means, so a simulation cannot be reproduced or judged without them. (UNVERIFIED)

A simulation parameter controlling how the equations of motion are advanced in time, including the timestep, the integration algorithm and how long the run lasts. The timestep matters most: too large a value makes the simulation unstable, and too small a value makes it slower than necessary. (UNVERIFIED)

An integration parameter that gives the length of simulated time between 2 successive steps of a molecular dynamics integration. It must be short enough to follow the fastest atomic motions, such as the vibration of bonds to hydrogen, for the integration to stay stable, while a longer step lowers the cost of covering a given length of simulated time. (UNVERIFIED)

An integration parameter that gives the total length of simulated time for which a simulation is run. It determines how many different conformations can be visited and which slow processes can be observed at all. In most programs it is set indirectly, as a number of steps multiplied by the time step. (UNVERIFIED)

A specific type of simulation duration that defines the length of a single stage within a multi-stage simulation protocol. This is used in methods like steered MD or umbrella sampling but also during density adaptation and equilibration workflows, where the overall process is broken down into smaller, sequential runs. The simulation time per stage ensures that each part of the protocol is run for a defined period. This is often specified as nsteps within a block for a specific stage.

An integration parameter giving the conditions under which an energy minimization stops. The usual conditions are that the largest force on any atom, or the root-mean-square of all the forces, has fallen below a threshold, or that the energy has stopped changing between steps. A minimization that stops too early leaves strain in the structure, which can make the first steps of the following simulation unstable. (UNVERIFIED)

A minimization convergence criterion based on the root-mean-square of the energy gradient, which measures how large the forces on the atoms are. The minimization stops when this root-mean-square value falls below the chosen threshold. It is a common way to define when a minimization has converged. (UNVERIFIED)

basicPropertyValues.val: AMBER 26 Reference Manual, p. 434, entry drms.

definition.val: A minimization convergence criterion giving the threshold on the energy gradient below which an energy minimization is stopped. A smaller value makes the geometry optimization stricter and needs more steps. (UNVERIFIED)

A simulation parameter that fixes which quantities are held constant during a run, and so which statistical ensemble is sampled. Holding particle number, volume and temperature gives one ensemble; holding pressure instead of volume gives another. The choice determines which averages taken from the trajectory are meaningful. (UNVERIFIED)

A thermodynamic ensemble parameter specifying how the temperature is held at its target, covering the thermostat algorithm, the target value and the coupling strength. A thermostat both holds the temperature and changes the dynamics, so these settings affect more than the average temperature. They must be reported with any result that depends on rates. (UNVERIFIED)

A temperature control parameter naming which algorithm holds the temperature, such as Berendsen, Nosé-Hoover or stochastic velocity rescaling. They differ in whether they produce the correct spread of energies or only the correct average. The Berendsen scheme does not, which is why it is used to bring a system to temperature and then replaced. (UNVERIFIED)

A temperature control parameter that specifies the temperature at which the simulation is to be held. The thermostat adjusts the velocities of the atoms so that the instantaneous temperature fluctuates around this value. It is used only when a thermostat is applied, not in a run at constant energy. (UNVERIFIED)

basicPropertyValues.val: AMBER 26 Reference Manual, p. 436, entry temp0.

definition.val: A temperature control parameter setting how strongly the system is coupled to the simulated heat bath. Strong coupling holds the temperature close to target and interferes with the natural motion; weak coupling leaves the dynamics alone and lets the temperature wander. Any quantity involving rates depends on this choice. (UNVERIFIED)

A thermostat coupling parameter specifying the time constant of the coupling between the system and the heat bath, which sets how quickly the kinetic temperature is driven towards the target temperature.

basicPropertyValues.val: AMBER 26 Reference Manual, p. 436, entry tautp.

definition.val: A thermostat coupling parameter giving how often, on average, a particle receives a random kick from the simulated bath in a stochastic thermostat. A high frequency reaches the target temperature quickly and turns the motion into a random walk; a low one preserves the real dynamics and controls temperature weakly. It is the stochastic counterpart of a coupling time constant. (UNVERIFIED)

basicPropertyValues.val: AMBER 26 Reference Manual, p. 216, entry gamma_ln.

definition.val: A thermodynamic ensemble parameter specifying how the pressure is held at its target, covering the barostat algorithm, the target value, the coupling strength and the compressibility. The barostat changes the volume of the simulation box so that the average pressure matches the target. These settings apply only to constant-pressure runs. (UNVERIFIED)

A pressure control parameter naming which algorithm holds the pressure at its target, such as Berendsen, Parrinello-Rahman or a Monte Carlo scheme. They differ in whether they generate the correct distribution of volumes or merely the correct average. The Berendsen scheme equilibrates quickly and does not give the correct distribution, which is why it is used to settle a system and then replaced. (UNVERIFIED)

A pressure control parameter that specifies the pressure at which a constant-pressure simulation is to be held. The barostat changes the volume of the simulation box so that the instantaneous pressure fluctuates around this value. It is used only in constant-pressure simulations. (UNVERIFIED)

basicPropertyValues.val: AMBER 26 Reference Manual, p. 438, entry pres0.

definition.val: A pressure control parameter giving the time constant over which a barostat relaxes the system pressure towards the target pressure.

basicPropertyValues.val: AMBER 26 Reference Manual, p. 438, entry taup.

definition.val: A pressure control parameter giving how much the system's volume changes for a given change in pressure. Some barostats need it to work out how far to scale the box when correcting pressure. For a system in water the value for water is normally used, because water fills most of the box. (UNVERIFIED)

basicPropertyValues.val: AMBER 26 Reference Manual, p. 438, entry comp.

definition.val: A simulation parameter controlling how interactions between atoms are computed, covering the cutoff distances, the long-range electrostatic method and the treatment at the cutoff. These settings determine how much of each interaction is actually included. They affect both cost and correctness, which is why they are reported with any published simulation. (UNVERIFIED)

An interaction parameter controlling how van der Waals and short-range electrostatic interactions are computed, covering the cutoff distance, the treatment at that cutoff, and the neighbour list settings. These settings decide how much of the interaction is included and what happens at the boundary. They are among the few settings that affect both speed and correctness directly. (UNVERIFIED)

A non-bonded interaction parameter naming how interactions are handled at the cutoff distance, such as truncating them sharply, shifting them so that they reach zero at the cutoff, or smoothly switching them to zero over a range. A sharp truncation makes the energy and the force change abruptly when a pair of atoms crosses the cutoff, which harms energy conservation. The choice therefore affects the stability of a simulation as well as its accuracy. (UNVERIFIED)

A non-bonded interaction parameter that specifies the single distance beyond which both van der Waals and electrostatic interactions are no longer calculated directly. Leaving out pairs farther apart than this distance is one of the main ways to reduce the cost of a simulation, and using 1 distance for both kinds of interaction is common. Programs that allow the 2 distances to be set separately use a more specific parameter for each. (UNVERIFIED)

basicPropertyValues.val: AMBER 26 Reference Manual, p. 456, entry cut.
AMBER 26 Reference Manual, p. 467, card CUT, which names this quantity the non-bonded cutoff distance.
NAMD 3.x User's Guide, p. 55, section 5.2.3, entry cutoff. States that the cutoff is the local interaction distance common to both electrostatic and van der Waals calculations.

definition.val: A non-bonded interaction parameter giving the distance at which a switching function starts to reduce the interaction, so that it reaches zero at the cutoff. Without such smoothing, the energy and the force change abruptly when a pair of atoms crosses the cutoff, which harms energy conservation. The gap between this distance and the cutoff sets how gradual that transition is. (UNVERIFIED)

A non-bonded interaction parameter giving how many steps pass between rebuilds of the neighbour list. Rebuilding often is safe and costly; rebuilding rarely is cheap and risks missing a pair that has moved into range. It is chosen together with the pairlist skin, since a thicker skin allows a longer interval. (UNVERIFIED)

basicPropertyValues.val: AMBER 26 Reference Manual, p. 456, entry nsnb.

definition.val: A non-bonded interaction parameter giving the extra distance beyond the cutoff within which pairs of atoms are recorded in the neighbour list. Including pairs that are not yet interacting means the list stays valid for several steps as atoms move, so it need not be rebuilt every step. Too small a value lets a pair reach interaction range unnoticed, which silently loses interactions. (UNVERIFIED)

An interaction parameter controlling how electrostatic interactions are computed. Its members cover which long-range method is used and the settings that method needs, such as grid spacing and real-space cutoff. These settings determine accuracy and cost together, so they are chosen as a set rather than individually. (UNVERIFIED)

An electrostatic parameter naming which algorithm computes the long-range electrostatic interactions, such as particle mesh Ewald, plain Ewald summation, or a reaction field. Electrostatic forces fall off slowly enough that simply ignoring them past a cutoff introduces visible artefacts. The choice of method is therefore part of what a published simulation must state. (UNVERIFIED)

An electrostatic parameter giving how far apart the points of the reciprocal-space grid lie in a particle mesh Ewald calculation. A finer grid is more accurate and costs more, and the cost rises with the cube of the refinement. It trades off against the real-space cutoff, so the 2 should be chosen together rather than separately. (UNVERIFIED)

basicPropertyValues.val: AMBER 26 Reference Manual, p. 500, entry fft_grids_per_ang.

definition.val: An electrostatic parameter used by the particle mesh Ewald (PME) method that gives the number of grid points along each box dimension for the reciprocal-space calculation. More grid points for the same box give a more accurate calculation at a higher cost. The numbers are usually chosen automatically from the box size and a target grid spacing, but can also be set directly. (UNVERIFIED)

An electrostatic parameter giving how strongly a medium screens the electrostatic interaction between charges within it, relative to a vacuum. It is 1 in vacuum and usually also in explicit solvent simulations, where the water molecules do the screening themselves. Implicit solvent models instead give the inside of the solute a low value and the surrounding solvent a high one, to stand in for solvent that is not present. (UNVERIFIED)

A dielectric constant that describes the interior of the solute in a continuum solvation calculation. It is set low, usually between 1 and 4, because the packed interior of a molecule screens charge poorly. Its value is one of the largest sources of variation between published binding free energy estimates. (UNVERIFIED)

basicPropertyValues.val: AMBER 26 Reference Manual, p. 82, entry epsin.
AMBER 26 Reference Manual, p. 952, entry indi.

definition.val: A dielectric constant that describes the bulk solvent surrounding a solute in a continuum solvation calculation. It is set high, near 80 for water, so that the solvent screens electrostatic interactions strongly. Together with the internal value it fixes the dielectric boundary at the molecular surface. (UNVERIFIED)

basicPropertyValues.val: AMBER 26 Reference Manual, p. 82, entry epsout.
AMBER 26 Reference Manual, p. 952, entry exdi.

definition.val: An electrostatic parameter giving the distance at which the directly summed part of an Ewald calculation stops. Raising it moves work out of the reciprocal-space part and into the real-space part, and lowering it does the reverse. The accuracy of the whole calculation depends on this distance together with the reciprocal-space grid and the coefficient that sets how the interaction is divided between the 2 parts. (UNVERIFIED)

basicPropertyValues.val: AMBER 26 Reference Manual, p. 499, entry es_cutoff.

definition.val: An interaction parameter giving the strength, direction and time dependence of a field applied to the system from outside. It is what specifies an applied electric field in a simulation of ion transport or of a membrane under voltage. Without it the field has no defined magnitude. (UNVERIFIED)

basicPropertyValues.val: AMBER 26 Reference Manual, p. 457, entry efx.

definition.val: An external field parameter that gives the strength of an applied external electric field along 1 Cartesian axis. The components along the 3 axes together set the direction and strength of a uniform field acting on the charged particles of the system. Such a field is used to simulate the effect of an applied field or voltage on the molecules. (UNVERIFIED)

A type of simulation parameter that controls the application of geometric constraints or restraints to the system. Constraints are used to fix certain degrees of freedom, while restraints are used to guide the system towards a particular conformation. These constraint and restraint parameter settings are used to control the flexibility of the system or to apply experimental data.

A parameter controlling how geometric constraints are applied, most often to hold bonds involving hydrogen at a fixed length. Fixing those bonds removes the fastest motion in the system, which permits a longer timestep, typically about twice as long. Its members say which bonds are held, by which algorithm, and how exactly. (UNVERIFIED)

A constraint parameter naming which algorithm enforces the geometric constraints, such as SHAKE, RATTLE, LINCS or SETTLE. The choice affects speed and how well the constraints are held, not what is being constrained. SETTLE is used for water specifically, because water's constraints have an exact solution that needs no iteration. (UNVERIFIED)

A constraint parameter naming which bonds are held at a fixed length, usually as a choice between all bonds, only the bonds involving hydrogen, or none. Constraining only the bonds involving hydrogen is the most common choice, because most force fields were parameterised that way and it permits a longer timestep. Constraining all bonds is slower and is not needed at timesteps up to about 2.5 femtoseconds. (UNVERIFIED)

A constraint parameter giving how close to its target length a constrained bond must be before the algorithm stops adjusting it. A tighter value holds the geometry more exactly and takes more iterations each step. Too loose a value lets energy drift over a long run, which is the usual sign it was set badly. (UNVERIFIED)

A type of constraint and restraint parameter that specifies how artificial restraining potentials are applied to the system. These are used to guide the simulation towards a specific conformation. The restraint parameter settings are essential for biased simulations and structure refinement. These are often set with keywords like restraint_wt and restraintmask.

A restraint parameter that specifies the force constant for a harmonic or other restraining potential. A larger restraint energy constant results in a stronger force pulling the restrained atoms towards their target values. This is a key parameter for controlling the strength of the applied restraints. This is often set with the keyword restraint_wt.

basicPropertyValues.val: AMBER 26 Reference Manual, p. 433, entry restraint_wt.

definition.val: A restraint parameter that names which atoms a restraining force applies to, written as a selection expression rather than a list. It is what lets part of a system be held in place while the rest moves freely, such as holding a protein still while water settles around it. A mask that selects the wrong atoms produces a simulation that runs normally and means something else. (UNVERIFIED)

basicPropertyValues.val: AMBER 26 Reference Manual, p. 433, entry restraintmask.

definition.val: A specific restraint energy constant used to apply a restraining potential to a spherical cap of water molecules around a solute. This is used in some simulation setups to prevent the solute from becoming exposed to the vacuum. The water cap force constant controls the strength of this spherical boundary potential. This is often set with the keyword fcap.

basicPropertyValues.val: AMBER 26 Reference Manual, p. 454, entry fcap.

definition.val: A simulation parameter that fixes what the system is made of and what state it is in, rather than how it is advanced in time. Examples are the box dimensions, the pH and the protonation states, the ionic strength and the state of the chain ends. Most are chosen once while the system is built, although some, such as the box size in a constant-pressure run, change while it runs. (UNVERIFIED)

A system setup parameter giving the acidity of the simulated solution. It determines which acidic and basic groups carry a proton, and so the charge on the molecule. In an ordinary simulation it is used once to assign fixed protonation states; in a constant pH simulation it is held during the run and the states respond to it. (UNVERIFIED)

A system setup parameter that specifies the molar concentration of salt in the simulation solvent. The ionic strength affects the screening of electrostatic interactions and is crucial for mimicking experimental buffer conditions. This is a key parameter for accurately modeling the electrostatic environment of the system. This is often set with the keyword ion_concentration or saltcon.

basicPropertyValues.val: AMBER 26 Reference Manual, p. 73, entry saltcon.
AMBER 26 Reference Manual, p. 984, entry ion_concentration.

definition.val: A system setup parameter that specifies the size and shape of the periodic box used to create a periodic system. The periodic box dimensions are essential for any simulation using periodic boundary conditions. They determine the overall density of the system.

A system setup parameter giving the chemical state of each end of a polymer chain: charged, neutral, or capped with a group that mimics the continuation of the chain. Capping is used when the simulated fragment is part of a longer chain in reality, so that an artificial charge is not introduced. A wrong choice adds or removes charge at exactly the place a fragment is most exposed. (UNVERIFIED)

A system setup parameter that specifies whether the simulation involves an alchemical transformation for a free energy calculation. This parameter indicates that some atoms/residues in the system have their properties changed over the course of the simulation. The alchemical transformation state is a key descriptor for identifying free energy calculations. This is often controlled by a perturbation flag (lambda, λ).

A simulation process parameter that specifies the number of independent simulation runs performed from the same or similar initial conditions. Running number of replicates helps to assess the statistical robustness and convergence of simulation results. This is a key parameter of the overall simulation experimental design.

A system setup parameter giving the target value of the tension, a force per unit length, acting in the plane of an interface in a constant-pressure simulation of a membrane or a liquid surface. The box is scaled in the plane of the interface to bring the tension towards this value, while the pressure normal to the interface is controlled separately. A value of 0, the AMBER default, describes an interface under no tension. (UNVERIFIED)

basicPropertyValues.val: AMBER 26 Reference Manual, p. 439, entry gamma_ten.

definition.val: A system setup parameter giving the number of QM/MM partitionings used in an adaptive solvent QM/MM simulation, in which solvent molecules can pass between the quantum and the classical region. Each partitioning assigns the solvent molecules in a transition region between the 2 regions differently to the quantum or the classical description, and the energy is a weighted average over the partitionings. With N solvent molecules in the transition region, N + 1 partitionings carry a nonzero weight. (UNVERIFIED)

basicPropertyValues.val: AMBER 26 Reference Manual, p. 211, entry n_partition.

definition.val: A type of simulation parameter that controls the application of a specific enhanced sampling method designed to accelerate the exploration of the system's conformational space. These parameters define the nature and strength of the biasing potential or other modifications to the standard simulation protocol.

A type of enhanced sampling parameter that controls a steered molecular dynamics (sMD) simulation, where an external force is applied to pull the system along a specific coordinate. These parameters define the pulling speed, force constant, and direction of the steering. The steered molecular dynamics parameter settings are essential for setting up non-equilibrium pulling simulations. These are often set with keywords like smd.

A steered molecular dynamics parameter that specifies the constant speed at which the steered coordinate is changed during a constant-velocity sMD simulation. The atom pulling velocity determines the rate at which the system is pulled in agreement with the selected reaction coordinate. This is often set with the keyword v.

A steered molecular dynamics parameter that specifies the stiffness of the harmonic potential used to pull the system along the reaction coordinate. A larger steered MD restraint energy constant results in a stiffer spring and less deviation from the target path. This is a key parameter for controlling the strength of the steering. This is often set with the keyword harm.

basicPropertyValues.val: AMBER 26 Reference Manual, p. 610, entry harm.

definition.val: A steered molecular dynamics parameter that specifies the total number of distinct stages or windows used in a staged sMD simulation protocol. This allows for the pulling to occur incrementally or for parameters to be changed between stages. The number of sMD stages is a key parameter for setting up complex pulling protocols. This is often set with the keyword nstage.

A type of enhanced sampling parameter that controls an umbrella sampling simulation, where a biasing potential is used to confine the system to specific windows along a reaction coordinate. These parameters define the location and strength of the biasing potential in each window. The umbrella sampling parameter settings are essential for setting up simulations to calculate a potential of mean force. These are often set in the input file for each window.

An umbrella sampling parameter that specifies the strength of the harmonic biasing potential applied in each umbrella sampling window. This force constant determines how strongly the system is restrained around the target value of the reaction coordinate for that window. The umbrella sampling restraint energy constant is a key parameter for ensuring sufficient sampling within each window. This is often set with the keyword anchor_strength.

An umbrella sampling parameter that specifies the total number of individual simulations (windows) performed in an umbrella sampling workflow. Each window is typically centered at a different value along the reaction coordinate. The number of umbrella sampling windows is a key parameter for ensuring adequate coverage of the entire reaction coordinate.

An umbrella sampling parameter that determines the center or boundaries of the harmonic potential for a specific umbrella sampling window. This parameter defines the region of the reaction coordinate that will be sampled in that window. The umbrella anchor position is a key parameter that is varied between different windows. This is often set with the keyword anchor_position.

A type of enhanced sampling parameter that controls an accelerated molecular dynamics (aMD) simulation. These parameters define the energy threshold and strength of the boost potential that is applied to flatten the energy landscape. The accelerated MD parameter settings are crucial for controlling the degree of enhanced sampling. These are often set in a specific amd section of the input file.

An accelerated MD parameter that specifies the energy threshold for the dihedral energy, below which the biased potential is applied. This parameter controls when the dihedral energy term is biased. The aMD dihedral energy threshold is a key parameter for tuning the aMD simulation. This is often set with the keyword EthreshD.

A scaling parameter used to flatten high potential energy barriers, allowing the simulation to explore conformational space much faster. It dictates the magnitude of the bias applied to the system's dihedral degrees of freedom. A smaller aMD dihedral alpha factor results in a larger boost. This is a key parameter for tuning the aMD simulation. This is often set with the keyword alphaD.

An accelerated MD parameter that specifies the energy threshold for the total potential energy, below which the biased potential is applied. This parameter controls when the total potential energy is biased. The aMD potential energy threshold is a key parameter for tuning the aMD simulation. This is often set with the keyword EthreshP.

An accelerated MD parameter that determines the strength of the biased potential applied to the total potential energy term. A smaller aMD potential alpha factor results in a larger boost. This is a key parameter for tuning the aMD simulation. This is often set with the keyword alphaP.

A type of enhanced sampling parameter that controls a Gaussian accelerated molecular dynamics (GaMD) simulation. These parameters define the upper limit of the standard deviation for the potential energy boost. The Gaussian accelerated MD parameter settings are crucial for controlling the balance between accuracy and enhanced sampling. These are often set in a specific gamd section of the input file.

A Gaussian accelerated MD parameter that specifies the upper limit of the standard deviation for the potential energy boost. This parameter controls the maximum strength of the applied bias. This is often set with keywords like sigma0P or sigma0D.

basicPropertyValues.val: AMBER 26 Reference Manual, p. 526, entry sigma0D.
AMBER 26 Reference Manual, p. 526, entry sigma0P.

definition.val: A type of enhanced sampling parameter that controls a random acceleration molecular dynamics (RAMD) simulation. These parameters define the strength of the randomly applied acceleration force. The random acceleration MD parameter settings are crucial for enhancing the exploration of conformational space. These are often set in a specific ramd section of the input file.

A random acceleration MD parameter that specifies the strength of the acceleration boost applied in a Random Acceleration Molecular Dynamics (RAMD) simulation. This parameter controls the magnitude of the random forces used to accelerate the system's exploration. The RAMD boost strength is a key parameter for tuning the RAMD simulation. This is often set with the keyword ramdboost.

basicPropertyValues.val: AMBER 26 Reference Manual, p. 458, entry ramdboost.

definition.val: A type of enhanced sampling parameter that controls a targeted molecular dynamics (TMD) simulation. These parameters define the target structure and the strength of the biasing potential used to guide the simulation towards it. The targeted MD parameter settings are essential for simulating large-scale conformational transitions between known start and end states. These are often set in a specific tmd section of the input file.

A targeted MD parameter that specifies the force constant for the RMSD restraint potential used to guide the simulation towards the target structure. A larger targeted MD force constant results in a stronger biasing force. This is a key parameter for controlling the strength of the targeted MD simulation. This is often set with the keyword tgtmdfrc.

basicPropertyValues.val: AMBER 26 Reference Manual, p. 532, entry tgtmdfrc.

definition.val: A targeted MD parameter that specifies the target root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) value for the restraint. The simulation is guided to reduce the RMSD of the current structure relative to a reference structure to this targeted MD RMSD target value. This is a key parameter for defining the endpoint of the TMD simulation. This is often set with the keyword tgtrmsd.

basicPropertyValues.val: AMBER 26 Reference Manual, p. 532, entry tgtrmsd.

definition.val: A type of enhanced sampling parameter that controls a nudged elastic band (NEB) simulation, which is used to find the minimum energy path between two conformations. These parameters define the number of intermediate structures (images) and the spring constants connecting them. The nudged elastic band parameter settings are essential for accurately mapping reaction pathways. These are often set in a specific neb section of the input file.

A nudged elastic band parameter that specifies the spring force constant connecting adjacent images along the reaction path. This parameter ensures that the images are evenly spaced and do not drift off the path. The NEB spring constant is a key parameter for the stability and convergence of the NEB calculation. This is often set with the keyword nebk.

basicPropertyValues.val: AMBER 26 Reference Manual, p. 550, entry nebk.

definition.val: A nudged elastic band parameter that specifies the number of intermediate structures (images) to optimize along the reaction path. A larger NEB number of images provides a more detailed representation of the path but is computationally more expensive. This is a key parameter for controlling the resolution of the NEB calculation. This is often set with the keyword neb_nimage.

basicPropertyValues.val: AMBER 26 Reference Manual, p. 550, entry neb_nimage.

definition.val: A type of enhanced sampling parameter that controls a well-tempered metadynamics simulation. These parameters define how the height of the added Gaussian hills is rescaled over time, ensuring that the simulation eventually converges. The well-tempered metadynamics parameter settings are crucial for obtaining converged free energy surfaces. These are often set in a specific metadynamics section of the input file.

A well-tempered metadynamics parameter that controls the rate at which the height of the added Gaussian hills decreases. A higher well-tempered pseudo-temperature results in a faster convergence but a less detailed exploration of the energy landscape. This is a key parameter for tuning the well-tempered metadynamics simulation. This is often set with the keyword wt_temperature.

basicPropertyValues.val: AMBER 26 Reference Manual, p. 613, entry wt_temperature.

definition.val: A simulation parameter that controls a calculation in which part of the system is treated with quantum mechanics and the rest with a force field. Its members set which atoms are in the quantum region, which quantum method is used, and how bonds crossing the boundary are handled. Such hybrid calculations are used mainly to study chemical reactions, such as those in enzyme active sites, where bonds are formed or broken. (UNVERIFIED)

A QM/MM parameter giving the total charge of the quantum region as a whole number. The quantum calculation needs a definite number of electrons, so this cannot be left to be worked out.
