Setting it wrong gives a calculation that runs to completion and describes a different chemical species. (UNVERIFIED)

basicPropertyValues.val: AMBER 26 Reference Manual, p. 159, entry qmcharge.

definition.val: A QM/MM parameter giving the distance from a quantum atom to the link atom placed along its bond to a classical atom. The link atom, usually a hydrogen, fills the free valence left where the boundary between the quantum and classical regions cuts a covalent bond. In AMBER all link atoms are placed at the same distance, by default 1.09 ångström. (UNVERIFIED)

basicPropertyValues.val: AMBER 26 Reference Manual, p. 175, entry lnk_dis.

definition.val: A QM/MM parameter giving the cutoff distance for electrostatic interactions between the quantum region and the classical region. Classical atoms within this distance of any quantum atom interact directly with the quantum region, and when a particle mesh Ewald treatment is used the value only divides the work between the direct and the reciprocal parts. In AMBER it is by default equal to the cutoff used for the classical region. (UNVERIFIED)

basicPropertyValues.val: AMBER 26 Reference Manual, p. 172, entry qmcut.

definition.val: A QM/MM parameter controlling a density functional tight binding calculation, covering which parameter files are used, how many charge iterations are allowed and how tightly they must converge. The parameter files are specific to each pair of elements, so a system containing an unparameterised pair cannot be run. Checking that first saves discovering it at run time. (UNVERIFIED)

A parameter giving the greatest number of self-consistent charge iterations a tight binding calculation may take. It stops a calculation that will not converge from running indefinitely. Reaching the limit means the charges are not converged and the result must not be used. (UNVERIFIED)

basicPropertyValues.val: AMBER 26 Reference Manual, p. 159, entry dftb_maxiter.

definition.val: A DFTB parameter giving the electronic temperature used to spread the occupation of orbitals near the highest occupied level according to a Fermi distribution, which helps the self-consistent charge iterations of a density functional tight binding calculation converge. The spreading mixes the highest occupied and lowest unoccupied orbitals a little, which helps in difficult cases where the occupation would otherwise switch between iterations. It is a numerical aid rather than a physical temperature, so it is used only when needed and the results are then checked carefully. (UNVERIFIED)

basicPropertyValues.val: AMBER 26 Reference Manual, p. 159, entry dftb_telec.

definition.val: A QM/MM parameter controlling the self-consistent field procedure, the iterative calculation that finds the electronic structure of the quantum region. Its members set how closely successive iterations must agree, how many iterations are allowed, and which scheme is used to speed up or stabilise convergence. They are usually left at their defaults and adjusted when a difficult system fails to converge. (UNVERIFIED)

A self-consistent field parameter giving the greatest number of iterations the calculation may take before it is treated as not converged. It stops a calculation that will not converge from running indefinitely. A result reached at the limit is not converged, although some programs continue with it, so it needs checking before it is used. (UNVERIFIED)

basicPropertyValues.val: AMBER 26 Reference Manual, p. 161, entry itrmax.

definition.val: A parameter giving how little the energy or the electron density must change between iterations for a self-consistent field calculation to be considered finished. A tighter value gives a more accurate result and takes more iterations. Forces need a tighter setting than energies, because they are more sensitive to a partly converged density. (UNVERIFIED)

basicPropertyValues.val: AMBER 26 Reference Manual, p. 160, entry scfconv.

definition.val: A parameter giving how much of the previous iteration's electron density is mixed into the next one. Mixing slows the calculation down and stops it oscillating between 2 near-solutions. It is raised when a difficult system will not converge and lowered otherwise, because it costs iterations. (UNVERIFIED)

basicPropertyValues.val: AMBER 26 Reference Manual, p. 479, entry damp.

definition.val: A self-consistent field parameter that controls the direct inversion in the iterative subspace procedure, which speeds up convergence by extrapolating from previous iterations. The values set how many previous iterations are kept and how many extrapolation attempts are made. Poor settings make a calculation converge slowly or oscillate without settling. (UNVERIFIED)

A DIIS parameter giving the number of self-consistent field iterations in which an extrapolation by direct inversion in the iterative subspace is attempted. In AMBER these attempts start only after 100 iterations have failed to converge, so the setting matters only for molecules that are hard to converge. A larger value gives the extrapolation more iterations in which to succeed. (UNVERIFIED)

basicPropertyValues.val: AMBER 26 Reference Manual, p. 162, entry ndiis_attempts.

definition.val: A DIIS parameter giving how many previous error vectors the convergence accelerator keeps and extrapolates from. It sets the size of the subspace used, so a larger value uses more history and more memory. Too few gives a poor extrapolation and too many can include iterations no longer relevant. (UNVERIFIED)

A simulation parameter controlling a constant pH run, covering how often protonation changes are attempted, how long the system is allowed to relax after one, and at what pH the simulation is held. These settings determine whether the protonation states are sampled properly or barely move. They are specific to this kind of simulation and appear nowhere else. (UNVERIFIED)

A constant pH parameter giving how many simulation steps pass between attempts to change a residue's protonation state. Attempting more often samples the protonation states better and costs more, because each attempt requires extra calculation. Attempting too rarely leaves a residue stuck in one state for most of the run. (UNVERIFIED)

nodes.lbl: number of CpHMD solvent relaxation steps

definition.val: A constant pH parameter that specifies the number of solvent relaxation steps performed after a protonation state change. Those steps let the solvent reorient around the residue that has just been charged or neutralised. (UNVERIFIED)

A simulation parameter controlling a run with a polarizable force field, covering how the induced dipoles are solved for and how tightly they must converge. A loose convergence makes the forces slightly inconsistent with the energy, which shows as energy drift. These settings do not arise at all with a fixed-charge force field. (UNVERIFIED)

A polarizable force field parameter giving how little the induced dipoles must change between iterations before they are accepted. A tighter value gives forces closer to the exact ones and costs more iterations each step. Too loose a value makes the forces slightly inconsistent with the energy, which shows up as energy drift. (UNVERIFIED)

basicPropertyValues.val: AMBER 26 Reference Manual, p. 465, entry dipole_scf_tol.

definition.val: An input setting that determines the mathematical, statistical or filtering rules applied when existing simulation data is processed. Examples are the distance below which 2 structures count as similar, the size of a block in an error estimate, and the spacing of an analysis grid. The same trajectory analysed with different settings gives different numbers, so they are part of the result. (UNVERIFIED)

A type of analysis parameter that controls a clustering algorithm used to group similar molecular conformations from a trajectory. These parameters define the distance metric, the cutoff for cluster membership, and the number of clusters to be generated. The clustering parameter settings are crucial for identifying the dominant conformational states sampled in a simulation.

A clustering parameter that specifies the distance threshold for grouping conformations into the same cluster. Two structures with a distance (e.g., RMSD) less than the clustering distance cutoff are considered to be in the same cluster. This is a key parameter for defining the granularity of the clustering. This is often set with the keyword epsilon or cutoff.

A clustering parameter giving how many groups the algorithm should produce. Algorithms such as k-means require it in advance, so it is chosen either from prior knowledge or by trying several values and comparing a quality measure. Choosing it badly either merges distinct conformations or splits one into several. (UNVERIFIED)

An analysis parameter that controls how a 3-dimensional grid of values is produced, such as a density or an electrostatic potential map. Its members set where the grid sits, how far apart its points are and what is computed at each. Spacing chosen too coarsely hides features; chosen too finely it produces files too large to handle. (UNVERIFIED)

A volumetric analysis parameter giving the distance between neighbouring points of a 3-dimensional grid. A finer grid resolves smaller features and produces a file whose size grows with the cube of the refinement. Too coarse a grid can hide small features, such as the sites of ordered water molecules. (UNVERIFIED)

basicPropertyValues.val: AMBER 26 Reference Manual, p. 138, entry grdspc.

definition.val: A volumetric analysis parameter naming which quantity is computed at each point of a 3-dimensional grid, such as a density, an interaction energy or a correlation function. The choice determines what the resulting map shows. The available choices depend on the analysis program. (UNVERIFIED)
A volumetric analysis parameter that specifies the number of points in each dimension of a three-dimensional grid. It controls the size and the resolution of the volumetric data. (UNVERIFIED)

An analysis parameter controlling a statistical calculation, such as the confidence level, the number of resampling trials or the block size. These settings determine what an error bar means, so a value quoted without them cannot be interpreted. They are part of the result rather than an implementation detail. (UNVERIFIED)

A statistical analysis parameter giving the value below which a result is called significant. It is the probability of calling a result significant when there is in fact no effect, so setting it at 0.05 accepts such a false result in 1 of every 20 tests where no effect exists. It must be chosen before the data are examined, or it means nothing. (UNVERIFIED)

A statistical analysis parameter giving the proportion of confidence intervals that would contain the true value if the whole procedure of sampling and calculating the interval were repeated many times. A level of 95% means 19 such intervals in 20 would contain it. It does not mean there is a 95% chance the true value lies in the particular interval computed. (UNVERIFIED)

A statistical analysis parameter giving how many times the data are resampled in a bootstrap estimate. More resamples make the estimate of the uncertainty itself more stable, at a cost that grows in proportion. They do not make the underlying data more informative, which is a common misunderstanding of this setting. (UNVERIFIED)

A statistical analysis parameter giving the width of the smooth bumps placed on each data point in a kernel density estimate. Too narrow a width shows every random fluctuation as a peak; too wide a one merges genuinely separate peaks into one. It is the single most consequential choice in such an estimate. (UNVERIFIED)

An analysis parameter that controls how a free energy is calculated from simulation data. The group covers settings for end-point methods such as MM-PBSA, for thermodynamic integration, for the analysis of umbrella sampling and for 3D-RISM solvation calculations. The same simulation data analysed with different settings can give different free energies, so the settings are reported with the result. (UNVERIFIED)

A free energy analysis parameter that controls a molecular mechanics Poisson-Boltzmann or generalized Born surface area calculation. Its members set the continuum solvent model and the surface area treatment. Different choices for these settings are a common reason why published binding free energies for the same system disagree. (UNVERIFIED)

A dielectric constant that describes an implicit membrane slab in a continuum solvation calculation. It is set low to represent the non-polar lipid core, which screens charge about as poorly as a protein interior. It is what makes burying a charge in the membrane region cost energy in the model. (UNVERIFIED)

basicPropertyValues.val: AMBER 26 Reference Manual, p. 953, entry emem.

definition.val: A parameter giving the radius of the sphere rolled over a molecule's van der Waals surface to define its solvent-accessible surface area. It is normally set to 1.4 ångström, the effective radius of a water molecule. It controls how far into clefts the solvent is considered to reach, and so it changes the non-polar part of the solvation free energy. (UNVERIFIED)

basicPropertyValues.val: AMBER 26 Reference Manual, p. 952, entry prbrad.

definition.val: A parameter giving the constant term added to the surface-area estimate of the non-polar solvation free energy. It accounts for the part of that energy which does not scale with area. It is fitted together with the surface tension coefficient, so the 2 should not be taken from different sources. (UNVERIFIED)

A parameter giving the coefficient that converts solvent-accessible surface area into non-polar solvation free energy. It has the same role as the surface tension of a large interface, but its value is obtained by fitting to data rather than by measurement. It is fitted together with the cavity offset. (UNVERIFIED)

A free energy analysis parameter that controls a thermodynamic integration calculation. Its members set how many intermediate coupling states are used and how they are spaced along the path. Too few or badly spaced states leave the integral under-sampled where the energy changes fastest. (UNVERIFIED)

A thermodynamic integration parameter giving how many intermediate coupling states are simulated along the transformation path. More windows make the numerical integration more accurate and the calculation proportionally more expensive. Too few leaves the integrand under-sampled where it changes fastest, which is usually near the end points. (UNVERIFIED)

A type of free energy analysis parameter that controls the analysis of umbrella sampling simulations to generate a potential of mean force. These parameters define the settings for the histogramming and reweighting procedure. The umbrella sampling analysis parameter settings are crucial for correctly combining the data from multiple windows. These are often set in the input file for a WHAM or MBAR analysis program.

nodes.lbl: potential of mean force convergence step size

definition.val: An umbrella sampling analysis parameter that specifies the increment or step size used when assessing the convergence of the calculated Potential of Mean Force (PMF). The PMF is calculated using progressively larger amounts of data to check for convergence. The potential of mean force convergence step size is a key parameter for ensuring that the calculated free energy profile is reliable. This is a key parameter for WHAM analysis.

A parameter controlling a 3D-RISM calculation, covering the grid on which the solvent distribution is computed, the closure relation used, and how tightly the solution must converge. The closure choice changes the answer, not merely its precision. These settings must be reported for a solvation free energy from this method to be interpretable. (UNVERIFIED)

A 3D-RISM parameter giving how little the solution must change between iterations before the calculation is declared finished. A tighter value gives a more accurate solvent distribution and needs more iterations. Too loose a value returns a result that looks complete and is still drifting. (UNVERIFIED)

A 3D-RISM parameter giving the distance beyond which interactions between the solute and the solvent are not evaluated. Raising it improves accuracy and raises cost, because the number of grid points within that distance of each solute atom grows with the cube of the distance. It is one of the main controls on how long such a calculation takes. (UNVERIFIED)

A type of analysis parameter that controls the analysis of simulation data to generate properties that can be compared with Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) experiments. These parameters define the settings for calculating NMR-related observables from a trajectory. The NMR analysis parameter settings are crucial for validating simulations against experimental data. These are often set in the input file for an NMR analysis program.

An NMR analysis parameter that specifies a particular form of distance averaging used in NMR structure calculation and refinement. This method involves averaging the inverse sixth power of the distance between two atoms, which is directly related to the Nuclear Overhauser Effect (NOE) intensity. The <r⁻⁶>⁻¹/⁶ averaged distance is a key parameter for back-calculating NOEs from a simulation trajectory. This is often referred to as R6 averaging.

A quantitative or qualitative output data item generated by a simulation or analysis process. It represents the actual measured state, derived metric, or calculated result of the system (e.g., instantaneous potential energy, calculated RMSD, assigned cluster IDs). (UNVERIFIED)

A computed observable describing the thermodynamic state of a system, or the energy exchanged as it changes state, such as energy, temperature, pressure, entropy and free energy. Most of these depend only on the current state and not on how the system reached it, and are estimated as averages over sampled configurations. Work done in a nonequilibrium process is an exception, because its value depends on the path taken. (UNVERIFIED)

A thermodynamic property measuring a capacity to do work that belongs to a simulated system or to part of it, such as its total energy, a single term of the force field, or the interaction between 2 of its parts. In a classical simulation the potential part is computed from the atom positions using the force field, and the kinetic part from the velocities. The terms are reported separately at intervals through a run, because a fault usually shows in a single term rather than in the total. (UNVERIFIED)

A component of a system's energy that depends only on where the atoms are, not on how fast they are moving. In a classical simulation it is computed from the force field, summing the bonded terms with the electrostatic and van der Waals interactions. The force on each atom is the negative of its gradient, and those forces drive the simulation forward. (UNVERIFIED)

A potential energy summing every bonded and non-bonded contribution for 1 configuration of the system. It is reported at intervals during a run and is among the first quantities checked when a simulation is suspected of going wrong. It usually settles to a stable average once the system has equilibrated. (UNVERIFIED)

A component of the potential energy arising from the Coulomb interaction between the partial charges on the atoms. It falls off slowly with distance, so it reaches much further than the other non-bonded term and needs special treatment in a periodic system. It is what makes polarity, solvation and ionic binding come out right or wrong. (UNVERIFIED)

A component of the electrostatic energy covering only pairs of atoms separated by exactly 3 bonds. Such pairs are close enough that the plain Coulomb term would double-count what the torsion term already describes, so many force fields scale it down by a fixed factor. The factor differs between force fields, which is one reason their parameters cannot be mixed. (UNVERIFIED)

A component of the potential energy covering the short-range interaction between atoms not bonded to each other: a steep repulsion when they approach too closely and a weaker attraction at slightly greater distance. The repulsion is what gives atoms an effective size. The attraction is what makes non-polar molecules condense into liquids at all. (UNVERIFIED)

A component of the van der Waals energy covering only pairs of atoms separated by exactly 3 bonds. Such pairs are close enough that the full interaction would double-count what the torsion term already describes, so many force fields scale it down or use separate parameters for these pairs. The treatment differs between force fields, which is one reason their parameters cannot be mixed. (UNVERIFIED)

A component of the potential energy stored in the bending of the angle between 3 bonded atoms away from its preferred value. It is softer than the bond stretching term, so angles deform more readily than bond lengths. It is the term that keeps, for example, a carbon atom with 4 single bonds close to a tetrahedral shape. (UNVERIFIED)

A component of the angle energy that adds a spring directly between the 2 outer atoms of a bonded triple, in addition to the angle term itself. It corrects the coupling between bending an angle and stretching the bonds around it, which the angle term alone cannot represent. It is used by the CHARMM force fields and not by most others. (UNVERIFIED)

A component of the potential energy associated with rotation about a bond, defined by 4 atoms in sequence and repeating as the rotation goes round. It is what makes some rotational positions preferred over others, which sets the shapes a molecule can adopt. It is the term most often refitted when a force field is improved, because conformational preferences depend on it most. (UNVERIFIED)

A component of the potential energy that holds a group of 4 atoms flat, or holds a centre in one of its 2 mirror forms. Unlike an ordinary torsion it is defined over atoms that are not in a chain, and in many force fields it is a harmonic term with a single preferred value rather than a repeating one. Without it, a planar group such as an aromatic ring or an amide could bend out of its plane. (UNVERIFIED)

A component of the potential energy arising from momentary fluctuations in an atom's electron cloud inducing matching fluctuations in its neighbours. It is always attractive and falls off rapidly with distance, so near neighbours contribute most. It is weak between any 2 atoms and dominant in large non-polar molecules simply because there are so many pairs. (UNVERIFIED)

A component of the potential energy arising from a molecule's electron cloud being distorted by the electric field of its surroundings. A force field with fixed atomic charges cannot represent it and absorbs its average effect into those charges instead. Representing it explicitly is what distinguishes a polarizable force field and what makes it several times more expensive. (UNVERIFIED)

A component of the reported energy arising from artificial potentials added to hold atoms near chosen positions, or to keep a distance, angle or other value near a target. A large value shows that the system is being held far from where it would otherwise go. It is not part of the system's physical energy, so its effect must be removed or corrected for when thermodynamic quantities are computed. (UNVERIFIED)

A component of the reported energy computed quantum mechanically for one region of a system. It appears only in calculations where part of the system is treated that way and the rest with a force field. It cannot be compared with a force field energy, because the 2 are measured from different zero points. (UNVERIFIED)

A QM energy giving the electronic energy of a region once the iterative self-consistent field (SCF) procedure has converged, as in a Hartree-Fock or density functional theory calculation. For Hartree-Fock it is the energy of the best single-configuration description of the electrons, which post-Hartree-Fock methods then improve by adding electron correlation. (UNVERIFIED)

A component of the system's energy that represents an artificial (non negative) energy term added to the potential to accelerate sampling in enhanced sampling simulations. This non-physical energy helps the system overcome high energy barriers more quickly. It is reported in the log files of methods like Accelerated MD as E_boost or amd_boost.

Accelerated Molecular Dynamics (aMD or GaMD) is a powerful enhanced sampling technique designed to speed up conformational transitions in biomolecular simulations. It works by applying a harmonic boost potential to the system's true potential energy surface whenever it drops below a predefined threshold. The accelerated MD boost energy is the key quantity used to reweight the biased trajectory to recover correct thermodynamic properties. It is often reported in log files as amd_boost.

A special potential term used in some older force fields to explicitly model hydrogen bonds. It is calculated using a 10-12 Lennard-Jones-like function between donor and acceptor atoms. This term is not commonly used in modern force fields but may be found in older simulation outputs. It is often reported as HBOND in energy summaries when such a potential is used.

A component of the reported energy contributed by the several copies of a region that a locally enhanced sampling simulation contains, which do not interact with each other. Because the force field parameters of the copies are scaled by 1 over the number of copies, the value is an average over the copies rather than the energy of a single real structure. The term exists only in this kind of simulation. (UNVERIFIED)

A thermodynamic property combining energy and entropy into the quantity that determines which way a process goes at fixed temperature. Its decrease in a process equals the largest amount of useful work the system can deliver under those conditions. Because it contains entropy it cannot be read off a single structure, only from an ensemble. (UNVERIFIED)

A free energy giving the change on taking 2 molecules from separate, solvated states to a bound complex. It is the quantity that determines binding affinity, so it is what a docking or free energy calculation is usually trying to predict. It is negative when binding is favourable. (UNVERIFIED)

A free energy giving the difference in binding free energy between 2 ligands binding the same receptor. It is usually computed by transforming 1 ligand into the other alchemically, which cancels the parts of the calculation the 2 have in common. That cancellation is why it can be computed more accurately than either absolute value. (UNVERIFIED)

A free energy giving the change on moving a molecule from vacuum into a solvent. It measures how favourable it is for the molecule to be surrounded by that solvent, and so it underlies solubility and partitioning. It appears as a leg in most thermodynamic cycles used to compute binding. (UNVERIFIED)

A solvation free energy where the solvent is water. It gives the change on moving a molecule from the gas phase into aqueous solution. It is the most common benchmark for testing whether a force field treats solute-water interactions correctly, because accurate experimental values exist for many small molecules. (UNVERIFIED)

A component of the solvation free energy arising from electrostatic interaction between the solute's charges and the solvent, which polarizes in response to them. It is favourable for any charged or polar molecule moved from vacuum into a polar solvent, and the part of it lost when polar groups are buried, for example on binding, is called the desolvation penalty. Continuum solvent models compute this electrostatic part and the non-polar part separately. (UNVERIFIED)

A component of the solvation free energy arising from everything other than electrostatics, chiefly the cost of forming a cavity and the dispersion attraction between solute and solvent. It is often estimated as proportional to the solvent-accessible surface area, although some methods compute the cavity and dispersion parts separately. (UNVERIFIED)

A non-polar solvation energy computed as a function of the solvent-accessible surface area of a molecule, usually a constant times the area plus an offset. It stands for the cost of opening a cavity in the solvent together with the dispersion attraction across its surface. It is the simplest of the non-polar treatments. (UNVERIFIED)

A polar solvation energy obtained by solving the Poisson-Boltzmann equation for a solute of low dielectric constant embedded in a continuum of high dielectric constant. It treats the electrostatics of solvation without approximating the shape of the molecule. It is more expensive and more faithful than the generalized Born alternative. (UNVERIFIED)

A polar solvation energy obtained from the generalized Born model, which approximates the Poisson-Boltzmann result with a closed-form expression using an effective radius for each atom. It is far faster, which is what makes it usable inside a running simulation rather than only in post-processing. Its accuracy depends on how the effective radii are computed. (UNVERIFIED)

A specific type of solvation free energy calculated using the 3D Reference Interaction Site Model (3D-RISM). This method provides a detailed, atomistic picture of the solvent structure around the solute and its thermodynamics. The 3D-RISM solvation energy is a key output of 3D-RISM calculations. This value is often reported as the excess chemical potential.

A type of thermodynamic property representing the free energy change of adding one particle to a system at constant volume and temperature. It is a direct measure of solvation free energy and is the primary output of methods like 3D-RISM. The calculated Excess Chemical Potential, often denoted µex or --exchem, is a key indicator of a molecule's solubility. This term is often found in the output of 3D-RISM calculations.

A thermodynamic property measuring how many microscopic arrangements a system can adopt while looking the same macroscopically. It enters the free energy with a negative sign multiplied by temperature, so a state with more arrangements is favoured, more strongly at higher temperature. It is far harder to compute from a simulation than the energy, because it depends on how much of the possible configurations the simulation visits, not only on an average over those it samples. (UNVERIFIED)

An entropy component giving the change in disorder when a solute is placed in a solvent. It combines the conformational freedom the solute loses with the reorganisation forced on the solvent around it. For a non-polar solute in water the solvent term dominates, which is the origin of the hydrophobic effect. (UNVERIFIED)

An information entropy of the statistical weights given to configurations when data from several biased simulations are combined, measuring how evenly those weights are spread. A low value means a few configurations carry most of the weight, so the effective sample is much smaller than the number of frames. It is checked before a reweighted average, such as the free energy of a single bin of a free energy surface, is trusted. (UNVERIFIED)

An entropy component arising from the positions a molecule's centre of mass can occupy. It falls when a molecule is confined, which is why binding always carries a translational entropy cost. It depends on concentration, so the standard state must be stated with any value. (UNVERIFIED)

An entropy component arising from the orientations a molecule can adopt. Like the translational component it falls on binding, because a bound molecule is held in a fixed orientation. The 2 together are the rigid-body entropy cost of forming a complex. (UNVERIFIED)

A thermodynamic property that should not change during a simulation in a given ensemble, and is therefore watched to check that the integration is sound. With no thermostat or barostat it is the total energy; with them it is that energy plus terms accounting for what they have added or removed. A steady drift in it means the timestep is too large or a setting is inconsistent, whatever else looks normal. (UNVERIFIED)

A thermodynamic property giving the work done on a system while it is driven away from equilibrium, obtained by integrating the applied force along the path taken. It differs between repetitions of the same process, so it is a distribution rather than a single number. A fluctuation theorem relates that distribution to the equilibrium free energy difference. (UNVERIFIED)

A type of output data descriptor that quantifies some aspect of the three-dimensional arrangement of atoms in a molecule or system. These descriptors are used to characterize the conformation, shape, size, and flexibility of molecules. They are the most common type of analysis performed on simulation trajectories.

A type of structural property that measures the average distance between the atoms of two superimposed molecular structures. It is the most common metric for quantifying the difference between two conformations, often used to track a simulation's stability relative to a starting structure. Analysis outputs frequently report the RMSD value over time.

A type of structural property that measures the fluctuation of each individual atom around its average position over the course of a simulation. It is used to identify flexible or mobile regions within a molecule, such as loops or termini in a protein. Analysis outputs often report the per-residue RMSF or atomicfluct to highlight these regions.

A type of structural property that measures the difference between two structures based on their internal pairwise atomic distances, rather than their Cartesian coordinates. This metric does not require structural alignment and can be more sensitive to changes in internal conformation. It is a useful alternative to standard RMSD for comparing flexible molecules.

Hydrogen mass repartitioning is a system setup method where a portion of the mass of a heavy atom is transferred to its bonded hydrogen atoms. This makes the hydrogens heavier, which slows down their bond vibrations and allows a larger time step to be used in a molecular dynamics simulation. For experts, this technique, often abbreviated HMR, is a common strategy to increase computational efficiency without significantly altering the system's dynamics.

A distance between an ion and the oxygen atoms of the water molecules in its first solvation shell, usually taken as the position of the first peak of the ion-oxygen radial distribution function. It is a standard target when ion parameters are fitted or tested, because it can be compared directly with X-ray and neutron scattering data. (UNVERIFIED)

A structural property giving how far the line from a middle atom to a first atom is turned from the line from that middle atom to a third atom, for 3 specified atoms. Following it through a trajectory is the simplest way to watch a local geometry change, such as a hydrogen bond opening. It is measured between any 3 atoms, whether or not they are bonded. (UNVERIFIED)

A type of structural property representing the torsion angle defined by four sequentially bonded atoms, which describes the rotation around the central bond. The dihedral angle is the most important descriptor for characterizing the overall conformation of a flexible molecule. Its value is a primary output of many structural analysis tools. This value is commonly referred to as dihedral or torsion.

A dihedral angle describing the rotation about one of the bonds in a protein backbone. The pair of angles either side of each alpha carbon determines the local shape of the chain, and so which secondary structure that stretch forms. Plotting the 2 against each other gives the Ramachandran plot, whose crowded and empty regions show which shapes are possible at all. (UNVERIFIED)

A specific type of dihedral angle that describes the conformation of an amino acid's side chain. These angles determine the spatial arrangement of the side chain's functional groups. They are critical for understanding molecular interactions and protein packing. These angles are commonly referred to as chi angles, such as chi1 or chi2.

A specific nucleic acid backbone dihedral angle is a torsion angle describing rotation about a bond in the sugar-phosphate backbone of DNA or RNA. The six backbone torsion angles (α, β, γ, δ, ε, and ζ), together with the glycosidic torsion angle (χ) and the sugar pucker, define the local conformation, flexibility, and overall geometry of the nucleic acid helix.

A type of structural property that measures the overall compactness of a molecule or a group of atoms. It is calculated as the root-mean-square distance of the atoms from their common center of mass. The radius of gyration is used to monitor large-scale conformational changes like protein folding or unfolding.

A structural property that quantifies the positional fluctuation or displacement of an atom, representing its mobility. It is calculated from the mean-square fluctuations of atomic positions in a simulation and is analogous to the crystallographic B-factor or temperature factor. High B-factor values indicate regions of high flexibility. This value is often referred to as bfactor or B-factor.

A structural property rating how similar the overall folds of 2 proteins are, on a scale from 0 to 1, with residue distances weighted on a length-dependent scale so that the score does not depend on protein length. The weighting also makes it less sensitive than RMSD to a few badly matched regions. A value above roughly 0.5 means the 2 usually share the same fold. (UNVERIFIED)

A structural property giving how many of the atom or residue contacts present in a reference folded structure are also present in the conformation being scored. It is usually reported as a fraction of the reference set rather than a raw count. It is the most common single-number reaction coordinate for folding. (UNVERIFIED)

A type of structural property that represents the average number of neighboring particles within a certain distance of a central particle. For an ion in water, the Coordination Number typically refers to the number of water molecules in its first solvation shell. It is a fundamental descriptor of local solvent structure and is used to validate force fields. This value is often abbreviated as CN.

A type of structural property that measures the surface area of a molecule that is accessible to a solvent. This quantity is crucial for understanding solvation effects. It is a key component in implicit solvent models and is often used to characterize a molecule's exposure to its environment. This value is commonly known as Solvent Accessible Surface Area or SASA.

A type of structural property that describes the specific three-dimensional conformation of a sugar ring, such as the ribose in DNA or RNA. The pucker is a critical determinant of the local and global structure of a nucleic acid helix. It is often described by a pseudorotation angle and can be analyzed to characterize A-form, B-form, or other helical types. This value is a standard output of nucleic acid analysis tools.

A structural property recording which of its 2 mirror forms a centre in a molecule takes. The 2 forms cannot be superimposed and often behave completely differently in a biological system. A force field cannot change one into the other, so an error here persists through an entire simulation unnoticed. (UNVERIFIED)

A type of structural property that describes the rotational position of a molecule or a group of atoms in three-dimensional space. It is often represented by a set of Euler angles, a rotation matrix, or a quaternion. Analyzing the orientation is essential for understanding the tumbling of molecules in solution or the alignment of components in a complex.

A specific type of orientation descriptor that represents the angle of rotation between the current orientation and a reference orientation. This provides a simple, scalar measure of how much a molecule has rotated. This value is often reported as ORIENTATION_ANGLE.

A specific type of orientation descriptor that represents the cosine of the angle of rotation between the current and reference positions. This value is often used in analyses of rotational correlation. This value is often reported as ORIENTATION_PROJ.

A base pair step parameter that describes the rotation of one base pair relative to the next around their short axes. A non-zero tilt causes the helix to bend. It is an important parameter for describing DNA curvature. This is a standard output of nucleic acid analysis programs.
A specific type of orientation descriptor that represents the angle of rotation of a molecule around a specific unit axis. The SPINANGLE is useful for analyzing spinning motions.

A molecular orientation descriptor giving the rotation that best superimposes a chosen group of atoms onto a set of reference coordinates, written as a unit quaternion: 4 numbers that together encode a rotation angle and a rotation axis. Unlike Euler angles, a quaternion has no orientations at which the description breaks down, so it is a reliable way to follow how a molecule turns during a simulation. (UNVERIFIED)

A type of structural property that provides a detailed, quantitative description of the geometry of a nucleic acid helix. These parameters are calculated by specialized analysis programs to characterize the structure of DNA and RNA. They are essential for comparing simulated structures to experimental data and for understanding sequence-dependent structural variations. These are the standard output of programs like do_x3dna or cpptraj.

A nucleic acid parameter that describes the relative position and orientation of the 2 bases within a single base pair. It measures how far the pair departs from an ideal flat pairing, and includes shear, stretch, stagger, buckle, propeller twist and opening. (UNVERIFIED)

A base pair parameter that quantifies the translational displacement of one base relative to the other along their short axis, within the plane of the base pair. A non-zero shear indicates a lateral displacement of the two bases from their ideal paired geometry, altering their relative alignment while maintaining the base-pair plane. This is a standard output of nucleic acid analysis programs.

A base pair parameter that quantifies the translational displacement of one base relative to the other along the axis of the hydrogen bonds. A non-zero stretch measures how much the base pair is pulled apart or compressed. It reflects the strength and dynamics of the hydrogen bonds holding the pair together. This is a standard output of nucleic acid analysis programs.

A base pair parameter that quantifies the translational displacement of one base relative to the other along the axis perpendicular to the base pair plane. A non-zero stagger indicates that the two bases are offset in the direction normal to the base-pair plane, resulting in a difference in their relative height and a deviation from an ideal coplanar geometry. This is a standard output of nucleic acid analysis programs.

A base pair parameter that describes the rotation of the two bases relative to each other around their long axis, roughly parallel to the hydrogen bonds. A non-zero buckle angle indicates that the bases are tilted relative to each other, producing a bent base-pair geometry. It contributes to the overall shape of the helix. This is a standard output of nucleic acid analysis programs.

A base pair parameter that describes the rotation of the two bases relative to each other around an axis connecting their glycosidic bonds. This propeller twist optimizes stacking with adjacent base pairs but can strain hydrogen bonds. It is a key determinant of helix stability and groove dimensions. This is a standard output of nucleic acid analysis programs.

An intra-base-pair parameter that describes the relative rotation of the two bases around the axis perpendicular to the base-pair plane. A non-zero opening angle indicates that the base pair deviates from its ideal planar geometry, altering the orientation of the hydrogen-bonding and increasing their exposure to the solvent. Large opening values are often associated with transient base-pair opening ("breathing") or fraying events. Opening is a standard structural parameter reported by nucleic acid analysis programs.

A type of nucleic acid parameter that describes the relative geometry and orientation between two successive base pairs in a helix. These parameters define the local helical structure. They are essential for characterizing the sequence-dependent variations in DNA and RNA structure. These parameters include shift, slide, rise, tilt, roll, and twist.

A base pair step parameter that describes the translational displacement of one base pair relative to the next along their short axes. A non-zero shift indicates a lateral sliding motion. It affects the alignment and stacking interactions between adjacent base pairs. This is a standard output of nucleic acid analysis programs.

A base pair step parameter that describes the translational displacement of one base pair relative to the next along their long axes. A non-zero slide is a major determinant of the width of the major and minor grooves. It is a key parameter for describing B-form DNA. This is a standard output of nucleic acid analysis programs.

A base pair step parameter that describes the translational distance between two adjacent base pairs along the central helical axis. The rise per step is a primary determinant of the overall length of the DNA or RNA helix. This is a standard output of nucleic acid analysis programs.

A base pair step parameter that describes the rotation of one base pair relative to the next around their long axes. A non-zero roll angle causes the helix to bend into the major or minor groove. It is a crucial parameter for DNA bendability and protein recognition. This is a standard output of nucleic acid analysis programs.

A base pair step parameter that describes the rotation of one base pair relative to the next around the central helical axis. The helical twist is the primary determinant of the number of base pairs per turn in a DNA or RNA helix. This is a standard output of nucleic acid analysis programs.

A nucleic acid parameter that quantifies the position of a base pair's reference frame relative to the global or local helical axis. Displacement is the distance (in Å) between the center of the base pair and the global helical axis, measured perpendicular to the helix axis. They include x-displacement and y-displacement.

A displacement parameter that measures the translation of a base pair away from the central helical axis towards the major or minor groove. The x-displacement is a key parameter for distinguishing between A-form and B-form DNA. This is a standard output of nucleic acid analysis programs.

A displacement parameter that measures the translation of a base pair away from the central helical axis along the axis of the base pair's hydrogen bonds. The y-displacement is typically small in canonical DNA structures. This is a standard output of nucleic acid analysis programs.

A computed observable describing how the electrons of a molecule are distributed and how they respond to a disturbance, usually obtained from a quantum mechanical calculation. Examples are atomic charges, dipole moments and polarizabilities. These properties govern chemical reactivity and how a molecule responds to light or to an electric field. (UNVERIFIED)

An electronic property giving the partial electric charge assigned to a single atom in a molecule. No such quantity exists in the underlying physics, because electrons are not divided between atoms; it is a convention for splitting a continuous distribution. Different conventions give different values for the same molecule, so the method must always be stated. (UNVERIFIED)

An atomic charge obtained by fitting point charges on the atoms so that together they reproduce the electrostatic potential around the molecule computed by a quantum mechanical calculation. Such charges are widely used to build force field parameters for new molecules, because they reproduce how the molecule interacts electrically with its surroundings. Charges on buried atoms are poorly determined by the fit, which is why restrained variants such as RESP exist. (UNVERIFIED)

An electronic property giving the size and direction of the separation between a molecule's positive and negative charge, equal to the charge multiplied by the distance separating it. It is what makes a molecule polar, and it determines how the molecule aligns in an electric field and how strongly it interacts with other polar molecules. For a neutral molecule it can be measured and does not depend on how charge is divided between atoms. (UNVERIFIED)

An electronic property describing a molecule's charge distribution in more detail than a dipole, through terms such as the quadrupole that capture progressively finer features of its shape. A molecule with no dipole can still interact strongly through these, as benzene does through its quadrupole. Some force fields, such as AMOEBA, place a dipole and a quadrupole on each atom as well as a point charge. (UNVERIFIED)

An electronic property giving how easily a molecule's electron cloud is distorted by an electric field. A larger, softer electron cloud distorts more, so polarizability rises with molecular size. It determines the strength of dispersion attraction, which is what holds non-polar molecules together. (UNVERIFIED)

A polarizability describing how a molecule's electron cloud responds to a strong electric field, beyond the part that responds in proportion to the field. It is what makes a material double the frequency of light passing through it, or change its refractive index with intensity. It matters for optical materials and is negligible at ordinary field strengths. (UNVERIFIED)

A polarizability describing how a molecule's response to an oscillating electric field, such as light, depends on the frequency of the oscillation. The response grows as the frequency approaches that of an electronic excitation of the molecule, so the same calculation also gives the energies at which the molecule absorbs light. It determines how the refractive index changes with the colour of light. (UNVERIFIED)

An electronic property giving the least energy needed to remove an electron from a molecule. A high value means the molecule holds its electrons tightly and is hard to oxidise. Together with the electron affinity it says how readily the molecule will give or take electrons in a reaction. (UNVERIFIED)

An electronic property giving the energy released when an electron is added to a molecule. A large value means the molecule accepts electrons readily and is easily reduced. It is the counterpart of the ionization potential, which measures losing one instead. (UNVERIFIED)

An electronic property read directly from the mathematical function describing a molecule's electrons, rather than from an energy difference. Orbital energies, orbital shapes and the electron density itself belong here. They depend on the method and basis set used, so they are comparable only between calculations done the same way. (UNVERIFIED)

A wavefunction property giving the total electronic energy of a system at a fixed arrangement of its nuclei. It is the main output of a quantum chemistry calculation and the quantity whose derivatives give the forces. It is meaningful only as a difference, because its absolute value depends on the method and basis set. (UNVERIFIED)

A wavefunction property saying whether a converged self-consistent field solution is a true energy minimum or only a saddle point, from which a small change in the orbitals would lower the energy. Such a solution passes the convergence test even though a lower-energy solution exists. Checking this is routine for open-shell and transition metal systems, where such unstable solutions are common. (UNVERIFIED)

An electronic property giving the total charge of a chosen group of atoms rather than of a single one. Grouping is more robust than per-atom charges, because the arbitrariness of dividing charge between neighbouring atoms partly cancels. It is used to state the charge of a quantum region or of a functional group. (UNVERIFIED)

A charge distribution descriptor giving the net charge of the core region in an adaptive QM/MM calculation, the atoms that are treated with quantum mechanics throughout the simulation. It is given as a whole number, because the quantum calculation needs the total charge of the atoms it treats. (UNVERIFIED)

A charge distribution descriptor giving the net charge of the buffer region in an adaptive buffered force-mixing QM/MM calculation, the shell of atoms around the atoms that move with quantum mechanical forces. Buffer atoms are included in the larger quantum calculation so that the atoms inside get accurate forces, but their own forces from that calculation are discarded. Their net charge is given as a whole number, because the quantum calculation needs the total charge of the atoms it treats. (UNVERIFIED)

A computed observable describing how a system moves and changes with time, rather than what shape it has at one instant. Diffusion coefficients, relaxation times and transition rates belong here. They are normally computed from a trajectory, because a single structure carries no information about time. (UNVERIFIED)

A kinetic property giving how fast particles spread out through random thermal motion. It is obtained from the slope of the mean squared displacement against time, or from the integral of the velocity autocorrelation function. It is one of the few simulated quantities that can be compared directly with a straightforward experiment. (UNVERIFIED)

A kinetic property giving the average of the squared distance a particle has moved from where it started, as a function of elapsed time. In a liquid it grows in proportion to time once the motion has become random, and the constant of proportionality gives the diffusion coefficient. Departure from that straight line marks motion that is still constrained rather than free. (UNVERIFIED)

A type of kinetic property that characterizes the rate at which nuclear spins return to thermal equilibrium after being perturbed in a Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) experiment. These relaxation times are sensitive to molecular motions on different timescales. They are key experimental observables that can be compared with simulation results to validate molecular dynamics. These are known as T1 and T2 relaxation times.

A specific type of NMR relaxation time, also known as the spin-lattice or longitudinal relaxation time. It characterizes the rate at which the nuclear spins exchange energy with their surrounding environment (the "lattice"). The T1 relaxation time is sensitive to fast molecular motions, on the order of the inverse of the Larmor frequency. This is a key parameter in NMR spectroscopy.

A specific type of NMR relaxation time, also known as the spin-spin or transverse relaxation time. It characterizes the rate at which the nuclear spins lose phase coherence with each other. The T2 relaxation time is sensitive to both fast and slow molecular motions, making it a rich source of dynamical information. This is a key parameter in NMR spectroscopy.

A type of kinetic property that represents the time scale over which a system's properties, such as the orientation of a bond, remain correlated. It is a measure of the "memory" of the system's dynamics. The correlation time is a key parameter in the interpretation of NMR relaxation data. This is often denoted tcorr or tau_c.

A physical quantity that can be measured by or is related to a spectroscopic experiment. These properties are often calculated from simulations and compared directly with experimental data to validate the accuracy of the simulation model. They provide a crucial link between computational models and the real world. These are the primary outputs of computational spectroscopy.

A type of spectroscopic property that measures the through-bond interaction between two nuclear spins, which causes splitting of NMR signals. The J-coupling is highly sensitive to the dihedral angle between the coupled nuclei, as described by the Karplus relationship. It is a key piece of experimental data used to determine molecular conformation. This is a standard output of NMR analysis programs.

A type of spectroscopic property that provides long-range structural information in NMR experiments by measuring the orientation of bond vectors in a weakly aligned molecule. Residual Dipolar Couplings (RDCs) are extremely valuable for determining the relative orientation of distant parts of a molecule. They provide powerful restraints for refining molecular structures.

The deuterium order parameter (SCD) measures the orientational order and dynamic disorder of lipid acyl chains in MD simulations. It allows for direct validation of membrane fluidity and structural phases against deuterium NMR experiments.

A type of spectroscopic property that measures the motional restriction of a bond vector, typically an N-H bond in a protein, on fast timescales. The S2 order parameter ranges from 0 (completely isotropic motion) to 1 (completely rigid) and is measured by NMR relaxation experiments. It is a powerful tool for characterizing internal protein dynamics. This is a standard output of NMR relaxation analysis.

A computed observable obtained by applying a statistical measure to a dataset, such as a set of structures from a trajectory or a set of predicted and reference values. Examples are error measures, distances and divergences between data sets or distributions, and clustering quality scores. (UNVERIFIED)

OBSOLETE. A specific type of correlation coefficient that measures the linear relationship between two continuous variables. It is the most common method for calculating correlation. This value is often reported in analysis as the Pearson correlation coefficient or simply 'r'. This is a standard output of statistical packages.

comments: Obsoleted 2026-07-29: duplicated both MOLSIM:000112 and STATO:0000280 - 'Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient' is the full formal name of Pearson's correlation coefficient. Replaced by the reused STATO term.

definition.val: OBSOLETE. A specific type of correlation coefficient that measures the monotonic relationship between two variables, based on their ranks rather than their raw values. It is less sensitive to outliers than the Pearson correlation. The Spearman rank correlation coefficient is a non-parametric measure of association. This is often reported as rho or Spearman's rho.

comments: Obsoleted 2026-07-29: duplicated STATO:0000201. STATO is the canonical OBO home for statistics and its definition of this term is fuller than MOLSIM's (it covers the monotonic-function reading, the perfect +/-1 case, and when to prefer it over Pearson's). Note the symbol 'rho' named in the retired definition is not carried on the STATO term, which has no synonyms, because MOLSIM must not annotate a foreign IRI.

definition.val: A correlation coefficient that measures how far 2 variables place items in the same order, computed by counting the pairs of items they order the same way and the pairs they order differently. It uses only the order of the values, so it does not change when the values are rescaled and it is much less sensitive to extreme outliers than a coefficient based on the values themselves. It suits comparisons where the ranking matters more than the exact numbers. (UNVERIFIED)

A statistical property giving the typical size of the difference between predicted and observed values, computed by squaring the differences, averaging them and taking the square root. Squaring first makes large errors count disproportionately, so a single bad prediction moves it noticeably. It is in the same units as the quantity itself, which makes it directly interpretable. (UNVERIFIED)

A statistical property giving the average size of the difference between predicted and observed values, ignoring sign. Because it does not square the differences, every error counts in proportion to its size and one large error does not dominate. It is the measure to prefer when outliers are expected and should not be allowed to control the score. (UNVERIFIED)

nodes.lbl: obsolete standard error of the mean (SEM)

definition.val: OBSOLETE. A type of statistical property that estimates the standard deviation of the sample mean, quantifying how precisely the sample mean represents the true population mean. It is calculated by dividing the sample standard deviation by the square root of the sample size. The standard error of the mean is a key measure of the uncertainty of a calculated average value. This is often abbreviated as SEM.

comments: Obsoleted 2026-07-29: duplicated STATO:0000037. STATO is the canonical OBO home for statistics; reused in place of this term. Note the '(SEM)' abbreviation carried by the retired label is not reproduced on the STATO term, because MOLSIM must not annotate a foreign IRI; STATO's own definition spells out the abbreviation.

definition.val: OBSOLETE. A type of statistical property, also known as R-squared, that indicates the proportion of the variance in the dependent variable that is predictable from the independent variable(s). It provides a measure of how well the observed outcomes are replicated by the model. The coefficient of determination is a key metric for assessing the goodness of fit of a regression model. This is often reported as R^2 or R-squared.

comments: Obsoleted 2026-07-29: duplicated STATO:0000564. STATO is the canonical OBO home for statistics; reused in place of this term.

definition.val: A type of statistical property that quantifies the degree to which two probability distributions share common regions. In umbrella sampling simulations, this is a critical diagnostic for ensuring that adjacent simulation windows have sampled sufficiently overlapping regions of phase space. The distribution overlap is a key metric for validating the results of umbrella sampling or replica exchange simulations. This is often reported as Phase space overlap (PSO).

A measure of how far the configurations sampled at 2 neighbouring alchemical states coincide. Free energy estimators need configurations typical of 1 state to be reachable from the other; where they are not, the estimate is biased whatever its apparent precision. It is checked per pair of neighbouring states, not once for the whole calculation. (UNVERIFIED)

A statistical property giving how likely something is, given that something else is already known to have happened. The transition probabilities of a Markov model are of this kind: the chance of being in 1 state next, given the state now. (UNVERIFIED)

OBSOLETE. A type of statistical property that measures the amount of variation or dispersion of a set of values. A low standard deviation indicates that the values tend to be close to the mean, while a high value indicates that the values are spread out over a wider range. It is a fundamental measure of the variability of a calculated property. This is often abbreviated as sd or stdev.

comments: Obsoleted 2026-07-29: duplicated STATO:0000237. STATO is the canonical OBO home for statistics; reused in place of this term.

definition.val: A statistical property giving how far apart 2 sets of points are, as the largest distance from any point of either set to the nearest point of the other. It is controlled by the worst-matched point rather than by the typical one. That makes it sensitive to a single outlying point, which is useful when the worst match matters and misleading when it does not. (UNVERIFIED)

A statistical property rating how well a set of groups describes the data, typically by comparing how tight the groups are against how far apart they lie. Such measures are used to choose how many groups to make, since most algorithms will produce any number asked for. No measure settles the question; they narrow it. (UNVERIFIED)

A clustering quality metric giving the average, over all groups, of how similar each group is to the one it most resembles. Similarity here combines how spread out the 2 groups are with how close their centres lie. A lower value means the groups are compact and well separated, so it is minimised rather than maximised. (UNVERIFIED)

A clustering quality metric giving the ratio of the variation between groups to the variation within them. A high value means the groups differ from each other far more than their members differ among themselves. It is computed for several possible numbers of groups, and the number giving the highest value is taken as the best. (UNVERIFIED)

A clustering quality metric giving the share of the total variation in the data that is accounted for by the differences between groups. A value near 1 means almost all the variation is captured by the grouping. It always rises as more groups are added, so it is read by looking for where it stops rising steeply rather than by taking its maximum. (UNVERIFIED)

A clustering quality metric giving, for each structure, how much closer it is to its own group than to the nearest other group, on a scale from −1 to 1. A value near 1 means it clearly belongs where it was put, near 0 that it sits on a boundary, and negative that it would fit another group better. Averaging it over all structures rates the whole grouping. (UNVERIFIED)

A statistical property giving how strongly 2 quantities are related when separated by a given distance or a given interval of time. Its shape says both how strong the relationship is and over what range it persists. Many quantities taken from a trajectory, such as radial distribution functions and diffusion coefficients, are correlation functions or are derived from them. (UNVERIFIED)

A correlation function giving how much a particle's velocity at one moment still resembles its velocity a given time later. It starts at its maximum and decays as collisions with neighbouring particles change the direction of motion. Its integral over time is proportional to the diffusion coefficient, a Green-Kubo relation. (UNVERIFIED)
A specific type of correlation function that measures the covariance of a signal with itself at different time points. It is similar to the autocorrelation function but is not normalized.

A correlation function giving the total departure from randomness in the positions of 2 particles in a liquid, counting both their direct influence on each other and influence passed through intervening particles. It is written h(r) and relates to the pair distribution function as h(r) = g(r) − 1. It is 1 of the 2 unknowns the RISM equations solve for. (UNVERIFIED)

A specific type of correlation function that describes the direct correlation between two particles in a liquid, excluding indirect effects mediated by other particles. It is a fundamental quantity in the statistical mechanics of liquids, related to the total correlation function by the Ornstein-Zernike equation. This is often denoted as c(r). (UNVERIFIED)

A correlation function giving how likely a particle is to be found at each distance from another particle, relative to a uniform distribution. Peaks mark the distances at which neighbours prefer to sit: the first peak gives the most likely distance of the nearest neighbours, and the first minimum after it marks the outer edge of the first solvation shell. It is the standard way the structure of a liquid is described, and it can be compared with X-ray and neutron scattering data. (UNVERIFIED)

A type of output data descriptor for calculated properties that do not fit into the other major categories like thermodynamic or structural properties. This includes mathematical quantities derived from the potential energy surface or other specific analysis metrics. These are often specialized outputs from analysis programs.

A vector of the first derivatives of the potential energy with respect to each atomic coordinate. Its negative is the force on each atom, which is what a simulation uses to move them. A minimization has converged when it is close to zero everywhere. (UNVERIFIED)

A matrix of the second derivatives of the potential energy with respect to every pair of atomic coordinates. It gives the curvature of the energy surface, so at a point where the gradient is zero it shows whether that point is a minimum, a saddle point or a maximum. Diagonalising it after weighting by the atomic masses gives the vibrational normal modes and their frequencies. (UNVERIFIED)

A descriptor giving how many interactions of a chosen kind, such as hydrogen bonds or close contacts, involve a particular atom or group. It reduces a pattern of contacts to a single number that can be followed over time. What it counts depends entirely on the distance and angle criteria used, which must be stated with it. (UNVERIFIED)

A descriptor giving a single number that expresses how alike 2 entities are, such as 2 molecular structures or 2 atom types, according to a stated measure. The scale and range depend on the measure chosen, such as the Tanimoto coefficient for molecular fingerprints. Such scores are used, for example, to rank compounds in virtual screening. (UNVERIFIED)

The Adaptive String Method (ASM) is a numerical technique used in computational chemistry and physics to find minimum free energy paths (MFEPs) or reaction pathways in complex, high-dimensional systems such as chemical reactions, conformational changes in biomolecules, or phase transitions. It is an improvement over the original string method because it adapts the distribution of points ("images") along the path to better capture regions of high curvature or complexity. For experts, this adaptive placement of images leads to a more efficient and accurate determination of the minimum free energy path.

Ensemble trajectory analysis is a method that involves analyzing a large collection of independent simulation trajectories together, rather than just a single long one. This approach provides a more robust and statistically reliable picture of a molecule's behavior by sampling a wider range of starting conditions and potential pathways. It is particularly important for studying complex processes like protein folding or for achieving converged statistics on a system's properties.

A ligand charge model that keeps the AM1-BCC approach, charges from a semi-empirical AM1 calculation followed by bond charge corrections, but with the corrections refitted for use with the second general AMBER force field (GAFF2). The corrections were fitted so that GAFF2 with these charges reproduces measured solvation free energies, such as hydration free energies, of organic molecules. AMBER recommends combining it with GAFF2 rather than with the first general AMBER force field. (UNVERIFIED)

A method that obtains atomic charges by taking the charges from a fast semi-empirical calculation and correcting them with terms fitted to reproduce measured dipole moments. The correction is what fixes the known bias of the underlying charges. It is fast enough to apply to large numbers of molecules. (UNVERIFIED)

A charge model refining the earlier CM1 scheme with corrections fitted against a larger set of measured dipole moments and covering more elements. The functional form is unchanged; the fitting set and the coverage are wider. It is used where semi-empirical charges are wanted quickly and reliably. (UNVERIFIED)

A charge model that assigns partial charges by passing charge between bonded atoms according to their electronegativity until the flow stops. It needs no quantum calculation at all, only the bond connectivity. It is fast enough for millions of molecules and crude enough that it is used for screening rather than for simulation. (UNVERIFIED)

A charge model in which atomic charges are recomputed in response to the surrounding electric field, and the calculation repeated until they stop changing. Each atom's charge affects the field its neighbours feel, so they cannot be solved one at a time. It is one of the ways a polarizable force field represents the response of the electron cloud. (UNVERIFIED)

A force field for RNA, built on AMBER ff99 with the bsc0 alpha and gamma backbone correction and with the glycosidic torsion chi refit by the Olomouc group. The refit removed the shift of chi into the high-anti region that made RNA duplexes open into non-native ladder-like structures in long simulations. It is the RNA force field recommended in AMBER. (UNVERIFIED)

This is a specialized force field for simulating proteins that pays extra attention to how proteins interact with water and charged ions. The AMBER ff15ipq force field was developed to improve the description of protein interactions with ions by using a novel charge model (Implicitly Polarized Charge, IPq) that better reproduces experimental hydration free energies. This force field is particularly recommended for simulations where the accurate modeling of protein-ion interactions or salt bridge dynamics is critical to the system's behavior.

A force field specifically parameterized for the simulation of protein mimetics, which are synthetic molecules designed to mimic natural proteins. It extends the existing ff15ipq force field to include parameters for non-standard, artificial, heterogenous building blocks, such as D-amino acids and beta-amino acids. This enables researchers to accurately model the structure and dynamics of these non-natural biopolymers.

Amber ff03 is a modified version of the ff99 AMBER force field. The main changes are that charges are now derived from quantum calculations that use a continuum dielectric to mimic solvent polarization, and that the φ and ψ backbone torsions for proteins are modified, with the effect of decreasing the preference for helical configurations. The changes are just for proteins; nucleic acid parameters are the same as in ff99.

This is a simplified version of the AMBER ff03 force field where the aliphatic hydrogen atoms on all amino acid side-chains are united to their corresponding carbon atoms. The aliphatic hydrogen atoms on all alpha carbon atoms are still represented explicitly to minimize the impact of the united-atom approximation on protein backbone conformations. In addition, aromatic hydrogens are also explicitly represented. Nucleic acid parameters are still in all atom and kept the same as in ff99.

A force field for DNA, built on AMBER ff99 with the bsc0 correction, that adds 3 refinements from the Olomouc group: to the epsilon and zeta backbone torsions, to the glycosidic torsion chi, and to the beta backbone torsion. It improves the description of the sugar-phosphate backbone and of helical twist over the preceding DNA parameters. It was later extended by OL21 and then by OL24, which AMBER now recommends for DNA. (UNVERIFIED)

A nucleic acid force field is a set of mathematical functions and parameters specifically designed to simulate the behavior of DNA and RNA molecules. These force fields contain parameters optimized to accurately reproduce the unique structural features of nucleic acids, such as the double helix, sugar puckering, and base stacking interactions. They are essential for any realistic simulation of genetic material or functional RNA molecules.

The AMBER bsc1 force field is a specific and widely used refinement for the dihedral angle parameters of the DNA backbone, designed for use with AMBER force fields. Developed by the Barcelona Supercomputing Center (BSC), it significantly improves the description of DNA's structural dynamics compared to the uncorrected force fields. It is considered a standard addition for obtaining accurate DNA simulations.

A force field for DNA whose bonded parameters and partial charges were derived from high-level quantum mechanical calculations rather than fitted to experimental data. The consistent derivation is what distinguishes it from force fields assembled from separately fitted terms. It targets DNA structure and dynamics specifically. (UNVERIFIED)

A force field for DNA from the Olomouc group that adds a refinement of the alpha and gamma backbone torsions to OL15. It was followed by OL24, which adds a refinement of the sugar pucker and is now the DNA force field AMBER recommends. (UNVERIFIED)

A force field for phospholipids in the AMBER family, introduced in 2012, that provided the first modular framework for lipids in AMBER, in which head groups and tails are parameterised separately and combined. The modularity allows lipids not in the original set to be assembled from existing pieces. It has been superseded by later revisions in the same series. (UNVERIFIED)

A lipid force field built on the general AMBER force field, with its non-bonded parameters and the related torsion terms refined specifically for lipids. It was the first lipid parameter set based on the AMBER energy function that allowed lipid bilayers to be simulated at constant pressure without an applied surface tension. It was introduced in 2012, together with the modular Lipid11 framework. (UNVERIFIED)

A classical force field parameter set fitted to reproduce the geometries of proteins energy-minimized with the AM1 semi-empirical quantum method. It is used to pre-minimize a protein cheaply before a more expensive AM1 calculation, so that the starting geometry is already close to the AM1 one. It was meant only to reproduce AM1 geometries and was not tested for other uses, such as classical molecular dynamics. (UNVERIFIED)

A classical force field parameter set fitted to reproduce the geometries of proteins energy-minimized with the PM3 semi-empirical quantum method. It is used to pre-minimize a protein cheaply before a more expensive PM3 calculation, so that the starting geometry is already close to the PM3 one. It is the PM3 counterpart of ParmAM1, and was not tested for other uses, such as classical molecular dynamics. (UNVERIFIED)

A force field parameterised for solid-state materials such as metals, oxides, semiconductors and polymers, or for their interfaces with liquids. It is fitted to reproduce material properties such as crystal structure, elastic constants and defect energies, rather than the behaviour of biomolecules in water. Many such force fields use many-body terms, because bonding in a metal or a semiconductor cannot be described by fixed pairs of bonded atoms. (UNVERIFIED)

A material force field that describes the interaction between water and the (111) crystal face of platinum, developed as part of a project on multiscale simulations in catalysis. It adds Lennard-Jones, Gaussian and angle-dependent terms between surface platinum atoms and water oxygens, and can be combined with any water model. At present it has parameters only for water over platinum (111). (UNVERIFIED)

A force field parameter set for the fluorescent dye molecules used to label biomolecules in experiments. It is built to be used alongside the standard AMBER protein and nucleic acid parameters without modification. It lets a labelled construct be simulated as it was actually measured, which matters when interpreting FRET distances. (UNVERIFIED)

A semi-empirical quantum method applying pairwise distance-dependent corrections to the PM3 parameterisation. The corrections markedly improve heats of formation for organic molecules.
