It uses the same underlying approximation and differs in the correction terms and their fitted values. (UNVERIFIED)

A semi-empirical quantum method extending MNDO with d orbitals on the heavier main-group elements. Without them, elements from the third row onwards are described badly, because their bonding involves those orbitals. It extends the method's usable range rather than changing how it treats the elements it already covered. (UNVERIFIED)

A model that adds the effect of a field imposed from outside the system, such as an electric or magnetic field. The field acts on the charges in the system but is not affected by them. It is how a simulation represents an applied voltage, or the environment of a membrane under a potential difference. (UNVERIFIED)

An external field model in which the field comes from one or more fixed charges placed in or around the system. The charges do not move and feel no force themselves. It is a way of representing a nearby charged object without simulating it. (UNVERIFIED)

The simplest approximation used for the exchange-correlation term in density functional theory, which treats the electron density at each point as though it were part of a uniform gas of that density. It uses no information about how the density varies from place to place. It is reasonable for metals and poor for molecules, where the density changes sharply. (UNVERIFIED)

A class of approximations for the exchange-correlation energy in density functional theory that uses both the electron density at each point and its gradient, that is, how fast the density changes there. Including the gradient corrects much of the error that the local density approximation makes for molecules. PBE and BLYP are widely used examples. (UNVERIFIED)

An exchange-correlation functional that mixes a fixed fraction of exact exchange, computed as in Hartree-Fock theory, with exchange and correlation from a generalized gradient approximation (GGA) functional. The mixture cancels part of the error each part makes alone, particularly the artificial repulsion of an electron from itself. It costs more than a pure GGA functional because exact exchange is expensive to compute, and B3LYP is the best-known example. (UNVERIFIED)

A constituent part of a hybrid model in which a small region is treated with quantum mechanics and the rest with a force field. The parts include the choice of quantum and classical regions, the quantum method and its settings, such as the basis set and integration grid, corrections such as an empirical dispersion term, and the treatment of the boundary between the regions. The boundary is the difficult part, because bonds crossing it must be handled without either description failing. (UNVERIFIED)

A set of points at which a function is evaluated so that an integral over space can be computed as a weighted sum. Density functional theory needs one because part of its energy cannot be integrated analytically. Its density controls both the accuracy of the result and a noticeable share of the cost. (UNVERIFIED)

A standard pruned integration grid for density functional theory calculations, proposed by Gill, Johnson and Pople in 1993, with 50 radial points and up to 194 angular points around each atom. Pruning means fewer angular points are used near the nucleus and far from it, where the integrand varies less, which keeps the grid small. It is a small, low-cost grid accurate enough for many routine calculations, and because it is defined in advance, every program that implements it uses the same grid. (UNVERIFIED)

An extra atom, usually a hydrogen, placed in a hybrid quantum and classical simulation to complete a bond cut by the boundary between the 2 regions. Without it the quantum region would have an unsatisfied valence and behave like a radical. It is not part of the real molecule and is invisible to the classical region. (UNVERIFIED)

The part of a force field giving how the energy rises as a covalent bond departs from its preferred length. It is almost always a simple spring, chosen because it is cheap and accurate for the small departures thermal motion produces. A spring cannot break, which is the deliberate limitation of a classical force field. (UNVERIFIED)

A force field component that gives how the energy rises as the angle between 3 bonded atoms moves away from its preferred value. It is usually a harmonic term, which behaves like a spring much softer than the one for bond stretching. Together with the bond term, it sets the local geometry of a molecule. (UNVERIFIED)

A force field component that gives how the energy varies with rotation about a bond, measured by the dihedral angle of 4 consecutive bonded atoms. It is usually written as a sum of cosine terms, so it repeats through a full turn, and the terms included set how many minima there are per turn. It is the main term that sets which shapes a flexible molecule prefers. (UNVERIFIED)

It is an electrostatic or van der Waals force between two atoms that are separated by at least three covalent bonds. It is typically composed of two parts: the van der Waals component, which models short-range repulsion and dispersion, and the electrostatic component, which models the Coulomb interaction between atomic partial charges.

A point in a force field that carries charge or interaction parameters but no mass, held at a fixed position relative to real atoms. It lets charge be placed where no nucleus sits, such as on a lone pair or slightly off a nucleus. The 4-point water models and the extra points on halogens are the common examples. (UNVERIFIED)

A way of modelling a metal ion with explicit bonds to the atoms coordinating it, so the geometry of the site is held by the same terms that hold any other bond. It reproduces the fixed arrangement of a metal centre in a protein. The bonds cannot break, so the ion cannot exchange its coordinating atoms or leave. (UNVERIFIED)

A way of modelling a metal ion as a charged sphere interacting only through electrostatics and van der Waals terms, with no bonds to its neighbours. The ion can then exchange its surroundings freely, as a real ion in solution does. It cannot reproduce the fixed geometry of a metal held in a protein site. (UNVERIFIED)

A non-bonded potential that adds a term falling off with the fourth power of distance to the usual repulsion and attraction, representing the ion polarizing the molecules around it. That extra attraction is what a fixed-charge model otherwise omits entirely for a highly charged ion. It lets one parameter set reproduce both an ion's hydration energy and its ion-water distance, which the standard form cannot. (UNVERIFIED)

A solvation model in which the solute, or the part of it being studied, is surrounded by a spherical droplet of explicit water rather than a fully periodic box. A restraining potential at the edge of the sphere usually keeps the water molecules from leaving. Using a droplet reduces the number of water molecules sharply, but water near the boundary behaves unlike bulk water, so results there are less reliable. (UNVERIFIED)

A representation of a single molecule as a set of atoms together with the rules governing how they interact. It fixes what is represented explicitly and what is left out, such as whether hydrogens appear individually. It is the unit a simulated system is assembled from. (UNVERIFIED)

A model in which a molecule is represented as a set of independent harmonic oscillators, each vibrating about a fixed position. It is not meant to describe any real molecule; it serves as a reference state whose free energy is known exactly. That known value is what absolute free energies of solids and of bound states are measured against. (UNVERIFIED)

An implicit solvent model that approximates the electrostatic part of the solvation free energy with a closed-form expression, using an effective radius for each atom that reflects how deeply it is buried. It avoids solving a partial differential equation, so it is fast enough to run inside a simulation rather than only afterwards. Its accuracy rests entirely on how those effective radii are computed. (UNVERIFIED)

A generalized Born implicit solvent model that keeps the functional form of the GBn neck model but refits its parameters, with separate values for each element and for proteins and nucleic acids. It reproduces Poisson-Boltzmann and explicit solvent results more closely than the earlier neck model. AMBER recommends it, combined with the ff14SBonlysc force field, for proteins, nucleic acids and their complexes. (UNVERIFIED)

An experimental refinement model is a computational model used to improve or interpret raw experimental data, particularly in structural biology. It combines a theoretical energy function, like a molecular mechanics force field, with terms that represent the experimental observations, such as X-ray diffraction patterns or NMR restraints.

A model of the disordered solvent in a crystal, used during experimental structure refinement to account for the scattering that ordered atoms do not explain. It treats that solvent as a uniform continuum of constant electron density rather than as individual water molecules. Without it, the low-resolution part of a diffraction pattern fits poorly. (UNVERIFIED)

A non-bonded potential energy function modified so that the energy stays finite when 2 atoms overlap completely. It removes the singularity in the Lennard-Jones and Coulomb terms that appears as an atom is created or annihilated in an alchemical calculation. Without it the calculation becomes numerically unstable near the end points of the coupling parameter. (UNVERIFIED)

A force field in which the total energy is the sum of independent terms, each depending on a fixed set of atoms and unaffected by the rest of the system. Independence is what makes the energy cheap to compute and easy to parallelise. It also means the parameters cannot respond to their environment, which is what a polarizable force field adds. (UNVERIFIED)

A model that describes a system through the probabilities of its possible microscopic arrangements, rather than by following any one of them. It connects what individual particles do to the temperature, pressure and free energy that are actually measured. Every thermodynamic quantity taken from a simulation rests on one. (UNVERIFIED)

comments: Not to be confused with STATO:0000107 "statistical model", which is a statistics and inference concept: a formalization of relationships between random variables. This term is the statistical-MECHANICS sense - the theoretical framework connecting the microscopic motion of atoms to macroscopic thermodynamic properties, for example the canonical ensemble. Renamed 2026-07-29 to remove that ambiguity; "statistical model" is retained as an exact synonym.

definition.val: A statistical mechanics model giving how the speeds of particles are spread at a given temperature, when the system is at thermal equilibrium. Most particles move near an average speed, with a long tail of fast ones and few very slow ones. Starting velocities in a simulation are drawn from it, and the observed distribution is checked against it to confirm the system has equilibrated. (UNVERIFIED)

A two-state transition model is a simplified statistical mechanics model used to describe a system that can exist in two distinct states, such as a protein in a folded or unfolded state. The model characterizes the probability of switching from one state to the other, often used to analyze the kinetics of conformational changes.

An integration grid for density functional theory calculations built by giving each atom its own spherical grid and blending these with weights that sum to 1 everywhere. The blending avoids double counting where atomic grids overlap. It is the standard way such molecular grids are built. (UNVERIFIED)

A set of points and weights on a sphere chosen so that a numerical integration over that sphere is exact for spherical harmonics up to a stated order. It reaches a given accuracy with far fewer points than an evenly spaced grid. It is the angular part of the grid a density functional theory calculation integrates on. (UNVERIFIED)

A rigid 3-site water model retuned from SPC/E so that proteins simulated in it rotate at the rates measured experimentally, giving better agreement with NMR relaxation data. Correct rotation matters because it sets the NMR relaxation properties computed from a simulation. It costs the same as SPC/E. (UNVERIFIED)

A rigid 3-site water model refitted from its predecessor against a wide set of measured properties simultaneously, rather than a few. Fitting to many targets at once gives better agreement across temperature and pressure than fitting to a handful. It keeps the 3-site form, so it costs no more than the model it replaces. (UNVERIFIED)

A rigid 3-site water model whose charges and geometry were optimised together, by a nearly exhaustive search over the electrostatic properties most relevant to liquid water, so that it reproduces a wide set of measured bulk properties. It is significantly more accurate than TIP3P and SPC/E over a wide range of temperatures, at the same cost. It also reproduces the charge hydration asymmetry of water, the different solvation of positive and negative ions of the same size. (UNVERIFIED)

A polarizable 3-site water model of the OPC family, based on the Drude oscillator idea, whose charge distribution responds to the electric field around it. Real water is markedly more polar in the liquid than as an isolated molecule, and a fixed-charge model must compromise between the 2. It removes that compromise with little extra computational cost, and its parameters were optimised to match 5 key properties of bulk water. (UNVERIFIED)

A coarse-grained water model in which 4 charged beads, joined in a tetrahedron, together represent a cluster of about 11 water molecules. Because its beads carry charges, it produces its own dielectric response instead of needing a uniform dielectric medium. It was developed as the explicit solvent for the SIRAH force field. (UNVERIFIED)

A crystallographic model component is a fundamental concept used to describe the structure of a crystal. It represents one of the key pieces of information, such as the repeating unit or the symmetry rules, that define how molecules are arranged in a crystalline solid.

The smallest portion of a crystal from which the whole structure can be built by applying the symmetry operations of its space group. It may hold 1 molecule, several, or a fraction of 1, depending on where the molecules sit relative to the symmetry elements. It is what a deposited crystal structure file usually contains. (UNVERIFIED)

A solvation shell refers to the layer of solvent molecules that are in direct contact with or in the immediate vicinity of a solute molecule. These solvent molecules are often more ordered and have different dynamic properties compared to the bulk solvent further away. Usually, analyzing the structure and dynamics of the first and second solvation shells is crucial for understanding the details of solute-solvent interactions.

A way of describing the 3-dimensional arrangement of atoms in a molecule, either as Cartesian coordinates or as internal coordinates such as bond lengths, angles and dihedral angles. Both describe the same shape, but internal coordinates leave out where the molecule sits and how it is turned in space, and they make a constraint or a symmetry easy to impose. The choice is usually dictated by the program. (UNVERIFIED)

A way of describing a molecule's geometry by giving each atom's position relative to atoms already placed, as a bond length, an angle and a rotation. It expresses shape directly, so a symmetry or a constraint can be imposed by fixing one number. It becomes unstable when 3 atoms it refers to lie nearly in a straight line. (UNVERIFIED)

The collection of fitted numbers that gives a force field its behaviour for a particular class of molecules, such as proteins, lipids or carbohydrates. The functional form stays the same across sets; the numbers change. A simulation states both the form and the set, because the form alone does not identify what was used. (UNVERIFIED)

A parameter set covering phosphorylated amino acids such as phosphoserine, phosphothreonine and phosphotyrosine, for use with the AMBER ff99SB protein force field and older AMBER protein force fields. Standard protein parameters do not include them, because phosphorylation is a modification rather than a standard residue. The newer phosaa14SB and phosaa19SB sets replace it for the ff14SB and ff19SB force fields. (UNVERIFIED)

A parameter set covering phosphorylated amino acids such as phosphoserine, phosphothreonine and phosphotyrosine, for use alongside the ff14SB protein force field. Standard protein parameters do not include them, because phosphorylation is a modification rather than a standard residue. It is matched to that protein force field and should not be used with another. (UNVERIFIED)

A parameter set covering phosphorylated amino acids such as phosphoserine, phosphothreonine and phosphotyrosine, for use alongside the ff19SB protein force field. Standard protein parameters do not include them, because phosphorylation is a modification rather than a standard residue. It is matched to that protein force field and should not be used with another. (UNVERIFIED)

A force field parameter set for the monovalent alkali and halide ions, published by Joung and Cheatham in 2008, with parameters fitted separately for each of 3 water models. Fitting per water model is the point: parameters that behave correctly with 1 water model do not with another. They were fitted to solvation free energies, ion-water interaction energies and the lattice energies and lattice constants of salt crystals. (UNVERIFIED)

A collection of mathematical functions combined to represent the shape of each electron orbital in a quantum chemistry calculation. The true orbitals cannot be written down, so they are built up from a finite set of simpler functions instead. The choice of these functions, together with the quantum method, largely sets both the accuracy and the cost of a calculation. (UNVERIFIED)

A set of mathematical functions used to approximate products of orbital basis functions, rather than the orbitals themselves, so that electron repulsion integrals can be computed more cheaply. It is what makes density fitting and resolution-of-identity methods fast. It must be matched to the orbital basis set it is paired with, or the speed-up costs accuracy. (UNVERIFIED)

A force field parameter set that extends the AMBER Lipid17 and Lipid21 lipid force fields with further head groups, such as lysophospholipids, phosphatidylinositols and cardiolipins, and with sterols such as ergosterol. It reuses the bonded and Lennard-Jones parameters of Lipid17 or Lipid21, with new partial charges fitted by the RESP method over several conformations. Its head groups are still in development and are less well tested than those of the main lipid force field. (UNVERIFIED)

A QM/MM model component that adds a deep neural network correction to the energy of a QM/MM potential, trained to improve both the interactions within the quantum region and those between quantum atoms and nearby classical atoms. The correction is non-electrostatic and acts only on classical atoms within a cutoff distance of the quantum region, which is what range-corrected refers to. It is typically used to bring a fast semi-empirical QM/MM model close to the accuracy of ab initio QM/MM. (UNVERIFIED)

A description of the full symmetry of a crystal, listing the rotations, reflections, translations and their combinations that leave the structure unchanged. There are 230 such groups in 3 dimensions, and every crystal belongs to exactly 1. Together with the asymmetric unit it determines the entire crystal. (UNVERIFIED)

A generalized Born implicit solvent model that computes effective Born radii with the scheme of Onufriev, Bashford and Case, which rescales the radii to account for the spaces between atomic spheres that earlier pairwise models missed. Its radii come closer to the true molecular volume at little extra cost. In AMBER it has 2 parameter variants, igb=2 and igb=5, which are recommended for most protein work and are used with the mbondi2 radii. (UNVERIFIED)

A generalized Born implicit solvent model that corrects the effective Born radii for the narrow regions between overlapping atomic spheres, which earlier formulations treated as more solvent-exposed than they are. The correction matters most in crevices and buried pockets. The letter n in the name stands for those neck regions. (UNVERIFIED)

A label classifying an atom by its element and its local bonding environment, in the scheme used by the SYBYL software and by the Mol2 file format. For instance, C.ar marks an aromatic carbon and C.2 a carbon with a double bond. Many modelling tools read these types from Mol2 files, for example when preparing a small molecule for docking or charge calculation. (UNVERIFIED)

A generalized distance coordinate restraint is a type of restraint that is applied to a complex coordinate defined as a combination of multiple distances, angles, or dihedrals. This allows for the restraining of complex conformational changes, such as the movement of a whole domain, that cannot be described by a single distance.

An electronic property giving how a molecule's electrons respond to a magnetic field, as a 3-by-3 array because the response depends on the field's direction relative to the molecule. A molecule with circulating electrons, such as an aromatic ring, responds much more strongly along one axis than the others. It is what underlies the ring current shifts seen in NMR spectra. (UNVERIFIED)

An alignment tensor is a mathematical object that describes the degree and direction of the average orientation of molecules in a sample that is not perfectly random. In an NMR experiment, molecules can be weakly aligned by a magnetic field, and the alignment tensor quantifies this small but measurable preference in orientation. This tensor is crucial for interpreting experimental data like residual dipolar couplings (RDCs), which provide powerful long-range structural information.

A force field component that is 1 of the numbers setting the Lennard-Jones van der Waals interaction of an atom type, such as its well depth (epsilon), its size (sigma), or the coefficient of the attractive or the repulsive term. Parameters for 2 different atom types are combined by a combining rule. Those combining rules differ between force fields, which is one reason their parameters cannot be mixed. (UNVERIFIED)

An implicit solvent model that represents a solute as a low-dielectric cavity in a high-dielectric continuum and solves for the electrostatic potential, including the screening by mobile salt ions. It makes no analytical approximation to the molecule's shape, so it is the reference the faster models are judged against. Solving it numerically is expensive, which is why it is usually applied to snapshots rather than during a simulation. (UNVERIFIED)

A Poisson-Boltzmann model in which the equation is linearized and solved in closed form under simplifying assumptions about geometry. It is far faster than solving the full non-linear equation numerically. It holds only where electrostatic potentials are small, so it is unreliable for highly charged systems. (UNVERIFIED)

A generalized Born implicit solvent model that accounts for charge hydration asymmetry, the fact that a negative ion and a positive ion of the same size are not solvated equally by water. It adds this asymmetry to the generalized Born equation to copy the response of a chosen explicit water model, and uses its own set of atomic radii. It was tested on small molecules, amino acid analogues and small proteins, and is available in the GBNSR6 program. (UNVERIFIED)

A generalized Born implicit solvent model in which ions are kept as explicit particles while the water is treated implicitly, with extra coefficients in the generalized Born equation that tune the interactions between solute atoms and ions and between ions. Interactions between solute atoms are computed with the standard generalized Born model, and it has been used together with the GB-Neck2 model. It was fitted to explicit-solvent ion distributions around DNA, and captures local effects of ions that a uniform salt concentration cannot. (UNVERIFIED)

A generalized Born implicit solvent model that computes each atom's effective Born radius numerically, by an integral over the molecular surface of the solute (the R6 integral), rather than by an analytical approximation. This makes it nearly as accurate as Born radii derived from Poisson-Boltzmann calculations, and almost independent of the choice of atomic radii. In AMBER it is used to estimate solvation free energies of single structures and cannot yet be used in molecular dynamics. (UNVERIFIED)

A model that estimates the free energy of a process by adding up tabulated free energies for moving each chemical group between environments, such as from water into a protein interior. The group values are measured once on small molecules and then reused. It is fast and additive, which also means it cannot capture effects that depend on how groups are arranged relative to one another. (UNVERIFIED)

A database holding the 2-dimensional and 3-dimensional structures of small organic compounds. Such collections supply the starting geometries and the reference conformations that force field parameters are fitted and tested against. They differ from protein structure archives in holding many small entries rather than few large ones. (UNVERIFIED)

A RISM model that solves the integral equations on a 3-dimensional grid around a solute, giving the spatial distribution of each solvent site. It shows where solvent molecules are likely to sit, including individual ordered water positions, without running a simulation. It needs the bulk solvent correlation functions from a 1-dimensional calculation as input. (UNVERIFIED)

An approximate equation relating the 2 unknown correlation functions in an integral equation theory of liquids, so that the system can be solved. Without it there are 2 unknowns and 1 equation. Different choices, such as hypernetted-chain or Kovalenko-Hirata, give measurably different solvation free energies from otherwise identical input. (UNVERIFIED)

The Kovalenko-Hirata (KH) closure is a mathematical approximation used in the statistical mechanical Ornstein-Zernike (OZ) integral equation theory (commonly utilized in 3D-RISM theory) to calculate solvent structure and solvation free energy.

An implicit solvent model in which the solvent excluded surface, the boundary between solute and solvent used in a Poisson-Boltzmann calculation, is predicted by a machine-learned model instead of being built geometrically. It produces the surface much faster than the classical construction while closely reproducing it. In AMBER it is used within Poisson-Boltzmann calculations through models such as GENIUSES. (UNVERIFIED)

A machine-learned potential that predicts only the difference between a cheap approximate calculation and an accurate one, rather than the full energy. The difference is smaller and smoother than the energy itself, so far less training data is needed to learn it well. The cheap calculation still has to be run, which is the cost of the approach. (UNVERIFIED)

A charge model that fits permanent point charges to the electrostatic potential and adds an induced dipole on each atom to represent the response to a field. The permanent part describes the isolated molecule and the induced part its response to the environment. It is 1 way of deriving the electrostatic parameters of a polarizable force field from quantum calculations. (UNVERIFIED)

A charge model that fits a dipole and higher terms on each atom, not only a point charge, to reproduce the electrostatic potential around a molecule. The extra terms capture features a point charge cannot, such as the anisotropy of a lone pair or the positive region on a halogen. It is more accurate and more expensive to use. (UNVERIFIED)

The AMBER FB15 (force-balanced 15) protein force field is a refinement of the AMBER94 ff with a systematic and thorough optimization of the intramolecular terms. The key difference in the optimized result is a significant lowering of the potential in regions away from the energy minima, which is expected to yield greater flexibility in finite temperature simulations. This force field is particularly useful for simulations of proteins, particularly when fluctuations away from equilibrium, conformational changes, and/or temperature dependence are expected to play important roles.

A force field in which non-polar hydrogens are merged into the heavy atom they are bonded to, so that a methyl group is 1 interaction site. This reduces the number of particles, so a simulation costs less than with an all-atom model. Polar hydrogens are kept as separate sites, because they take part in hydrogen bonds. (UNVERIFIED)

A charged particle attached by a harmonic spring to an atom in a polarizable force field, used to represent how that atom's electron cloud shifts in an electric field. The local electric field pulls the particle and its atom apart, and the 2 charges together form an induced dipole, so polarization is reproduced without modelling electrons. The particle is either given a small mass and moved with the other atoms, usually with its own thermostat held at a very low temperature, or its position is solved for at every step. (UNVERIFIED)

A RISM model that solves the integral equations for a homogeneous fluid, giving site-to-site correlation functions that depend only on distance. It describes the structure of the bulk solvent itself, with no solute present. Its output is the required input for a 3-dimensional calculation around a solute. (UNVERIFIED)

A statistical mechanical model of molecular liquids that predicts how solvent molecules arrange themselves around a solute by solving integral equations for site-to-site correlation functions. It gives an atomistic picture of solvation without simulating individual solvent molecules moving. It sits between an implicit solvent model and explicit solvent in both cost and detail. (UNVERIFIED)

A RISM model corrected so that its results reproduce the known dielectric constant of the solvent. Standard RISM does not, which distorts long-range electrostatics. The correction matters most for solvation free energies of charged solutes. (UNVERIFIED)

A thermodynamic property giving the average kinetic energy of the particles in a system, expressed on a conventional scale. In a simulation it is computed from the velocities and fluctuates strongly, because the system is small. A value quoted from a short stretch of trajectory can differ from the target by several degrees for that reason alone. (UNVERIFIED)

A QM/MM model component that replaces the fixed Lennard-Jones terms between quantum and classical atoms with exchange repulsion and dispersion terms that depend on the current partial charge of each quantum atom. An atom that loses electron density becomes smaller and less polarizable, and one that gains it becomes larger, which fixed Lennard-Jones parameters cannot represent. It matters most in reactions, where atoms change their charge and bonding as the reaction proceeds. (UNVERIFIED)

A semi-empirical extended tight binding method, the first of its family, parameterised to give good molecular geometries, vibrational frequencies and non-covalent interaction energies for elements across most of the periodic table. Its name records those 3 targets: geometries, frequencies and non-covalent interactions. It is used to optimise structures and screen conformations quickly. (UNVERIFIED)

A semi-empirical tight binding method that adds atom-centred multipoles and a density-dependent dispersion treatment to the earlier method in its family. Those additions improve the description of non-covalent interactions without the separate hydrogen bond and halogen bond corrections that the earlier method needed. It is the member of the family in general use. (UNVERIFIED)

A correction to the PM3 semi-empirical quantum method that replaces the core-core repulsion between atoms of different molecules with specially fitted functions, to improve the interactions of organic molecules with water and of water molecules with each other. Separate parameters are used for water-water pairs and for organic-organic and organic-water pairs, and a later version treats hydrogens that attract water differently from hydrogens that repel it. In AMBER it is available in semi-empirical Born-Oppenheimer molecular dynamics. (UNVERIFIED)

A correction to the PM3 semi-empirical quantum method in which the core-core repulsion functions, within and between molecules, are replaced by specially fitted functions, to improve the description of hydrogen-bonded systems such as liquid water. Its first version has parameters only for hydrogen and oxygen, and a second version adds chlorine. In AMBER it is available in semi-empirical Born-Oppenheimer molecular dynamics. (UNVERIFIED)

A force field that allows chemical bonds to form and break during a simulation, so the list of bonded atoms is not fixed in advance. Bond-order force fields such as ReaxFF do this by computing the strength of each bond from the current distances between atoms, while other approaches, such as the empirical valence bond method, mix the energies of several fixed bonding patterns. It can describe reactions in systems far larger than a quantum method can handle, at a cost well above that of a conventional force field. (UNVERIFIED)

A reactive force field in which the strength of every bond is recomputed from interatomic distances at each step, so bonds can form and break. Charges are also recomputed, since they change as bonds do. It reaches system sizes no quantum method can while still describing reactions, at a cost much higher than that of a conventional force field. (UNVERIFIED)

A force field component that replaces the Lennard-Jones parameters for 1 particular pair of atom types, overriding the values the combining rule would give, as done in the CHARMM force fields. It is used where the combining rule gives poor results for a pair, for example for some ions with carboxylate oxygens. It is applied pair by pair rather than by changing the atom types themselves. (UNVERIFIED)

An algorithm that computes the induced dipole on each atom in a polarizable force field. Each induced dipole changes the field felt by the others, so they must be solved together rather than one at a time. That coupling is what makes a polarizable simulation several times more expensive than a fixed-charge one. (UNVERIFIED)

A polarization algorithm that computes the induced dipoles in a set of polarizable atoms by giving each atom a point polarizability and solving the resulting linear equations self-consistently. It captures how the dipole induced on one atom polarizes its neighbours in turn. Its induced dipoles can grow without limit when 2 atoms come too close, a problem called the polarization catastrophe, which later schemes such as Thole's avoid by damping the interaction at short range. (UNVERIFIED)

nodes.lbl: RESP permanent virtual site charge model

definition.val: A charge model that fits point charges to the electrostatic potential while allowing some of them to sit at fixed positions away from any nucleus. Placing charge off-nucleus reproduces directional features, such as a lone pair, without the cost of higher multipole terms. It is the cheaper alternative to a multipole description. (UNVERIFIED)

A potential energy function formed as a straight-line interpolation between the functions of an initial and a final state, controlled by a coupling parameter running from 0 to 1. It is what makes a continuous path between 2 chemically different states possible in an alchemical calculation. It behaves badly when atoms appear or disappear, which is why the soft-core variant exists. (UNVERIFIED)

A data format defining, for each residue that can gain or lose a proton, the topology and charges of every protonation state it can take and the reference energy of each. A constant pH simulation reads it to know what states are available and what switching between them costs. A residue absent from the library cannot titrate. (UNVERIFIED)

A force field component that adds an energy correction read from a 2-dimensional grid indexed by a pair of neighbouring backbone rotation angles. The pair of angles is treated together rather than as 2 independent terms, which is what lets the correction fix their coupling. It was introduced to bring simulated backbone conformational populations into line with experiment. (UNVERIFIED)

A restraint potential is an artificial energy function that is added to the force field to guide a simulation. This potential adds an energy penalty when the system deviates from a user-defined geometric target, such as a specific distance, angle, or RMSD value.

A statistical mechanical theory that describes solvent around a solute by treating the solvent as a fluid whose density and orientation vary with position. It assigns energy and entropy to each region rather than to the system as a whole. That local assignment is what lets individual water sites be scored for displacement by a ligand. (UNVERIFIED)

A simulation technique in which the box is treated as one cell of an infinite lattice of identical copies, so a particle leaving one side re-enters the opposite side. It removes the surface that a finite box would otherwise have, where molecules would behave unlike those in bulk. The box must be large enough that a molecule does not interact with its own image. (UNVERIFIED)

An expanded ensemble simulation is an enhanced sampling method where the simulation samples not only the coordinates of the system but also an additional thermodynamic variable, such as temperature or an alchemical coupling parameter. The system can move dynamically between different temperatures or states, which helps it to overcome energy barriers and sample a wider range of conformations. For experts, this method is a powerful framework that generalizes techniques like replica-exchange and lambda-dynamics for calculating free energies.

A software program that assembles the parts of a simulation into a system that is ready to run. It places the molecule in a box, fills the box with solvent, adds ions to reach the intended charge and concentration, and writes the topology and coordinate files. It is the step at which a structure becomes a simulatable system. (UNVERIFIED)

A system preparation program in AmberTools that adds a stated number of copies of a solvent molecule or ion to a crystal unit cell or supercell, placing each at a random position and orientation where it does not clash with the biomolecule. Added molecules are allowed closer to one another than to the biomolecule, because enough solvent must be added to keep the cell at its crystallographic size. It is part of the AmberTools route for building simulations of biomolecular crystals. (UNVERIFIED)

An electrostatics analysis tool is a type of software designed to calculate and visualize the electrostatic properties of a molecule. These tools typically take a molecular structure with assigned atomic charges and compute quantities like the electrostatic potential on the molecule's surface or the total electrostatic energy of solvation. They are essential for understanding how a molecule will interact with other charged molecules and its polar solvent environment.

A numerical solver that computes the electrostatic potential around a molecule in solvent by solving the Poisson-Boltzmann equation on a grid that is refined where the potential changes fastest. Refining only where needed gives the accuracy of a fine grid at much lower cost. It is the usual way continuum electrostatics is computed for a large biomolecule. (UNVERIFIED)

A set of van der Waals radii that is the third modification of the Bondi set in AMBER, with further adjustments to the radii of some atoms based on protein simulations. It is the radii set recommended for the GB-Neck2 generalized Born model (igb=8). For nucleic acids its radii are currently the same as mbondi2. (UNVERIFIED)

An analysis program that processes the output of a constant pH molecular dynamics run and reports pKa values and titration curves for the titratable residues. It reads the record of protonation state changes rather than the trajectory. It is what turns a constant pH simulation into a number that can be compared with experiment. (UNVERIFIED)

A defined set of functions and rules through which one piece of software uses another. It fixes what can be asked for and what comes back, so the 2 sides can change independently as long as the agreement holds. It is how a simulation engine is driven from a script rather than from a command line. (UNVERIFIED)

A programming platform and interface for running general computation on NVIDIA graphics processors. A graphics processor performs thousands of simple operations at once, which suits computing forces on many atoms simultaneously. Many simulation engines use it to run several times faster than on central processors alone, at the cost of working only on one manufacturer's hardware. (UNVERIFIED)

A software program that computes free energy differences from the data produced by molecular simulations. It implements estimators such as the weighted histogram analysis method or the multi-state Bennett acceptance ratio, which combine data from many biased or alchemical runs, or endpoint methods that use only the start and end states. It is usually the last step of a free energy workflow, turning the output of many runs into 1 number. (UNVERIFIED)

An analysis program, part of the FE-ToolKit library in AmberTools, that computes the free energy of 1 alchemical transformation, an edge, in 1 or 2 environments using the multi-state Bennett acceptance ratio and thermodynamic integration. It writes a report with error estimates, time series and convergence checks, and a breakdown of the relative free energy into its parts. The results for many edges are then combined in a network analysis by a companion script. (UNVERIFIED)

A software library is a collection of pre-written code and subroutines that provide specific functionalities to be used by other programs. Libraries are not executed directly by end-users but are imported or linked by developers to perform specialized tasks, such as mathematical computations or file parsing.

A software library for computing discrete Fourier transforms, which convert data between a description in space or time and one in frequency. Particle mesh Ewald performs one at every step, so its speed sets a large part of a simulation's cost. The library measures the machine it is running on and chooses its method accordingly. (UNVERIFIED)

A simulation engine distributed with AmberTools that is now used mainly for force field parameter development, including fitting bonded terms and CMAP surfaces and deriving IPolQ charges. It began as a test platform for new molecular dynamics algorithms and keeps a modest ability to run basic simulations, including many small generalized Born simulations at once for validating parameters. It is a development tool rather than a production engine. (UNVERIFIED)

A small script that performs one well-defined supporting task inside a larger workflow, such as converting between file formats or pulling one value out of an output file. It does no science itself; it makes the pieces that do fit together. A published workflow usually depends on several of them. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility script in AmberTools, part of the pyMSMT toolbox, that converts a PDB file holding a single metal ion into a mol2 file carrying the ion's charge, which the user specifies. It was written for users of the metal centre parameter builder MCPB.py, which needs the metal ions as mol2 files. (UNVERIFIED)

A set of atomic radii fitted for use with the generalized Born model of the same authors. Radii and generalized Born model are fitted together, so using 1 with a different model degrades both. It is the default radii set for that model in AMBER. (UNVERIFIED)

The ndfes software, included in the FE-ToolKit package, is used to analyze biased umbrella sampling to estimate free energy surfaces in an arbitrary number of reaction coordinate dimensions using either the variational free energy profile (vFEP), multistate Bennett acceptance ratio method (MBAR), or the highly-related weighted thermodynamic perturbation and generalized weighted thermodynamic perturbation methods.

ParmEd is a software package and Python library designed for manipulating and converting molecular topology and parameter files from various simulation packages, with a primary focus on the AMBER force field format. It allows users to programmatically modify force field parameters, change molecular connectivity, and convert between different file formats.

A system preparation program that cleans a Protein Data Bank structure file so the AMBER tools can read it. It renumbers residues, corrects atom naming, and reports problems such as missing atoms, alternate locations and unusual residues. It is run before force field parameters are assigned, because those steps fail on an unprepared file. (UNVERIFIED)

A system setup program in AmberTools that builds a larger simulation cell by repeating a crystallographic unit cell along chosen directions. It is needed when the unit cell is too thin for the cut-off distance used for non-bonded interactions, because a periodic simulation cell must be able to hold a sphere of at least that radius plus a small buffer. Repeating the cell makes the box big enough, and can also reduce artefacts from the strict symmetry that periodic copies impose. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility script in AmberTools, part of the pyMSMT toolbox, that cuts a segment out of a protein structure and caps the cut ends, producing clusters suitable for quantum calculations. The user chooses which residues to keep whole, which to keep only as side chains and which to cap as acetyl or N-methyl groups, and it writes Gaussian input files. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility program in AmberTools, written in Python to replace the older resp program, that fits atomic charges to an electrostatic potential computed by quantum chemistry, with restraints that keep poorly determined charges small. Besides the standard RESP charge model for additive force fields, it fits models with induced and permanent dipoles for polarizable force fields. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility program in AmberTools that writes the input files for the 2 stages of a restrained electrostatic potential fit with resp or py_resp.py, starting from the electrostatic potential file made by espgen. It records which charges, and for polarizable models which permanent dipoles, must be equal, and the restraint weights for each stage. It performs no fitting itself. (UNVERIFIED)

Pytraj is a Python library that provides a programmable interface to the powerful trajectory analysis capabilities of the cpptraj engine from the AmberTools suite. It allows users to write Python scripts to perform a wide range of analyses, such as calculating RMSD, distances, and hydrogen bonds, directly on simulation trajectories. Pytraj enables the creation of complex, automated, and reproducible analysis workflows that integrate seamlessly with other Python data science tools.

A quantum chemistry engine in AmberTools that performs semi-empirical calculations, either on its own or as the quantum part of a QM/MM simulation run with sander. It implements methods such as AM1, PM3, PM6 and MNDO, and the density functional tight binding methods DFTB2 and DFTB3. Antechamber calls it to compute the AM1 charges from which AM1-BCC charges are derived. (UNVERIFIED)

A quantum chemistry engine for Hartree-Fock and density functional theory calculations that was written from the outset to run on graphics processors rather than adapted to them later. Designing for that hardware gives it a large speed advantage on the calculations it supports, which suits very large molecules and the quantum part of QM/MM simulations. It supports fewer methods than a general-purpose package. (UNVERIFIED)

A software library used by the AmberTools PBSA program, built on LibTorch, the C++ form of the PyTorch machine learning framework, to run trained machine learning models for parts of a Poisson-Boltzmann surface area calculation, such as building the molecular surface. It lets those models run on central or graphics processors without a Python interpreter. The options that need it work only when LibTorch is installed. (UNVERIFIED)

A system setup program that rebuilds a complete crystallographic repeating unit from a structure file by applying the symmetry operations recorded in it. A deposited file usually contains only the smallest unique part, leaving the rest to be generated. The program performs that generation so the full contents of the cell can be simulated. (UNVERIFIED)

A graphical system preparation program that builds a molecular system for AMBER interactively: loading a structure, applying a force field, adding solvent and ions, and writing the topology and coordinate files. It is the graphical front end to the same engine the command-line tool uses. The 2 produce identical output from identical commands. (UNVERIFIED)

A program that controls how source code is turned into a working executable, working out what must be compiled, in what order and with which options, and calling the compiler and linker to do it. It also finds the libraries the program depends on. Which options it was given affects how fast the resulting program runs, and sometimes what it can do. (UNVERIFIED)

A build system tool that reads a single description of how a program is assembled and generates the native build files, such as Makefiles or Visual Studio projects, for each platform. It lets one set of instructions serve Linux, macOS and Windows. Many simulation packages, including GROMACS and AMBER, are built with it, so which version was used is part of reproducing an installation. (UNVERIFIED)

The Intel oneAPI Math Kernel Library (oneMKL) is a collection of highly optimized mathematical functions for science, engineering, and financial applications, specifically tuned for Intel processors. It provides high-performance implementations of routines for linear algebra (BLAS, LAPACK, ScaLAPACK), Fast Fourier Transforms (FFT), and other core mathematical operations. For biomolecular simulation software, linking against oneMKL can significantly boost performance by accelerating the fundamental mathematical computations underlying the simulation algorithms.

A package manager is a tool that automates the process of installing, upgrading, configuring, and removing software packages and their dependencies. It simplifies the management of the complex web of software required for scientific computing by handling the details of where to find packages and which versions are compatible. For simulation scientists, package managers like Conda are crucial for creating stable and reproducible software environments.

Miniconda is a minimal, bootstrap installer for the Conda package manager, which is widely used in the scientific computing community. It includes only the Conda package manager and Python, allowing users to create customized software environments by installing only the packages they need. For researchers, Miniconda provides a lightweight way to set up isolated and reproducible environments for their simulation and analysis software.

A utility script distributed with AmberTools that fetches and applies official updates and fixes to an existing installation. It contacts the update server, downloads what applies to the installed version, and patches the source. Which updates have been applied is part of what identifies the version a result came from. (UNVERIFIED)

An analysis program that solves the 1-dimensional reference interaction site model (RISM) equations for a pure solvent, giving its structural and thermodynamic properties. Its output describes the bulk liquid with no solute present. It must be run before any 3-dimensional RISM calculation, which takes those results as input. (UNVERIFIED)

A quantum chemistry engine for Hartree-Fock and density functional theory calculations, distributed with AmberTools, that runs in parallel on central processors and on NVIDIA and AMD graphics processors. Evaluating the electron repulsion integrals, where most of the computing time goes, on graphics processors gives it its speed. It serves as the quantum part of QM/MM simulations with AMBER, where the calculation must be repeated at every step. (UNVERIFIED)

A quantum chemistry program for very high accuracy electronic structure calculations, implementing coupled cluster methods to arbitrary excitation level and their multi-reference forms. Those methods are the benchmark other methods are measured against. Its most exact methods are limited to small molecules, but its local natural orbital approximations bring coupled cluster accuracy to molecules of hundreds of atoms. (UNVERIFIED)

A quantum chemistry engine that performs density functional calculations using orbitals confined to a fixed radius around each atom, with the resulting integrals tabulated in advance. Confining the orbitals is what makes the tabulation possible and the calculation fast. It is used for large systems where full density functional theory would be too slow. (UNVERIFIED)

A quantum chemistry engine implementing density functional tight binding, an approximation that replaces most of the electronic integrals with values tabulated in advance. It is 2 to 3 orders of magnitude faster than full density functional theory while remaining quantum mechanical. Its accuracy depends on parameters fitted for each pair of elements, so it works only for element combinations that have been parameterised. (UNVERIFIED)

A quantum chemistry program implementing the GFN family of extended tight binding methods, semi-empirical methods parameterised for most of the periodic table. It is fast enough to optimise geometries, compute vibrational frequencies and search conformations for molecules of hundreds of atoms. It is widely used as a preliminary step before a more expensive calculation. (UNVERIFIED)

A software framework that connects separate simulation programs so that each can compute the part of a system it is best suited to. It passes coordinates, energies and forces between them and keeps them in step. It is what allows a quantum chemistry program and a molecular dynamics program to run 1 simulation together. (UNVERIFIED)

A software library that lets a classical simulation program request energies and forces from the TeraChem quantum chemistry program over a network connection. The 2 programs run separately and exchange data at each step. It is what allows a quantum and a classical engine to run one hybrid simulation together. (UNVERIFIED)

A simulation engine built to run reactive force field simulations, where bonding is recomputed at every step rather than fixed. Recomputing the bond network is what makes such a simulation expensive, and the engine is written around doing it in parallel. It is used for reactions in materials and at surfaces. (UNVERIFIED)

A structure preparation program that adds hydrogen atoms to a macromolecular structure and chooses their positions. It also decides how to orient groups whose 2 possible arrangements X-ray data cannot distinguish, such as the ends of asparagine and glutamine side chains. Crystallography rarely sees hydrogens, so a structure file usually arrives without them and a simulation cannot start until they are there. (UNVERIFIED)

A system setup utility that places the hydrogen atoms of water molecules taken from an experimental structure. Crystallography sees the oxygen of an ordered water and not its hydrogens, so their orientation must be worked out. It chooses orientations that make sensible hydrogen bonds with the surroundings. (UNVERIFIED)

A Python library and set of command-line tools for analysing and manipulating Protein Data Bank structure files and for running molecular dynamics simulations with AMBER, GROMACS and NAMD through 1 interface. It covers structure preparation, minimization, dynamics and trajectory processing, and PACKMOL-Memgen uses it to estimate the volume of a protein. (UNVERIFIED)

A system preparation program that builds an initial arrangement of molecules inside a defined region by packing them to satisfy stated counts and spatial constraints while keeping them from overlapping. It solves a constrained optimisation rather than placing molecules at random. It is how a mixed or layered starting system is built when a regular lattice will not do. (UNVERIFIED)

AMBAT is a software tool used to construct three-dimensional models of cell membranes for use in AMBER molecular simulations. Consisting of a set of scripts, it automates the complex process of arranging lipid molecules to form a proper bilayer and can then embed a protein structure within that prepared membrane. As part of the AmberTools suite, AMBAT (Amber Membrane Builder and Analysis Tool) provides a script-based workflow for both the initial construction of lipid bilayer systems and for subsequent analysis of membrane properties, serving as a specialized tool for preparing membrane protein simulations.

synonyms.val: Amber Membrane Builder and Analysis Tool

definition.val: A software program that derives force field parameters by adjusting them until the force field reproduces reference data, usually quantum calculations. It is used when no existing parameter covers a molecule and assignment by analogy is not good enough. Its output is a parameter set, not a prepared system. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility program that searches automatically for force field parameters giving the best agreement with reference data, by trying many combinations rather than fitting one term at a time. Searching the whole space at once can find a combination that fitting terms separately misses. It is used for parameter development rather than for preparing a single system. (UNVERIFIED)

comments: described in https://doi.org/10.1002/jcc.1079

definition.val: A utility program in AmberTools that checks whether every parameter a molecule needs is present in the chosen force field, and writes an additional parameter file supplying the missing ones by analogy. Missing parameters otherwise stop system preparation with an error. Parameters it supplies by analogy are guesses and are flagged as such in its output. (UNVERIFIED)

An interactive utility included in the AmberTools software package for deriving force field parameters. It assists users in calculating new parameters for bond lengths and angles based on a set of built-in empirical rules. This tool is particularly useful when parameterizing a new molecule for which no existing force field parameters are available. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility program in AmberTools that optimizes chosen force field parameters, often dihedral terms, so that the energies or forces the force field gives over many conformations of a molecule match quantum chemical reference values. It is used when parameters are missing and cannot be supplied by analogy, or when existing ones are not accurate enough. It can also fit 1 set of parameters across several molecules at once. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility program in AmberTools that builds force field parameters for a metal centre in a protein, from quantum calculations on the metal and the groups around it. A metal site has no standard parameters, because its geometry and charge depend on which groups coordinate it. It automates a procedure that is otherwise long and easy to get wrong. (UNVERIFIED)

A Python toolbox in AmberTools for modelling metal sites in biomolecules for molecular dynamics, covering both bonded and non-bonded models of the metal. It bundles several programs, including the metal centre parameter builder MCPB.py, the ion parameterization program IPMach.py and the metal site search program PdbSearcher.py. It is a toolbox rather than a single program. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility program in AmberTools that assigns a force field atom type to every atom of a molecule, from its element and its bonding environment. Every parameter a molecule receives follows from those assignments. It is run before parameters are looked up, and its output is worth inspecting for unusual chemistry. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility program in AmberTools that turns AM1 Mulliken charges, computed beforehand by a fast semi-empirical calculation, into AM1-BCC charges by adding tabulated bond charge corrections that depend on atom and bond types. The corrections are fitted so the result approximates charges fitted to a far more expensive quantum calculation of the electrostatic potential. Antechamber calls it automatically when these charges are requested. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility program in AmberTools that assigns each bond in a molecule 1 of the 6 bond types defined for AM1-BCC charges: single, double, triple, aromatic single, aromatic double and delocalized. It works from the connectivity table alone, or adjusts simple bond types already present in the input file. Antechamber uses the result when it applies the AM1-BCC bond charge corrections. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility program in AmberTools that writes the input files for the 2 stages of a restrained electrostatic potential (RESP) fit of atomic charges. It detects which atoms are equivalent and must receive equal charges, and records the restraint weights and any charges or charge groups the user wants fixed. The fit itself is performed by a separate program. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility program in AmberTools that writes a residue template, a prep file, for a new molecule from a file holding its structure, atom types and charges. It builds the main chain and the internal coordinate tree itself, or takes the main chain atoms, the head and tail atoms that join neighbouring residues, and atoms to delete from a main chain file given by the user. It is run once per new building block, and its output is reused thereafter. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility program in AmberTools that builds the residue template, in prepi format, for a modified amino acid, nucleotide or other polymer unit, removing the capping groups used during the charge calculation. It runs a sequence of antechamber programs from a single input file, including a RESP charge fit over 1 or more conformations. It is meant for cases too complex for prepgen alone, such as charges averaged over several conformations. (UNVERIFIED)

A quantum chemistry engine that divides a large molecule into overlapping regions, solves each separately, and assembles the result. Doing so makes the cost grow in proportion to the system size rather than far faster, which is what puts whole proteins within reach. The overlap between regions is what keeps the joins from introducing errors. (UNVERIFIED)

A diagnostic utility program in AmberTools that checks a small molecule structure file for problems that would make the antechamber programs fail, such as unusual elements, unfilled valences, atom clashes, doubtful bonds and atoms not linked to the rest of the molecule. It then tries to assign bond and atom types and reports any errors and warnings. Since AmberTools 17 the same checks run inside antechamber by default. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility script in AmberTools, part of the pyMSMT toolbox, that fits Lennard-Jones parameters for an ion, in the 12-6 or 12-6-4 model, to a target hydration free energy, a target ion-oxygen distance, or both. It runs thermodynamic integration simulations of the ion in a chosen water model at trial parameters and adjusts them until the targets are met within a tolerance. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility script in AmberTools, part of the pyMSMT toolbox, that searches a list of PDB files for the metal centres of a chosen element. It records each centre's ligating atoms, bond distances and geometry in an environment file and a summary file. It is the Python version of the earlier Pdbsearcher program and recognises metal ions more reliably from PDB naming. (UNVERIFIED)

A system preparation script in AmberTools that writes the input files a replica exchange molecular dynamics run needs: 1 input file per replica, the group file listing them and, for a multidimensional run, the file describing each exchange dimension. It builds them from a reference input file and lists of the temperatures, pH values, redox potentials or Hamiltonians to be exchanged. A replica exchange run needs as many input files as it has replicas, which is too many to write reliably by hand. (UNVERIFIED)

The nfe-umbrella-slice script is a utility used in the analysis of umbrella sampling simulations, likely as part of a larger free energy calculation workflow. Its purpose is to extract a specific portion or "slice" of the simulation data from the collective output of all umbrella windows. Experts use this for tasks such as assessing the convergence of the free energy profile by analyzing how it changes as more data is included.

A system preparation script, part of AmberTools, that writes the input file a constant pH molecular dynamics run needs. It records which residues may change protonation state and the parameters the titration algorithm uses. Without it the simulation has no list of titratable sites. (UNVERIFIED)

The ceinutil.py script is a utility used to prepare the input files for constant redox-potential MD simulations in AMBER. It allows the user to specify which residues can change their redox state and defines the parameters for the simulation. This script is essential for setting up simulations that model the behavior of molecules in a specific electrochemical environment.

A system preparation script that writes the input file for a simulation holding both pH and redox potential constant. It records which residues may change protonation state and which may change oxidation state. It is the constant pH preparation script extended to redox-active sites. (UNVERIFIED)

The cyana_rest_to_amberRST script iscript converts CYANA .upl upper distance limit files into AMBER .RST format, allowing for the inclusion of restraints in molecular dynamics simulations. This conversion tool is commonly used to prepare input data for AMBER's sander or pmemd applications.

This script is a utility for creating a restraint file (RST) for a simulation that uses direct dipolar coupling (DIP) data from NMR experiments. It likely reads experimental dipolar coupling values and generates the corresponding energy restraint terms in a format that can be read by a simulation program like AMBER. This automates the process of incorporating this specific type of experimental data into a simulation.

A utility script in AmberTools, part of FRETrest, that adds pseudo atoms to a structure or topology file to stand for the mean positions of fluorescent dyes, as found by accessible volume simulations. It is the first of 2 steps in adding Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) restraints to a simulation; FRETrest.py then tethers the pseudo atoms and applies the restraints. It reads a FRET configuration file that names the labelling positions. (UNVERIFIED)

The FRETrest.py script is a utility used to generate distance restraints for a molecular dynamics simulation based on experimental data from Förster Resonance Energy Transfer (FRET) experiments. It translates the efficiency of energy transfer between two fluorescent labels into a distance distribution that can be used to bias the simulation.

The ambpdb utility is a command-line tool in the AmberTools suite that converts AMBER's native topology (.prmtop) and coordinate (.inpcrd or .rst7) files into the standard Protein Data Bank (PDB) format.

A system preparation script that derives the separate receptor and ligand topology files needed for an end-point binding free energy calculation by stripping atoms from the topology of the complex. Deriving them this way guarantees the 3 topologies are consistent. Building them independently is the common source of mismatched-topology errors. (UNVERIFIED)

A Perl script, part of the AmberTools free energy workflow FEW, that collects the binding free energies and their main energy contributions from MM-PBSA or MM-GBSA calculations on several ligands into 1 table. For each ligand it lists the electrostatic, van der Waals, nonpolar solvation and polar solvation contributions and the total binding free energy. It does not handle the hybrid PB2 model or energy decomposition runs. (UNVERIFIED)

A Perl script, part of the AmberTools free energy workflow FEW, that collects the differences in electrostatic and van der Waals interaction energies from the linear interaction energy results of several ligands into 1 table. It reads each ligand's result file together with a list of ligand names and their measured binding data. The table can then be used to fit the coefficients of a linear interaction energy model. (UNVERIFIED)

A Perl script, part of the AmberTools free energy workflow FEW, that chooses which pairs of ligands in a series to connect by thermodynamic integration so that the transformations need, overall, the smallest structural changes. It reads a matrix of pairwise similarity scores, for example from shape overlays with ROCS, and applies Kruskal's algorithm. Relative binding free energies are then computed between the most similar pairs. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility script in AmberTools that prepares trajectories from the decharging step of an alchemical binding free energy calculation for BAR/PBSA analysis, which adds the electronic polarization that additive force fields leave out. It strips solvent and ions, writes Poisson-Boltzmann input files with chosen atomic radii and solute dielectric constant, and runs the calculations in parallel with sander. The analysis is used first to calibrate ligand and protein radii and then to scan the dielectric constant of the solute. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility script that converts output files from AMBER simulations into the specific data format required by the edgembar free energy analysis program. It processes AMBER's energy or log files to extract the necessary potential energy values for each frame of the simulation. This script is an essential data preparation step for using the edgembar tool to analyze free energy calculations that were performed with the AMBER software. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility script in the FE-ToolKit library that performs the free energy analysis of a whole network of alchemical transformations, combining the results edgembar wrote for each edge into a consistent set of relative free energies for all molecules. It can hold chosen edges to experimental values, leave edges out and pick a reference molecule, and writes the analysis as an HTML report. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility script in the FE-ToolKit library that extracts the data edgembar needs from a sander simulation that transforms the system step by step between a molecular mechanics and a QM/MM description. It writes energy time series for multi-state Bennett acceptance ratio and thermodynamic integration analysis, or the nonequilibrium work values when the simulation used Jarzynski sampling. It works like edgembar-amber2dats.py, which handles ordinary alchemical simulations. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility script in the FE-ToolKit library that chooses the number and spacing of the coupling parameter values, the lambda schedule, for an alchemical free energy calculation. It analyses short preliminary simulations run with many states and places the new states so that neighbouring states overlap equally, measured by phase space overlap or predicted replica exchange acceptance. Spacing chosen this way avoids wasting simulations where neighbouring states overlap strongly and leaving gaps where they barely overlap. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility script in the FE-ToolKit library that prepares the output of 1 AMBER umbrella sampling simulation for analysis with ndfes. It writes a new file of the restrained coordinate values, a dumpave file, with the columns needed, and prints the matching line of the metafile that tells ndfes the window's umbrella centre, force constant, temperature and data file. It is usually run in a loop over all windows. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility script in the FE-ToolKit library that finds the equilibrated part of an umbrella sampling simulation by forward and reverse analysis of the time series of its biasing potential. It can then write a shorter trajectory or data file that keeps only statistically independent samples from that part, optionally with cpptraj. It is normally run before the data are prepared for free energy analysis with ndfes. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility script in the FE-ToolKit library that merges 1 or more ndfes metafiles, the input files that list each biased simulation with its umbrella centre, force constant and data file, into a new metafile. It is used to analyse the combined sampling of several independent trials or of several iterations of the finite temperature string method. It can also move a metafile to another directory by adjusting the relative paths it lists. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility script in the FE-ToolKit library that prints the free energy surface stored in an ndfes checkpoint file as plain text, 1 line per occupied histogram bin. Each line gives the bin centre on each reaction coordinate, the free energy and its standard error or 95% confidence interval, a reweighting entropy that warns when few samples dominate the bin, and the number of samples. The output is used to plot the free energy surface. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility script in the FE-ToolKit library that averages free energy surfaces stored in ndfes checkpoint files, such as those from independent repeats of a simulation, and writes the result as a new checkpoint file. Each input surface is shifted to fit the average as closely as possible, and the spread between the repeats is used to give a better uncertainty for the best free energy estimate. (UNVERIFIED)

A program in the FE-ToolKit library that finds and evaluates paths on a multidimensional free energy surface computed by ndfes. It evaluates the free energy along a given curve, optimizes a minimum free energy path between 2 states, or prepares the next set of simulations for the finite temperature string method. A minimum free energy path is the route of lowest free energy connecting 2 stable states, and it shows how a conformational change or reaction proceeds. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility script in the FE-ToolKit library that prepares an initial guess for the finite temperature string method from restraint definitions for 2 or more states, such as reactant and product. It writes input and restraint files for a chosen number of windows connected by linear interpolation, and shell scripts that generate a starting structure for each window by a series of short simulations from the nearest prepared structure. The path is then refined by later string iterations. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility script in the FE-ToolKit library that prepares the latest set of simulations of a finite temperature string calculation for analysis. It acts as a wrapper that runs ndfes-CheckEquil.py, ndfes-PrepareAmberData.py and ndfes-CombineMetafiles.py, after which ndfes estimates the free energy surface and ndfes-path updates the path. The finite temperature string method refines a minimum free energy path by repeated rounds of simulation along it. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility script in AmberTools that computes the reference energy a new titratable residue needs in constant pH or constant redox potential simulations. It titrates the model compound with repeated short constant pH runs, adjusting the reference energy until the residue is 50% protonated at a pH equal to the model compound's pKa. It is an alternative to computing the reference energy by thermodynamic integration. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility script that extracts the electrostatic potential and the points it was computed at from quantum chemistry output, and writes them in the form a charge fitting program expects. It is a format conversion between 2 steps of charge derivation. It performs no fitting itself. (UNVERIFIED)

A pipeline script in AmberTools that sets up and runs restrained electrostatic potential (RESP) charge fits over several conformations and several molecules at once. It generates conformers with antechamber and RDKit, reads the electrostatic potential from Gaussian or GAMESS output or computes it with QUICK, then writes the fitting input with pyresp_gen.py and performs the fit with py_resp.py. It is meant to make the derivation of RESP charges easier and more standardised. (UNVERIFIED)

The chamber script is a utility within the AmberTools suite that facilitates the conversion of CHARMM-formatted force field files into a format that can be used by AMBER. It processes CHARMM topology (PSF) and parameter (PAR) files, allowing users to run simulations with CHARMM force fields using the AMBER simulation engines.

match_atomname is a utility program within the AmberTools suite that takes an input file and a reference file in pdb, ac, prepi, prepc and mol2 format and it automatically detects the corresponding atom name in the reference for each atom name in the input. An output file in the same format as that of the input is generated using the matched atom names. Designed to recover atom-name information lost after running Gaussian calculations.

A software library implementing the message passing standard, providing the functions a parallel program calls to send and receive data between machines. The standard says what the functions do; a library is a working version of them. Which one is installed mainly affects performance. (UNVERIFIED)

An implementation of the message passing standard that moves data directly between graphics processors on different machines, without routing it through their central processors. Avoiding that detour removes a large part of the delay in a simulation running across several machines with accelerators. It requires network hardware that supports direct access. (UNVERIFIED)

A software library for finding a few eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a very large matrix without forming the whole matrix. Normal mode analysis of a large structure needs exactly that, since only the slowest modes are of interest. Computing every mode would cost far more for a system of that size. (UNVERIFIED)

An analysis program, the predecessor of cphstats in AMBER, that computed predicted pKa values and fractions of protonation for the titratable residues from the output of a constant pH molecular dynamics run. Its standard output format is kept by cphstats, which replaced it. (UNVERIFIED)

A system preparation program that rewrites a topology file to contain several non-interacting copies of a chosen region of a molecule, as locally enhanced sampling requires. The copies feel the rest of the system but not each other. It is run before the simulation, because the method cannot be switched on afterwards. (UNVERIFIED)

A formal system of instructions and syntax rules in which computer programs are written. Which one a tool is written in affects how fast it runs and how easily it can be changed or extended. Reproducing a computational result may require the same language version. (UNVERIFIED)
