NAB, or Nucleic Acid Builder, is a specialized programming language designed specifically for the purpose of constructing and manipulating three-dimensional models of nucleic acids and proteins. For experts, NAB provides a powerful and scriptable way to build complex or non-standard biomolecular structures that would be difficult to create with standard graphical tools. Originally distributed with the AmberTools software suite, it is now only available from an independent GitHub repository.
The FE-ToolKit is a collection of tools designed to facilitate the setup, execution, and analysis of alchemical free energy simulations and umbrella sampling.

An analysis program that computes a theoretical small-angle X-ray scattering profile from a structure together with a solvent distribution from 3D-RISM theory. Including the ordered solvent layer matters because that layer scatters measurably. It differs from the trajectory-based tool in obtaining the solvent from theory rather than from sampling. (UNVERIFIED)

An analysis program in AmberTools that computes a theoretical small-angle X-ray scattering profile from snapshots of 2 explicit-solvent simulations: a sample containing the biomolecule with water and ions, and a blank containing the solvent alone. Subtracting the blank and averaging over the sampled conformations makes the result comparable with a measurement on a solution. It differs from saxs_rism in taking the solvent from simulation rather than from 3D-RISM theory. (UNVERIFIED)

A collection of separate programs distributed and installed together, sharing file formats and conventions so that the output of one is directly usable by the next. AmberTools and GROMACS are examples. The distinction from a single program matters, because a suite's name is often used loosely for the one program in it that a study actually ran. (UNVERIFIED)

A software suite in AmberTools that analyses volumetric data, such as 3-dimensional densities of water and ions, produced by simulations, 3D-RISM or Poisson-Boltzmann calculations, or by experiments such as crystallography and cryo-electron microscopy. Its functions, used mainly through the metatwist program, include converting map formats, reducing maps to radial or helical profiles, filtering them, and placing water and ions at density peaks. (UNVERIFIED)

An analysis program in AmberTools, the command-line front end to the MoFT library, that processes 3-dimensional density maps of solvent and ions from simulations, 3D-RISM calculations or experiments. It computes radial distribution functions and twisted or untwisted maps of ion and water density around nucleic acid helices, filters and converts maps, and places explicit water molecules and ions at density peaks. (UNVERIFIED)

A trajectory analysis program, formerly part of the AMBER suite, that read a script of commands and computed properties such as root mean square deviation, distances and angles from a coordinate file. It has been superseded by cpptraj, which is faster and handles more formats. Older published workflows still refer to it. (UNVERIFIED)

An analysis method that converts a continuous solvent density map into a list of discrete water positions, by repeatedly taking the highest remaining peak and removing the density around it. A simulation needs individual water molecules, and a theory-derived map gives only a density. It is the step that turns one into the other. (UNVERIFIED)

A simulation engine, distributed with the AMBER package rather than with the free AmberTools, optimised for speed on large systems and on graphics processing units. It supports fewer methods than the general-purpose engine sander but runs the common ones far faster. It is the engine most production molecular dynamics in AMBER is run with. (UNVERIFIED)

A simulation engine, distributed with AmberTools, that performs energy minimisation, molecular dynamics and some free energy calculations. It is the general-purpose engine of the suite and supports the widest range of methods. It is slower than pmemd, the optimised engine of the separately licensed AMBER package, which is the trade for that breadth. (UNVERIFIED)

A software service, reached through a web browser, that runs a computational tool or searches a database on the user's behalf and returns the result. Nothing is installed locally, so people can use methods they could not otherwise run. The cost is that the input leaves the user's machine, and the exact software version used may not be recorded. (UNVERIFIED)

GLYCAM-Web is a collection of online tools and web servers that assist researchers in building three-dimensional models of carbohydrates and glycoproteins. It uses the GLYCAM force field to generate realistic structures and provides tools for tasks like predicting the conformation of glycosidic linkages.

The Glycoprotein Builder is a web-based tool that automates the process of constructing three-dimensional models of glycoproteins. It allows users to start with a protein structure and graphically attach various glycan (sugar chain) structures to specific amino acid residues. For researchers, this tool greatly simplifies the otherwise complex and tedious task of building a complete, simulation-ready model of a glycosylated protein.

An open-source software library for working with chemical structures, covering reading and writing file formats, computing molecular descriptors, generating 3-dimensional conformations and comparing molecules. It is the foundation most cheminformatics workflows in Python are built on. It handles the chemistry around a simulation rather than the simulation itself. (UNVERIFIED)

A software library for running molecular dynamics, designed to be called from a program or script rather than run as a command. It is built with graphics processors in mind and is among the fastest engines available on them. Because it is a library that is easy to extend, it is often used to build and test new simulation methods. (UNVERIFIED)

A standard specifying how parts of a parallel program running on separate machines exchange data by sending messages to one another. Because the machines share no memory, every piece of shared information must be sent explicitly. It is how a single simulation is spread across the nodes of a cluster. (UNVERIFIED)

A programming interface that lets parts of a program run on several processor cores that share the same memory, by marking sections of the code rather than rewriting it. It is how most simulation engines use the cores of a single machine. It does not spread work across separate machines, which needs a different mechanism. (UNVERIFIED)

A software library, and the standard interface it defines, for low-level linear algebra routines such as multiplying a matrix by a vector or by another matrix. Hardware vendors supply versions tuned for their own processors, so the same program runs at very different speeds depending on which is installed. Almost every numerical library is built on top of it. (UNVERIFIED)

A software library providing routines for linear algebra problems such as solving systems of equations, finding eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and least-squares fitting. Normal mode analysis, principal component analysis and many other analyses reduce to calls into it. Its speed determines how large a matrix those analyses can handle. (UNVERIFIED)

DL-Find is a software library that provides a collection of robust algorithms for geometry optimization tasks. It contains routines for efficiently finding energy minima (stable structures) and first-order saddle points (transition states) on a potential energy surface. This library acts as an optimization engine that can be incorporated into other simulation or quantum chemistry programs to perform complex structural searches and reaction path calculations.

A software library of AMBER-compatible molecular mechanics routines, written for the NAB molecular manipulation language, that computes energies and forces for minimization and molecular dynamics with an emphasis on implicit solvent models such as generalized Born, Poisson-Boltzmann and RISM. It has been moved out of AmberTools into a separate repository together with NAB and its C interface. (UNVERIFIED)

x3DNA is a comprehensive software package for the analysis, rebuilding, and visualization of three-dimensional nucleic acid structures. It takes a DNA or RNA structure file as input and calculates a wide range of standard helical and base pair parameters that are used to describe the detailed geometry of the helix. It is a cornerstone tool in the field of nucleic acid structural biology for characterizing and comparing experimental or simulated structures.

A software library that computes energies and forces from data-driven many-body potentials, MB-pol for water and MB-nrg for ions and small molecules, for use by molecular dynamics programs such as LAMMPS and i-PI. These potentials add explicitly fitted terms for pairs and triples of molecules to a polarizable model that covers the remaining many-body effects. Fitting them to high-level quantum calculations gives close to quantum chemical accuracy from small clusters to liquids. (UNVERIFIED)

A match analysis tool is a program that compares two or more molecular structures or datasets to find and quantify their similarities. This can involve superimposing two protein structures to calculate their RMSD or searching a database of small molecules to find ones that have a similar shape or chemical features to a query compound.

A software framework, part of the AmberTools free energy workflow FEW, that automates the calculation of ligand binding free energies by the MM-PBSA and MM-GBSA methods from snapshots of molecular dynamics simulations. It offers 4 variants of the Poisson-Boltzmann calculation and 3 of the generalized Born calculation, applied either to 1 trajectory of the complex or to separate trajectories of complex, receptor and ligand. (UNVERIFIED)

A software framework, part of the AmberTools free energy workflow FEW, that prepares and analyses the simulations needed for a linear interaction energy estimate of ligand binding. It sets up runs of each ligand bound to its receptor and free in solution, and computes from them the ligand's electrostatic and van der Waals interaction energies, treating many ligands with 1 consistent protocol. The energy differences are turned into binding free energies with empirical coefficients, which can be fitted by linear regression against measured data. (UNVERIFIED)

A software framework, part of the AmberTools free energy workflow FEW, that automates relative binding free energy calculations between 2 ligands by thermodynamic integration. It sets up the transformation simulations at each coupling state and, once they have run, integrates the results to give the free energy difference. It is the thermodynamic integration counterpart to the linear interaction energy workflow. (UNVERIFIED)

An algorithm that computes an approximate solution to a mathematical equation or a system of equations that has no exact formula for its solution or is too large to solve directly. Many such solvers improve a trial solution step by step until it is accurate enough. Examples are the conjugate gradient methods used to solve the large systems of linear equations that arise in implicit solvent models such as the Poisson-Boltzmann equation. (UNVERIFIED)

An iterative algorithm for solving a large system of linear equations whose matrix is not symmetric. The ordinary conjugate gradient method requires a symmetric matrix and can fail without one. In Poisson-Boltzmann continuum electrostatics it is used with discretization schemes, such as the immersed interface method, that produce a matrix that is not symmetric. (UNVERIFIED)

nodes.lbl: modified direct inversion in the iterative subspace solver algorithm

definition.val: A numerical solver algorithm that speeds up an iterative calculation by combining several saved trial solutions, weighted so that the combined error left in the equations, the residual, is as small as possible. Each new trial solution is built from this combination with a set step size, and in AMBER the method accelerates the solution of the 1D-RISM and 3D-RISM integral equations of solvation theory. It is a modified form of the method used to converge self-consistent field calculations in quantum chemistry. (UNVERIFIED)

An algorithm that advances the positions and velocities of the atoms from one step to the next, using the forces computed at the current step. It approximates the continuous equations of motion by a series of short, discrete time steps. Integrators differ in accuracy, stability at large time steps, cost, and how well they conserve energy over a long run. (UNVERIFIED)

An integration algorithm that updates positions from the current velocity and the forces at the current and previous steps, and updates velocities from the forces at the previous, current and new steps. It produces the same positions as the Verlet algorithm but computes velocities more accurately at each point. That matters when a quantity depending on velocity, such as kinetic energy, is being reported. (UNVERIFIED)

nodes.lbl: modified incomplete Choleski conjugate gradient solver algorithm

definition.val: A numerical solver algorithm that solves a large, sparse, symmetric system of linear equations by the conjugate gradient method, first transforming the system with an approximate, deliberately incomplete Cholesky factorisation of its matrix to reduce the number of iterations. An exact factorisation would cost as much as solving the system directly, so only part of it is kept. It is the default solver for the finite-difference Poisson-Boltzmann equation in the pbsa program of AMBER. (UNVERIFIED)

An algorithm that computes the approximate value of a definite integral from values sampled at discrete points. It is used wherever the function being integrated is known only at the points where it was measured or computed. The free energy of a thermodynamic integration calculation is obtained this way. (UNVERIFIED)

A numerical integration algorithm for integrating a function over the surface of a sphere, using a fixed set of points and weights chosen to be exact for spherical harmonics up to a given order. It reaches a given accuracy with far fewer points than an evenly spaced arrangement. It supplies the angular part of the grid used in density functional theory. (UNVERIFIED)

An algorithm that computes a property or finds a pattern in raw simulation data. It is the concrete procedure an analysis method is carried out by, as distinct from the idea of the method itself. Two programs implementing the same method can use different algorithms and give slightly different numbers. (UNVERIFIED)

An analysis algorithm that examines or transforms data recorded as a sequence in time. A trajectory is such a sequence, so techniques built for signals apply to it directly. Examples are smoothing, filtering and splitting a series into its component frequencies. (UNVERIFIED)

A signal processing algorithm that removes frequencies above or below a chosen cut-off frequency while passing the remaining frequencies with a response that is as flat, that is as free of ripples, as possible. Flatness in the kept range is what it optimises, at the cost of a gradual rather than sharp cut-off. It is used to separate slow collective motion in a trajectory from fast thermal noise. (UNVERIFIED)

A numerical integration algorithm that approximates the area under a curve by joining neighbouring points with straight lines and summing the resulting trapezoids. It needs only the sampled values and treats the function as a straight line between each pair of neighbouring points. It is a common way to integrate the thermodynamic integration curve over the coupling parameter. (UNVERIFIED)

An algorithm designed to produce a sequence of numbers that shows no discernible pattern and so appears to be random. In computational science, such generators supply the element of chance that stochastic simulation methods need. In simulation these are pseudo-random generators, which compute the sequence from a starting value called a seed, and they supply the random numbers used by stochastic thermostats and Monte Carlo methods. (UNVERIFIED)

A pseudo-random number generator of the family developed by Marsaglia, built from simple shift and multiply operations on a small internal state. The simplicity makes them fast and easy to implement, which is why they appear inside simulation engines. They pass standard statistical tests while using far less state than a long-period generator. (UNVERIFIED)

nodes.lbl: Mersenne Twister random number generator algorithm

definition.val: A pseudo-random number generator, based on a twisted generalized feedback shift register, whose sequence repeats only after a period of 2^19937 - 1 in its standard MT19937 form. It is the default generator in many scientific libraries. It is not suitable where an adversary must not predict the sequence, which does not arise in simulation. (UNVERIFIED)

nodes.lbl: permuted congruential random number generator algorithm

definition.val: A pseudo-random number generator that advances a linear congruential generator and passes its state through an output function, such as an xor-shift followed by a rotation whose size is taken from the state, to remove the patterns of the plain congruential sequence. The result has much better statistical quality than a linear congruential generator while staying small and fast. (UNVERIFIED)

A pseudo-random number generator that updates 128 bits of state with xor, shift and rotate operations and produces each output by adding and rotating parts of the state. It is fast and passes current statistical test suites, and its small state makes it cheap to keep one per thread. Giving each thread its own generator and seed helps keep a parallel simulation reproducible. (UNVERIFIED)

MDposit is a web-based platform and portal designed for the sharing, visualization, and analysis of molecular dynamics simulation data. It serves as a distributed database interface that allows users to browse, access, and interactively view trajectories from different research groups. This tool aims to facilitate the dissemination and reuse of large-scale simulation datasets within the scientific community.

An algorithm that computes the discrete Fourier transform of N values, converting data between a description in time or space and one in frequency, in a time that grows as N log N. Computing the same transform directly would cost far more, growing with the square of N. It makes particle mesh Ewald affordable, because that method needs a forward and an inverse transform of the charge grid at every step. (UNVERIFIED)

A clustering algorithm that grows a group outward from any point with enough neighbours within a chosen distance, and leaves sparse points unassigned. It needs no target number of groups and can find groups of any shape. Structures left unassigned are treated as rare conformations rather than forced into a group, which suits a trajectory well. (UNVERIFIED)

A clustering algorithm that divides structures into a fixed number of groups by repeatedly assigning each to the nearest group centre and then recomputing the centres. The number of groups must be chosen in advance, which is its main limitation. It also assumes groups are roughly round and of similar size, which conformations often are not. (UNVERIFIED)

A clustering algorithm that picks group centres as points which have many close neighbours and are also far from any point with still more neighbours. Those 2 conditions identify a peak in the crowding rather than an arbitrary starting point. Every other point then joins the nearest denser point, which assigns the whole set in one pass. (UNVERIFIED)

An optimization algorithm for non-linear least-squares fitting of a model to data that blends 2 methods: cautious gradient descent steps when far from the best fit and fast Gauss-Newton steps when close to it. Shifting between them according to how well the fit is going makes it converge reliably even from a poor starting guess. It is often used to fit force field parameters to experimental or quantum mechanical reference data. (UNVERIFIED)

A force field component that holds the complete definition of each molecular building block, or residue, giving its atoms, their types and charges, and the bonds between them, usually stored as a data file. It lets a topology be assembled from a sequence without every atom being specified. A residue absent from it cannot be built automatically. (UNVERIFIED)

An optimization algorithm that keeps a set of trial points, 1 more than the number of variables, forming a simplex, and repeatedly replaces the worst point by reflecting it through the center of the others, expanding or shrinking the set as needed. It never needs a derivative, only the ability to evaluate the function. That makes it usable where derivatives are unavailable or unreliable, at the cost of converging slowly. (UNVERIFIED)

A set of effective atomic radii fitted for use with the SMx family of implicit solvent models. The radii absorb part of the error of the underlying model, which is why they are specific to it. Substituting a general-purpose set such as Bondi changes the computed solvation energies. (UNVERIFIED)

A numerical integration algorithm that evaluates a function at specially chosen points, with matching weights, so the result is exact for polynomials up to a given degree. Choosing the positions as well as the weights doubles the degree that a given number of points can handle. It needs the function to be evaluable anywhere, not only at points already sampled. (UNVERIFIED)

An algorithm that computes the area of a molecule's surface that a solvent molecule can reach, called the solvent accessible surface area. Numerical methods, such as the Shrake-Rupley method, place test points on a sphere around each atom enlarged by the radius of a solvent probe and count those that no other atom covers, while analytical methods, such as LCPO, estimate the area from how much the atom spheres overlap. The result is used to estimate the nonpolar part of the solvation free energy in implicit solvent models and to measure how exposed parts of a molecule are. (UNVERIFIED)

An algorithm that estimates solvent-accessible surface area from a sum over overlapping pairs of atoms, with fitted coefficients, rather than by placing test points. Having a closed form makes it fast enough to run at every step of a simulation, and to be differentiated so it contributes forces. Point-based methods can be more accurate but are slower, and counting points does not give smooth forces. (UNVERIFIED)

An algorithm that measures how far 2 structures differ, by first superposing them to remove any overall shift or rotation and then taking the root mean square of the remaining distances between matched atoms. Without the superposition step, moving a molecule across the box would register as a large change in shape. The choice of which atoms to superpose on decides what the number means. (UNVERIFIED)

An algorithm that finds the optimal superposing rotation as the eigenvector of the largest eigenvalue of a 4-by-4 symmetric matrix built from the 2 sets of points, instead of by decomposing a 3-by-3 matrix as the Kabsch algorithm does. The eigenvector is a unit quaternion, a set of 4 numbers that always describes a proper rotation, so the result can never be a reflection, which matrix methods must check for separately. It gives the same optimal superposition as the Kabsch algorithm. (UNVERIFIED)

An optimization algorithm that builds an approximation to the curvature of a function from the slopes seen at successive steps, and uses it to choose each new step. Approximating the curvature rather than computing it converges in far fewer steps than using slope alone, without the cost of second derivatives. It stores a full matrix, which limits it to problems with a moderate number of variables. (UNVERIFIED)

A minimization algorithm that chooses each step from the current downhill direction combined with the previous step's direction, so that it does not undo progress already made. That memory is what lets it follow a long narrow valley, where steepest descent zig-zags. It is the usual choice once the worst overlaps in a structure have been removed. (UNVERIFIED)

An optimization algorithm that finds a minimum by searching along one direction at a time and gradually replacing those directions with better ones built from the progress made. It never needs a derivative, only function values. It suits problems where derivatives are unavailable or too noisy to trust. (UNVERIFIED)

An integration algorithm that updates different forces at different intervals, evaluating fast-changing forces, such as bonded forces, every step and slow-changing forces, such as long-range forces, only every few steps. When the slow forces are the expensive ones, evaluating them less often saves much computing time. Making the outer interval too long makes the simulation unstable, because the slow-force updates can fall into resonance with the fastest motions. (UNVERIFIED)

A multiple time-stepping algorithm that splits the forces into groups that change quickly or slowly and nests their updates, integrating the fast forces with a short inner timestep and applying the slow forces as impulses at a longer outer timestep. It is derived so that the scheme stays time-reversible, and it conserves energy well as long as the outer timestep is short enough, about 4 fs in typical biomolecular simulations, to avoid resonance with the fastest motions. (UNVERIFIED)

An algorithm that computes long-range forces quickly by grouping distant particles into a hierarchy of cells and treating each distant group as a single source. Seen from far enough away, a group acts almost like a single point, so computing the effect of each member separately is wasted work. It reduces the cost from growing with the square of the particle count to growing close to linearly. (UNVERIFIED)

A multiple time-stepping algorithm that estimates an expensive force, such as the 3D-RISM solvation force, at intermediate steps from forces already computed at earlier steps instead of computing it in full. The current coordinates are written as a weighted combination of the coordinates at earlier fully computed steps, and the same weights are applied to the forces from those steps. This allows long intervals between full calculations, but unlike r-RESPA the scheme does not conserve energy and is not time-reversible. (UNVERIFIED)

An algorithm that decides, during a simulation, which atoms belong in the quantum region at each moment. It is needed when molecules such as solvent move into and out of the region of interest, because a fixed list would keep treating molecules that have left as quantum and miss molecules that have arrived. The difficulty is changing the assignment without a jump in the energy or forces. (UNVERIFIED)

A region selection algorithm that uses 2 distance thresholds, a nearer one for entering the quantum region and a farther one for leaving it. The gap between them stops an atom sitting near the boundary from switching back and forth every step. With a single threshold, atoms that cross and re-cross the boundary make the region definition change rapidly. (UNVERIFIED)

An algorithm that approximately solves the equations of quantum mechanics for a molecular system, to obtain how its electrons are distributed and the energy of that arrangement. The equations can be solved exactly in closed form only for systems with a single electron, so practical methods each make an approximation. Methods differ in which approximation they make and in how much computing time they need. (UNVERIFIED)

An algorithm that makes a quantum calculation on a large molecule possible by splitting it into overlapping pieces, solving each, and combining the results. The cost of a conventional calculation grows much faster than the size of the system, while the cost of this approach grows roughly in proportion to it. The pieces must overlap, or the boundaries between them introduce errors. (UNVERIFIED)

A multiple time-stepping algorithm built on the velocity Verlet integrator in which slowly varying forces are computed only at major steps and applied as impulses, while fast-varying forces are recomputed at every minor step in between. In the mdgx program of AMBER, bond, angle and 1-4 non-bonded terms are recomputed at every minor step, and the other non-bonded and dihedral terms only at major steps. (UNVERIFIED)

A thermostat algorithm that couples the system to a thermostat variable, that variable to a second one, and so on along a chain, extending the Nosé-Hoover thermostat. The chain corrects a failure of the single-variable form, which may not reach the canonical distribution for small or stiff systems, such as a harmonic oscillator, because their dynamics do not explore all accessible states. (UNVERIFIED)

A thermostat algorithm that rescales the velocities towards the target temperature by a factor that includes a random part, chosen so that the kinetic energy follows the canonical distribution instead of being driven to a single value. It reaches the target temperature as quickly as simple rescaling schemes such as the Berendsen thermostat, while sampling the canonical ensemble correctly, which they do not. (UNVERIFIED)

An integration algorithm of the velocity-Verlet family in which the thermostat acts in the middle of each step, between 2 half-step updates of the coordinates, rather than at the start or end of the step. Placing it there makes the sampled distribution of coordinates exact for a harmonic system and much more accurate in general, so a larger timestep can be used for the same accuracy in structural properties. It can be combined with thermostats such as the Langevin and Andersen thermostats. (UNVERIFIED)

A polarization algorithm that gives each induced dipole a small fictitious mass and lets it move under its own equation of motion, instead of solving for it exactly at every step. If the mass is small enough the dipoles stay close to the exact solution while never being solved for. It removes the iteration that otherwise dominates the cost. (UNVERIFIED)

A thermostat algorithm in which the thermostat acts for a full time step in the middle of each integration step, between 2 half-step updates of the coordinates, rather than at the beginning or end of the step. This placement keeps the sampled distribution of coordinates accurate at much larger timesteps, which makes the sampling of structural and thermodynamic properties more efficient. It works with several thermostats, such as the Langevin and Andersen thermostats, and can be combined with Monte Carlo or stochastic cell rescaling barostats. (UNVERIFIED)

A set of atomic radii for Poisson-Boltzmann calculations, assigned by AMBER atom type and charge and optimized by Tan and Luo for the standard residues of the AMBER force fields. They define the dielectric boundary between solute and solvent and are the default radii in the AMBER Poisson-Boltzmann program. Molecules built with general AMBER force field atom types do not use them and take their radii from the topology instead. (UNVERIFIED)

A conjugate gradient algorithm that weights the previous search direction by the dot product of the new gradient with the change in gradient since the last step, divided by the squared length of the old gradient. The Fletcher-Reeves variant instead uses only the ratio of the squared lengths of the new and old gradients. When progress stalls and the gradient barely changes, the weight falls towards 0, so the search restarts by itself along the steepest descent direction. (UNVERIFIED)

A quasi-Newton optimization algorithm, a variant of the BFGS algorithm, that approximates the curvature of a function from the last few steps taken instead of storing the full curvature matrix. Storing that matrix is not practical when there are hundreds of thousands of variables, as in a large molecular system. Keeping only recent history gives most of the benefit at a fraction of the memory. (UNVERIFIED)

A minimization algorithm that chooses each step by approximately solving the Newton equations, which use the curvature of the energy surface, with an inner linear conjugate gradient calculation that is stopped early. Using curvature as well as slope needs far fewer steps than slope alone, and the inner calculation needs only products of the curvature matrix with vectors, so the full matrix of second derivatives never has to be stored. Stopping the inner calculation early saves time while the step is still far from the minimum. (UNVERIFIED)

An enhanced sampling algorithm is a computational procedure that modifies a standard simulation to accelerate the exploration of a molecule's possible states or to observe rare events. These algorithms are designed to overcome the high energy barriers that can trap a simulation in a single state for a long time.

An enhanced sampling algorithm where multiple independent simulation replicas (walkers) simultaneously explore the conformational space and contribute to a single, shared biasing potential. This parallelization significantly accelerates the convergence of methods like metadynamics or adaptive biasing force.

The IUPAC International Chemical Identifier (InChI) is a standardized text string that provides a unique, machine-readable signature for a specific chemical substance. It is algorithmically generated from a molecule's structural information and it is sensitive to its chirality, ensuring that a given compound will always produce the same identifier regardless of how it is drawn. This code serves as a universal label for linking chemical information across different databases and software.

The ICOSA algorithm is a computational method used to rapidly calculate the solvent-accessible surface area (SASA) of a molecule. It works by placing a sphere of dots, arranged in a pattern based on an icosahedron, around each atom and then counting how many of these dots are not covered by neighboring atoms. This numerical approach provides a fast and efficient way to estimate the molecular surface area, a property that is crucial for implicit solvent models and for analyzing a molecule's exposure to its environment.

A minimization algorithm that moves the atoms at each step in the direction of the force on them, which is the steepest downhill direction from where they are. It is robust, because a small enough step in that direction always lowers the energy. It becomes very slow in a long narrow valley, where the steepest direction points across the valley rather than along it. (UNVERIFIED)

An algorithm that identifies which parts of a protein form regular repeating shapes, such as helices and sheets, from the coordinates of its backbone. It works by finding the pattern of hydrogen bonds between backbone groups, or by examining backbone angles. It is what turns a list of coordinates into the helix-and-arrow picture of a protein. (UNVERIFIED)

The DSSP (Define Secondary Structure of Proteins) algorithm is the most widely used and standard algorithm for assigning secondary structure to the residues of a protein. It works by identifying the characteristic hydrogen-bonding patterns between the backbone amide and carbonyl groups that define alpha-helices and beta-sheets. The detailed, per-residue output of the DSSP algorithm is a standard tool for protein structure analysis and validation.

OBSOLETE. A trajectory analysis algorithm is a computational procedure that processes the time-series of atomic coordinates from a simulation to calculate a specific property. These algorithms are the engines of analysis tools, turning raw simulation output into interpretable scientific data. For experts, this includes the specific algorithms for tasks like imaging periodic trajectories, calculating correlation functions, or clustering conformations.

comments: candidate for removal per https://github.com/CPCLab/molsim-ontology/issues/21

definition.val: An analysis algorithm that unwraps the trajectories of molecules from a constant-pressure simulation with periodic boundary conditions, by adding to each molecule's unwrapped position its displacement from the previous frame, measured in Cartesian space. It removes the jumps that appear when a molecule crosses the box boundary and is put back into the central box, while handling changes in box size between frames. It is used mainly to calculate diffusion coefficients from mean-squared displacements. (UNVERIFIED)

An algorithm that draws a smooth curve through a set of points by fitting a cubic polynomial between each neighbouring pair and matching their slopes and curvatures where they join. The matching is what stops the curve having visible corners. It is often used to draw a smooth free energy profile from values computed at discrete points. (UNVERIFIED)

A signal processing algorithm that decomposes a signal into contributions at each frequency and each moment at once, by matching it against a short wave shape, the wavelet, that is stretched and shifted across the data. A plain frequency analysis, such as a Fourier transform, does not show when each frequency occurs. That matters for a trajectory, where a motion may appear only during part of the run. (UNVERIFIED)

An algorithm that applies the methods of statistics to summarise data, estimate a quantity, or judge how reliable a result is. Simulation output is a finite sample, so averages, probability distributions and their uncertainties all have to be estimated from it. Examples are fitting a probability distribution to sampled values and estimating the error bar on an average. (UNVERIFIED)

A statistical algorithm that estimates the distribution behind a set of points by placing a small smooth peak, called a kernel, such as a Gaussian, on each point and adding them together. It assumes no particular shape for the distribution, unlike fitting a named family. How wide the kernels are decides whether it reveals real structure or smooths it away. (UNVERIFIED)

A residue name is a standardized short code, typically three or four letters, used in structure files to identify a specific type of molecular building block. For example, 'ALA' is the residue name for the amino acid alanine, and 'DG' can represent a deoxyguanosine nucleotide.

A short code identifying a sugar residue in the GLYCAM carbohydrate force field, encoding which sugar it is, its ring form, its anomeric configuration, its D or L form, and which of its positions are linked to other residues. Sugars branch, so the same sugar appears in many linkage patterns and each needs its own template. That is why the code carries linkage information where amino acid codes do not. (UNVERIFIED)

An atom name is a unique label given to an atom within a specific residue to distinguish it from other atoms of the same element. For example, in an amino acid, the names 'CA' and 'CB' are used to differentiate the alpha-carbon from the beta-carbon.

The atom of a residue designated to form the bond joining it to the neighbouring residue in a chain. Building a polymer from residue templates requires knowing which atom on each side makes that bond. Without it, templates could be listed in order and never joined. (UNVERIFIED)

The atom of a residue template that bonds to the preceding residue in a chain. In a protein it is the backbone nitrogen. Together with the tail atom it defines the direction in which templates are joined. (UNVERIFIED)

The atom of a residue template that bonds to the following residue in a chain. In a protein it is the backbone carbonyl carbon. A template with no tail atom defined cannot be followed by another, which is how a chain terminus is expressed. (UNVERIFIED)

OBSOLETE. Miller indices are a set of three integers (h, k, l) that uniquely describe the orientation of a plane of atoms within a crystal lattice. These indices are determined from the positions of the spots in an X-ray diffraction pattern and are fundamental to crystallography. They are used to define the specific crystal faces and to calculate the theoretical diffraction pattern from a structural model.

comments: Marked for removal. See: https://github.com/CPCLab/molsim-ontology/issues/26

definition.val: A classification recorded in a topology stating what general kind of building block a residue is, such as protein, nucleic acid, water, ion or solvent. Analysis tools use it to select parts of a system without naming every residue. A mis-set value makes a selection quietly omit or include the wrong atoms. (UNVERIFIED)
A constituent part of a 3-dimensional data map, being either a grid point or the value stored at it. The grid points fix where the map is sampled and the values say what was found there. (UNVERIFIED)

A single cell of a 3-dimensional grid, holding one value for the small volume of space it covers. It is to a volume what a pixel is to an image. Analyses that map a property through space, such as where water sits around a protein, report their results one of these at a time. (UNVERIFIED)
A classification assigned to an atom to describe its fundamental chemical identity or its specific physical and computational properties within a molecular model.

comments: Previous definition: An atom type is a classification assigned to an atom in a force field that defines its interaction parameters based on its chemical environment. It encodes not just the chemical element but also its hybridization state and bonding pattern, so a carbonyl carbon will have a different atom type than an aromatic carbon.

definition.val: A description of an atom's surroundings used by a machine-learned force field, computed from the positions of its neighbours rather than assigned from a table. A conventional atom type is a fixed label such as "aromatic carbon"; this instead varies continuously with the local geometry. That is what lets such a model describe environments it was never given a label for. (UNVERIFIED)

A code identifying an amino acid that has been chemically altered, such as by phosphorylation or methylation. The standard 3-letter codes cover only the 20 unmodified residues, so a modified one needs a code of its own. The code is what links the residue to the extra parameters its modification requires. (UNVERIFIED)

A path image is a single, discrete snapshot or structure that represents one point along a continuous pathway between two molecular states. A collection of these images is used in methods like the Nudged Elastic Band (NEB) to map out a reaction path or conformational transition.

Trajectory post-processing is the general process of cleaning and preparing raw simulation trajectory files before performing detailed scientific analysis. This typically involves essential steps like removing the overall rotation and translation of a target molecule to keep it centered, and fixing any molecules that appear "broken" by the periodic boundary conditions. These routine procedures are necessary to create a clean trajectory that is suitable for correct visualization and accurate calculation of structural properties.

A system preparation stage in which a correspondence is established between the atoms of 2 structures, saying which atom of one corresponds to which atom of the other. An alchemical transformation needs it to know which atoms change and which stay the same. A wrong correspondence produces a calculation that runs to completion and gives a wrong answer. (UNVERIFIED)

A preparation process that produces the 2 files that describe the system for a simulation: a topology file saying what the system is made of, and a coordinate file saying where every atom is at the start. The topology lists the atoms, the bonds between them and the force field parameters, and it does not change during the run. The coordinates change at every step, which is why the 2 are kept apart. (UNVERIFIED)

A kinetic property describing the random tumbling of a molecule in a liquid, caused by collisions with the solvent around it, usually expressed as a rotational diffusion coefficient or a rotational correlation time. How fast the molecule tumbles depends on its size and shape and on how viscous the solvent is. NMR relaxation measurements are sensitive to it, which is how a simulated value can be checked. (UNVERIFIED)

A modelling method that rebuilds an all-atom structure from a coarse-grained one, placing the atoms each grouped site stands for. Information was discarded when the coarse model was built, so the rebuilt atoms are a plausible arrangement rather than a recovered one. It is used to inspect a coarse-grained result in atomic detail, or to continue a simulation at finer resolution. (UNVERIFIED)

NMR refinement is a computational process used to generate or improve a three-dimensional model of a molecule using experimental data from Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectroscopy. The method involves finding a structure, or an ensemble of structures, that is both stereochemically realistic and consistent with a set of experimental restraints, such as distances between atoms derived from the Nuclear Overhauser Effect. This process is essential for translating the raw data from an NMR experiment into a high-resolution atomic model.

A simulation preparation stage in which the LEaP program of AMBER, run as tleap or xleap, assembles a molecular system and assigns force field parameters, producing the topology and coordinate files an AMBER simulation needs. It covers loading the structure, choosing the force field, adding solvent and counter-ions, and writing the output. It is the step at which a structure becomes a system that can be simulated. (UNVERIFIED)

A procedure applied at intervals during a simulation that sets the total linear momentum of the system to zero, and in some cases also the total angular momentum, so that the system as a whole does not translate or rotate. Small numerical errors, for example in the long-range forces, can set the whole system slowly moving, and the kinetic energy of that overall motion would be counted wrongly as thermal motion and raise the reported temperature. Removing it keeps the reported temperature a measure of the internal motion only. (UNVERIFIED)

A chemical change made to a protein after it has been built from its amino acid sequence, such as attaching a phosphate, a sugar or a lipid. It can switch the protein's activity on or off, mark it for destruction, or send it to a particular part of the cell. Standard force fields do not include the modified residues, so extra parameters are needed to simulate one. (UNVERIFIED)

A post-translational modification in which a branched sugar chain is attached to the nitrogen of an asparagine side chain. It is among the most common modifications of proteins on the cell surface and of secreted proteins. The sugar chains are large, flexible and highly variable, which makes them among the hardest parts of a protein to simulate. (UNVERIFIED)

A post-translational modification in which sugars are attached to the oxygen of a side chain, most often of serine or threonine, and are added 1 at a time rather than as a preassembled block. The resulting chains range from a single sugar to long chains, as in the mucins. Their size and variability make such glycosylated proteins hard to model and simulate. (UNVERIFIED)

A model specifying the mathematical form assumed for the many-electron wavefunction in a quantum chemistry calculation, such as a single determinant or a combination of several configurations. It fixes what electronic structure the calculation is able to represent before any basis set is chosen. A single determinant cannot describe bond breaking or a near-degenerate ground state. (UNVERIFIED)

A wavefunction model in which every occupied molecular orbital holds exactly 2 electrons of opposite spin. It applies to molecules with no unpaired electrons, which is most stable organic molecules in their ground state. It is the default assumption of a quantum chemistry calculation unless an open-shell model is asked for. (UNVERIFIED)

A wavefunction model in which electrons of opposite spin may occupy different spatial orbitals, used mainly for molecules with unpaired electrons such as radicals and many metal complexes. This extra freedom describes unpaired electrons well, but the result can mix in other spin states, which is called spin contamination. It is the basis of unrestricted Hartree-Fock and unrestricted density functional theory calculations. (UNVERIFIED)

A region of a polypeptide chain classified by the local shape of its backbone, which in the regular forms is held in place by hydrogen bonds between nearby backbone groups. The regular forms are helices and beta strands, and the irregular stretches between them are classed as turns, bends or coil. One chain contains many such regions. (UNVERIFIED)

A beta sheet is a common shape in proteins where parts of the amino acid chain line up side-by-side like ribbons in a flat, pleated sheet. It is a secondary structure motif formed by two or more extended polypeptide chains, called beta-strands, which are linked laterally by a regular pattern of hydrogen bonds between their backbone atoms. These sheet structures form the rigid core of many proteins and are critical for creating binding surfaces for other molecules. (UNVERIFIED)

A parallel beta sheet is a type of beta sheet where the adjacent protein chains all run in the same direction, like lanes on a one-way highway. In this arrangement, the neighboring beta-strands are all aligned in the same N-terminus to C-terminus direction, which results in a pattern of angled, evenly spaced hydrogen bonds between the strands. This arrangement is typically found buried in the core of a protein and often requires long loop connections between the strands.

An anti-parallel beta sheet is a type of beta sheet where the adjacent protein strands run in opposite directions, like traffic on a two-way street. In this arrangement, the neighboring beta-strands are aligned in opposite N-terminus to C-terminus directions, resulting in a pattern of straight, perpendicular hydrogen bonds between the strands. This arrangement is generally more stable than the parallel form and is a very common structural motif found in many proteins.

OBSOLETE. A helix is a common shape in proteins and DNA where the molecular chain is twisted into a spiral or corkscrew. It is a secondary structure motif characterized by a repeating pattern of backbone dihedral angles that causes the polymer chain to follow a helical path, which is stabilized by a regular pattern of internal hydrogen bonds. The alpha-helix in proteins and the double helix of DNA are two of the most fundamental and recognizable structures in biology.

comments: Retired 2026-08-05 in favour of the Sequence Ontology term, which covers the same concept in the ontology whose scope owns protein secondary structure. The MOLSIM hierarchy position is preserved: the SO class is asserted under MOLSIM:001781 secondary structure so the DSSP category set stays in one place.

definition.val: OBSOLETE. The 3-10 helix is a type of spiral shape found in proteins that is tighter and more narrow than the common alpha-helix. It is a secondary structure motif characterized by a repeating hydrogen bond between the backbone carbonyl of a residue and the backbone amide of the residue three positions down the chain (i → i+3). While less common than the alpha-helix, short segments of 3-10 helix are often found at the ends of alpha-helices, acting as a cap to the structure.

comments: Retired 2026-08-05 in favour of the Sequence Ontology term, which covers the same concept in the ontology whose scope owns protein secondary structure. The MOLSIM hierarchy position is preserved: the SO class is asserted under MOLSIM:001781 secondary structure so the DSSP category set stays in one place.

definition.val: OBSOLETE. The alpha-helix is the most common spiral shape found in proteins, resembling a coiled ribbon. It is a right-handed secondary structure motif characterized by a repeating hydrogen bond between the backbone carbonyl of a residue and the backbone amide of the residue four positions down the chain (i → i+4). This highly stable and common structure forms a fundamental building block for the architecture of most proteins.

comments: Retired 2026-08-05 in favour of the Sequence Ontology term, which covers the same concept in the ontology whose scope owns protein secondary structure. The MOLSIM hierarchy position is preserved: the SO class is asserted under MOLSIM:001781 secondary structure so the DSSP category set stays in one place.

definition.val: OBSOLETE. The pi-helix is a wide spiral shape found in proteins that is less stable than the common alpha-helix. It is a secondary structure motif characterized by a repeating hydrogen bond between the backbone carbonyl of a residue and the backbone amide of the residue five positions down the chain (i → i+5). Because its internal packing is less favorable, the pi-helix is usually found only as a short, single-turn insertion within other helical structures. Once thought to be rare, short π-helices are found in 15% of known protein structures and are believed to be an evolutionary adaptation derived by the insertion of a single amino acid into an α-helix.

comments: Retired 2026-08-05 in favour of the Sequence Ontology term, which covers the same concept in the ontology whose scope owns protein secondary structure. The MOLSIM hierarchy position is preserved: the SO class is asserted under MOLSIM:001781 secondary structure so the DSSP category set stays in one place.

definition.val: A secondary structure element in which a short stretch of 3 to 5 residues reverses the direction of a protein chain, usually held by a hydrogen bond between backbone groups near its 2 ends. Turns let 2 stretches of chain run back alongside each other, which helps a chain fold into a compact shape. (UNVERIFIED)

A bend is a region in a protein chain that creates a sharp turn, changing the direction of the polypeptide. It is a short structural motif, typically involving a few amino acid residues, that is characterized by a specific pattern of backbone dihedral angles that reverses the direction of the chain.

A secondary structure element in which a stretch of polypeptide chain is drawn out into a nearly straight zig-zag, with backbone dihedral angles in the extended region of the Ramachandran plot. It is the conformation of a beta strand, and strands in this conformation pair up through backbone hydrogen bonds to form a beta sheet. The zig-zag places successive side chains on alternating sides of the strand. (UNVERIFIED)
A beta bridge is an isolated, localized hydrogen bond between two amino acid residues from different segments of a protein, mimicking the interactions found in β-sheets.

A conformational transition is the process where a molecule changes from one stable three-dimensional molecular arrangement to another. This can be a large-scale event, such as a protein switching between an active and an inactive state, or a more local change like the flipping of a sugar ring. Studying these transitions is fundamental to understanding how molecular function is controlled by changes in structure.

A crankshaft motion refers to a specific, localized, correlated movement of a protein's backbone. Specifically, it is an oscillation or rotation of a rigid peptide plane along an axis defined by two adjacent Cα carbon atoms.

The Solvent MoDeL (MDL) file is an explicit molecular model input used for 1D-RISM and 3D-RISM (Reference Interaction Site Model) calculations in software like Amber. It supplies atomic coordinates, partial charges, and Lennard-Jones parameters for solvent molecules or ions.

In computational chemistry and molecular dynamics, the mean solvation force is the average net force exerted by solvent molecules on a solute molecule, with all solvent degrees of freedom thermally averaged out. It represents the derivative of the potential of mean force (PMF) and drives conformational changes and structural binding in liquids.

The atom position is the precise location of an atom in three-dimensional space. It is described by a set of three Cartesian coordinates (X, Y, Z) that specify its location relative to a defined origin. The collection of all atom positions for a molecule at a given instant constitutes a single "frame" of a simulation trajectory, and the evolution of these positions over time is the fundamental output of a molecular dynamics simulation.

An interaction energy component arising when a small amount of electron density moves from one molecule to another at close range. It is a quantum mechanical effect that a force field with fixed atomic charges cannot represent, yet it contributes measurably to hydrogen bonds and to interactions with metal ions. Capturing it explicitly needs a quantum mechanical treatment or a force field with a dedicated charge transfer term. (UNVERIFIED)

An energy chosen as the zero point against which other energies in a calculation are reported. In a free energy calculation it is usually a known or simplified state, and every other state is quoted as a difference from it. Comparisons between systems are meaningless unless the same choice was made for both. (UNVERIFIED)

A physical property is a measurable characteristic of a substance or system that describes its physical state, such as its temperature, pressure, or density. In molecular simulations, these properties are calculated as averages over the course of the trajectory to describe the macroscopic state of the simulated system. These calculated properties are the primary outputs used to validate a simulation against experimental data and to understand the material characteristics of the molecular model.

A physical property giving how strongly a single atom scatters X-rays, as a function of scattering angle. It rises with the number of electrons the atom has and falls as the angle increases, because the electron cloud has a finite size. It is the per-atom term from which structure factors are built. (UNVERIFIED)

A program written in a language that is interpreted as it runs rather than compiled first, used to drive a sequence of steps automatically. Being interpreted makes it quick to change and slow to execute, which suits work that is mostly waiting on other programs. Most of the workflow around a simulation is scripts rather than compiled code. (UNVERIFIED)

An energy arising from the forces between 2 or more separate molecules, or between distinct parts of 1 molecule, computed as the energy of the whole minus the sum of the energies of the parts held at the same geometry. It gathers the electrostatic and van der Waals contributions into a single number. It measures how strongly the parts are held together, but it is not a free energy, because it contains no entropy. (UNVERIFIED)

An interaction energy between a solute and all the water molecules around it. It sums the electrostatic and van der Waals contributions over every solute-water pair. Following it through a trajectory shows how the solute's contact with water changes as it moves. (UNVERIFIED)

An interaction energy summing the interactions of every water molecule with every other water molecule in a system. It measures how strongly the solvent holds itself together, separately from anything the solute does. Changes in it show how a solute disturbs the interactions between the water molecules around it. (UNVERIFIED)

The REMD round-trip time is a diagnostic metric that measures how long it takes for a single simulation copy to travel through the full range of temperatures in a Replica Exchange Molecular Dynamics simulation. In this method, multiple simulations are run at different temperatures, and this metric tracks the time for one replica to go from the lowest to the highest temperature and back again. A short round-trip time indicates that the simulation is sampling conformations efficiently, which is necessary to obtain reliable results.

Lifetime curve data is a graph that shows how long a specific molecular interaction, such as a hydrogen bond, typically lasts in a simulation. The curve usually plots the probability that an interaction, once formed, will still exist after a certain amount of time has passed. This data is generated by calculating the autocorrelation function of an interaction's existence over a trajectory, and fitting the curve provides a characteristic lifetime for that interaction.

An average taken over a window that moves along a series, giving one value for each position of the window. It removes short-term fluctuation so that a slower trend can be seen. The width of the window sets what counts as fluctuation and what counts as trend. (UNVERIFIED)

A measure of how far 2 sets of collective modes span the same motions, computed from the inner products between their eigenvectors. A value near 1 means the 2 sets describe the same motion, and a value near 0 means they do not. It is how the modes from 2 simulations, or from a simulation and an experiment, are compared. (UNVERIFIED)

A single number summarising how strongly the parts of a molecule move together, computed as the root mean square of all the pairwise correlation values. It reduces a whole correlation matrix to 1 figure, so 2 simulations can be compared directly. It says how much correlated motion there is but not where. (UNVERIFIED)

An interaction energy density giving, for each cell of a 3-dimensional grid around a solute, the mean interaction energy between the solute and the solvent molecules in that cell, per unit volume. Negative regions mark places where solvent is held favourably by the solute. Because it is per volume, it reflects both how strongly the solvent there interacts with the solute and how much solvent is present. (UNVERIFIED)

An interaction energy density giving, for each cell of a 3-dimensional grid around a solute, the mean interaction energy of the solvent molecules in that cell with all other solvent molecules in the system, per unit volume. Comparing it with the bulk value shows where a solute has disturbed the solvent's own network of interactions. Solvent that interacts less well with other solvent than in the bulk is a sign of a place where a ligand could displace it favourably. (UNVERIFIED)

An energy giving the mean non-bonded energy of each solvent molecule found in a small region of space, such as 1 cell of a grid around a solute, with electrostatics computed by particle mesh Ewald. It includes the molecule's interactions with both the solute and the other solvent molecules, and it is obtained by dividing the PME solvent energy density of the region by the number density of solvent there. Comparing it with the bulk value shows where solvent is more or less stable than in pure solvent. (UNVERIFIED)

An energy density giving, for each cell of a 3-dimensional grid around a solute, the mean non-bonded energy of the solvent molecules in that cell per unit volume, with electrostatics computed by particle mesh Ewald. It includes the solvent's interactions with both the solute and the rest of the solvent, so it shows where solvent is energetically stabilised and where it is strained. It differs from a solvent density map in reporting energy rather than how much solvent is present. (UNVERIFIED)

An interaction energy giving the mean interaction energy of a water molecule with all the other water molecules, expressed per water molecule found in a given region, such as 1 cell of a grid around a solute. Expressing it per molecule makes regions holding different amounts of water comparable with each other and with bulk water. A value less negative than in bulk marks water that is held less strongly by the surrounding water than in the bulk. (UNVERIFIED)

An electronic property giving, at each point of a 3-dimensional grid around a solute, the mean dipole moment of the solvent molecules there per unit volume. It shows how solvent molecules orient themselves around a solute, which a plain density map cannot. Regions where the dipoles all point the same way mark strong local electric fields. (UNVERIFIED)

A structural property giving, for each cell of a 3-dimensional grid around a solute, the mean number of neighbours of the solvent molecules in that cell multiplied by the number of solvent molecules per unit volume there. It therefore combines how crowded each molecule's surroundings are with how much solvent the cell holds. Dividing it by that number density gives the neighbour count per molecule. (UNVERIFIED)

A coordination number giving the average number of neighbouring solvent molecules, usually water, around each solvent molecule found in a small region of space, such as 1 cell of a grid around a solute. Dividing by the number of solvent molecules in that region makes it a count per molecule, so regions holding different amounts of solvent can be compared. In grid inhomogeneous solvation theory (GIST), 2 water molecules count as neighbours when their oxygen atoms are within 3.5 Å of each other. (UNVERIFIED)

A measure of how closely the 4 nearest neighbours of a water molecule sit at the corners of a regular tetrahedron around it. Water in its ordinary hydrogen-bonded network is close to tetrahedral, and disruption shows as a fall in the value. It is how water near a surface or an ion is shown to be structured differently from bulk water. (UNVERIFIED)

A tetrahedral order parameter rescaled to run from −1/3 to 1, where 1 is a perfect tetrahedron and 0 is a random arrangement. The rescaling puts the value of random water at 0, so a number can be read directly as how much more ordered than random the arrangement is. It is the form usually reported. (UNVERIFIED)

A chemical shift restraint simulation is a method where experimental Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) chemical shifts are used to guide a molecular dynamics simulation. An additional energy term is added that penalizes the simulation if the back-calculated chemical shifts from the trajectory do not agree with the experimental values. For experts, this method is a powerful tool for refining the accuracy of a structural ensemble to be consistent with experimental NMR data.

A pseudocontact shift restraint simulation is a technique that uses a specific type of NMR data, known as pseudocontact shifts (PCS), to guide a simulation. PCS provide long-range distance and angular information relative to a paramagnetic metal center in the molecule. For structural biologists, using PCS restraints is a powerful method for determining the structure and dynamics of proteins and their complexes.

A direct dipolar coupling restraint simulation is a method that incorporates experimental NMR data from residual dipolar couplings (RDCs) to guide a MD simulation. RDCs provide information about the orientation of chemical bonds relative to an external magnetic field.

nodes.lbl: residual chemical shift anisotropy restraint simulation

definition.val: A residual chemical shift anisotropy (RCSA) restraint simulation is a technique that uses NMR RCSA data to guide a MD simulation. RCSA provides information about the orientation of the chemical shift tensor for specific atoms, which is sensitive to local structure and dynamics.

An energy term printed in a simulation's energy output that tracks part of an algorithm rather than any physical interaction. Thermostats and barostats that add extra degrees of freedom report such terms, as does the correction term of adaptive QM/MM, so that a conserved total can still be checked. Such a term is not part of the potential energy and must not be added to it. (UNVERIFIED)

An electrostatic method that represents the solvent beyond a cutoff distance as a uniform medium that polarizes in response to the charges inside, rather than as individual molecules. The polarized medium pushes back with a field that is added to the direct interactions. It is much cheaper than Ewald summation and less accurate, particularly for a system carrying a net charge. (UNVERIFIED)

A collective variable is a simplified coordinate that helps describe a complex process in a simulation, such as the distance between two proteins as they bind. Instead of tracking thousands of atomic coordinates, a collective variable reduces the system's motion to one or a few key parameters that capture the essence of the event. These variables are frequently used in enhanced sampling methods to focus computational effort on exploring a specific conformational change or reaction pathway.

A distance collective variable is a simple coordinate that measures the separation between two specific atoms or groups of atoms. It is one of the most common variables used in simulations to track processes like a drug molecule unbinding from its target protein. Monitoring this distance provides a straightforward way to follow the progress of an association or dissociation event.

nodes.lbl: center of mass distance collective variable

definition.val: A center of mass distance collective variable measures the separation between the centers of mass of two groups of atoms, such as two entire proteins or a protein and a ligand. This provides a robust measure of the distance between whole molecular entities, averaging out the fast motions of individual atoms.

nodes.lbl: difference of center of mass distances collective variable

definition.val: This is a complex coordinate that tracks the difference between two separate center-of-mass distance measurements. It defines a reaction coordinate by calculating the absolute difference between two distinct COM distance measurements.

nodes.lbl: linear combination of distances collective variable

definition.val: A linear combination of distances is a mathematical expression used in molecular simulations to define a collective variable (CV). It sums or subtracts multiple specific atomic distances, each multiplied by a defined weight, creating a single reaction coordinate to track conformational changes like folding or chemical reactions.

An angle collective variable is a low-dimensional geometric descriptor that measures the angle formed by three specific atoms or groups of atoms during a simulation. This variable is used to monitor hinge-like motions, such as the opening and closing of domains in a protein.

nodes.lbl: center of mass angle collective variable

definition.val: A center of mass angle collective variable measures the angle formed by the centers of mass of three distinct groups of atoms. This is useful for describing the large-scale orientation of entire protein domains or molecules relative to one another, smoothing out the rapid fluctuations of individual atoms.

A torsion collective variable is a coordinate that tracks the value of a specific dihedral angle, which describes the rotation around a chemical bond. These variables are fundamental for describing the detailed three-dimensional shape of a flexible molecule. They are often used in enhanced sampling simulations to accelerate the rotation of protein side chains or to explore different backbone conformations.

nodes.lbl: center of mass torsion collective variable

definition.val: A center of mass torsion collective variable is a dihedral angle defined by the centers of mass of four distinct groups of atoms, rather than four single atoms. This allows for the description of torsional or twisting motions between large molecular domains or subunits.

nodes.lbl: sum of cosines of dihedrals collective variable

definition.val: This is a collective variable created by summing the cosine values of several different dihedral angles within a molecule. This mathematical combination creates a smooth, continuous variable that describes the collective rotational state of multiple bonds at once. It is often used in enhanced sampling methods to create a simplified coordinate that captures a complex, multi-dimensional conformational change.

nodes.lbl: sum of sines of dihedrals collective variable

definition.val: This is a collective variable created by summing the sine values of several different dihedral angles within a molecule. This mathematical combination creates a smooth, continuous variable that describes the collective rotational state of multiple bonds at once. It is often used in enhanced sampling methods to create a simplified coordinate that captures a complex, multi-dimensional conformational change.

A paired dihedral collective variable is a coordinate that combines two different dihedral angles, often the phi and psi backbone angles of a protein, into a single analysis. This is most commonly used to generate a two-dimensional free energy map, known as a Ramachandran plot, which reveals the energetically allowed conformations of the protein backbone. This analysis is fundamental for understanding protein structure and flexibility.

A pattern dihedral is a specialized Collective Variable (CV) used in MD to track the conformational transitions of a molecular system, such as protein folding or crystal polymorphs. It measures a weighted linear combination of multiple specific dihedral angles to act as a low-dimensional structural parameter, often replacing a complex set of atomic coordinates.

The radius of gyration is a collective variable that measures the overall compactness of a molecule or a group of atoms. It quantifies how spread out the atoms are from the molecule's center of mass, with a smaller value indicating a more compact shape. This variable is commonly used as a simple metric to monitor large-scale conformational changes, such as the process of a protein folding into its native structure or unfolding.

A multi-RMSD collective variable is a coordinate that simultaneously measures a molecule's structural similarity to several different reference structures. This is useful for tracking a molecule's transitions between multiple known functional states, such as an active, inactive, and an intermediate conformation. By monitoring which reference structure the molecule is closest to, this variable can map out the complex conformational landscape connecting different states.

A number of bonds collective variable is a coordinate that counts the number of specific chemical bonds that exist at any given moment in a simulation. This variable is only meaningful when using a reactive force field that allows chemical bonds to form and break. It serves as a simple and direct way to track the progress of a chemical reaction by monitoring the creation or destruction of key covalent bonds.

A handedness collective variable is a mathematical measure that quantifies the chirality, or "handedness," of a molecular structure, such as the left-handed versus right-handed twist of a helix. This variable provides a continuous value that can track a molecule's transition between different chiral states during a simulation.

A complex quantity describing how strongly and with what phase a crystal scatters a wave in a given direction, summed over the atoms in its repeating unit. Its magnitude is what a diffraction experiment measures; its phase is not, which is the central difficulty of crystallography. The electron density follows from both by Fourier transform. (UNVERIFIED)

A physical computing device or component, such as a processor, a whole computer or cluster, or the network between machines, on which simulation software runs. It is recorded with a simulation because it determines how long the run takes and can decide whether the run can be repeated bit for bit. Averaged scientific results should not depend on the hardware used. (UNVERIFIED)

A parameter giving the effective size of an atom, as the distance at which another atom begins to be repelled strongly. It is the radius of the hard sphere that best represents where Pauli repulsion overtakes the weak attraction between 2 non-bonded atoms. These radii set the molecular surface used in solvation models and in most measures of packing. (UNVERIFIED)

The Larmor frequency is the specific rate at which a magnetic particle, like an atomic nucleus, wobbles or "precesses" when placed in a strong external magnetic field. This is analogous to the way a spinning top wobbles in the Earth's gravitational field. This frequency is the fundamental principle behind all Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) experiments, as it determines the exact frequency of energy the nucleus will absorb.

A function that varies smoothly between 0 and 1 across a shell of space, used to blend an atom's quantum and classical descriptions as it crosses the boundary. Blending removes the jump in energy that an abrupt reassignment would cause. The width of the shell trades smoothness against how many atoms are in a mixed state at once. (UNVERIFIED)

A simulation analysis that tests whether a simulation has run long enough for the quantity of interest to stop drifting. It follows a chosen property, such as total energy or a structural measure, and checks whether its running average settles over the later part of the trajectory. Without it, a reported average may reflect only the part of the trajectory that happened to be sampled. (UNVERIFIED)

A modeling and setup tool is a type of software used to construct and prepare a molecular system before a simulation is run. This involves tasks like building a molecule from scratch, repairing a structure from an experimental database, or surrounding a protein with water molecules to mimic its natural environment. For an expert, these tools are essential for creating a chemically correct and physically stable starting point, which is a prerequisite for any meaningful simulation.

A software program that performs the calculation at the centre of a simulation, computing the energy of a molecular system and the forces on its atoms and, in a dynamics run, advancing the atom positions step by step. It takes a prepared system and a set of parameters and produces energies, optimised structures or a trajectory. Other programs in a simulation workflow mostly prepare its input or analyse its output. (UNVERIFIED)

A dynamics analysis method that reduces the motion in a trajectory to the few collective movements that account for most of the total fluctuation, using principal component analysis. The largest components are usually functionally meaningful, such as hinge bending between domains, while the smallest are thermal noise. It lets a trajectory of thousands of coordinates be discussed in terms of 2 or 3 motions. (UNVERIFIED)

A matrix whose entry at row i and column j gives the correlation between the fluctuations of quantities i and j. In trajectory analysis the quantities are usually the displacements of atoms or residues, so the matrix says which parts of the molecule move together. It is the input from which correlated motion and network analyses are computed. (UNVERIFIED)

A structural analysis method that identifies which parts of a molecule are rigid and which move, usually by computing the root-mean-square fluctuation of each atom or residue about its average position. The result separates a stable core from mobile loops and termini. Its results can be compared with experimental B-factors, which measure atomic mobility in crystal structures. (UNVERIFIED)

A contact map is a simplified 2D picture that shows which parts of a molecule are touching other parts of itself or other molecules. Contact maps provide a representation of molecular interactions or a protein foldings.
